o: People over 45, smokers, and those with weakened immune systems
People who only drink bottled water
Children under ten years old
Fit, healthy non-smokers in their twenties
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Risk rises with age (over 45), smoking, heavy drinking and weakened immunity or chronic illness.

n.3: Fit, healthy young non-smokers are at lower risk, not higher.
n.1: Drinking bottled water does not affect the risk, which comes from inhaling aerosols.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: What are the early symptoms of Legionnaires' disease usually like?
o: Itchy eyes and a runny nose only

No symptoms of any kind at any stage

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: It usually starts with flu-like symptoms including high temperature, headache and muscle pains before developing into pneumonia.

n.2: The disease does produce symptoms, which can become severe.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Where is legionella bacteria naturally found?
o: Only in the air, never in water
In natural water sources such as rivers and lakes, usually in small harmless numbers
Only inside sealed bottles of fizzy drink
Only in sea water
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionella occurs naturally in rivers, lakes and ground water in low numbers, and becomes a risk when it multiplies in man-made water systems.

n.2: It lives in water systems, not in sealed soft drinks.
n.0: It lives in water; it only becomes airborne when water is broken into droplets.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: You visit an elderly relative in a care home and read that a resident has Legionnaires' disease. Are you at risk of catching it from that resident?
o: Yes, it spreads easily from person to person like a cold
Yes, by sharing a cup of tea with them
Yes, but only if you shake their hand
No, it does not spread person to person; the concern is the water system
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is not passed between people, so the focus is on controlling the building's water system, not isolating the resident.

n.0: It does not spread from person to person like a common cold.
n.2: It is not spread by touch or shaking hands.
n.1: It is not spread by sharing food or drink.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: You feel unwell with a high fever, headache and a cough a few days after staying somewhere with poorly maintained showers. What is the responsible thing to do?
o: Take no action because the disease is caught only from drinking water
Assume it cannot be Legionnaires' disease because you feel able to walk about
See a doctor promptly and mention you may have been exposed to contaminated water spray
Wait several weeks to see if it clears before telling anyone
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Because Legionnaires' disease is a potentially fatal pneumonia, early medical help and telling the doctor about possible aerosol exposure are important.

n.3: Delaying treatment of a potentially fatal lung infection is dangerous.
n.1: Feeling able to move about does not rule out a serious infection that can worsen quickly.
n.0: The disease is caught by inhaling contaminated spray, not by drinking water, so exposure is still possible.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A colleague says the mist drifting off an outdoor cooling tower is harmless because 'it's just water vapour'. Why is this belief dangerous?
o: Vapour cannot be inhaled deep enough into the lungs to cause infection
The drift can carry fine aerosols containing Legionella that people nearby may inhale
Cooling towers cannot support Legionella because the water is constantly moving
Only warm indoor showers, never outdoor sources, can spread the bacteria
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Cooling towers are a recognised high-risk aerosol source; their drift can carry respirable droplets containing Legionella that people downwind can inhale, causing infection.

n.2: Movement alone does not prevent colonisation; towers can harbour and multiply Legionella.
n.0: Fine aerosols are exactly what reach deep into the lungs, which is how infection occurs.
n.3: Outdoor cooling towers are one of the most significant aerosol sources for community outbreaks.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Two people drink from the same untreated water storage tank and one later develops Legionnaires' disease. What does this tell us about how the other person was NOT exposed?
o: Drinking the water is not a route of infection, so swallowing it did not expose them
The bacteria were killed the moment the water was swallowed
They were protected simply because they are younger than 45
They must have a natural immunity that the first person lacked
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is caught by inhaling contaminated aerosols, not by drinking water; swallowing contaminated water is not a recognised route of infection.

n.2: Age lowers or raises risk of severe illness but is unrelated to the route being drinking versus inhalation.
n.3: No reliable natural immunity explains this; the point is the route, not immunity.
n.1: Infection depends on inhaling aerosols, not on any bactericidal effect of swallowing.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A worker develops flu-like symptoms about a week after using a poorly maintained site shower, which then worsen into pneumonia. How does this timing fit Legionnaires' disease?
o: It is consistent, as symptoms typically begin around 2 to 10 days after exposure
It proves the illness was passed to them by a co-worker who was already ill
It is too slow; Legionnaires' disease always shows within a few hours of exposure
It rules Legionella out because pneumonia can only follow months later
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: The incubation period is typically about 2 to 10 days, beginning with flu-like symptoms that can progress to pneumonia, so a week's delay fits the pattern.

n.2: Symptoms take days, not hours, to appear.
n.3: Pneumonia develops within days of onset, not months.
n.1: Legionnaires' disease does not spread person to person.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which individual would generally be considered at HIGHER risk of severe illness if exposed to Legionella?
o: A 24-year-old non-smoking woman in good health
A 52-year-old man who smokes and has a chronic lung condition
A 30-year-old man with no underlying medical conditions
A 19-year-old woman who exercises regularly
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Being over 45, male, a smoker and having chronic lung disease are all recognised factors that increase the risk of serious illness from Legionella.

n.0: Young, healthy non-smokers are at comparatively lower risk of severe disease.
n.2: A young man with no underlying conditions carries lower risk than an older smoker with lung disease.
n.3: A young, fit woman with no risk factors is at comparatively low risk.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A new starter asks whether they should wear a mask around a patient who has Legionnaires' disease to avoid catching it from them. What is the correct response?
o: Only if the patient has a fever, as that is when it becomes contagious
Yes, because the illness spreads easily in enclosed rooms between people
Yes, because coughing spreads Legionnaires' disease directly to others
No, because Legionnaires' disease is not passed from person to person
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is not transmitted person to person; it is caught only by inhaling contaminated aerosols, so no such precaution against the patient is needed.

n.2: Coughing does not transmit the disease between people.
n.1: There is no person-to-person spread in enclosed spaces.
n.0: Fever does not make an infected person contagious; the disease never spreads this way.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which of these water outlets presents the LEAST concern as a Legionella aerosol source?
o: A spray tap in a rarely used washroom
A shower head that has not been used for several weeks
A sealed, non-aerosolising drinking-water bottle dispenser tap that fills a glass without spray
A garden hose left charged with warm water in the sun
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Infection requires inhalable aerosols; an outlet that fills a glass without producing a spray creates little to no respirable aerosol, so it presents the least concern.

n.3: A warm, stagnant hose can both grow bacteria and spray aerosols when used.
n.1: A little-used shower can allow growth and then release aerosols on first use.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Pontiac fever is best described as which of the following?
o: An allergic reaction to chlorine used in water treatment
A skin infection caught by touching contaminated water
A more severe, rapidly fatal form of Legionella infection
A milder, self-limiting illness caused by Legionella without the pneumonia
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Pontiac fever is a milder, self-limiting flu-like illness caused by Legionella that does not develop into the pneumonia seen in Legionnaires' disease.

n.2: Pontiac fever is milder, not more severe, and is not typically fatal.
n.0: It is caused by Legionella, not by an allergic reaction to chlorine.
n.1: It results from inhaling aerosols, not skin contact, and is not a skin infection.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: During a toolbox talk, someone claims 'young, fit people never get Legionnaires' disease'. Why is this statement misleading?
o: Because young fit people are actually the highest-risk group of all
Because fitness has no bearing whatsoever on any aspect of the illness
Because anyone can be infected if they inhale contaminated aerosols, though some groups are at higher risk of serious illness
Because Legionnaires' disease only affects people under 45
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Anyone inhaling enough contaminated aerosol can be infected; being older, male, a smoker or having certain conditions raises the risk of serious illness but does not make others immune.

n.0: Young, fit people are not the highest-risk group; older people with risk factors are.
n.3: The disease is not limited to those under 45; over-45s are in fact at higher risk.
n.1: Fitness and health status do influence the risk of severe illness, so this overstates the point.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Why are the lungs the critical route by which Legionella causes disease?
o: Because the stomach's acid actively spreads the bacteria to the lungs
Because infection occurs when fine aerosols carrying the bacteria are breathed deep into the lungs
Because swallowed bacteria multiply fastest in the airways
Because the bacteria can only survive in dry lung tissue
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Infection happens when respirable aerosols containing Legionella are inhaled and reach deep into the lungs, where the bacteria can cause pneumonia.

n.3: Legionella thrives in water, not dry tissue; the point is inhalation of aerosols.
n.0: Stomach acid does not transport bacteria to the lungs; drinking is not a route.
n.2: Swallowing water is not a recognised infection route at all.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A hot tub at a leisure site is being investigated after several guests fell ill. Why are spa pools a notable Legionella risk?
o: They agitate warm water, producing large volumes of inhalable aerosol
They are always kept below temperatures where bacteria can grow
They are filled with drinking water that guests swallow
They pose a risk only through direct skin contact with the water
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Spa and hot tubs vigorously agitate warm water, generating large amounts of breathable aerosol that can carry Legionella to bathers and bystanders.

n.2: The risk is inhaling aerosols, not swallowing the water.
n.1: Warm spa temperatures often sit in a range that can support bacterial growth.
n.3: Skin contact is not the route; inhaling the aerosol is.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which statement about the early symptoms of Legionnaires' disease is correct?
o: It presents first as a digestive upset with no respiratory signs ever
It causes immediate breathlessness within minutes of exposure
It starts with flu-like symptoms such as high temperature and muscle aches
It begins with a distinctive rash before any other symptom
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease typically begins with flu-like symptoms, including a high temperature, headache and muscle aches, before progressing to pneumonia.

n.3: A distinctive rash is not a hallmark early sign.
n.0: While some gastrointestinal symptoms can occur, respiratory illness (pneumonia) is central, so 'no respiratory signs ever' is wrong.
n.1: Symptoms develop over days, not within minutes of exposure.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A firefighting sprinkler system and an irrigation sprinkler are both on a site's water risk list. Why are sprinklers included?
o: Because they are the only outlets capable of person-to-person spread
Because the pipework is always too cold to grow any bacteria
Because they store drinking water that could be swallowed
Because they can discharge water as a spray, creating aerosols that may be inhaled
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Sprinklers disperse water as a fine spray, producing aerosols that can carry Legionella into the air where people may inhale them, which is why they are assessed.

n.2: The concern is aerosol inhalation, not drinking the water.
n.1: Standing water in sprinkler pipework can warm and support growth.
n.0: Legionnaires' disease does not spread person to person by any route.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Someone with well-managed diabetes and a heavy-smoking colleague both work near a spray source. In terms of Legionella severity risk, how should this be understood?
o: Managing diabetes removes it entirely from the list of recognised risk factors
Both diabetes and smoking are recognised factors that can raise the risk of serious illness
Only the smoker is at any increased risk; diabetes is irrelevant
Neither diabetes nor smoking has any effect on the risk of severe illness
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Both diabetes and smoking are among the recognised factors that increase the risk of severe Legionella infection, so both individuals warrant awareness.

n.3: Both conditions are recognised risk factors, so they do affect severity risk.
n.2: Diabetes is a recognised risk factor, not irrelevant.
n.0: Good management helps overall health but diabetes remains a recognised susceptibility factor.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Why can a shower head that has not been used for a long period be a particular Legionella concern when first used again?
o: Because a dry shower head is the ideal place for bacteria to breed
Because stagnation can let bacteria multiply, then the first use releases aerosols
Because unused water becomes too acidic for the bacteria to survive
Because cold, moving mains water is the highest-risk condition
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Stagnant water in a little-used outlet can allow Legionella to multiply, and the first use then discharges an aerosol that may carry the bacteria into the air to be inhaled.

n.0: Legionella needs water to multiply, not a dry head.
n.3: Cold, flowing mains water is comparatively low risk; stagnant warm water is the concern.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which description of Legionnaires' disease is accurate?
o: A contagious chest cold passed between people by coughing
A potentially fatal form of pneumonia caused by Legionella bacteria
A mild throat infection that always clears without treatment
A stomach bug spread by swallowing contaminated water
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is a potentially fatal pneumonia (lung infection) caused by Legionella bacteria inhaled in contaminated aerosols.

n.2: It is a serious pneumonia that can be fatal, not a mild self-clearing throat infection.
n.3: It is not a stomach bug and is not caught by swallowing water.
n.0: It is not contagious and does not spread between people.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A supervisor asks staff to list the aerosol-generating sources at a site. Which of the following belongs on that list?

A sealed pressure vessel with no outlet to the air
A capped, disused pipe with no water flow
A bucket of still water with no agitation
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: A wash-down hose produces a fine spray, creating inhalable aerosols that could carry Legionella, so it belongs on the aerosol-source list.

n.1: A sealed vessel with no release to air does not create an inhalable aerosol.
n.2: A capped, dead pipe with no flow does not itself generate an aerosol during use.
n.3: Still water without agitation produces little to no breathable aerosol.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: How does Pontiac fever typically differ from Legionnaires' disease in its outcome?
o: Pontiac fever is caused by a completely different, non-Legionella organism
Pontiac fever is more often fatal than Legionnaires' disease
Pontiac fever usually requires longer hospital treatment than Legionnaires' disease
Pontiac fever generally resolves on its own without developing into pneumonia
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Pontiac fever is the milder, self-limiting form of Legionella infection that typically resolves without progressing to the pneumonia characteristic of Legionnaires' disease.

n.1: Pontiac fever is generally not fatal, unlike the more serious Legionnaires' disease.
n.0: It is caused by Legionella, the same genus, not a different organism.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Why is it important for water hygiene operatives to understand which groups are more susceptible to Legionella?
o: To help appreciate why controlling aerosol sources matters, especially where vulnerable people may be exposed
Because only susceptible people can ever transmit the bacteria to others
Because susceptibility changes the way the bacteria are inhaled
So susceptible people can be told they are completely immune once identified

n.1: The disease is not transmitted person to person by anyone.
n.2: Susceptibility affects severity of illness, not the physical way aerosols are inhaled.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A visitor at a garden centre becomes unwell days after walking through a mist being sprayed over plant displays. Why is the misting system a plausible source to investigate?
o: Because the disease spreads from other unwell visitors in the crowd
Because visitors would have drunk the mist as they walked past
Because misting produces fine aerosols people can inhale, which can carry Legionella
Because mist is only a risk if the water is ice cold

n.0: The disease does not pass between people in a crowd.
n.3: Warm water favours growth; ice-cold water is not the risk condition.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which combination of personal factors is most strongly associated with a higher risk of serious Legionella illness?

Being physically active with no chronic conditions
Being teetotal with no history of lung or heart disease
Being under 25, female and a non-smoker

n.2: Avoiding alcohol and having no lung or heart disease are protective rather than risk-raising.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A worker insists they 'definitely caught Legionnaires' from a workmate who had it last week'. Why is this explanation incorrect?
o: Because a workmate's illness would make the worker immune, not ill
Because only cooling towers, never any other source, can cause infection
Because Legionnaires' disease is not spread from person to person
Because the incubation period is far too short for that to happen

n.3: The incubation period is around 2 to 10 days, but the real reason is that person-to-person spread does not occur at all.
n.1: Many aerosol sources besides cooling towers can cause infection.
n.0: Exposure to an ill workmate confers no immunity and is not a route of infection.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which everyday feature explains why domestic and workplace showers are treated as a Legionella risk?
o: They deliver a spray of warm water that creates inhalable aerosols
They allow the disease to pass between people using them in turn
They keep water permanently at temperatures that kill all bacteria
They are the only outlets that dispense water for drinking
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Showers spray warm water, generating fine aerosols that can be inhaled; if the water is contaminated with Legionella, this is how infection can occur.

n.3: Showers are not drinking outlets, and drinking is not the route anyway.
n.2: Shower water is often in the warm range that can support growth, not one that kills all bacteria.
n.1: There is no person-to-person spread between successive users.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Why should a report of 'flu that turned into pneumonia' in someone who recently used a suspect water system be taken seriously?
o: Because this progression fits the pattern of Legionnaires' disease and warrants investigation
Because only people who feel unwell within an hour of exposure need concern
Because flu and Legionnaires' disease can never be confused with one another
Because pneumonia after exposure is impossible and indicates a false alarm

n.2: Early Legionnaires' disease can resemble flu, so they can indeed be confused, which is why it must be taken seriously.
n.3: Progression to pneumonia is exactly what can occur, not an impossibility.
n.1: Symptoms typically appear over 2 to 10 days, not within an hour.

o: Inhaling aerosols from a contaminated shower
Swallowing contaminated water while drinking
Breathing in spray drifting from a cooling tower
Inhaling mist from a contaminated spa pool
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is caught by inhaling contaminated aerosols; swallowing water while drinking is not a recognised route of infection.

n.3: Inhaling spa pool mist is a recognised route.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: At a hotel, an elderly guest and a young child both used the same spa pool; the elderly guest developed severe pneumonia and the child was unaffected. What does this most likely reflect?

That the child must have swallowed the water and so was protected
That the disease was passed from the guest to no one because the child was immune from birth
That the elderly guest, being older, was at greater risk of serious illness
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Older age is a recognised factor increasing the risk of serious Legionella illness, which helps explain why the elderly guest became severely ill while the child did not.

n.0: Spa pools do generate infectious aerosols; that is why one guest fell ill.
n.1: Swallowing water is not protective and is not a route of infection.
n.2: There is no person-to-person spread and no relevant innate immunity; the difference is susceptibility to severe illness.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Why is heavy alcohol consumption relevant when considering who is more vulnerable to Legionella?
o: Because heavy drinkers are recognised as being at increased risk of serious illness
Because alcohol changes the route by which the bacteria are inhaled
Because only heavy drinkers can transmit the disease to others
Because alcohol makes the bacteria multiply faster in a person's lungs

n.2: The disease is not transmitted person to person by anyone, drinkers included.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A trainee summarises: 'Legionella only matters if the water is hot enough to scald.' Why is this summary wrong?
o: Because the aerosol risk depends on water being sprayed and inhalable, not on it being scalding
Because Legionella can only ever be found in water above scalding temperature
Because scalding-hot water is actually the ideal condition for the bacteria
Because cold water is completely incapable of ever carrying the bacteria
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: The infection risk comes from inhaling aerosols of contaminated water; whether an outlet is a hazard depends on it producing an inhalable spray, not on the water being scalding.

n.2: Scalding-hot water is not the ideal growth condition; very hot temperatures tend to suppress the bacteria.
n.1: Legionella is not confined to scalding water; it favours warm conditions.
n.3: Cold outlets can still carry and aerosolise the bacteria under the right conditions.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which statement best captures why Legionnaires' disease is regarded as a serious health concern?
o: It is dangerous only because it spreads rapidly between people
It is a minor infection that never needs medical attention
It is serious only when caught by drinking contaminated water
It is a form of pneumonia that can be fatal, particularly in more vulnerable people
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is a potentially fatal pneumonia, and the danger is greatest for more vulnerable individuals, which is why it is treated as a serious concern.

n.1: It is a serious illness requiring medical treatment, not a minor one.
n.0: It does not spread between people, so that is not the reason it is serious.
n.2: It is caught by inhaling aerosols, not by drinking contaminated water.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A maintenance team is about to open and flush a rarely used spray tap that has stood full of warm water for months. Why should they treat this task with particular care regarding Legionella?
o: Because the main danger is swallowing droplets rather than inhaling them
Because spray taps cannot create aerosols small enough to inhale
Because the first spray could release aerosols from water in which bacteria may have multiplied
Because the water will certainly be safe once it has been standing that long
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Warm, stagnant water in a little-used spray tap can allow Legionella to multiply, and operating it can release aerosols the workers may inhale, so the task needs care.

n.3: Long standing warm water is more likely to be contaminated, not safe.
n.0: The danger is inhaling the aerosol, not swallowing droplets.
n.1: Spray taps do produce fine, inhalable aerosols, which is the whole concern.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which of these correctly pairs the illness with its nature?
o: Legionnaires' disease is a skin condition; Pontiac fever is a stomach infection
Legionnaires' disease is a serious pneumonia; Pontiac fever is a milder, self-limiting illness
Legionnaires' disease is mild and self-limiting; Pontiac fever is a fatal pneumonia
Both Legionnaires' disease and Pontiac fever are contagious chest infections
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is a serious, potentially fatal pneumonia, whereas Pontiac fever is the milder, self-limiting form of Legionella infection.

n.3: Neither is contagious; Legionella does not spread person to person.
n.0: Neither is a skin condition or a stomach infection; both stem from inhaled Legionella.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Why are people with chronic kidney or heart disease specifically highlighted in Legionella awareness training?
o: Because only people with these conditions can be infected at all
Because these conditions place them among those at greater risk of serious illness
Because such conditions make a person's breath spread the bacteria further
Because these conditions change how aerosols are formed at the outlet
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Chronic conditions such as kidney or heart disease are among the recognised factors placing a person at greater risk of serious illness if exposed to Legionella.

n.2: The disease does not spread via breath or between people at all.
n.0: Anyone can be infected by inhaling contaminated aerosols; these conditions raise severity risk, not exclusivity.
n.3: A person's health does not change how aerosols form at an outlet.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: An operative feels feverish and achy two days after working amid heavy spray from a suspect system, and dismisses it as 'just a cold'. Why is caution warranted?
o: Because early Legionnaires' disease can resemble flu-like illness and may progress to pneumonia
Because feeling unwell after exposure means the person is now immune
Because symptoms appearing this quickly rule Legionella out entirely
Because a cold and Legionnaires' disease produce identical long-term outcomes
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Early Legionnaires' disease often looks like a flu-like illness before progressing to pneumonia, so flu-like symptoms after exposure to a suspect system should not be lightly dismissed.

n.3: The outcomes differ greatly; Legionnaires' disease can be fatal, unlike a common cold.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which factor about the aerosol itself most influences whether inhaling it could cause Legionnaires' disease?

Whether the water tastes unpleasant when swallowed
Whether the droplets are fine enough to be breathed deep into the lungs
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: It is the fine, respirable droplets that can be carried deep into the lungs; these are the ones that matter for causing infection when they contain Legionella.

n.2: Taste relates to swallowing, which is not the route of infection.
n.0: The colour or clarity of the spray does not determine infectivity.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A member of the public asks whether they can catch Legionnaires' disease from a family member who has it. What is the correct explanation?

No, but only because the family member is no longer contagious after a week
No, it is not passed between people; it comes from inhaling contaminated aerosols
Yes, close family contact is the most common way it spreads
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is not transmitted between people; it is contracted only by inhaling contaminated aerosols, so a family member cannot catch it from the patient.

n.0: Sharing drinking water does not transmit it; drinking is not a route.
n.1: The reason is that it never spreads person to person, not a change in contagiousness over time.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Considering both aerosol sources and susceptible people, why is a care home with communal showers a setting that deserves particular attention?
o: Because Legionnaires' disease spreads more easily between residents living together
Because residents are generally young and at low risk

n.3: At 60°C and above the bacteria are killed rather than multiplying.
n.0: Freezing temperatures do not allow the bacteria to multiply.

How Legionella Grows.q: What happens to legionella bacteria in water held below 20°C?
o: They multiply faster than at any other temperature
They immediately die within seconds
They stay dormant and do not multiply
They turn the water into a spray on their own
How Legionella Grows.w: Below 20°C legionella becomes dormant and does not multiply, though it is not killed.

n.0: Cold water slows growth; it does not speed it up.
n.1: Cold water does not kill the bacteria; it only makes them dormant.
n.3: Bacteria cannot create a spray; aerosols come from equipment like showers and taps.

How Legionella Grows.q: At roughly what temperature is legionella killed quickly?
o: 60°C and above
How Legionella Grows.w: Water at 60°C and above kills legionella quickly, which is why hot water should be stored hot.

n.3: 37°C is close to the ideal temperature for growth, not for killing the bacteria.
n.0: At 20°C the bacteria begin to multiply rather than die.
n.1: At 10°C the bacteria are dormant but not killed.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which condition helps legionella to multiply in a water system?
o: Water kept constantly moving and very hot
Water stored below 5°C at all times
Water that is regularly flushed and turned over
Stagnant water with sludge, scale, rust or biofilm to feed on
How Legionella Grows.w: Stagnation together with nutrients such as biofilm, scale, rust and sludge provides ideal conditions for legionella to grow.

n.0: Keeping water moving and hot discourages growth.
n.1: Very cold water keeps the bacteria dormant, preventing multiplication.
n.2: Regular flushing removes stagnation and helps prevent growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which of these acts as a nutrient source that helps legionella grow?
o: Fresh air
Clean flowing chlorinated water
Biofilm, scale, rust and organic sediment inside pipes and tanks
Bright sunlight
How Legionella Grows.w: Deposits such as biofilm, scale, rust, sludge and organic matter feed the bacteria and shelter them from disinfectant.

n.1: Clean, well-treated flowing water does not provide the nutrients or stagnation the bacteria need.
n.0: Air is not a nutrient source for the bacteria.
n.3: Sunlight is not a food source and does not promote growth inside water systems.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which situation is most likely to create the aerosol that spreads legionella?
o: A sealed, full cold water storage tank with a tight lid
A running shower or a spray tap breaking water into a fine mist
Water sitting still in a covered bucket
A closed pipe with no outlets
How Legionella Grows.w: Showers, spray taps and cooling towers break water into fine droplets that can be inhaled, which is how the bacteria reach the lungs.

n.0: A properly sealed storage tank does not create a breathable spray.
n.3: A closed pipe with no outlet produces no aerosol.
n.2: Still water in a covered container does not form an inhalable mist.

How Legionella Grows.q: You find a shower in a spare room that has not been used for several weeks. What is the safest way to bring it back into use?
o: Turn it on at full mist and stand close to check the temperature
Flush it through, keeping your face away from the spray and avoiding creating a mist, ideally at a high temperature
Give the shower head a quick wipe with a dry cloth only
Leave it as it is because unused showers are always safe
How Legionella Grows.w: Little-used outlets should be flushed regularly, avoiding breathing in the spray, because stagnant water is where legionella multiplies.

n.0: Standing in the mist of a long-unused shower risks inhaling any bacteria that have grown.
n.3: Unused, stagnant outlets are a higher risk, not a safe one.
n.2: A dry wipe does not remove bacteria or clear the stagnant water inside the pipework.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why are little-used ('dead leg') sections of pipework a particular legionella risk?
o: They are always exposed to freezing conditions
Water there is always kept above 60°C
Water stagnates in them, allowing bacteria to multiply undisturbed
They contain extra chlorine that feeds the bacteria
How Legionella Grows.w: Water sits still in rarely used pipe sections, and stagnation lets legionella grow and form biofilm.

n.1: Dead legs often sit at warm room temperature, not above 60°C.
n.3: Chlorine is a disinfectant that kills bacteria; it is not a food source.
n.0: Dead legs are a risk because water stagnates, not because they freeze.

How Legionella Grows.q: A stored hot water calorifier is found running at 48°C rather than the intended 60°C. Why does this specific reading matter for Legionella growth?
o: 48°C is cold enough to keep the bacteria fully dormant, so there is no concern
48°C instantly kills any Legionella present, so the low reading is actually beneficial
48°C sits inside the 20–45°C growth band's upper edge and is too cool to reliably kill the bacteria, allowing multiplication
Temperature has no effect on a calorifier because nutrients alone control growth
How Legionella Grows.w: Stored hot water should be at 60°C. At 48°C the water is near or within the range where Legionella multiplies and is not hot enough to kill it, so numbers can rise. HSG274 Part 2 requires 60°C storage and 50°C at outlets within one minute.

n.0: Dormancy occurs below 20°C, not at 48°C; at 48°C the bacteria are active and can multiply.
n.1: Legionella is killed reliably around 60°C, not at 48°C, which is too cool to disinfect.
n.3: Temperature is the primary control; keeping water hot or cold prevents multiplication even where nutrients exist.

How Legionella Grows.q: Legionella bacteria multiply most rapidly at a temperature closest to which of the following?
o: Around 37°C, close to human body temperature
Around 55°C, typical of correctly distributed hot water
Around 8°C, typical of chilled mains water
Around 70°C, typical of a boiler flow
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella multiplies across roughly 20–45°C, with the fastest growth near 37°C, close to human body temperature. This is why lukewarm water is the highest-risk condition.

n.2: Around 8°C the bacteria are dormant and do not multiply; cold water should be kept below 20°C.
n.1: Around 55°C the bacteria begin to die rather than multiply.
n.3: Around 70°C Legionella is killed almost immediately, so no growth occurs.

How Legionella Grows.q: Cold water drawn from an infrequently used outlet is measured at 24°C after running for two minutes. What does this tell you about Legionella risk?
o: The reading is irrelevant because cold water cannot support Legionella at any temperature
The cold water is warmer than 20°C and now within the range where Legionella can multiply
The outlet is fine because only hot water systems grow Legionella
The water is safely cold and needs no further attention
How Legionella Grows.w: Cold water should stay below 20°C. At 24°C after two minutes' run-off, the cold system has warmed into the 20–45°C growth band, so Legionella can multiply. HSG274 Part 2 targets below 20°C for cold water.

n.3: Water at 24°C is above the 20°C threshold and is not safely cold.
n.0: Warm cold-water systems are a well-recognised source of Legionella growth.
n.2: Cold water systems that run warm are just as capable of supporting growth as hot systems that run cool.

How Legionella Grows.q: At which approximate temperature is Legionella reliably killed within a short time?
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella is killed rapidly at around 60°C, which is why hot water is stored at that temperature. At 60°C the great majority of bacteria die within a couple of minutes.

n.0: 20°C is the lower edge of the growth band, where the bacteria become active rather than being killed.
n.3: 37°C is near ideal for multiplication, not for killing the bacteria.
n.2: 45°C is still within the growth range; the bacteria are not reliably killed until much hotter.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is a layer of biofilm on the inside of a pipe or tank important to how Legionella grows?
o: Biofilm removes all nutrients from the water and starves the bacteria
Biofilm raises the water temperature above 60°C and destroys the bacteria
Biofilm provides shelter and a source of nutrients that support Legionella multiplication
Biofilm only forms in water hotter than 50°C where growth is impossible
How Legionella Grows.w: Biofilm is a slime layer of micro-organisms that both shelters Legionella from disinfectants and temperature and supplies nutrients, promoting growth. Controlling biofilm is central to HSG274 Part 2.

n.1: Biofilm does not heat water; it insulates and protects bacteria rather than killing them.
n.0: Biofilm supplies nutrients rather than removing them, encouraging growth.
n.3: Biofilm forms readily in warm, stagnant water within the growth range, not in water too hot to support growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: A capped-off length of redundant pipework still connected to a live main is left in place. Why does this 'dead leg' increase Legionella risk?
o: It cools the whole system below 20°C and forces the bacteria into dormancy
Water stagnates in it, warms to room temperature and accumulates nutrients, encouraging growth
It sterilises the connected pipework by trapping heat
It continuously flushes fresh chlorinated water through the system
How Legionella Grows.w: A dead leg holds water that does not move, allowing it to reach ambient temperature and collect sediment and nutrients, creating ideal conditions for Legionella. HSG274 Part 2 recommends removing dead legs.

n.0: A dead leg tends to sit at room temperature within the growth range, not below 20°C.
n.3: By definition there is no flow through a dead leg, so no flushing occurs.
n.2: Trapped stagnant water is not sterile; it favours growth rather than preventing it.

How Legionella Grows.q: Besides suitable temperature, which combination of conditions most favours Legionella multiplication?
o: High pressure and completely sterile pipework
Stagnation together with nutrients such as scale, rust, sludge and organic matter
Frequent draw-off and a total absence of any deposits
Fast continuous flow and freshly chlorinated water
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella needs warmth plus stagnant water and nutrients. Scale, rust, sludge, sediment and organic matter feed the bacteria and support biofilm, so still, dirty water in the growth range is highest risk.

n.3: Continuous flow and disinfectant residual suppress growth rather than promoting it.
n.2: Frequent draw-off and clean pipework work against growth by preventing stagnation and removing nutrients.
n.0: High pressure and sterile pipework do not provide the stagnation and nutrients the bacteria need.

How Legionella Grows.q: How do free-living amoebae and other protozoa in a water system affect Legionella?
o: They have no interaction with Legionella whatsoever
They consume all the Legionella and eliminate it from the system
They can host the bacteria, allowing Legionella to multiply inside them and shelter from disinfection
They raise the pH so high that the bacteria cannot survive
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella can invade and multiply inside protozoa such as amoebae, which shelter the bacteria from heat and biocides and provide nutrients. This is why controlling biofilm, where protozoa live, is important.

n.1: Rather than being destroyed, Legionella exploits protozoa as hosts and multiplies within them.
n.3: The relationship is about hosting and shelter, not a pH change.
n.0: There is a strong interaction: protozoa are a recognised reservoir for Legionella.

How Legionella Grows.q: Growth of Legionella in a system only becomes a health risk to people when which of the following occurs?
o: The contaminated water is dispersed as a fine, breathable aerosol that can be inhaled
A person touches a tap handle contaminated with the bacteria
The contaminated water is swallowed while drinking a glass of it
The water is heated above 60°C before it reaches the outlet
How Legionella Grows.w: The risk is realised when water containing Legionella is broken into a fine aerosol of droplets small enough to reach the lungs, for example from showers, sprays or cooling towers. Inhalation is the route of infection.

n.2: Legionnaires' disease is contracted by inhaling aerosol, not from drinking the water.
n.1: Touching a contaminated surface is not the recognised route of infection.
n.3: Heating above 60°C kills the bacteria, reducing rather than creating the risk.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is an oversized cold water storage tank that serves only a small daily demand a Legionella concern?
o: The extra capacity guarantees a strong disinfectant residual throughout
The large surface area cools the water enough to kill the bacteria
The stored water turns over slowly, so it stagnates and can warm into the growth range
The large volume keeps the water permanently below 20°C and dormant
How Legionella Grows.w: An oversized, underused tank has a low turnover, so water sits for long periods. Slow-moving water stagnates and can drift up towards ambient temperature, favouring growth. HSG274 Part 2 advises matching capacity to demand.

n.3: Slow turnover in a warm plant room lets stored water rise towards room temperature rather than staying cold.
n.1: A large tank does not chill water to a killing temperature; if anything it warms slowly.
n.0: Slow turnover allows any disinfectant residual to decay, weakening rather than guaranteeing it.

How Legionella Grows.q: A cold water tank sits in an unventilated roof space next to hot flow pipework in summer, and its temperature climbs to 26°C. What is the significance?
o: The water is now hot enough to be treated as pasteurised
The warmth kills the bacteria before they can multiply
It is unimportant because roof tanks are always exempt from temperature control
The heat gain has pushed the cold water into the 20–45°C range, so Legionella can now multiply
How Legionella Grows.w: Heat gain from the surroundings has warmed the cold water above 20°C into the growth range. Cold water should be kept below 20°C, so tanks should be insulated and kept away from heat sources.

n.2: Cold water storage temperature control applies to roof tanks; they are not exempt.
n.1: 26°C is well within the growth range and does not kill the bacteria.
n.0: Pasteurisation needs far higher temperatures; 26°C is simply warm, high-risk water.

How Legionella Grows.q: What happens to Legionella bacteria in water held steadily below 20°C?
o: They convert the water into biofilm
They multiply faster than at any other temperature
They can survive in a dormant state but do not multiply
They are immediately and completely destroyed
How Legionella Grows.w: Below 20°C Legionella survives but remains largely dormant and does not multiply. This is why keeping cold water below 20°C is a key control, even though it does not kill the bacteria.

n.1: Fastest multiplication is near 37°C, not below 20°C where the bacteria are dormant.
n.3: Cold does not kill Legionella; the bacteria persist and can grow again if the water warms.
n.0: Bacteria do not turn water into biofilm; biofilm is a separate slime layer they inhabit.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why does scale build-up from hard water inside a pipe or fitting contribute to Legionella growth?
o: Scale raises the water temperature above 60°C and sterilises it
Scale dissolves the biofilm and starves the bacteria
Scale prevents any water from ever contacting the pipe wall
Scale provides surface area and nutrients that harbour biofilm and shelter the bacteria
How Legionella Grows.w: Scale creates a rough surface and, with rust and sediment, forms deposits where biofilm establishes and Legionella shelters and feeds. Removing scale and sediment is part of controlling growth under HSG274 Part 2.

n.0: Scale does not heat water; it insulates surfaces and can even protect bacteria from heat.
n.2: Scale is a deposit water flows over and around; it does not seal the bacteria away from water.
n.1: Scale supports biofilm rather than dissolving it, so it encourages growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: A building has been closed for six weeks with no water use. Regarding Legionella growth, what is the main concern on reopening?
o: The lack of use will have sterilised the system completely
Prolonged stagnation will have allowed the bacteria to multiply and biofilm to develop throughout the system
The pipework will have cooled to a temperature that kills all bacteria
There is no concern because bacteria die without people present
How Legionella Grows.w: Six weeks with no flow means water has stagnated, temperatures have drifted towards ambient, disinfectant residual has decayed and biofilm has grown, all favouring Legionella. Systems should be flushed and checked before reuse.

n.0: Stagnation promotes growth; it does not sterilise a system.
n.2: Lack of use does not create killing temperatures; water tends towards room temperature.
n.3: The absence of occupants does not remove the water conditions that let Legionella multiply.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between temperature and Legionella across a water system?
o: Keeping water in the 20–45°C band is the safest way to control growth
Legionella grows equally well at all temperatures from freezing to boiling
Only nutrients matter; temperature makes no difference to growth
Keeping water either below 20°C or hot enough to kill the bacteria controls growth; the 20–45°C band is where it thrives
How Legionella Grows.w: Temperature control works by avoiding the 20–45°C danger band: cold water below 20°C keeps bacteria dormant and hot water around 60°C kills them. The band between is where multiplication occurs.

n.0: The 20–45°C band is precisely the danger range, not a safe target.
n.2: Temperature is the primary control alongside stagnation and nutrients; it matters greatly.
n.1: Growth is confined to a specific range; the bacteria are dormant when cold and killed when hot.

How Legionella Grows.q: Rubber, natural fibre washers and some jointing compounds are discouraged in water systems mainly because they can influence Legionella growth. How?
o: They chill the water below the growth range
They release a continuous disinfectant that suppresses bacteria
They have no effect on microbial growth at all
They can release nutrients that feed bacteria and support biofilm formation
How Legionella Grows.w: Certain materials such as some rubbers and natural fibres can degrade and provide nutrients that encourage bacterial and biofilm growth. Water fittings should meet approved standards to limit this, supporting HSG274 Part 2 control.

n.0: These materials do not cool water; they can act as a nutrient source instead.
n.1: They tend to feed growth rather than release any disinfectant.
n.2: The choice of materials does affect microbial growth, which is why suitable fittings are specified.

How Legionella Grows.q: Hot water reaching a distant outlet on a large system is measured at only 43°C. Why is this a growth concern even though the water leaves the calorifier at 60°C?
o: 43°C means the water has never been heated at all
43°C at the outlet is hot enough to kill any Legionella immediately
Heat loss along the run has cooled the water into the 20–45°C range, so Legionella can multiply near that outlet
Outlet temperature is irrelevant as long as storage is at 60°C
How Legionella Grows.w: Hot water should reach outlets at 50°C within one minute. At 43°C the water has cooled into the growth band during distribution, allowing multiplication near the outlet despite correct storage. This points to heat loss or poor circulation.

n.1: 43°C is within the growth range and does not kill the bacteria.
n.3: Distribution temperature matters as much as storage; outlets must reach 50°C.
n.0: The water was heated to 60°C but has lost heat on the way, which is the actual problem.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is sediment or sludge collecting at the base of a calorifier or cold water tank a particular concern for Legionella growth?
o: It settles out all the bacteria and safely removes them from the water
It provides nutrients and a sheltered habitat where Legionella and biofilm can thrive
It has no bearing on growth because bacteria live only in flowing water
It maintains the water at a lethal temperature
How Legionella Grows.w: Accumulated sludge, rust and sediment supply nutrients and a protected surface for biofilm, where Legionella multiplies and is shielded from temperature and disinfectant. Removing deposits by cleaning is a recognised control.

n.0: Settled sediment concentrates nutrients and bacteria rather than safely removing them.
n.3: Sediment does not heat water; the base of a tank is often cooler and higher-risk.
n.2: Legionella thrives in stagnant, sediment-rich zones, not only in flowing water.

How Legionella Grows.q: A little-used shower in a plant room delivers warm, cloudy first-draw water and is rarely run. Which factors combine to make this a Legionella growth hotspot?
o: Stagnation, warmth in the growth range and nutrients, with a shower producing breathable aerosol
High flow, cold water and clean pipework
Frozen water and a total lack of nutrients
Continuous circulation and disinfection
How Legionella Grows.w: Infrequent use means stagnation, the plant room warms the water into the growth band, and cloudiness suggests sediment and nutrients. A shower also generates fine aerosol, combining growth conditions with a route of exposure.

n.1: This outlet has low flow and warm water, the opposite of these protective conditions.
n.3: Rare use means no circulation and decayed disinfectant, not continuous protection.
n.2: The water is warm and cloudy with nutrients, not frozen and clean.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which of the following best explains why simply keeping a system clean of deposits helps control Legionella growth?
o: Removing scale, rust, sludge and biofilm takes away the nutrients and shelter the bacteria rely on
Cleaning permanently lowers the water temperature below 20°C
Cleaning makes the water too pure for aerosols to form
Cleaning replaces the need for any temperature control
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella depends on nutrients and shelter from deposits and biofilm. Removing them by cleaning and descaling reduces the food source and protective habitat, an important part of HSG274 Part 2 control alongside temperature.

n.1: Cleaning removes deposits but does not by itself set the water temperature.
n.3: Cleaning complements temperature control; it does not replace it.
n.2: Water purity does not stop aerosols forming; aerosol is a physical process at outlets.

How Legionella Grows.q: In terms of Legionella, why is a mixer tap or thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) area sometimes described as a higher-risk point for growth?
o: Because the water there is always stored above 60°C
Because hot and cold blend to a warm temperature within the growth range close to the outlet
Because mixing removes all nutrients from the water
Because it delivers only cold water below 20°C
How Legionella Grows.w: A TMV blends hot and cold to a comfortable warm temperature, which sits in the 20–45°C growth band right at the outlet and downstream fittings. This is why TMVs are fitted close to the outlet and maintained carefully.

n.0: The blended water is deliberately warm, not stored above 60°C.
n.3: The output is warm mixed water, not cold water below 20°C.
n.2: Mixing does not remove nutrients; it simply produces a warm temperature ideal for growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which description of Legionella's nutrient needs is correct?
o: It obtains nutrients from biofilm, scale, rust, sludge, sediment and other organic matter in the system
It manufactures its own food from sunlight and needs none from the water
It grows only in chemically pure, nutrient-free water
It requires added sugar to be dosed into the water to survive
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella draws nutrients from the organic and inorganic matter found in water systems, including biofilm, corrosion products, scale and sediment. Limiting these deposits limits the food available for growth.

n.2: Pure, nutrient-free water is unfavourable to growth; the bacteria need a food source.
n.1: Legionella does not photosynthesise; it feeds on organic matter and other micro-organisms.
n.3: No dosing is needed; ordinary system deposits supply ample nutrients.

How Legionella Grows.q: A section of hot water pipework is poorly lagged and runs through a cool basement, so the water in it drifts to around 40°C between draw-offs. What is the growth implication?
o: The section is protected because hot water can never grow Legionella
The water freezes and the bacteria are destroyed
The cooled hot water sits in the growth range, allowing Legionella to multiply in that section
The cooling makes the water safe because it is now below 45°C
How Legionella Grows.w: Hot water that cools to about 40°C between uses sits squarely in the 20–45°C growth band, so Legionella can multiply there. Adequate lagging and circulation keep hot water hot and prevent this cool-hot-water risk.

n.3: Being below 45°C does not make water safe; it is inside the growth range.
n.0: Hot water systems that run cool are a recognised growth risk, not protected.
n.1: 40°C is warm, not freezing; the bacteria are not destroyed and can multiply.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is regular use, or planned flushing, of every outlet important in controlling how Legionella grows?
o: It heats all cold water above 60°C
It prevents water stagnating, drawing fresh water through and refreshing temperature and any disinfectant residual
It replaces the need to keep hot water hot and cold water cold
It permanently sterilises the pipework with no further action needed
How Legionella Grows.w: Movement of water stops stagnation, brings through fresh water at the correct temperature and helps maintain any disinfectant residual, denying Legionella the still conditions it needs. Weekly flushing of little-used outlets is standard practice.

n.0: Flushing moves water through; it does not heat cold water to 60°C.
n.3: Flushing manages stagnation but does not permanently sterilise a system; it must be repeated.
n.2: Flushing supports temperature control but does not replace keeping hot water hot and cold water cold.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which everyday piece of equipment is a classic aerosol generator that can turn Legionella growth in a system into a health risk?
o: A sealed, mains-fed drinking water bottle filler with no spray
A closed radiator circuit that never opens to air
A kettle used only to boil water for drinks
A shower head producing a fine spray of warm water
How Legionella Grows.w: A shower head breaks warm water into fine, breathable droplets, the aerosol that can carry Legionella into the lungs. Aerosol-producing outlets are a priority for control because they link growth to exposure.

n.0: A non-spraying bottle filler produces little or no breathable aerosol.
n.1: A sealed radiator circuit does not disperse water as an aerosol into the room air.
n.2: A kettle boils water, killing bacteria, and does not generate a fine warm spray.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why can Legionella survive a short-term rise in temperature or a dose of disinfectant that would be expected to kill free-floating bacteria?
o: Because it forms heat-proof spores like some other bacteria
Because biofilm and host protozoa shelter it from heat and chemicals
Because it multiplies faster than any treatment can act
Because it changes the water chemistry to neutralise the disinfectant
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella hidden within biofilm or inside protozoa is protected from heat and biocides that would kill bacteria suspended in the water. This is why control must tackle biofilm and sediment, not just treat the bulk water.

n.0: Legionella does not form the resistant spores that some other bacteria produce; its protection comes from biofilm and hosts.
n.2: Its resistance comes from shelter, not from outpacing treatment by rapid multiplication.
n.3: The bacteria do not chemically neutralise disinfectant; they are shielded from it.

How Legionella Grows.q: A maintenance report notes 'low system turnover and warm ambient conditions'. Why does this phrasing point to a Legionella growth risk?
o: Neither factor has any link to Legionella growth
Low turnover keeps water permanently below 20°C
Together they mean stagnant water warming into the growth range, ideal for multiplication
Warm ambient conditions kill the bacteria on contact
How Legionella Grows.w: Low turnover means water stands still (stagnation) while warm surroundings raise it into the 20–45°C band. Combined, these give Legionella the still, warm conditions it needs to multiply, so both should be addressed.

n.1: Low turnover lets standing water warm towards ambient, not stay cold below 20°C.
n.3: Warm ambient conditions promote growth; they do not kill the bacteria.
n.0: Both stagnation and warmth are core drivers of Legionella growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which statement about where Legionella typically grows within a system is correct?
o: It grows only inside sealed pressure gauges
It cannot grow on any surface and lives only suspended in flowing water
It grows only in the open air above the water surface
It grows mainly on the inner surfaces, within biofilm, scale and sediment, rather than only free in the water
How Legionella Grows.w: Much Legionella growth occurs on wetted surfaces within biofilm and among scale and sediment, which shelter and feed it. Water sampling can under-represent this, so surfaces and deposits must be controlled.

n.2: Legionella is a waterborne organism that grows in the water and on wetted surfaces, not in open air above it.
n.0: It is not confined to sealed gauges; it colonises pipework, tanks and fittings.
n.1: Surfaces and biofilm are a primary habitat; the bacteria are not limited to flowing water.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is it misleading to assume a system is safe just because a water sample taken from a tap shows low bacterial numbers?
o: Because tap samples heat the water and kill everything in the pipe
Because samples always overstate the true level of Legionella
Because Legionella can still be established in biofilm and sediment that a single water sample may not detect
Because low numbers prove the system can never grow Legionella
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella sheltered in biofilm, sediment and protozoa may not appear in a one-off water sample, yet it can seed the system later. This is why temperature, cleanliness and flow controls matter, not just sample results.

n.3: A low result does not prove the system cannot grow Legionella; conditions can change and biofilm persists.
n.1: Samples can under-represent, not overstate, bacteria held in biofilm and deposits.
n.0: Taking a sample does not heat or sterilise the pipework; the hidden reservoir remains.

How Legionella Grows.q: Two adjoining outlets are compared: one used many times daily, one used once a month. Why is the monthly outlet the greater Legionella growth risk?
o: Its water stagnates for long periods and can warm and gather nutrients between uses
Rarely used outlets are physically incapable of forming biofilm
Its frequent flushing keeps it constantly fresh
It is always supplied with hotter water than the busy outlet
How Legionella Grows.w: The monthly outlet leaves water standing for weeks, allowing stagnation, temperature drift into the growth band and nutrient build-up. Frequently used outlets refresh their water and are less prone to these conditions.

n.2: A monthly outlet is not frequently flushed; that describes the busy outlet.
n.3: There is no reason a rarely used outlet receives hotter water; it often cools between uses.
n.1: Rarely used outlets are especially prone to biofilm because water sits still in them.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which set of conditions together represents the greatest risk of Legionella multiplying to harmful levels?
o: Water at 65°C, circulating, freshly cleaned, no spray
Water frozen solid with no nutrients present
Water at 6°C, high turnover, clean pipework, no aerosol
Water at 40°C, stagnant, sediment-laden, feeding a spray outlet
How Legionella Grows.w: Warm water in the growth range, standing still, rich in nutrients and feeding an aerosol-producing outlet brings together every factor: temperature, stagnation, nutrients and a route of exposure. This is the highest-risk combination.

n.2: At 6°C with high turnover and no aerosol, the bacteria are dormant and exposure is unlikely.
n.0: At 65°C and circulating, Legionella is killed and there is no aerosol to carry it.
n.1: Frozen, nutrient-free water offers none of the conditions the bacteria need.

How Legionella Grows.q: How does poor circulation in a hot water return loop encourage Legionella growth?
o: It removes all nutrients from the returning water
It keeps water moving too fast for bacteria to settle
It forces the whole loop above 60°C and kills the bacteria
It lets parts of the loop cool into the growth range and water to stagnate in poorly served branches
How Legionella Grows.w: Inadequate circulation lets sections of the loop and its branches fall below the target hot temperature into the 20–45°C band and stagnate, giving Legionella warm, still conditions. Balanced circulation keeps the whole loop hot.

n.2: Poor circulation causes cool spots below 60°C, not uniform killing temperatures.
n.1: The problem is water moving too slowly, allowing stagnation, not too fast.
n.0: Poor circulation does not strip nutrients; deposits build up in the sluggish areas.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is corrosion (rust) inside steel pipework relevant to Legionella growth?
o: Corrosion continuously releases a biocide that suppresses growth
Corrosion products provide nutrients and a rough, sheltered surface that support biofilm and bacterial growth
Corrosion seals the pipe so no water can touch the bacteria
Corrosion raises water temperature above the killing point
How Legionella Grows.w: Rust and corrosion debris supply nutrients and create rough, sheltered surfaces where biofilm forms and Legionella lodges. Controlling corrosion and removing debris helps limit the conditions for growth.

n.2: Corrosion roughens and pits surfaces; it does not seal water away from the bacteria.
n.0: Corrosion products feed growth rather than releasing any biocide.
n.3: Corrosion does not heat water to a killing temperature; it provides food and shelter.

How Legionella Grows.q: An expansion vessel and a rarely opened emergency safety shower are both on a site risk assessment. Why are components like these flagged for Legionella growth?
o: They keep large volumes of water constantly hot above 60°C
They are self-cleaning and never accumulate deposits
They contain no water and so cannot support bacteria
They hold water that seldom moves, allowing stagnation, warming and nutrient build-up
How Legionella Grows.w: Expansion vessels and emergency showers hold water that is rarely exchanged, so it stagnates, drifts into the growth range and gathers nutrients. Such infrequently used components need regular flushing and inspection.

n.0: These components are not maintained hot at 60°C; their water typically sits at ambient.
n.1: Little-used components accumulate sediment and biofilm rather than staying clean.
n.2: They do hold water, which is exactly why they can support growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which single summary best captures the conditions Legionella needs to grow to harmful numbers?
o: Sterile, nutrient-free water at any temperature
Water kept constantly below 20°C or above 60°C and always moving
Fast-flowing water with a strong disinfectant residual and no deposits
Warm water in the 20–45°C range, stagnant, with nutrients from biofilm, scale, rust or sediment, then dispersed as aerosol
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella multiplies when water is warm (20–45°C), still and nutrient-rich, and becomes a health risk when that water is dispersed as a breathable aerosol. Controls target each of these factors under HSG274 Part 2.

n.1: Water kept cold or hot and moving is a control condition, the opposite of what favours growth.
n.0: Sterile, nutrient-free water lacks the food the bacteria need and does not favour growth.
n.2: Fast flow, disinfectant residual and no deposits all suppress growth rather than promote it.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, what is the main duty an employer owes to their employees?
o: To carry insurance and nothing more
To provide free protective clothing whatever the cost
To ensure their health, safety and welfare so far as is reasonably practicable
To pay compensation whenever an accident occurs
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 2 of the Act places a general duty on employers to ensure the health, safety and welfare of employees so far as is reasonably practicable.

n.1: PPE is provided where a risk assessment requires it, and the duty is qualified by what is reasonably practicable, not unlimited cost.
n.3: The Act is about preventing harm; paying out after an accident is not the primary legal duty.
n.0: Employers' liability insurance is a separate legal requirement and does not discharge the wider safety duty.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 also places a duty on employees. What must every employee do?
o: Write the company's risk assessments themselves
Take reasonable care of themselves and others, and co-operate with their employer
Ignore hazards outside their own trade
Only follow safety rules when a manager is watching
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 7 requires employees to take reasonable care for their own safety and that of others and to co-operate with the employer on health and safety.

n.0: Producing risk assessments is the employer's duty, not the individual operative's.
n.3: The duty of care applies at all times, not only when supervised.
n.2: The duty to take reasonable care extends to others affected by your work, not just your own trade.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which set of regulations treats legionella bacteria as a biological hazard that must be assessed and controlled at work?
o: The Road Traffic Act
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (COSHH)
The Data Protection Act
The Working Time Regulations
The Law & Responsibilities.w: COSHH 2002 covers biological agents such as legionella and requires the risk to be assessed and adequately controlled.

n.0: The Road Traffic Act governs driving, not workplace health hazards.
n.3: The Working Time Regulations deal with hours of work, not biological hazards.
n.2: The Data Protection Act governs personal data, not hazardous substances.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What does the abbreviation ACOP stand for in relation to L8?
o: Annual Certificate of Practice
Approved Code of Practice
Approved Contractor Order Policy
Advisory Committee on Plumbing
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 is the Approved Code of Practice, giving practical advice on complying with the law on legionella.

n.3: There is no such committee behind L8; ACOP is a defined legal term.
n.0: L8 is not a certificate; it is guidance with special legal status.
n.2: ACOP does not refer to a contractor order policy.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What is the special legal status of an Approved Code of Practice such as L8?
o: It is optional advice with no bearing on the law
It only applies to hospitals
It replaces the Health and Safety at Work Act entirely
If you follow it you are doing enough to comply with the law; if you do not, you must show you did something equally effective
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Following an ACOP is normally enough to comply; departing from it means you must demonstrate compliance by some equally good means.

n.0: An ACOP has a defined legal standing and can be cited in court, so it is not merely optional.
n.2: An ACOP supports the law; it does not replace primary legislation.
n.1: L8 applies wherever there is a legionella risk, not only hospitals.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: HSG274 is best described as which of the following?
o: A product warranty document
Practical technical guidance on controlling legionella in specific systems
A criminal statute passed by Parliament
A first aid manual
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSG274 is HSE technical guidance giving practical detail on controlling legionella in different types of water system.

n.2: HSG274 is guidance, not an Act of Parliament.
n.3: It concerns water system control, not first aid.
n.0: It is not a warranty; it is health and safety guidance.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which part of HSG274 covers hot and cold water systems?
o: Part 6
Part 1
Part 2
Part 4
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSG274 Part 2 gives the practical guidance for controlling legionella in hot and cold water systems.

n.1: Part 1 covers evaporative cooling systems, not hot and cold water.
n.3: There is no Part 4 dealing with hot and cold water; that is Part 2.
n.0: There is no Part 6 for hot and cold water systems.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Who is the 'duty holder' with the legal responsibility to assess and manage the legionella risk on a site?
o: The water company that supplies the mains
The employer or person in control of the premises
Whichever operative last worked on the tank
The person who reports a fault
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder is the employer or person in control of the premises, and they carry the legal responsibility to assess and manage the risk.

n.2: An individual operative is not the duty holder simply because they did the last task.
n.0: The mains supplier is not responsible for the building owner's internal systems.
n.3: Reporting a fault is a good act but does not make someone the duty holder.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: The duty holder appoints a competent person to take day-to-day charge of controlling the legionella risk. What is this person usually called?
o: The insurance assessor
The site visitor
The mains inspector
The responsible person
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The appointed competent person who manages the control measures is known as the responsible person.

n.1: A 'site visitor' has no defined role in the control scheme.
n.2: A mains inspector is not the appointed manager of the internal water system risk.
n.0: An insurance assessor deals with claims, not day-to-day legionella control.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which regulations place a clear duty on employers to carry out a suitable and sufficient risk assessment?
o: The Highway Code
The Consumer Rights Act
The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999
The Building Societies Act
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations require employers to make a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks.

n.0: The Highway Code concerns road use, not workplace risk assessment.
n.3: The Building Societies Act is financial legislation.
n.1: The Consumer Rights Act deals with goods and services to consumers.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Legionnaires' disease diagnosed as caught at work must be reported to the authorities under which reporting requirement?
o: PAT
MOT
RIDDOR
GDPR
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Legionnaires' disease contracted at work is reportable to the HSE under RIDDOR.

n.1: MOT relates to vehicle roadworthiness, not disease reporting.
n.3: GDPR governs personal data protection.
n.0: PAT refers to portable appliance testing, not disease reporting.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which body is the main enforcing authority for the legionella duties under health and safety law?
o: The Health and Safety Executive (HSE)
The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency
The Advertising Standards Authority
The Environment Agency
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The HSE is the principal enforcing authority for health and safety law covering legionella.

n.3: The Environment Agency deals mainly with environmental discharges, not this enforcement.
n.2: The Advertising Standards Authority regulates advertising.
n.1: The DVSA regulates drivers and vehicles.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A written scheme for controlling the risk has been prepared for a site. What is your duty as an operative in relation to it?
o: Rewrite the scheme to suit yourself
Carry out your tasks in the way the scheme sets out and record what you do
Ignore it because it is only guidance
Keep it locked away and unread
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Operatives must follow the written scheme, complete their tasks correctly and keep records as required.

n.0: Altering the control scheme is not an operative's role; that lies with the responsible person.
n.2: The scheme is a legal control measure that must be followed, not ignored.
n.3: The scheme must be used and understood, not hidden away.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under COSHH, what must be done before employees are exposed to a substance or agent hazardous to health such as legionella?
o: Everyone must be issued a respirator regardless of task
The system must be shut down permanently
A sample must be sent to the police
The risk must be assessed and adequate control measures put in place
The Law & Responsibilities.w: COSHH requires the risk to be assessed and controlled adequately before exposure occurs.

n.0: Respirators are only required where the assessment identifies the need; blanket issue is not the rule.
n.1: Permanent shutdown is not required; the risk is managed, not eliminated by closing systems.
n.2: There is no requirement to involve the police with samples.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are flushing a rarely used outlet as instructed. Part-way through you notice a nearby tap has no cold water at all. It is outside your task. What should you do?
o: Turn off the whole building's water yourself
Wait a few weeks to see if it fixes itself
Say nothing because it is not on your job sheet
Report the fault to the responsible person so it can be investigated
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Everyone has a duty to report problems so the responsible person can act, even where it falls outside their own task.

n.2: Ignoring a fault because it is off your sheet breaches the duty to report.
n.0: Isolating the whole building without authority is not your decision and could cause harm.
n.1: Delaying a report allows a potential risk to persist.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why must a person appointed to manage legionella control be 'competent'?
o: Competence only means holding a driving licence
It is a courtesy title with no real meaning
They need the training, knowledge and experience to do the work correctly and safely
Competence is decided by length of service alone
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Competence means having the necessary training, knowledge, skills and experience to carry out the duties properly.

n.0: A driving licence is unrelated to competence in legionella control.
n.1: Competence is a genuine legal requirement, not a courtesy.
n.3: Time served does not by itself prove the required knowledge and skills.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: The responsible person is away on leave for two weeks. How should continuity of legionella control be maintained?
o: Control measures are suspended and restarted later
A trained and competent deputy should be appointed to cover their duties
All monitoring simply stops until they return
The tasks pass to whoever happens to be on site
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A competent deputy should be appointed so the control duties continue without a gap during absences.

n.2: Stopping monitoring during absence would break the control regime.
n.3: Duties should go to a suitably competent deputy, not an untrained bystander.
n.0: Suspending control measures allows conditions for legionella to develop.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative argues that because L8 is 'only a code of practice' it can be ignored. Why is this wrong?
o: Codes of practice are legally binding statutes
Only the Environment Agency can quote L8
An ACOP has special legal status and can be used in court as evidence of failing to comply
L8 has been withdrawn and no longer exists
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An ACOP carries special legal standing, and failing to follow it can be used in court unless equal compliance is shown.

n.0: An ACOP is not itself a statute, but it still carries legal weight; the claim it can be ignored is the error.
n.3: L8 is current guidance, not withdrawn.
n.1: The HSE, not the Environment Agency, is the enforcing authority that relies on L8.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act, what must an employee NOT do to safety equipment provided for their protection?
o: Report if it is damaged
Store it correctly
Clean it after use
Interfere with or misuse it
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 8 makes it an offence to intentionally interfere with or misuse anything provided for health and safety.

n.2: Cleaning equipment properly is good practice, not prohibited.
n.1: Storing equipment correctly is expected, not prohibited.
n.0: Reporting damage is exactly what an employee should do.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Who has the ultimate legal responsibility for ensuring the legionella risk assessment is carried out?
o: The visiting auditor
