The chemical supplier
The duty holder
The most junior operative
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder holds the legal responsibility for ensuring a suitable risk assessment is carried out.

n.3: A junior operative carries out tasks but does not hold the legal duty to ensure assessment.
n.1: A chemical supplier provides products, not the site's legal duty of assessment.
n.0: An auditor checks compliance but does not carry the duty holder's responsibility.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: During a routine temperature check you find a hot outlet running well below the expected temperature. What is the correct action?
o: Cross out the low reading and write a passing figure
Record the reading and report it to the responsible person
Assume the thermometer is faulty and move on
Adjust the boiler settings yourself without telling anyone
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Out-of-range readings must be recorded accurately and reported so control can be reviewed and corrective action taken.

n.3: Altering plant settings without authority is not the operative's role.
n.0: Falsifying records is dishonest and dangerous, hiding a real risk.
n.2: Dismissing the reading without checking could conceal a genuine control failure.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between L8 and HSG274?
o: L8 is the approved code of practice; HSG274 gives the detailed practical technical guidance
Neither has any connection to legionella
They are two names for the same single document
HSG274 overrides L8 in all cases
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 sets the code of practice while HSG274 provides the supporting practical and technical detail.

n.3: HSG274 supports L8 rather than overriding it.
n.2: They are separate publications, not one document.
n.1: Both are specifically about controlling legionella.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are a contractor asked to do work not covered by the site's written scheme or your training. What should you do?
o: Guess the method and carry on to save time
Stop and check with the responsible person before going ahead
Refuse to speak to anyone and leave silently
Sign off the work as complete anyway
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Work must be within your competence and the written scheme; if it is not, you should stop and consult the responsible person.

n.0: Guessing a method on a safety-critical system risks creating a hazard.
n.2: Leaving without informing anyone abandons the duty to communicate.
n.3: Signing off work not properly done is falsifying records.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under COSHH, how often should the assessment for a legionella risk be reviewed?
o: Only once when the building is first built
Only if an outbreak has already occurred
Regularly, and whenever there is reason to think it is no longer valid
Never, once it is signed
The Law & Responsibilities.w: COSHH requires the assessment to be reviewed regularly and whenever it may no longer be valid, such as after changes to the system.

n.0: A single assessment at construction cannot reflect later changes in use or plant.
n.3: Assessments are living documents that must be kept up to date.
n.1: Waiting for an outbreak defeats the purpose of preventive assessment.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative says the risk assessment is 'the water company's job'. Why is this incorrect?
o: Nobody is required to assess the risk
The water company is legally bound to assess every building's pipework
The duty holder in control of the premises must assess the risk in their own systems
Only the HSE can carry out risk assessments
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Responsibility for assessing the risk in the building's own water systems rests with the duty holder, not the mains supplier.

n.1: The water company is not responsible for assessing risks inside private premises.
n.0: The law clearly requires the risk to be assessed by the duty holder.
n.3: The HSE enforces the law but does not carry out duty holders' assessments for them.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What is the purpose of keeping records of the checks and tasks carried out under the control scheme?
o: To replace the need to do the actual tasks
To satisfy the marketing department
To show the control measures are being carried out and to help identify problems
To create paperwork that no one ever needs to see
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Records demonstrate that control measures are being applied and provide a history that helps spot trends and problems.

n.3: Records are a working tool that must be available for review, not pointless paperwork.
n.0: Recording a task does not remove the need to actually perform it.
n.1: Record keeping is a legal and technical requirement, not a marketing exercise.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You arrive to service a cold water storage tank and find the lid missing and debris inside. It is not the job you were sent for. What is the responsible action?
o: Remove the debris with your bare hands and say nothing
Report the uncovered tank and contamination to the responsible person straight away
Fit any lid you can find from another site without checking
Leave it open and complete only your original task
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An uncovered, contaminated tank is a clear risk that must be reported promptly so it can be dealt with correctly.

n.2: Fitting a random unsuitable lid could introduce further contamination and is not authorised.
n.3: Leaving the tank open ignores an obvious and reportable hazard.
n.0: Using bare hands is unhygienic and unsafe, and failing to report hides the problem.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations require the significant findings of a risk assessment to be recorded when the employer has how many or more employees?
o: Two hundred or more
Fifty or more
Five or more
One or more
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Employers with five or more employees must record the significant findings of their risk assessment.

n.3: The recording threshold is five, not one, although good practice is to record in any case.
n.1: The threshold is far lower than fifty.
n.0: The threshold is not set at two hundred employees.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following best describes 'so far as is reasonably practicable' in the Health and Safety at Work Act?
o: Balancing the risk against the time, trouble and cost of controlling it
Ignoring risk if control is inconvenient
Doing whatever is cheapest regardless of risk
Spending unlimited money whatever the risk
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Reasonably practicable means weighing the level of risk against the effort and cost needed to control it.

n.2: Cost cannot be put ahead of a serious risk; the test is a balance, not the cheapest option.
n.1: Inconvenience does not excuse leaving a significant risk uncontrolled.
n.3: The test is proportionate, not a requirement to spend without limit.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative on your team says they were never trained but has been told to carry out chlorination. What should happen?
o: They should ask a member of the public to help
They should sign the record to say they did it either way
They should attempt it and learn as they go
They should not do the task until they are trained and competent for it
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Tasks must only be done by people with the training and competence to do them safely and correctly.

n.2: Attempting a chemical task untrained risks harm to themselves and others.
n.1: Signing a record for work not properly done is falsification.
n.0: Members of the public are not trained operatives and must not carry out control tasks.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why is legionella specifically covered by COSHH?
o: Because it is a biological agent that is hazardous to health
Because it is a flammable liquid
Because it is a controlled explosive
Because it is a road transport hazard
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Legionella bacteria are a biological agent hazardous to health, which brings them within COSHH.

n.1: Legionella is a living organism, not a flammable liquid.
n.2: It is not an explosive substance.
n.3: COSHH covers it as a health hazard, unrelated to road transport rules.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are working on a customer's site and are unsure who the responsible person is. What is the best course of action?
o: Assume there is no responsible person
Start work and hope someone tells you later
Report only to another contractor you happen to know
Ask before starting so you know who to report to and take instruction from
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Knowing who the responsible person is ensures you can take instruction and report problems to the right person before work begins.

n.1: Starting blind means faults may not reach the right person.
n.0: A duty holder should have appointed a responsible person; assuming none exists is unsafe.
n.2: Reporting to an unrelated contractor does not put the information where it needs to go.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which statement about the duty holder's responsibilities is correct?
o: They must identify and assess the risk and put in place a means of controlling it
They are only responsible for water they can see
They only need to act after someone becomes ill
They can pass all legal responsibility to a cleaning contractor by verbal agreement
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder must identify and assess the risk and ensure control measures are in place and maintained.

n.3: Legal responsibility for the duty cannot simply be handed off by a casual arrangement.
n.2: The duty is preventive and does not wait for illness to occur.
n.1: The duty covers the whole system, including parts not readily visible.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A supervisor tells you to skip a scheduled temperature monitoring round because 'it's always fine'. What should you do?
o: Do half of the outlets to save time
Skip it as instructed and record it as done
Delete the outlet from the record permanently
Carry out the monitoring as the written scheme requires and record the results
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The written scheme's monitoring must be carried out and recorded honestly, as it is a legal control measure.

n.1: Recording monitoring as done when it was skipped is falsification.
n.0: Partial monitoring does not meet the requirements of the scheme.
n.2: An operative has no authority to remove monitoring points from the scheme.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What does the term 'suitable and sufficient' mean when applied to a risk assessment?
o: It properly identifies the risks and the measures needed to control them
It is as short as possible with no detail
It is copied word for word from another building
It only lists the equipment on site
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A suitable and sufficient assessment properly identifies the significant risks and the control measures required.

n.1: An assessment must contain enough detail to be useful, not be deliberately brief.
n.3: Listing equipment alone does not assess how the risk arises or is controlled.
n.2: A copied generic assessment may not reflect the actual system and its specific risks.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Legionnaires' disease is reportable under RIDDOR when it is believed to have been caught in what circumstance?
o: Only when the person is over 65
Where the person's work exposed them to legionella bacteria
Only if the person works outdoors
Never, because it is not work-related
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A case is RIDDOR-reportable where there is reasonable evidence the illness was linked to work exposure to legionella.

n.0: Age does not determine whether a case is reportable.
n.2: The setting need not be outdoors; indoor water systems are a common source.
n.3: Work-related cases are reportable, so it is not correct that it is never reportable.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You find that a colleague has been signing monitoring sheets without actually taking the readings. What is the correct response?
o: Copy their approach to keep up with the workload
Report it to the responsible person because the records are false and the risk is unmanaged
Say nothing to avoid causing trouble
Backdate your own sheets to match theirs
The Law & Responsibilities.w: False records mean the risk is not truly being monitored, so this must be reported so control can be restored.

n.0: Copying false record-keeping compounds the danger and the dishonesty.
n.2: Staying silent allows an unmanaged risk to continue.
n.3: Backdating records is itself falsification and hides the problem further.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which of these is a duty placed on employees rather than the employer under health and safety law?
o: Funding all control equipment
Preparing the site legionella risk assessment
Co-operating with the employer so they can meet their legal duties
Appointing the responsible person
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Employees have a legal duty to co-operate with their employer on health and safety matters.

n.1: Preparing the risk assessment is the employer's or duty holder's duty.
n.3: Appointing the responsible person is a duty holder responsibility.
n.0: Providing and funding equipment is an employer duty, not an employee one.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: If a duty holder chooses not to follow the exact advice in ACOP L8, what must they be able to demonstrate?
o: That they saved money by doing less
That another company is now to blame
That the risk no longer needs controlling
That they have controlled the risk to the same standard by another effective method
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Departing from an ACOP is permitted only if you can show you achieved compliance to an equally effective standard.

n.0: Saving money does not justify a lower standard of control.
n.2: The legal duty to control the risk remains regardless.
n.1: Shifting blame does not discharge the duty to control the risk.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A cold water storage tank temperature is found to be rising toward the range where legionella can multiply. Whose job is it to make sure this is acted upon?
o: The water meter reader
The responsible person, informed by the operative's report
The member of the public who reported feeling unwell
The HSE inspector on their next visit
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The operative reports the finding and the responsible person ensures corrective action is taken.

n.2: A member of the public has no role in managing the control scheme.
n.3: Action cannot wait for a possible future HSE visit.
n.0: A meter reader has no responsibility for the control scheme.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act, an employer's duty to non-employees such as visitors and the public is:
o: To conduct the undertaking so they are not exposed to risks to their health and safety, so far as is reasonably practicable
Non-existent, as the Act only protects employees
Only owed to paying customers
Limited to putting up a warning sign
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 3 extends the duty to persons not in the employer's employment who may be affected by the work.

n.1: The Act clearly protects people beyond the direct employees.
n.3: A sign alone does not discharge the wider duty to control the risk.
n.2: The duty is owed to anyone affected, not only paying customers.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why should an operative understand the site's written scheme of control before starting work?
o: So they can charge the customer more
So they can change the control temperatures
So they can decide the scheme is unnecessary
So they carry out the correct tasks, in the correct way, and know what to report
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Understanding the scheme ensures tasks are done correctly and that faults are recognised and reported properly.

n.1: Changing control temperatures is a decision for the responsible person, not the operative.
n.2: The scheme is a legal control measure, not something an operative can dismiss.
n.0: The scheme is about controlling risk, not adjusting charges.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A landlord manages a block of flats with shared water systems. Under the law, they are best described as:
o: A duty holder responsible for assessing and controlling the legionella risk
Exempt because they do not live in the building
A member of the public with no duties
Responsible only for the boiler warranty
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A landlord in control of premises with a water system is a duty holder and must assess and control the risk.

n.1: Not living in the building does not remove the duty for premises under their control.
n.3: The duty covers the whole system risk, not just a warranty.
n.2: As the person in control, the landlord has clear legal duties.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You notice the site risk assessment on the wall is dated over five years ago and the building has since been extended. What does this suggest?
o: The assessment likely needs reviewing because the system has changed
Only the HSE may point this out
Nothing, as assessments never expire
The extension means the old assessment is automatically correct
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A material change such as an extension is a trigger to review whether the assessment is still valid.

n.2: Assessments must be kept current and reviewed after changes, so they are not timeless.
n.3: An extension adds new pipework and risk, so the old assessment cannot be assumed correct.
n.1: Anyone noticing this should raise it; it is not solely for the HSE to identify.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is the correct order of legal weight, from primary law to practical guidance?
o: ACOP L8, then the Act, then HSG274
They all carry exactly equal legal force
Health and Safety at Work Act, then ACOP L8, then HSG274 guidance
HSG274, then ACOP L8, then the Act
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The Act is the primary legislation, L8 is the approved code of practice supporting it, and HSG274 is practical guidance.

n.3: Guidance does not sit above the primary Act; the order is reversed.
n.0: An ACOP supports the Act rather than outranking it.
n.1: They have different standings; primary law, ACOP and guidance are not equal.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A member of the public tells you a shower in a leisure centre changing room has not worked for months. You are on site to service the pool plant. What should you do?
o: Ignore it because showers are not your job today
Pass the information to the responsible person so the little-used outlet can be assessed
Tell the member of the public to fix it themselves
Turn the shower on and leave it running unattended
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A little-used outlet can allow stagnation, so the information should reach the responsible person to be assessed and acted upon.

n.0: The duty to report a potential risk applies even when it is outside your immediate task.
n.2: Members of the public are not the ones who should be carrying out control work.
n.3: Leaving a shower running unattended is not a controlled or safe response.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What is the main reason an operative must report faults promptly rather than at the end of the month?
o: There is no real reason; timing does not matter
A delay can allow conditions for legionella to develop and put people at risk
Monthly reporting looks tidier on paperwork
Prompt reports annoy the responsible person
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Prompt reporting allows quick corrective action before conditions favour legionella growth.

n.2: Appearance of paperwork is irrelevant next to controlling a health risk.
n.3: Reporting promptly supports the responsible person's duties rather than hindering them.
n.0: Timing matters greatly because delay increases risk.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which document would an operative primarily follow for the day-to-day tasks and frequencies on a site?
o: The company's holiday policy
The site-specific written scheme of control
A generic advertising brochure
The building's fire certificate
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The written scheme of control sets out the specific tasks, methods and frequencies for that site.

n.2: A brochure is marketing material, not a control document.
n.3: A fire certificate concerns fire safety, not legionella control tasks.
n.0: A holiday policy is unrelated to water hygiene tasks.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: If the HSE inspects a site and finds the legionella risk is not being managed, which of these can they do?
o: Serve an improvement or prohibition notice and, in serious cases, prosecute
Only offer friendly advice with no powers
Repair the water system themselves for free
Issue a parking ticket
The Law & Responsibilities.w: As the enforcing authority the HSE can serve enforcement notices and bring prosecutions where the law is breached.

n.1: The HSE has real enforcement powers, not just advice.
n.2: The HSE enforces the law; it does not carry out the duty holder's repairs.
n.3: Parking tickets are nothing to do with the HSE's health and safety role.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative completes a task but realises they did it slightly wrong. What is the responsible thing to do?
o: Tell the responsible person so it can be corrected and recorded accurately
Do nothing and hope it was fine
Record it as fully correct to avoid questions
Blame the previous contractor in the record
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Being honest about a mistake lets it be corrected and keeps the records accurate and reliable.

n.2: Recording a task as correct when it was not is falsification and hides a possible risk.
n.1: Ignoring a known error leaves a potential problem unaddressed.
n.3: Shifting blame does not fix the error or keep the record truthful.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which document is the Approved Code of Practice (ACOP) for controlling legionella?
o: The Highway Code
L8, 'Legionnaires' disease: The control of legionella bacteria in water systems'
The building's daily cleaning rota
A manufacturer's shower installation leaflet
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 is the HSE Approved Code of Practice that sets the standard for controlling legionella, supported by the HSG274 guidance.

n.0: The Highway Code deals with road use, not water hygiene.
n.3: A product leaflet is not an official code of practice.
n.2: A cleaning rota is a local task list, not the ACOP.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under health and safety law, who is the 'duty holder' with overall responsibility for controlling the legionella risk?
o: The most junior member of staff on site
The employer or person in control of the premises
Any visitor who happens to use the building
The water company that supplies the mains
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder is the employer or person in control of the premises, who must assess and control the risk.

n.2: Visitors have no legal duty to control the risk.
n.3: The water supplier is responsible only up to the boundary, not for the building's internal systems.
n.0: Responsibility rests with the duty holder, not automatically with junior staff.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What must the duty holder do about managing the day-to-day legionella controls?
o: Wait until someone becomes ill before acting
Rely only on tenants noticing any problems
Leave the system alone once it is installed
Appoint a competent 'responsible person' to manage the controls
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder must appoint a competent responsible person to take day-to-day charge of managing and monitoring the controls.

n.2: Water systems need ongoing management, not a fit-and-forget approach.
n.1: The legal duty cannot be passed to tenants simply noticing faults.
n.0: The law requires prevention in advance, not waiting for illness to occur.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which two pieces of legislation place general legal duties to control the legionella risk?
o: The Working Time Regulations and the Equality Act
The Road Traffic Act and the Licensing Act
The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and COSHH 2002
The Data Protection Act and the Consumer Rights Act
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and the COSHH Regulations 2002 create the legal duties to assess and control the risk.

n.3: These laws cover data and consumer purchases, not water hygiene risk.
n.1: These laws cover driving and alcohol licensing, not legionella control.
n.0: These laws cover working hours and discrimination, not legionella control.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What is the role of HSG274 in relation to legionella control?
o: It is a marketing brochure for cleaning products
It is a warranty document for boilers
It is HSE technical guidance on how to control legionella in water systems
It is a criminal court sentencing guideline
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSG274 is the HSE's practical technical guidance that supports the L8 ACOP, including Part 2 on hot and cold water systems.

n.3: It is health and safety guidance, not a court sentencing document.
n.1: It is not a product warranty.
n.0: It is official guidance, not sales material.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are carrying out water hygiene checks and notice a stored hot water temperature is far too low. What should you do?
o: Record the reading and report it promptly to the responsible person as required by the written scheme
Say nothing to avoid causing extra work
Ignore it because it is not part of your written tasks
Wait several months and mention it at the next annual review
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The written scheme requires readings to be recorded and problems reported promptly so control can be restored quickly.

n.2: Everyone has a duty to report problems they find, even outside their usual tasks.
n.1: Staying silent leaves a known risk uncontrolled.
n.3: A control failure needs prompt action, not delay until the next review.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A colleague asks you why you bother writing down every temperature and inspection. What is the correct reason?
o: They are not needed and can be thrown away straight away
To show the controls are working and provide evidence the risk is being managed
Purely so staff can practise their handwriting
Only to decorate the plant room wall
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Records demonstrate that the written scheme is being followed and that the risk is being properly controlled over time.

n.0: Records must be kept, not discarded; they are a legal expectation.
n.3: Their purpose is evidence and control, not decoration.
n.2: Their value is as proof of monitoring, not handwriting practice.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What does 'competent' mean when appointing a responsible person for legionella control?
o: They own the most tools
They happen to be available on the day
They have the right training, knowledge and experience to manage the risk
They are simply the longest-serving employee regardless of knowledge
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A competent person has the necessary training, knowledge, skills and experience to carry out the control duties properly.

n.3: Length of service alone does not make someone competent.
n.0: Owning tools is not a measure of competence for managing the risk.
n.1: Being available is not the same as being competent.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are a new operative and have not read the site's written control scheme yet. Before you start work on the water system, what should you do?
o: Guess what to do so you do not have to ask anyone
Copy whatever the last operative did without checking
Read and follow the written scheme, and ask the responsible person about anything you are unsure of
Skip the paperwork because it slows you down
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Everyone must follow the site's written scheme and raise any uncertainty with the responsible person before working on the system.

n.0: Guessing on safety-critical work risks leaving the system uncontrolled.
n.1: Copying past actions may repeat mistakes and ignores the agreed scheme.
n.3: The written scheme sets out the required controls and must not be skipped.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative argues that because ACOP L8 is only an Approved Code of Practice and not an Act of Parliament, its guidance can be ignored so long as the job gets done. Under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, what is the true legal standing of L8?
o: Following it is one way to comply; if you do not, you must show your controls are at least equally effective, and a court can treat a breach as proof of a legal failing unless you prove otherwise
It has no legal weight at all and is purely advisory background reading
It only applies to the water supplier and places no duties on contractors working on systems
It is fully mandatory law and any deviation is automatically a criminal offence regardless of the controls in place
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An ACOP has a special legal status: you may follow it, or adopt controls that are at least equally effective. If prosecuted for a breach of the law and it is shown you did not follow the ACOP, a court can find you at fault unless you prove you complied in some other equally effective way.

n.1: An ACOP is not merely advisory; it carries a special evidential status in court.
n.3: An ACOP is not itself absolute law and permits equally effective alternative controls, so deviation is not automatically an offence.
n.2: L8 duties fall on anyone in control of the relevant premises or system, including contractors.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A duty holder claims they have discharged all their legal duties simply by appointing a competent responsible person for Legionella control. Under the HSWA 1974 and MHSWR, is this correct?
o: No, the duty holder retains overall legal responsibility and must ensure the risk is assessed and controlled, resourcing and monitoring the arrangements
No, but only because a deputy must also be appointed before any duty is discharged
Yes, provided the responsible person has a recognised certificate the duty holder has no further role
Yes, appointing a competent person transfers the entire legal duty away from the duty holder
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Appointing a competent responsible person is required, but overall legal responsibility for assessing and controlling the risk stays with the duty holder (employer/person in control). They must resource, monitor and ensure the arrangements actually work.

n.3: Legal duty cannot be transferred away by appointing someone; the duty holder remains accountable.
n.2: A certificate does not remove the duty holder's ongoing responsibility to oversee the arrangements.
n.1: A deputy is good practice for continuity, but the real reason is that overall duty always remains with the duty holder.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: On a domestic hot and cold water system, which HSE guidance document sets out the technical guidance most directly relevant to National Water Hygiene work?
o: HSG274 Part 2, which covers hot and cold water systems
HSG274 Part 3, which covers other risk systems such as spa pools
INDG458, which is a short introductory leaflet only
HSG274 Part 1, which covers evaporative cooling systems
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSG274 is HSE's technical guidance supporting ACOP L8, and Part 2 specifically addresses hot and cold water systems, which is the domain most relevant to water hygiene operatives.

n.3: Part 1 covers evaporative cooling systems such as cooling towers, not hot and cold water.
n.1: Part 3 covers other risk systems such as spa pools, not general hot and cold water systems.
n.2: INDG458 is a brief overview leaflet and is not the detailed technical guidance for hot and cold water systems.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: While flushing a rarely used outlet, an operative notices the thermostatic mixing valve is delivering blended water at only 35 degrees C and the local temperature monitoring records are two months out of date. What is the correct action under the written scheme and their legal duties?
o: Shut down the entire building water supply immediately without informing anyone
Adjust the valve settings themselves and backdate the monitoring records to close the gap
Record the finding and report the fault to the responsible person so it can be assessed and acted upon
Ignore it because temperature control of individual outlets is not part of a water hygiene operative's role
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Operatives must follow the written scheme and report faults or abnormal readings to the responsible person, who assesses and directs corrective action. Reporting creates the record and triggers the proper management response.

n.1: Adjusting valves outside your remit and falsifying records is unsafe and unlawful.
n.3: Monitoring and reporting temperature abnormalities is a core part of the operative's role.
n.0: Unilaterally shutting the whole supply without informing anyone is not the correct managed response; the fault must be reported and assessed.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which single piece of legislation places the broad, overarching duty on employers to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of employees and others affected by the work, and underpins all Legionella control law?
o: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002
The Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013
The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSWA 1974 is the primary, overarching legislation placing general duties on employers and the self-employed to protect employees and others so far as is reasonably practicable. The other regulations sit beneath it.

n.1: COSHH deals specifically with hazardous substances, including biological agents, but is a regulation made under the wider Act.
n.0: MHSWR sets out risk-assessment duties but is subordinate to the primary Act.
n.2: RIDDOR is about reporting specified incidents, not the overarching general duty.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A Legionella bacterium is a biological agent. Which regulations most directly require employers to assess and control the risk from exposure to it as a hazardous substance?
o: The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015
The Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992
The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (COSHH)
The Law & Responsibilities.w: COSHH covers hazardous substances including biological agents such as Legionella bacteria, requiring assessment and control of exposure. L8 and HSG274 give the practical guidance for meeting these duties.

n.2: PUWER concerns the safety of work equipment, not control of a biological agent.
n.1: The PPE Regulations cover provision and use of protective equipment, not the substance risk assessment itself.
n.0: CDM concerns management of construction projects, not the specific control of Legionella exposure.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A site's responsible person leaves the company suddenly and no deputy was ever appointed. For several weeks nobody is directing the Legionella control scheme. From a legal standpoint, what does this situation primarily represent?
o: A matter only for the water supplier to resolve, not the duty holder
A failing by the duty holder, who must ensure competent management of the risk continues without interruption
A problem that only becomes legally relevant if someone actually contracts Legionnaires' disease
An acceptable temporary gap because control duties pause when no responsible person is in post
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder must ensure the risk continues to be managed by a competent person at all times, which is why appointing deputies and providing continuity is expected. A management gap is a failing of the duty holder's ongoing duty.

n.3: Legal duties to control the risk do not pause when a post is vacant.
n.0: Responsibility for on-site control rests with the duty holder, not the water supplier.
n.2: The legal failing exists as soon as control lapses, regardless of whether illness has yet occurred.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An HSE inspector visits a site and finds a water system being operated in a way that involves a risk of serious personal injury. Which enforcement action allows the inspector to require that activity to stop, immediately or after a set time?
o: A fixed penalty ticket issued on the spot
An improvement notice
A prohibition notice
A simple caution letter with no legal force
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A prohibition notice is used where there is a risk of serious personal injury and can require an activity to stop immediately or by a specified time. It is the enforcement tool aimed at stopping dangerous activity.

n.1: An improvement notice requires a contravention to be remedied within a period but does not stop the activity.
n.3: A caution letter is not the formal power used to halt dangerous activity.
n.0: HSE does not use on-the-spot fixed penalty tickets for this; formal notices or prosecution are used.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An HSE inspector identifies a breach of health and safety law that must be put right, but there is no immediate risk of serious injury. Which notice is most appropriate?
o: A prohibition notice requiring the work to cease at once
An improvement notice specifying the breach and a time period to remedy it
A verbal warning that carries no obligation to act
An automatic criminal conviction without any notice
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An improvement notice is served where there is a contravention that must be remedied; it specifies the breach and sets a time period for compliance. It is the appropriate tool when there is no immediate serious risk.

n.0: A prohibition notice is reserved for situations involving a risk of serious personal injury.
n.3: A conviction follows a prosecution and court process, not the serving of an improvement notice.
n.2: A verbal warning is not the formal legal instrument; an improvement notice imposes an enforceable obligation.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A care home has a confirmed case of Legionnaires' disease traced to its hot and cold water system. Beyond controlling the immediate risk, what reporting duty does the responsible party have?
o: It only needs to be recorded in the site logbook and no external report is required
None, because Legionnaires' disease is a private medical matter for the individual only
It is reportable to the enforcing authority under RIDDOR as a reportable disease
It must be reported only if more than one person is affected
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Legionnaires' disease is a reportable disease under RIDDOR where it is linked to work exposure. The responsible party must report it to the enforcing authority as well as controlling the risk.

n.1: It is not solely a private medical matter; a work-linked case triggers a legal reporting duty.
n.3: The reporting duty does not depend on the number of people affected.
n.0: A logbook entry alone is insufficient; an external RIDDOR report is required.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, what is the fundamental first step an employer must take in managing the risk from Legionella?
o: Delegate all decisions to the water supplier and take no further action
Wait for the HSE to inspect and tell them what to do
Immediately install chemical dosing on every water system before any assessment
Carry out a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risk of exposure
The Law & Responsibilities.w: MHSWR requires a suitable and sufficient risk assessment as the foundation of managing any workplace risk, including Legionella. Controls then flow from what that assessment identifies.

n.2: Installing controls before assessing the risk is not the required first step and may be disproportionate or ineffective.
n.1: Employers must act proactively, not wait to be told by the regulator.
n.0: The duty cannot be delegated away to the water supplier; the employer must assess and act.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A responsible person delegates temperature monitoring to an operative who has never been trained or shown competent to do the task. Under L8 and MHSWR, what is the primary legal problem with this?
o: The task must legally be done only by the HSE, not by staff
Persons carrying out control tasks must be competent, suitably informed, instructed and trained for the work
The problem is only that the operative is not paid enough for the responsibility
There is no problem, because any employee can carry out water monitoring
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 and MHSWR require that those carrying out Legionella control tasks are competent, with the necessary information, instruction and training. Assigning safety-critical monitoring to an untrained person breaches this.

n.3: Not any employee may do it; competence and training are legal requirements.
n.0: Monitoring is carried out by the duty holder's arrangements, not by the HSE.
n.2: Pay is not the health and safety issue; the issue is competence and training.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A contractor is asked to sign a written scheme of control they have not read, being told 'it's just a formality'. What is the correct understanding of the written scheme's legal role?
o: It is the documented plan for controlling the risk that operatives are legally expected to understand and follow
It replaces the need for any risk assessment to have been carried out
It is a formality with no bearing on how the work is actually done
It only matters to office staff and never to the people doing the work
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The written scheme of control sets out how the risk is to be prevented or controlled and must be implemented and followed. Operatives are expected to understand and work to it, not sign it blind.

n.2: It directly governs how the work must be done; it is not a mere formality.
n.3: It is precisely the people doing the work who must follow it.
n.1: The written scheme follows from, and does not replace, the risk assessment.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following best describes 'so far as is reasonably practicable', the standard applied to many duties under HSWA 1974?
o: Only doing something if the HSE specifically orders it
An absolute duty that must be met regardless of any other factor
Balancing the level of risk against the time, trouble, cost and effort needed to control it
Whatever the duty holder can afford after all other spending
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Reasonably practicable involves weighing the risk against the sacrifice (time, cost, effort) needed to reduce it; where the risk is significant relative to the effort, the control must be taken.

n.3: Affordability alone does not define the standard; the balance is against the level of risk.
n.1: It is not an absolute duty; it explicitly allows a proportionate balance.
n.0: The duty exists independently and does not depend on an HSE order.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: In the context of EUSR National Water Hygiene work on public water supplies, what additional overriding responsibility do operatives carry when working on systems connected to drinking water?
o: To disconnect backflow protection to make their tasks easier
To sample water only for taste and appearance, ignoring contamination risk
To protect the public drinking-water supply from contamination during their work
To increase water pressure at every opportunity to improve flow
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Water hygiene work on drinking-water systems carries a duty to protect the public supply from contamination, which is central to why the water industry requires the National Water Hygiene scheme and Blue Card.

n.3: Raising pressure indiscriminately is not a responsibility and can cause harm.
n.1: Contamination risk cannot be ignored; taste and appearance are not adequate measures of safety.
n.0: Backflow protection prevents contamination and must never be defeated for convenience.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An employer wants to know who, in law, can be a 'duty holder' with responsibility for Legionella risk. Which description is correct?
o: The employer, or any person in control of the premises or system in connection with their work
Only a qualified plumber can be a duty holder
Only the HSE can ever be a duty holder
Only the original building architect remains the duty holder for life
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder is the employer or any person in control of the premises or the water system in connection with a trade, business or undertaking. Control, not job title, determines the duty.

n.2: The HSE is the enforcing authority, not the duty holder.
n.1: Being a plumber is not what makes someone a duty holder; control of the premises or system does.
n.3: Duty follows current control, not the person who originally designed the building.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: An operative is told by a site manager to skip a scheduled flushing task because 'the risk assessment is overdue for review anyway'. What is the correct response consistent with legal duties?
o: Skip the task, since an overdue review cancels the control scheme
Do nothing and assume the manager has authority to waive all controls
Continue to follow the current written scheme and report the overdue review to the responsible person
Rewrite the risk assessment on the spot to remove the flushing task
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The existing written scheme remains in force until properly reviewed and revised. The operative should keep following it and report the overdue review to the responsible person so it can be actioned.

n.0: An overdue review does not cancel existing controls; they remain in force.
n.3: Operatives do not unilaterally rewrite risk assessments to drop controls.
n.1: A manager cannot lawfully waive required controls, and doing nothing leaves the risk uncontrolled.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under Section 7 of the HSWA 1974, what duties are placed directly on employees such as water hygiene operatives?
o: No duties at all, as all duties rest solely with the employer
To personally fund any safety equipment they need
To take reasonable care of their own and others' safety and to cooperate with their employer on health and safety
To design the entire Legionella control scheme themselves
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 7 places duties on employees to take reasonable care for the health and safety of themselves and others affected by their acts, and to cooperate with the employer on health and safety matters.

n.3: Designing the whole control scheme is a duty-holder/management function, not the individual employee's Section 7 duty.
n.0: Employees do have personal legal duties under the Act.
n.1: Employers, not employees, are responsible for providing necessary safety equipment.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A responsible person keeps no records of monitoring, inspections or remedial actions for the water system. Why is this a legal and practical failing?
o: Because records are only needed if the system is over ten years old
Because only the water supplier is ever required to keep records
Because records are optional and their absence has no consequence
Because L8/HSG274 expect control measures and monitoring to be recorded and retained to demonstrate the scheme is being managed
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Keeping records of the assessment, control scheme, monitoring and remedial actions is expected under L8/HSG274 so the duty holder can demonstrate the risk is being effectively managed and reviewed.

n.0: Record-keeping is not tied to the system being over a certain age.
n.2: Records are not optional; their absence undermines the ability to show effective control.
n.1: The duty holder responsible for the premises must keep records, not only the water supplier.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: During a prosecution following an outbreak, the duty holder states they had a risk assessment but never acted on its recommendations. How is this likely to be viewed under health and safety law?
o: As irrelevant, since assessments carry no legal weight
As acceptable, provided the assessment was signed by a manager
As a serious failing, because the law requires identified controls to be implemented, not just documented
Favourably, because merely having an assessment satisfies the law
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An assessment must lead to the implementation of appropriate controls. Identifying risks but failing to act on them is a serious failing of the duty to prevent or adequately control exposure.

n.3: Having an assessment is not enough; the required controls must be put into effect.
n.0: Risk assessments are a legal requirement and carry significant weight.
n.1: A signature does not excuse failing to implement the identified controls.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best captures the relationship between ACOP L8 and HSG274?
o: HSG274 replaced L8 entirely, so L8 no longer exists
They are two names for exactly the same document
L8 is the technical how-to guide and HSG274 is the legal ACOP
L8 sets out the ACOP and legal framework, while HSG274 provides the detailed technical guidance to achieve control
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 contains the ACOP and outlines the legal framework and duties, and HSG274 supplements it with detailed practical/technical guidance across its parts for achieving effective control.

n.2: The roles are reversed: L8 is the ACOP and HSG274 is the technical guidance.
n.1: They are distinct documents with different roles.
n.0: HSG274 supplements L8; it did not abolish it.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative discovers a dead leg (a section of redundant pipework holding stagnant water) during routine work. Under their reporting duty, what should they do?
o: Record and report it to the responsible person so it can be assessed and, where appropriate, removed
Leave it, as dead legs are not relevant to Legionella risk
Cap the live supply so nothing can be flushed anywhere on site
Cut it out themselves without telling anyone, to save time
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Dead legs promote stagnation and Legionella growth. The operative's duty is to record and report the finding to the responsible person, who assesses and arranges appropriate remedial action such as removal.

n.3: Carrying out unauthorised modifications outside the managed scheme is not correct and may create new risks.
n.1: Dead legs are a well-recognised Legionella risk factor and are relevant.
n.2: Capping the live supply is a disproportionate and unsafe response and does not address the dead leg properly.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What does the appointment of a 'competent' responsible person for Legionella control principally require?
o: That the person holds any first-aid certificate
That the person has the necessary training, knowledge, experience and skills to manage the risk
That the person volunteers, whether or not they understand the task
That the person is the most senior manager on site regardless of knowledge
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Competence means having sufficient training, knowledge, experience and skills to carry out the role of managing and controlling the Legionella risk effectively.

n.3: Seniority alone does not equal competence for this specialised role.
n.0: A first-aid certificate is unrelated to competence for Legionella management.
n.2: Willingness to volunteer does not substitute for the required competence.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A landlord of let residential properties asks whether Legionella duties apply to them. Which answer is correct?
o: Only if the property has a cooling tower installed
No, duties never apply to residential landlords in any circumstances
Only if a tenant specifically requests a risk assessment in writing
Yes, landlords have a duty to assess and manage the risk of exposure to their tenants in connection with their letting business
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Landlords who provide residential accommodation as part of their business have a duty to assess and control the Legionella risk to tenants, applying the same principles of assessment and proportionate control.

n.1: The duty does apply to landlords in connection with their letting business.
n.0: The duty is not limited to premises with cooling towers; hot and cold water systems are covered.
n.2: The duty exists regardless of whether a tenant requests an assessment.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Following a failure to control Legionella risk that leads to prosecution, which outcome is possible under the HSWA 1974 for the most serious cases?
o: Only a written apology is ever required
Penalties are capped at a small fixed administrative fee
The HSE simply reissues the guidance with no further action
Unlimited fines and, in the gravest cases, imprisonment of those responsible
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Breaches of the HSWA can lead to prosecution with unlimited fines and, in the most serious cases, imprisonment, reflecting the potentially fatal consequences of failing to control Legionella.

n.0: An apology is not the legal remedy; formal penalties can follow.
n.1: Penalties are not capped at a small administrative fee; fines can be unlimited.
n.2: Prosecution and penalties, not merely reissuing guidance, follow serious breaches.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why does ACOP L8 place emphasis on the management arrangements (roles, responsibilities, lines of communication) rather than only on technical controls?
o: Because only paperwork, not physical control, reduces risk
Because clear management responsibility and communication are essential for control measures to be carried out reliably and faults acted upon
Because management arrangements remove the need to monitor the system
Because technical controls are legally irrelevant
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Even good technical controls fail without clear roles, responsibilities and communication so that tasks are done, results reviewed and faults acted upon. L8 stresses management to make control effective in practice.

n.3: Technical controls are essential; management arrangements make them work, not replace them.
n.0: Physical control measures directly reduce risk; paperwork alone does not.
n.2: Management arrangements support monitoring; they do not remove the need for it.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: An operative is offered a shortcut by a colleague to falsify a chlorination certificate for a new water main so the job can be signed off faster. Considering both health and safety law and the duty to protect the public supply, what is the correct course?
o: Sign it but note privately that it may be inaccurate
Refuse and ensure the required disinfection and verification are genuinely completed and truthfully recorded
Ask the colleague to sign it instead so the operative is not implicated
Accept, since paperwork rarely affects the actual water quality
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Falsifying records endangers the public water supply and breaches legal duties. The correct course is to ensure the disinfection is genuinely carried out and verified, and recorded truthfully.

n.3: Records underpin confidence that the water is safe; falsification directly risks public health.
n.0: Signing a document known to be false is dishonest and unlawful regardless of private notes.
n.2: Passing the falsification to a colleague does not make it lawful or safe.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Who is the enforcing authority responsible for the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 as it relates to Legionella control in most industrial and commercial premises?
o: The Environment Agency in every case
The Health and Safety Executive (or local authority, depending on the premises)
The building insurance provider
The water company alone
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The HSE is the primary enforcing authority for the Act, with local authorities enforcing in certain premises such as some retail and office environments. They can issue notices and prosecute.

n.3: The water company is not the enforcing authority for the Act.
n.0: The Environment Agency has other environmental roles but is not the enforcer of these HSWA Legionella duties.
n.2: Insurers are not statutory enforcing authorities.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A duty holder installs a control measure that differs from the specific method described in ACOP L8 but can demonstrate, with evidence, that it controls the risk at least as effectively. Is this permissible?
o: Only if the HSE grants a signed exemption certificate beforehand
Yes, because an ACOP permits alternative measures that are at least equally effective in controlling the risk
Only if the alternative measure is cheaper than the L8 method
No, any deviation from the exact wording of L8 is automatically unlawful
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The special status of an ACOP allows compliance either by following it or by adopting measures that are at least equally effective. Evidenced equivalent control is legally acceptable.

n.3: Equally effective alternatives are expressly permitted; deviation is not automatically unlawful.
n.0: No pre-issued HSE exemption certificate is required to use an equally effective method.
n.2: Cost is not the test; the test is whether control is at least equally effective.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative's core legal contribution to Legionella control on site is best summarised as which of the following?
o: Setting the organisation's health and safety policy
Carrying out assigned tasks to the written scheme, working safely, and reporting faults and abnormal results promptly
Prosecuting other duty holders who fail to comply
Deciding the overall control strategy and appointing the responsible person
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The operative implements the written scheme, works safely and reports faults or abnormal readings so that management can act. Strategy, policy and enforcement sit with others.

n.3: Deciding strategy and appointing the responsible person are duty-holder functions.
n.0: Setting the health and safety policy is a management responsibility, not the operative's role.
n.2: Prosecution is the role of the enforcing authority, not the operative.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why does the law require a review of the Legionella risk assessment when there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid, for example after significant changes to the water system?
o: Because reviews are needed only to satisfy insurers and serve no safety purpose
Because the assessment expires automatically every seven days by law
Because system changes can introduce new risks that existing controls may not address, so the assessment and scheme must stay current
Because only the water supplier is allowed to change the assessment
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Changes such as new pipework, altered use or occupancy can create new risks. The assessment and written scheme must be reviewed so controls remain suitable, sufficient and effective.

n.0: Reviews serve a genuine safety purpose, not merely an insurance one.
n.1: There is no automatic seven-day expiry; review is triggered by change or suspicion of invalidity.
n.3: The duty holder, not solely the water supplier, is responsible for keeping the assessment current.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: An operative repeatedly reports the same uncorrected temperature fault, but the responsible person takes no action over several months. What does the operative's continued reporting, properly recorded, principally achieve in law?
o: It removes the need for the responsible person to act
It transfers the entire legal liability onto the operative
It automatically closes the fault after three reports
It demonstrates the operative has discharged their duty to report, and creates a record that the failure to act lies with management
The Law & Responsibilities.w: By reporting and recording the fault, the operative fulfils their own duty and creates evidence. The failure to act then rests with the responsible person and duty holder, not the operative.

n.1: Proper reporting does not transfer liability onto the operative; it evidences they did their part.
n.0: The responsible person's duty to act is not removed by the operative's reports.
n.2: Reporting does not automatically resolve or close a fault; corrective action is still required.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under COSHH and supported by L8/HSG274, what is the correct order of priority when deciding how to control the Legionella risk?
o: Always choose the cheapest option regardless of effectiveness
Prevent the risk where reasonably practicable; where prevention is not possible, control it through appropriate measures
Rely first on personal protective equipment and only then consider anything else
Do nothing until an outbreak provides evidence a control is needed
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The principle is to prevent the risk of exposure where reasonably practicable, and where that is not possible, to control it using suitable measures such as temperature or treatment regimes.

n.2: PPE is a lower-order measure and is not the first line of control.
n.0: Cost alone must not override the effectiveness of control.
n.3: Controls must be proactive; waiting for an outbreak is unlawful and dangerous.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A new operative asks why holding the EUSR National Water Hygiene card matters legally when working on public water supplies. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It exempts the holder from all other health and safety duties
It provides evidence of the hygiene awareness and competence the water industry requires to protect the public supply, and is commonly a condition of site access
It is a personal souvenir with no bearing on competence or access to sites
It replaces the need for the duty holder to have any control scheme
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The National Water Hygiene scheme and Blue Card evidence the hygiene awareness and competence the water industry expects, helping protect the public supply, and is widely required for access to water-industry sites.

n.2: The card is evidence of competence and is often required for site access, not a souvenir.
n.3: It does not remove the duty holder's obligation to have a control scheme.
n.0: It does not exempt the holder from other legal duties; those still apply.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: An operative is unsure whether a task they have been given falls within the site's written scheme or their own competence. What is the legally and professionally correct action before proceeding?
o: Proceed anyway and interpret the scheme however seems reasonable at the time
Stop and clarify the task with the responsible person before carrying it out
Carry out a different task instead without recording anything
Refuse to communicate and simply leave the site without notice
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Where scope or competence is unclear, the correct action is to stop and clarify with the responsible person, consistent with the duty to work within the scheme and to take reasonable care.

n.0: Proceeding on personal interpretation risks working outside competence and the scheme.
n.3: Leaving without notice abandons the task and fails the duty to communicate and cooperate.
n.2: Substituting an unrecorded task neither resolves the uncertainty nor meets record and reporting duties.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the main purpose of a legionella risk assessment for a water system?
o: To identify and assess the sources of risk in the water system and who could be exposed
To set the price of any remedial plumbing work needed
To prove the water is safe to drink from every outlet
To record the water temperature once a year for the building file
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A legionella risk assessment identifies and assesses the sources of risk in the water system and the people who could be exposed.

n.3: A single annual temperature reading is not an assessment of risk across the system.
n.2: Legionella controls concern inhaled aerosols, not the drinking quality of the water.
n.1: Costing remedial work is not the purpose of assessing the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Under the ACOP L8 approach, which should you try to do FIRST when managing legionella risk?
o: Wait until a case of illness is reported
Prevent the risk where reasonably practicable, then control what remains
Add extra biocide to every part of the system
Fit more monitoring meters before doing anything else
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: You should prevent the risk of exposure so far as is reasonably practicable first, and control any risk that cannot be prevented.

n.3: Monitoring measures a risk but does not prevent or control it on its own.
n.2: Dosing biocide everywhere is a control, not the first-choice prevention step.
n.0: Waiting for illness means the risk was never managed.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A legionella risk assessment should specifically consider people who are especially vulnerable. Which group is an example?
o: Elderly, sick or immunocompromised people who may be exposed
Delivery drivers who never enter the building
Contractors who work outside on the grounds
People who only use the site car park
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment must consider those more susceptible to infection, such as the elderly, the sick and people with weakened immune systems.

n.1: People who do not enter the building are not exposed to its water aerosols.
n.3: Using only the car park gives no exposure to the water system.
n.2: Working outside on the grounds is not exposure to building water aerosols.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these is a potential source of risk that a legionella risk assessment should look for?
o: The colour of the pipework insulation
A power socket in the plant room
The brand name printed on the cold tank
Anywhere water is stored, can stagnate or is between 20 and 45 degrees C
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Stored, stagnant or warm water in the 20-45 degrees C range provides the conditions in which legionella can multiply.

n.1: An electrical socket is not part of the water system risk.
n.0: Insulation colour does not affect legionella growth.
n.2: The manufacturer's brand name has no bearing on the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why does a legionella risk assessment pay attention to outlets and equipment that create a spray or mist?
o: Because sprays make the floor slippery
Because misting outlets are harder to clean
Because aerosols can carry legionella deep into the lungs when breathed in
Because spray uses more water and raises the bill
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Legionella causes illness when contaminated water aerosols are inhaled, so sources of spray or mist are key to assess.

n.3: Water cost is not the health reason for assessing aerosols.
n.1: Cleaning difficulty is not why aerosols matter for legionella.
n.0: Slip hazards are a separate safety issue, not the legionella reason.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A large office block closes one entire wing and takes its taps and showers out of use for several months. What is the correct action for the water system?
o: Do nothing because the wing is closed to people
Turn off the whole building's cold water supply
Remove the wing from the asset register and forget it
Review the risk assessment and manage the now little-used outlets, for example by flushing them
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A change of use creates stagnation risk, so the assessment must be reviewed and the disused outlets kept under control, such as by regular flushing.

n.0: Closed but still-connected outlets stagnate and become a growing risk.
n.1: Shutting the whole supply is disproportionate and affects the occupied areas.
n.2: Ignoring the wing hides a real and increasing legionella risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the written scheme of control (the written scheme) for?
o: To list the names of everyone who has ever visited the site
To set out how the risk will be prevented or controlled and how the system is managed safely
To record only the cost of chemicals used
To advertise the building to new tenants
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme describes the water system and sets out the measures to be taken to prevent or control the risk.

n.0: A visitor log has nothing to do with controlling legionella.
n.2: Chemical costs are not the purpose of the written scheme.
n.3: Marketing the building is unrelated to controlling the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which item should a written scheme of control include?
o: A photograph of the front door
The control measures, how they are monitored, and who is responsible
Only the postcode of the building
The favourite colour of the site manager
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme should describe the control measures, the checks and monitoring, and the roles and responsibilities for carrying them out.

n.2: A postcode alone does not describe how the risk is controlled.
n.0: A photo of the door tells you nothing about the water system controls.
n.3: Personal preferences are irrelevant to the scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A written scheme of control should also say what to do in one important situation. Which one?
o: What action to take if the control measures fail
How to book a meeting room
Which supermarket is nearest the site
What music to play in reception
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme must set out the remedial action to take if monitoring shows the control measures are not working.

n.2: The nearest shop is not a legionella control matter.
n.1: Room booking has nothing to do with water safety.
n.3: Reception music is irrelevant to the scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An up-to-date schematic diagram of the water system is useful in the risk assessment mainly because it:
o: Records the electricity meter readings
Shows where the staff car park spaces are
Shows how the system is laid out, including tanks, pipe runs and outlets that may pose a risk
Proves the building meets fire regulations
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A schematic diagram maps the system so that storage, dead-legs and outlets that could pose a risk can be identified and managed.

n.3: Fire regulation compliance is a separate matter.
n.1: Car parking layout is unrelated to the water system.
n.0: Electricity readings are not part of the water schematic.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why should an asset register or list of the water system's parts be kept with the assessment?
o: To decide the colour scheme of the plant room
To calculate the building's council tax
So the parts can be sold second-hand
So all relevant plant, tanks and outlets are known and none are overlooked when managing the risk
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An asset register records the system's components so that every relevant item is accounted for and included in the control scheme.

n.2: Selling parts is not the reason for the register.
n.0: Decor choices are irrelevant to managing risk.
n.1: Council tax has nothing to do with the water assets.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: When should a legionella risk assessment be reviewed?
o: Regularly, and whenever there is reason to think it may no longer be valid
Never, once it has been signed off
Once every twenty years
Only when the building is sold
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment should be reviewed regularly and specifically whenever there is reason to believe it is no longer valid.

n.3: Waiting until a sale ignores changes that happen in between.
n.2: A twenty-year gap would leave the assessment badly out of date.
n.1: An assessment that is never reviewed becomes unreliable.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these changes would be a reason to review the risk assessment?
o: The office repaints a corridor
The car park line markings are refreshed
A new manager starts on reception
New plant or pipework is added, or the use of the building changes
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Changes to the system, such as new plant or altered use, can create new risks and require the assessment to be reviewed.

n.0: Repainting a corridor does not alter the water system.
n.2: A new reception manager does not change the plumbing.
n.1: Repainting parking lines has no effect on water risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An outbreak or suspected case of legionnaires' disease linked to a site should trigger which action for the assessment?
o: Removing the written scheme from the file
Painting over the affected pipework
Ignoring it until the next annual check
An immediate review of the risk assessment and control measures
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A case or outbreak is a clear reason the assessment may no longer be valid and must be reviewed straight away.

n.2: Delaying the review allows exposure to continue.
n.0: Discarding the scheme removes the very controls needed.
n.1: Painting pipework does nothing to address the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The risk assessment and written scheme should be kept how?
o: Recorded and kept up to date so they reflect the system as it is now
Written once and never changed
Held only in one person's memory
Shredded after the first year
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Records must be kept and updated so the assessment and scheme always reflect the current system and controls.

n.1: An unchanged document soon fails to match a changing system.
n.2: Relying on memory leaves nothing others can follow or audit.
n.3: Destroying the records loses the basis for managing the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Who should carry out or oversee a legionella risk assessment?
o: A person who is competent, with the right knowledge, skills and experience
Anyone who happens to be free that day
A visitor with no water knowledge
The newest apprentice on their first morning, unsupervised
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment must be done by someone competent, with sufficient knowledge, skills and experience to identify and assess the risk.

n.1: Availability does not make a person competent to assess the risk.
n.2: A visitor without knowledge cannot judge the system's risks.
n.3: An unsupervised first-day apprentice lacks the needed competence.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A café installs a new decorative water feature that produces a fine spray in the seating area. What should happen to the legionella risk assessment?
o: It should be deleted as the feature is decorative
Nothing, because it only holds a small amount of water
It should be reviewed because a new aerosol-producing source has been added
It should be replaced with the fire risk assessment
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Adding new plant that creates aerosols is a relevant change, so the assessment must be reviewed to cover the new source.

n.1: Even a small volume of sprayed water can carry legionella.
n.0: Being decorative does not remove the aerosol risk.
n.3: A fire assessment does not address legionella at all.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Storing hot and cold water at the wrong temperatures matters because legionella multiplies best:
o: Only in boiling water
In water roughly between 20 and 45 degrees C
Only in water below freezing
At any temperature equally
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Legionella grows most readily in water in the approximate range of 20 to 45 degrees C, which the assessment aims to avoid.

n.2: Freezing water does not let the bacteria multiply.
n.0: Boiling temperatures kill the bacteria rather than grow them.
n.3: Growth is strongly temperature-dependent, not equal at all temperatures.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A hotel converts several guest bathrooms into a rarely used storeroom, leaving the showers connected but unused. What is the key risk this creates?
o: Stagnation in the unused showers, which should be flushed or removed and the assessment reviewed
A rise in the electricity bill only
A shortage of towels
Damage to the bathroom tiles
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Little-used or dead outlets allow water to stagnate and legionella to grow, so they must be managed and the assessment reviewed.

n.1: Electricity cost is not the water safety concern here.
n.3: Tile condition is unrelated to legionella risk.
n.2: Towel supply has nothing to do with the water system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Monitoring in the written scheme is mainly there to:
o: Check that the control measures are working as intended
Replace the need for any control measures
Prove the building is fully occupied
Increase the number of forms staff must sign
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Monitoring confirms whether the chosen controls are keeping the risk under control and flags when they are not.

n.3: Paperwork volume is not the purpose of monitoring.
n.1: Monitoring supports controls; it does not remove the need for them.
n.2: Occupancy levels are not what monitoring is checking.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which statement about preventing legionella risk is correct?
o: Longer runs of unused pipework are always safer
Prevention is impossible, so only monitoring matters
Adding more storage tanks always reduces risk
Removing unnecessary storage and dead-legs helps prevent risk before controls are even needed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Designing out storage, stagnation and dead-legs prevents conditions for growth, which is preferable to controlling them later.

n.1: Prevention is a recognised and preferred step, not impossible.
n.2: Extra unnecessary storage adds stagnation risk rather than removing it.
n.0: Unused dead-legs stagnate and increase risk, not reduce it.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A school is closed over a long summer holiday. What should the written scheme cover for this period?
o: Keeping water moving, for example flushing outlets, so it does not stagnate while the building is empty
Removing the risk assessment for the holiday
Leaving every tap running continuously day and night
Switching off all record keeping until term starts
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: During long closures the scheme should keep water fresh, such as by regular flushing, to prevent stagnation.

n.3: Records should continue, as the risk does not stop over the holiday.
n.1: Removing the assessment leaves the closure unmanaged.
n.2: Leaving all taps running wastes water and is not the specified control.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The risk assessment should identify who could be exposed. What does 'exposed' mean here?
o: People who have read the safety policy
People who could breathe in water droplets or mist from the system
People who live nearest to the building
People who pay the water bill
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Exposure to legionella happens when people inhale contaminated aerosols, so the assessment identifies who could breathe them in.

n.0: Reading a policy is not the same as being exposed to aerosols.
n.3: Paying the bill has no bearing on inhalation exposure.
n.2: Simply living nearby is not exposure unless aerosols reach them.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A factory takes over the empty unit next door and connects it to the same mains water supply. What should be done?
o: Ignore the new pipework as it is short
Only assess the new unit if someone falls ill
Review and extend the risk assessment and written scheme to include the new pipework and outlets
