Assume the existing assessment already covers the new unit
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Adding pipework and outlets is a relevant change, so the assessment and scheme must be updated to cover the extended system.

n.3: The old assessment cannot cover parts of the system it never examined.
n.1: Waiting for illness means managing the risk too late.
n.0: Even short new pipework can contain dead-legs and outlets that need managing.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these best describes a 'dead-leg' that a risk assessment should look for?
o: A pipe carrying hot water at high speed
A length of pipe with little or no water flow, where water can stagnate
The main incoming water supply
A tap used many times every day
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A dead-leg is pipework with little or no throughput, allowing water to stagnate and legionella to grow.

n.0: Fast-flowing hot water is not a stagnation point.
n.2: The busy main supply is not a low-flow dead-leg.
n.3: A frequently used tap keeps water moving rather than stagnant.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: If monitoring shows a control measure has failed, the written scheme should ensure staff know to:
o: Erase the failed reading from the log
Wait for a member of the public to complain
Take the pre-agreed remedial action and record what was done
Do nothing until the annual review
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The scheme sets out remedial actions so that a control failure is corrected promptly and the action recorded.

n.3: Delaying to the annual review leaves the risk uncontrolled.
n.0: Deleting the reading hides the problem and breaks the record.
n.1: Relying on public complaints is not a control response.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why should roles and responsibilities be written down in the scheme of control?
o: So it is clear who is responsible for each task and nothing is missed
To make the document longer
So blame can be handed out after an incident
To keep the information secret from staff
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Naming who does what ensures every control task has an owner and is actually carried out.

n.2: The aim is prevention and clarity, not apportioning blame.
n.1: Length is not a goal in itself.
n.3: Staff need to know their duties, not be kept in the dark.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A care home admits more residents who are frail and elderly than before. How does this affect the legionella risk assessment?
o: It has no effect, as the pipework is unchanged
It means the scheme can be relaxed
It should be reviewed, as more vulnerable people are now exposed to the system
It only matters if the water pressure changes
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A rise in the number of especially vulnerable people is a relevant change in who is exposed, so the assessment must be reviewed.

n.0: Risk depends on who is exposed, not only on the pipework.
n.1: More vulnerable people call for equal or tighter control, not relaxation.
n.3: Vulnerability of occupants matters regardless of water pressure.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What kind of information about temperature is useful to record when assessing and controlling risk?
o: The temperature of the car park
Hot and cold water temperatures at sentinel and other outlets
The outside air temperature only
The oven temperature in the kitchen
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Recording water temperatures at outlets shows whether the system is kept out of the range that lets legionella grow.

n.2: Outside air temperature does not tell you the water's temperature.
n.0: Car park temperature is irrelevant to the water system.
n.3: Oven temperature is unrelated to water safety.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A previously vacant building is brought back into full use after standing empty for a year. What should be done before people use the water?
o: Only test the water if someone reports a smell
Review the risk assessment and ensure the system is cleaned, flushed and safe after standing idle
Assume standing water is fine and open normally
Remove the assessment because the building was empty
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Long stagnation is a serious risk, so the assessment must be reviewed and the system brought back into safe condition before use.

n.2: Water standing for a year can harbour heavy growth and is not fine.
n.0: Waiting for a complaint means exposing people first.
n.3: An empty period is a reason to keep the assessment, not remove it.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these is a reasonable prevention measure the assessment might recommend?
o: Removing redundant pipework and unused outlets that only serve to hold stagnant water
Leaving disused showers connected indefinitely
Adding extra unused tanks in case they are needed later
Fitting more dead-legs to balance the system
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Taking out redundant pipework and outlets removes stagnation points and prevents conditions for legionella growth.

n.2: Extra unused tanks create more storage and stagnation, not less.
n.3: Adding dead-legs increases stagnation risk.
n.1: Leaving disused showers connected keeps a stagnation source.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The written scheme describes the water system. Why is an accurate description important?
o: So the document looks professional
So the controls are applied to the system as it actually is, not to an outdated layout
So the water can be billed correctly
So the building can be insured
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An accurate description ensures the control measures match the real system, so nothing risky is missed.

n.0: Appearance is not the reason an accurate description matters.
n.2: Water billing is separate from controlling legionella.
n.3: Insurance is not the purpose of the system description.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A gym adds a new communal shower block used by many members each day. What should the water safety arrangements do?
o: Only assess the showers if attendance falls
Exclude showers because they are used often
Cover the new showers in the assessment and scheme, as showers create aerosols
Treat the showers the same as the car park
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: New showers generate aerosols and are heavily used, so they must be brought into the assessment and control scheme.

n.1: Frequent use reduces stagnation but does not remove the aerosol risk.
n.0: Falling attendance would raise stagnation risk, not remove the need to assess.
n.3: A car park has no water aerosol risk to compare with.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Keeping the risk assessment 'live' means:
o: Storing it on the newest computer
Updating it whenever the system or its use changes, not just once a year
Printing a fresh copy each morning
Reading it aloud at every staff meeting
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A live assessment is kept current by updating it whenever a relevant change occurs, so it always reflects the real risk.

n.2: Reprinting an unchanged document does not keep it current.
n.0: Where it is stored does not make its content up to date.
n.3: Reading it aloud does not update its content.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A hospital ward is temporarily closed for refurbishment, isolating part of the pipework. What is the correct approach?
o: Review the assessment and manage the isolated section so it does not become a stagnant source when reconnected
Remove that ward from all records
Leave the isolated pipe full and forget it until reopening
Increase the water pressure to compensate
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Isolated pipework can stagnate, so the assessment must be reviewed and the section managed before it is put back into use.

n.2: Leaving it full and forgotten lets legionella grow unchecked.
n.1: Deleting records loses control of a real part of the system.
n.3: Raising pressure does not address stagnation in the isolated section.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which best describes 'sentinel outlets' referred to when monitoring a system?
o: Outlets that are never used
The outlets nearest to and furthest from each tank or heater, used as representative check points
Only the outlets in the plant room
The most expensive taps in the building
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Sentinel outlets are the nearest and furthest points on hot and cold systems, chosen as representative places to monitor temperature.

n.3: Cost has nothing to do with choosing sentinel points.
n.0: Unused outlets are not representative check points for the working system.
n.2: Plant-room outlets alone do not represent the whole distribution.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An office doubles its staff and adds a second kitchen with new taps and a boiling-water unit. What is the right response?
o: Only act if the water tastes different
Remove the original kitchen from the records
No action, as tap water is always safe
Review the assessment and update the scheme to include the new outlets and heater
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Adding outlets and a water heater is a relevant change, so the assessment and scheme must be updated to cover them.

n.2: Tap water is not automatically free of legionella risk in a changed system.
n.0: Taste is not a reliable indicator of legionella risk.
n.1: The original kitchen remains part of the system and stays in the records.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The assessment should record the findings so that:
o: The paperwork weighs a certain amount
Only the assessor ever needs to see them
They can be filed and never opened
The significant risks and the controls decided upon are clear and can be acted on
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Recording the findings makes the significant risks and the chosen controls clear so responsible people can act on them.

n.1: Others must be able to follow the findings, not just the assessor.
n.2: Findings that are never opened cannot guide any control.
n.0: The physical bulk of paperwork is not the point of recording.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why might a risk assessment recommend keeping cold water genuinely cold?
o: To reduce the water bill
To keep it below the temperature range where legionella multiplies
To make pipes easier to paint
To make the water taste sweeter
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Keeping cold water below about 20 degrees C helps stop legionella multiplying, which is a core control.

n.3: Temperature control is about safety, not taste.
n.0: It is not primarily a cost-saving measure.
n.2: Painting pipes is unrelated to the temperature control.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A landlord takes over a block of flats and finds no legionella risk assessment exists. What should be done first?
o: Only assess the flats that are occupied
Assume the previous owner dealt with it
Wait until a tenant complains before assessing
Arrange a competent legionella risk assessment of the water systems
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Where no valid assessment exists, a competent assessment of the water systems must be carried out to identify and assess the risk.

n.2: Waiting for a complaint leaves the risk unassessed and unmanaged.
n.1: Assuming without evidence provides no basis for control.
n.0: Empty flats can hold stagnant water and must also be assessed.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What should happen to the written scheme when a control method in it is changed, for example a new disinfection regime?
o: Only change it at the next building sale
Leave the old method written down for the records
The written scheme should be updated to reflect the new control method
Throw the scheme away and rely on memory
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The scheme must be kept up to date so it always describes the controls actually in use.

n.1: Leaving the outdated method written down misleads whoever follows it.
n.3: Relying on memory removes the documented basis for control.
n.0: Delaying to a sale leaves the scheme wrong in the meantime.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A risk assessment considers 'the water systems'. Which of these is part of that?
o: Cold water tanks, hot water cylinders, pipework, taps and showers
The car park drainage gullies
The building's phone lines
The window cleaning cradle
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The water systems assessed include storage, heaters, distribution pipework and the outlets people use.

n.2: Phone lines are not part of the water system.
n.3: A window cleaning cradle is not part of the assessed water system.
n.1: Car park drainage is separate from the building's water system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An assessment finds a little-used tap at the end of a long pipe. Which control fits the 'prevent then control' principle best?
o: Remove the redundant tap and pipe if not needed, otherwise flush it regularly
Paint the tap to mark it as unused
Leave it and hope it is never a problem
Cap the pipe but keep the stagnant water inside
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Removing redundant pipework prevents the stagnation risk; if it must stay, regular flushing controls the remaining risk.

n.2: Hoping is not a control and leaves the risk in place.
n.3: Capping while trapping stagnant water leaves a growth reservoir.
n.1: Painting the tap does nothing about the stagnant water.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why should the person managing the scheme be told promptly about a temperature reading that is out of range?
o: So the thermometer can be blamed
So the log can be closed for the year
So the reading can be quietly ignored
So corrective action can be taken quickly before the risk grows
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Prompt reporting lets the responsible person act quickly to bring the control back on target before risk increases.

n.2: Ignoring an out-of-range reading leaves the risk uncontrolled.
n.0: Blaming the instrument does not correct the water risk.
n.1: Closing the log does not address the failed control.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A building changes from offices to a residential use with showers and baths in every unit. What must be reconsidered?
o: Just the colour of the bathroom fittings
Nothing, as it is the same building
Only the reception signage
The whole risk assessment, because the use, outlets and exposed people have all changed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A major change of use with new aerosol-producing outlets and different occupants requires the assessment to be reconsidered in full.

n.2: Signage does not reflect the changed water risk.
n.0: Fitting colour is irrelevant to the assessment.
n.1: The same walls do not mean the same water risk after a change of use.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these is the best reason to keep records of monitoring and inspections?
o: To fill up storage space
To hide the results from managers
To avoid ever having to do the checks again
To show the controls have been carried out and to spot trends that need action
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Records demonstrate that controls were done and help identify trends so problems can be acted on early.

n.0: Using up space is not a reason to keep records.
n.2: Records do not replace the ongoing need to carry out checks.
n.1: Records are meant to inform managers, not be hidden from them.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A cooling tower is added to a site that previously had none. How significant is this for the risk assessment?
o: Not significant, as it is outdoors
Only relevant if it is painted a bright colour
Relevant only to the electricity supplier
Very significant, as cooling towers can spread aerosols widely and the assessment must cover them
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Cooling towers create and disperse aerosols that can carry legionella, so adding one is a major change the assessment must address.

n.0: Being outdoors can spread aerosols further, not remove the risk.
n.1: Colour has no bearing on the aerosol risk.
n.2: The electricity supplier is not who manages the legionella risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the correct overall order of the approach in the written scheme of control?
o: Monitor first, then decide whether to write anything down
Only act after the first case of illness
Control everything with chemicals and skip describing the system
Describe the system, prevent risk where possible, control the rest, monitor, and set out what to do if control fails
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A sound scheme describes the system, prevents risk, controls what remains, monitors the controls and sets out remedial action for failures.

n.0: You cannot monitor sensibly before the system and controls are defined.
n.2: Skipping the description means controls may miss parts of the system.
n.1: Waiting for illness abandons the whole preventive approach.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A tenant reports that the hot water at their tap now runs only lukewarm, which was not the case before. What does this suggest about the assessment and controls?
o: The tenant should simply be told to run the tap longer forever
The written scheme should be discarded
The control may no longer be valid, so the assessment should be reviewed and the fault investigated
Lukewarm water is always perfectly safe, so no action is needed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Hot water failing to reach its intended temperature suggests a control has slipped, so the assessment should be reviewed and the cause put right.

n.3: Lukewarm water sits closer to the growth range and is not automatically safe.
n.0: Telling the tenant to run the tap does not fix the underlying temperature fault.
n.1: Discarding the scheme removes the controls rather than correcting the fault.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which statement about who is responsible for managing legionella risk is correct?
o: No one needs to be responsible if a contractor visits sometimes
Only the water supplier is responsible for the building's systems
Responsibility ends once the assessment is first written
A named responsible person should be appointed to manage the assessment and control scheme
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A competent responsible person should be appointed to take day-to-day charge of the assessment, scheme and controls.

n.0: Occasional contractor visits do not remove the need for an appointed responsible person.
n.2: Responsibility continues through ongoing review and control, not just the first write-up.
n.1: The water supplier is not responsible for the internal systems within the building.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Under the ACOP L8, who is responsible for making sure a legionella risk assessment is carried out for a building's water system?
o: The water hygiene operative who takes the temperatures
The tenants who use the building's outlets
The duty holder (for example the employer or person in control of the premises)
The local water supply company that provides the mains
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The duty holder, such as the employer or person in control of the premises, has the legal duty to ensure a legionella risk assessment is done.

n.0: The operative carries out monitoring tasks but does not hold the legal duty for the assessment.
n.1: Tenants use the outlets but are not the ones legally responsible for the assessment.
n.3: The water company supplies the mains but is not responsible for the building's internal system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the main purpose of a legionella risk assessment?
o: To identify and assess the sources of risk from legionella in the water system
To record the daily hot water bill for the building
To list every member of staff who works in the building
To decide the colour coding used for cleaning equipment
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A risk assessment exists to identify and assess the sources of legionella risk so that suitable controls can be put in place.

n.1: Energy costs are not the purpose of a legionella risk assessment.
n.2: A staff list is not what the assessment is for.
n.3: Cleaning colour codes are a separate matter and not the aim of the assessment.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: If the risk assessment finds a foreseeable legionella risk, what must the duty holder put in place?
o: A notice telling users to run taps whenever they wish
Nothing further, because the assessment on its own is enough
A written scheme of control setting out how the risk is prevented or controlled
A single verbal instruction given once to staff
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Where a risk is identified, a written scheme of control must be prepared describing how the risk is managed.

n.3: A one-off verbal instruction is not a documented, controlled scheme.
n.0: An informal notice does not meet the requirement for a written scheme of control.
n.1: The assessment alone is not enough; a written scheme is required when a risk is found.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of the following should a written scheme of control normally include?
o: A copy of the building's fire evacuation plan
Only the phone number of the water supply company
The names of everyone who has ever visited the site
A schematic of the system, who is responsible, the controls, monitoring and what to do if control fails
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A written scheme should describe the system, responsibilities, control measures, monitoring and the action to take if control is lost.

n.1: A supplier phone number alone is nowhere near a complete written scheme.
n.0: The fire plan is a separate document and not part of the water control scheme.
n.2: A visitor list has nothing to do with controlling legionella.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which change would most clearly make a legionella risk assessment need reviewing?
o: New plant is installed or the use of the building changes
A new poster is put up in the staff canteen
The building is repainted the same colour
A member of staff changes their car parking space
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Installing new plant or changing how the building is used can alter the risk, so the assessment must be reviewed.

n.1: A canteen poster does not affect the water system risk.
n.2: Repainting in the same colour does not change the water system.
n.3: A change of parking space has no bearing on legionella risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A legionella risk assessment should be reviewed following which of the following events?
o: A change of the office stationery supplier
An outbreak or suspected case linked to the water system
A staff member returning from annual leave
The end of the financial year
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An outbreak or suspected case is a clear trigger to review the assessment, as controls may need strengthening.

n.0: The stationery supplier has no link to water safety.
n.3: The financial year end is an accounting date, not a risk trigger.
n.2: Routine staff leave does not change the water system risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What does keeping an up-to-date schematic drawing of the water system in the written scheme help operatives to do?
o: Decide the paint colour scheme for the plant room
Set the temperature of the building's central heating radiators
Work out the monthly electricity charges for the building
Understand the layout so all parts, including dead legs, can be found and managed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An accurate schematic lets operatives locate all parts of the system, including little-used sections, so nothing is missed.

n.2: A schematic is not used for calculating electricity charges.
n.0: Paint choices are unrelated to a water system schematic.
n.1: Radiator settings are part of heating, not the water safety schematic.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the first thing a Legionella risk assessment must establish before any control measures are considered?
o: The temperature setpoint of the calorifier thermostat
The brand of biocide to be dosed into the system
Whether a risk of exposure to Legionella exists and, if so, its sources
The name of the external contractor who will do the monitoring
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 requires the assessment first to identify and assess the risk — whether a foreseeable risk of exposure to Legionella exists and where the sources of that risk are — as the basis for everything that follows.

n.1: Selecting a biocide is a control decision that can only be made after the risk and sources are understood.
n.3: Arranging who monitors is a management step that follows identification of the risk.
n.0: A specific setpoint is a control measure, not the initial finding the assessment must reach.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Besides identifying sources of risk, what else must the risk assessment identify about the people around the system?
o: Who could be exposed, giving particular attention to those especially at risk
Which members of staff hold a current first-aid certificate
The job titles of everyone who has ever entered the plant room
The home addresses of employees for emergency contact
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment must identify who may be exposed to the aerosol, paying particular attention to those who may be especially susceptible, such as the elderly, the very young or those with weakened immunity.

n.2: A historical list of everyone who entered the room does not identify who is exposed to the risk of infection.
n.1: First-aid cover is unrelated to identifying who is exposed to Legionella aerosols.
n.3: Home addresses have no bearing on assessing exposure to the water system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A care home installs a new spa pool in a communal lounge but does not revisit its existing water risk assessment. Why is this a breach of L8?
o: Only the local authority, not the duty holder, can amend an assessment
Risk assessments only need reviewing every five years regardless of changes
A spa pool never needs to appear in a written risk assessment
The assessment must be reviewed whenever there is a significant change, such as new plant, that could affect the risk
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 requires the assessment to be reviewed regularly and specifically whenever there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid, including significant changes such as new plant, a new aerosol source or a change of use.

n.2: A spa pool is a significant aerosol-generating source and must be assessed — it is one of the highest-risk items.
n.1: There is no fixed five-year rule; review is triggered by change and by ongoing suitability, not a fixed calendar alone.
n.0: The duty holder is responsible for keeping the assessment current; the local authority does not amend it for them.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which record is central to a Legionella risk assessment because it shows every part of the water system?
o: The site fire evacuation plan
A list of approved cleaning chemical suppliers
A schematic diagram of the water system, kept up to date
The annual electrical inspection certificate
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An up-to-date schematic (asset register/diagram) of the water system is fundamental; it lets the assessor see all plant, pipework, storage and outlets so no source of risk is missed.

n.0: A fire plan addresses a different hazard and does not map the water system.
n.1: A supplier list does not describe the physical water system.
n.3: An electrical certificate is unrelated to identifying water risk sources.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The written scheme for controlling Legionella risk must set out several things. Which of the following is one of them?
o: The postcode lottery results for the local area
The marketing plan for the building's owner
The purchase price of every fitting in the building
The clear allocation of responsibilities for carrying out the control measures
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme must set out the control measures, how and when they are checked and monitored, and who is responsible for carrying them out — clear allocation of duties is a required element.

n.2: The cost of fittings is not a control-scheme requirement.
n.1: A marketing plan has nothing to do with managing water risk.
n.0: This is irrelevant filler with no bearing on the scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: In the hierarchy of managing Legionella, which approach should the duty holder consider first?
o: Raising every outlet temperature above boiling point
Dosing the system continuously with the strongest available biocide
Waiting for a positive sample before taking any action
Preventing the risk — for example by avoiding water storage and stagnation where reasonably practicable
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The duty holder should first consider whether the risk can be prevented — for instance by removing dead legs, avoiding unnecessary storage and designing out stagnation — and only then control any residual risk.

n.1: Continuous heavy biocide dosing is a control measure, applied only when prevention is not reasonably practicable.
n.2: Waiting for a positive result is reactive and does not prevent the risk arising.
n.0: Water cannot practically be held above boiling point at outlets; this is not a recognised control.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which temperature band is regarded as the range in which Legionella bacteria most readily multiply, and which prevention aims to keep water out of?
o: 5 to 15°C
Below 0°C
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Legionella multiplies most readily between about 20°C and 45°C; prevention keeps cold water below 20°C and hot water hot so water spends as little time as possible in this band.

n.3: Below freezing the bacteria do not multiply, so this is not the band to avoid.
n.2: This band is below the growth range; well-run cold water sits here safely.
n.0: These temperatures kill the bacteria rather than allow multiplication.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A newly appointed manager finds the site risk assessment was written by an office administrator with no water-hygiene training. What is the concern under L8?
o: The assessment must be rewritten in a different font
The assessment is fine because anyone employed on site may write it
Only assessments written by the water supplier are ever valid
The assessment may not be suitable and sufficient because it was not done by a competent person
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 requires the risk assessment to be carried out by a competent person with the necessary knowledge, skills and experience; an untrained author casts doubt on whether it is suitable and sufficient.

n.1: Employment on site does not confer the competence the assessment demands.
n.0: Formatting is irrelevant to the validity of the assessment.
n.2: The water supplier need not write it; a competent person acting for the duty holder may.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What must the written scheme state should happen if a control measure is found not to be working?
o: The remedial action to be taken when control limits are not met
That the outlet is simply painted a warning colour
Nothing — the scheme only covers normal operation
That the failure is logged and reviewed at the next annual audit only
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme must describe the action to be taken, including remedial steps, if monitoring shows the control measures are not effective, so failures are corrected promptly.

n.3: Deferring action to an annual audit allows the risk to persist; response must be prompt.
n.2: A scheme that ignored failure would leave the risk uncontrolled; it must cover what to do when control fails.
n.1: Marking an outlet does not restore control of the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why does a Legionella risk assessment pay particular attention to sources that generate a spray or mist?
o: Because infection follows from breathing in an aerosol of contaminated water droplets
Because misting fittings use more electricity
Because spray taps are always cheaper to replace
Because sprays look untidy in a plant room
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Legionnaires' disease is contracted by inhaling small airborne droplets containing the bacteria, so identifying aerosol-generating sources — showers, spray taps, cooling towers, spa pools — is a key part of the assessment.

n.3: Appearance is not a health consideration in the assessment.
n.1: Energy use is not the reason aerosol sources are prioritised.
n.2: Replacement cost is irrelevant to why aerosols are a risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A landlord's risk assessment lists 'monthly temperature checks' but names nobody to do them and gives no record sheet. Which required feature of a written scheme is missing?
o: The colour scheme for the plant room walls
The manufacturer's warranty for the boiler
A copy of the tenant's rent agreement
A statement of who is responsible and a means of recording the monitoring
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A written scheme must allocate responsibility for each task and provide for recording the results of monitoring; naming a frequency alone, with no responsible person or record, leaves the scheme incomplete.

n.2: A rent agreement is unrelated to water-hygiene monitoring.
n.0: Decor is not part of the control scheme.
n.1: A boiler warranty does not fulfil the monitoring or responsibility requirement.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: How long should records of the risk assessment and monitoring of control measures generally be retained?
o: Records are never needed if the water looks clear
Only until the end of the working day
They may be destroyed as soon as they are written
For a suitable period, so trends can be reviewed and control demonstrated over time
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 expects records to be kept for a suitable period so that the effectiveness of the scheme can be reviewed over time and compliance demonstrated; monitoring results in particular should be retained long enough to show trends.

n.2: Immediate destruction would defeat the purpose of recording and prevent trend review.
n.0: Clear-looking water proves nothing; records are still required.
n.1: A single day is far too short to show whether control is being maintained.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A building has stood empty during a long refurbishment and water has sat unused in the pipework. What does this change mean for the existing risk assessment?
o: The assessment only needs review once the building is demolished
The assessment is automatically cancelled and need not be replaced
The assessment should be reviewed, as prolonged stagnation is a change that may affect the risk
Nothing changes because the building is the same shape
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A change of use or a period during which the system is left stagnant is exactly the kind of change that can invalidate an assessment, so it must be reviewed and controls applied before normal use resumes.

n.3: The physical shape is irrelevant; the water conditions have changed materially.
n.1: An assessment is never simply cancelled; it must be reviewed and kept current.
n.0: Waiting until demolition ignores the risk to people using the reoccupied building.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these best describes the relationship between the risk assessment and the written scheme of control?
o: The written scheme replaces the need to assess risk at all
The written scheme is prepared as a result of, and to manage, the risks the assessment identifies
They are the same single document with two names
The written scheme must be produced before any assessment is attempted
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment identifies the risks; where a risk is identified that cannot be prevented, a written scheme is then prepared to manage it, setting out the control measures. The scheme flows from the assessment.

n.2: They are distinct documents with different purposes, though they are linked.
n.3: The scheme cannot sensibly precede the assessment that defines what it must control.
n.0: A scheme does not remove the ongoing duty to assess and review risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: During a review, an assessor discovers a capped-off branch of pipe that no longer feeds any outlet. Why is this noted as a risk?
o: Capped pipework is always illegal to leave in place
It voids the building's insurance policy
It forms a dead leg where water stagnates and can allow bacteria to multiply
It reduces the water pressure at other taps
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A dead leg holds a volume of water that is not drawn through, allowing it to stagnate and warm into the growth range, so the assessment should flag it for removal or management.

n.0: Redundant pipework is not inherently unlawful, but it should be identified and ideally removed.
n.3: The concern is stagnation and bacterial growth, not a pressure effect.
n.1: Insurance status is not the water-hygiene reason for flagging a dead leg.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The written scheme specifies checking that cold water reaches outlets below a set temperature. What is the purpose of setting such a control limit?
o: To give a measurable standard against which monitoring can judge whether control is being maintained
To justify buying more expensive thermometers
To limit how often staff can use the taps
To make the paperwork look more detailed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Control limits give monitoring an objective benchmark; if a reading falls outside the limit, the scheme's remedial action is triggered, so the limit is what makes monitoring meaningful.

n.2: Control limits govern water conditions, not how often taps are used.
n.3: The purpose is functional control, not the appearance of the paperwork.
n.1: Equipment cost is not the reason for setting a limit.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Who holds the legal duty to ensure a suitable and sufficient Legionella risk assessment is carried out for premises?
o: The most junior member of the maintenance team
The duty holder — typically the employer, or person in control of the premises
Any visitor who happens to notice a problem
The water regulator, on the duty holder's behalf
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The duty holder — the employer or person in control of the premises — is legally responsible for ensuring the assessment is done and kept up to date, even if the work itself is delegated to a competent person.

n.2: Visitors have no legal duty for the premises' water safety.
n.0: A junior worker may carry out tasks but does not hold the overarching legal duty.
n.3: The regulator enforces the law; it does not carry the duty holder's responsibility for them.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A risk assessment concludes that the risk from a small, simple system is 'insignificant'. What does L8 still expect the duty holder to do?
o: Stop using the water supply entirely
Discard all paperwork immediately because no risk means no records
Install a cooling tower to be on the safe side
Record that conclusion and review it periodically and if circumstances change
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Even where the risk is assessed as insignificant, the duty holder should record the assessment and its conclusion and review it periodically, and again if anything changes, to confirm it remains valid.

n.1: A conclusion of insignificant risk still has to be recorded and revisited, not discarded.
n.2: Adding a cooling tower would introduce a major new risk, the opposite of what is needed.
n.0: Ceasing to use the supply is neither required nor practical for a low-risk system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An outbreak of respiratory illness is linked to a site. Regarding the water risk assessment, what should the duty holder do?
o: Delete previous monitoring records to start afresh
Assume the assessment is still valid and change nothing
Wait a full year before looking at the assessment again
Review the assessment, since an outbreak is a clear trigger to check it is still valid
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An outbreak, or any reason to suspect the assessment is no longer valid, is a specific trigger to review it promptly and check whether the controls have failed or the risk has changed.

n.1: An outbreak is precisely the situation in which the assessment must not be assumed valid.
n.2: Delaying review for a year during a suspected outbreak would be indefensible.
n.0: Records must be preserved, especially during an investigation, not deleted.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why does keeping the water-system schematic accurate matter so much when the risk assessment is reviewed?
o: Schematics are required purely for planning-permission purposes
A tidy diagram makes the plant room easier to photograph
The diagram is only needed to satisfy the architect
An out-of-date schematic can hide dead legs or added plant, so risks may be missed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: If the schematic does not reflect alterations — new branches, removed outlets, added storage — the reviewer cannot see all sources of risk, so keeping it current is essential to a suitable and sufficient review.

n.1: Photographic tidiness is not the purpose of the schematic.
n.0: Its role is water-safety management, not planning permission.
n.2: The diagram serves the risk assessment, not the architect's records.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A written scheme sets a monitoring frequency for flushing infrequently used outlets. What risk is this control primarily addressing?
o: The risk of limescale forming on the tap spout
The risk of stagnation in outlets that are used rarely, allowing bacterial growth
The risk of the water bill increasing
The risk of the outlet being stolen
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Little-used outlets let water sit and warm, favouring Legionella growth; scheduled flushing draws fresh water through and is a recognised control the written scheme should specify and record.

n.0: Limescale is a nuisance but is not the reason flushing is scheduled for infrequent outlets.
n.3: Theft is not a water-hygiene risk addressed by flushing.
n.2: Flushing may use a little water; controlling bacterial growth, not the bill, is its purpose.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which statement best reflects how often a Legionella risk assessment should be reviewed?
o: Once when written, and then never again
Strictly every ten years to the day, and at no other time
Only if a member of the public makes a written complaint
Regularly, and additionally whenever there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 expects periodic review and, on top of that, review whenever there is reason to think the assessment is no longer valid — such as changes to the system, its use, or a suspected case of disease.

n.0: A one-off assessment cannot stay valid as systems and uses change over time.
n.2: A public complaint is not the only, or main, trigger for review.
n.1: There is no fixed ten-year rule; review is driven by suitability and change.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A duty holder argues that because they employ a specialist contractor to manage the water systems, they no longer need to understand the risk assessment. Why is this view mistaken?
o: Because employing a contractor doubles the number of assessments required
Because contractors are not allowed to touch water systems
Because the duty holder retains legal responsibility and must ensure the assessment is suitable and acted upon
Because the assessment must instead be understood only by the cleaner
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Delegating the work does not transfer the legal duty; the duty holder must still ensure a competent assessment is made, understand its findings and see that the controls are implemented and reviewed.

n.1: Contractors routinely and lawfully manage water systems; that is not the issue.
n.3: Responsibility does not pass to the cleaner; it remains with the duty holder.
n.0: Using a contractor does not multiply the number of assessments required.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Within the written scheme, what is the purpose of clearly recording who does each monitoring task?
o: So that the busiest person can be blamed if anything goes wrong
So the names can be shared with marketing partners
So the document reaches a required page count
So responsibility is unambiguous and tasks are not left undone through confusion
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Allocating each task to a named, competent person ensures accountability and that nothing falls between roles; the scheme's controls only work if someone is clearly responsible for carrying them out.

n.1: Sharing names with marketing is irrelevant and inappropriate.
n.0: The aim is reliable completion of tasks, not apportioning blame.
n.2: Page count is not a consideration in the scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An assessor identifies a large cold-water storage tank that far exceeds the building's daily demand. Why is oversized storage recorded as a risk factor?
o: Bigger tanks always cost more to insure
The extra water makes the building harder to heat
Excess stored water turns over slowly and can stagnate and warm, aiding bacterial growth
Larger tanks are heavier and stress the roof
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Storage far above demand means water dwells longer before being drawn off, giving it time to warm into the growth range and stagnate; the assessment should flag it, favouring right-sized storage as prevention.

n.3: Structural loading is a building concern, not the water-hygiene reason for the flag.
n.0: Insurance cost is irrelevant to the Legionella risk.
n.1: Heating the building is not why oversized storage is a hygiene risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What does 'suitable and sufficient' mean when applied to a Legionella risk assessment?
o: It uses the same template as every other building in the country
It has been signed by the most senior director
It is long enough to fill a lever-arch file
It identifies and evaluates the actual risks in enough detail to decide the controls needed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A suitable and sufficient assessment properly identifies the sources and who is exposed, and evaluates the risk in enough depth to determine what control measures are needed for that particular system.

n.2: Length alone says nothing about whether the real risks were identified.
n.0: A generic template ignoring the system's specifics is not sufficient.
n.1: A senior signature does not make an inadequate assessment suitable.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A hotel converts a disused wing back into guest bedrooms after two years. Which action best reflects L8 before the wing reopens?
o: Remove the wing from the schematic to simplify records
Open the rooms and monitor water only if a guest complains
Review the risk assessment and bring the wing's controls up to date before it is used
Leave the assessment unchanged because the rooms existed before
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Bringing dormant plant back into use is a change that can invalidate the assessment; it should be reviewed, the schematic updated and controls applied so the reoccupied wing is safe from the first day of use.

n.1: Waiting for a complaint exposes guests before any control is confirmed.
n.3: That the rooms once existed does not account for two years of stagnation.
n.0: Deleting the wing from records hides a real part of the system and its risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why is an accurate asset register or list of system components valuable to the risk assessment?
o: It ensures all components that could harbour or spread Legionella are accounted for and managed
It is only needed by the finance department for depreciation
It sets the resale value of the plant
It records the guarantee dates for warranty claims
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Knowing every component — tanks, calorifiers, showers, spray taps, cooling plant — lets the assessor account for each potential source and assign controls, so nothing capable of harbouring or spreading the bacteria is overlooked.

n.2: Resale value is a financial matter, not a water-hygiene one.
n.3: Warranty tracking is incidental and not why the register matters here.
n.1: Depreciation accounting is not the assessment's purpose for the register.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A written scheme lists control measures but says nothing about how their effectiveness will be checked. What key element is missing?
o: The car-parking arrangements for contractors
The provision for monitoring the controls to confirm they remain effective
A list of the building's previous owners
A glossary of plumbing terms for visitors
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A written scheme must not only state the controls but set out how and when they are monitored, so the duty holder can confirm they are working; without monitoring, control failures would go undetected.

n.2: Past ownership has no place in the control scheme.
n.0: Parking arrangements are unrelated to water-safety controls.
n.3: A glossary is not a required element and does not verify the controls.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: When identifying who is at risk, why does the assessment give particular attention to groups such as the elderly, the very young and the immunocompromised?
o: They are more likely to tamper with the plumbing
They use hot water more cheaply than other people
They are legally exempt from all water charges
They tend to be more susceptible to infection if exposed to the bacteria
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 highlights that some people are more susceptible — the elderly, the very young, those with weakened immunity or respiratory illness — so premises serving them warrant particular care in identifying and controlling the risk.

n.0: Tampering is not why these groups are singled out.
n.1: Cost of water use has no bearing on susceptibility.
n.2: Water charges are unrelated to the health-risk reasoning.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A duty holder wants to reduce risk by design. Which of the following is a prevention measure rather than a control-and-monitor measure?
o: Taking routine samples for laboratory analysis
Recording weekly shower-head temperatures on a log sheet
Dosing the hot water with a chemical biocide
Removing an unused length of pipework so water can no longer stagnate in it
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Prevention designs the risk out — here, removing a dead leg so stagnant water cannot accumulate. The others manage a risk that remains, by controlling or monitoring it, which the hierarchy places after prevention.

n.1: Logging temperatures is monitoring of a retained risk, not prevention.
n.2: Biocide dosing controls an existing risk rather than removing its cause.
n.0: Sampling checks the state of the system; it does not prevent the risk arising.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An assessor reviewing a factory notes that its process uses a humidifier producing a fine water mist over the shop floor. Why must this feature the risk assessment?
o: It is relevant solely to the energy audit
It is an aerosol-generating source that could disperse contaminated droplets to be inhaled
It only affects the humidity readings on a chart
Humidifiers are always banned in factories
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A humidifier or any equipment creating a water mist is an aerosol source; if the water is contaminated, droplets can be inhaled, so the assessment must identify it and set controls for the water feeding it.

n.3: Humidifiers are not banned; they must be assessed and controlled.
n.0: It is a health-risk source, not just an energy consideration.
n.2: The concern is inhalable aerosol, not merely a humidity reading.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The written scheme should describe the correct operation of the water system. Why is this description important?
o: So the system can be advertised to potential buyers
So the description can replace all training for staff
So the document can be entered into a design competition
So that operators know the conditions the controls are meant to maintain and can spot deviations
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Describing how the system should run — temperatures, flows and conditions — gives operators a clear reference so they can recognise when it drifts out of control and trigger the scheme's remedial actions.

n.2: A design competition is not a purpose of the scheme.
n.0: Advertising the system is unrelated to safe operation.
n.1: A written description supports, but does not replace, proper competent training.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Two years after it was written, a site's risk assessment has never been looked at again despite a major re-plumbing of the building. What is the main failing?
o: The assessment was not reviewed after a significant alteration that could affect the risk
The assessment was written on the wrong grade of paper
The assessment used too few technical words
The assessment should have been thrown away after twelve months
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Significant alterations to the pipework are a clear trigger to review the assessment; leaving it untouched means new dead legs, routes or plant may be uncontrolled and unassessed.

n.2: The vocabulary used is not the compliance failing here.
n.3: Assessments are reviewed and updated, not discarded after a year.
n.1: The medium it is written on is irrelevant to its validity.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Overall, what is the fundamental purpose of producing and maintaining the risk assessment and written scheme together?
o: To transfer all legal duties away from the employer
To create paperwork that only insurers ever read
To satisfy a filing requirement with no practical effect
To identify the risk and then set out and sustain the measures that keep people safe from exposure
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Taken together they identify where and to whom the risk arises and then define, allocate, monitor and sustain the controls that prevent exposure — the whole point being to protect people's health, not merely to hold records.

n.2: They exist to control real risk, not merely to fill a filing requirement.
n.1: Their audience is those who manage and are exposed to the system, not just insurers.
n.0: They support the duty holder in meeting duties; they do not transfer legal responsibility away.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Legionella bacteria multiply most readily in water that sits within which temperature range?
o: 0 to 15°C
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The recognised danger zone where Legionella grows most readily is roughly 20 to 45°C.

n.0: Below about 20°C the bacteria stay dormant and do not multiply significantly.
n.2: Between 46 and 59°C growth slows and the bacteria begin to die off.
n.3: At 60°C and above the bacteria are killed quickly, so this range is a control not a risk.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why is temperature control regarded as the traditional and primary method of controlling Legionella in a hot and cold water system?
o: It keeps water either too cold or too hot for the bacteria to thrive
It is cheaper than fitting any thermostats
It removes the need to keep any records
It allows outlets to be used far less often
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Keeping cold water cold and hot water hot holds the system outside the 20 to 45°C growth range.

n.2: Records must still be kept to prove the controls are working.
n.3: Regular use of outlets is still needed to prevent stagnation.
n.1: Cost is not the reason; effective bacterial control is.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: At what temperature should water be stored in a calorifier (hot water cylinder) to control Legionella?
o: At least 60°C
At least 50°C
At least 70°C
At least 55°C
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above to keep the bacteria from multiplying.

n.1: 50°C is the minimum at the outlet, not the storage temperature.
n.3: 55°C is below the required storage minimum of 60°C.
n.2: 70°C is higher than needed for storage and risks scalding and energy waste.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Hot water should reach the tap at a minimum of 50°C within how long of the tap being run?
o: Five minutes
Two minutes
One minute
30 seconds
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Hot water must reach at least 50°C within one minute of running the tap.

n.3: Thirty seconds is shorter than the recognised one-minute allowance.
n.1: Two minutes is the run time used for cold water, not hot.
n.0: Five minutes is far too long and would indicate a fault.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: In a healthcare premises, what minimum hot water temperature should be reached at the outlet within one minute?
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: In healthcare settings the hot water target at the outlet is at least 55°C within one minute.

n.1: 50°C is the general minimum but healthcare requires a higher figure.
n.0: 52°C is not the recognised healthcare figure.
n.3: 60°C is the storage temperature, not the outlet target.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Cold water should be kept below which temperature to control Legionella?
o: Below 18°C
Below 25°C
Below 20°C
Below 15°C
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Cold water should be kept below 20°C to stay out of the bacterial growth range.

n.3: Below 15°C is ideal but the control limit is 20°C.
n.0: 18°C is not the recognised limit.
n.1: 25°C is inside the danger zone and unsafe.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What does the term 'sentinel outlets' mean on a hot and cold water system?
o: The outlets located in plant rooms only
The nearest and furthest outlets on a loop or system
Any outlet fitted with a thermostatic mixing valve
The two outlets used most often by staff
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Sentinel outlets are the outlets nearest to and furthest from where water enters the system or loop.

n.3: Frequency of use does not define a sentinel outlet.
n.2: Having a mixing valve does not make an outlet a sentinel.
n.0: Sentinels are chosen by position on the system, not by being in plant rooms.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: How often should the temperatures at sentinel outlets normally be checked?
o: Monthly
Annually
Quarterly
Weekly
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Sentinel outlet temperatures are normally checked monthly.

n.3: Weekly checks are more frequent than the routine requirement.
n.2: Quarterly is too infrequent for sentinel monitoring.
n.1: Annual checks apply to a wider set of outlets, not sentinels.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the minimum flow temperature that should be recorded leaving a calorifier?
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The calorifier flow temperature should be at least 60°C.

n.0: 50°C is the outlet minimum, not the calorifier flow.
n.1: 55°C is below the required flow figure.
n.2: 65°C is higher than the minimum required, though not itself unsafe.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the minimum return temperature that should be recorded coming back to a calorifier on a circulating hot water system?
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The return temperature to the calorifier should be at least 50°C.

n.2: 45°C is inside the danger zone and below the required return figure.
n.3: 55°C is higher than the minimum needed for the return leg.
n.0: 60°C is the flow and storage figure, not the return minimum.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You run a hot tap and after one minute the thermometer reads 48°C. What is the correct response?
o: Run the tap for another five minutes then leave it
Turn the calorifier down to stop scalding
Record the reading and report it as out of range
Accept it as it is above 45°C
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 48°C is below the 50°C minimum, so the reading is recorded and reported to the responsible person.

n.3: Being above 45°C is not the standard; the outlet must reach 50°C.
n.1: Turning storage down would make the problem worse, not better.
n.0: Leaving it after a long run does not fix an out-of-range outlet.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A colleague suggests turning the hot water storage down to 55°C so users are less likely to be scalded. Why is this wrong?
o: It would make the outlet checks quicker
Scalding cannot happen from stored water
55°C allows Legionella to survive in storage
It would use more energy overall
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Storing below 60°C allows Legionella to survive and multiply, so storage must stay at 60°C or above.

n.3: Energy use is not the safety reason for keeping 60°C.
n.1: Scalding can occur, which is exactly why the safe control is a mixing valve, not lower storage.
n.0: Speed of checks is irrelevant to the decision.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the correct way to reduce the risk of scalding at an outlet without lowering the storage temperature?
o: Store the water at 50°C instead
Fit a thermostatic mixing valve at the outlet
Fit a longer pipe run to the tap
Only use the tap for cold water
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A thermostatic mixing valve blends the hot supply down at the point of use while storage stays at 60°C.

n.0: Storing at 50°C would allow bacterial growth.
n.2: A longer pipe run does not control the delivered temperature safely.
n.3: Removing hot use does not address the scalding control needed.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: When taking a hot water outlet temperature with a surface probe, how long should you normally allow the tap to run before recording?
o: Until the basin is full
Exactly ten seconds
Until the temperature stabilises, up to one minute
Five minutes regardless of reading
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: You run the tap until the temperature stabilises, which for hot water is within one minute.

n.1: Ten seconds is too short for the reading to settle.
n.0: Filling the basin is not how the run time is judged.
n.3: Running for a fixed five minutes wastes water and is not the method.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You take a cold tap reading and after two minutes it reads 22°C. What should you do?
o: Accept it because it is close to 20°C
Turn the tap off and mark it as passed
Record the reading and report it as out of range
Wait ten minutes and only record if it rises
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 22°C after two minutes is above the 20°C limit, so it is recorded and reported.

n.0: Being close is not the same as meeting the below-20°C limit.
n.1: Marking it as passed would be a false record.
n.3: Waiting longer does not correct an out-of-range cold outlet.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Who should an out-of-range temperature reading be reported to?
o: The equipment manufacturer
The nearest member of the public
The responsible person for water safety
Nobody, if it is only one outlet
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Out-of-range readings are reported to the responsible person so corrective action can be taken.

n.1: Members of the public are not responsible for the water system.
n.3: Even a single failing outlet must be reported.
n.0: The manufacturer is not the person managing the site risk.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why must temperature readings be written down at the time they are taken?
o: Only because the public asks to see them
So the readings can be changed later if needed
Because the thermometer will not work otherwise
To provide a record proving controls are being monitored
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Recording readings provides evidence that the control scheme is being monitored and maintained.

n.2: The thermometer works regardless of whether you record.
n.1: Records must never be altered after the event.
n.0: The record is for the duty holder and inspectors, not only public request.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A cold water tap reads 24°C straight away and drops only to 23°C after two minutes. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The cold supply is being warmed somewhere, such as near a hot pipe
This is a normal and acceptable cold reading
The tap is used too often
The thermometer is faulty
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A cold outlet staying above 20°C suggests warming, often from nearby heat sources, and must be investigated.

n.3: A single high reading is more likely a real fault than a probe error.
n.1: 23°C is above the 20°C limit and is not acceptable.
n.2: Frequent use would tend to keep cold water cooler, not warmer.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which set of outlets, in addition to sentinels, is typically checked on a longer interval such as annually?
o: Outlets that have mixing valves removed
A representative selection of other outlets across the system
Only the outlets that failed last time
Outlets in the car park
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A representative range of other outlets is checked on a longer cycle, often annually, to confirm system-wide control.

n.2: Checks are not limited only to previously failed outlets.
n.3: Outlets are chosen across the served system, not by irrelevant locations.
n.0: Removing mixing valves is not how outlets are selected.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What temperature confirms that a calorifier is storing hot water safely?
o: Any temperature above 45°C
60°C or above
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Stored hot water at 60°C or above controls Legionella.

n.2: 58°C is below the storage minimum.
n.1: 59°C is still just below the required 60°C.
n.0: Above 45°C alone is not enough; growth continues up to about 45°C and survives to 60°C.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You are asked to check the two sentinel outlets on a hot water loop. Which outlets are these?
o: The two most decorative taps
Two taps chosen at random
The two taps closest to the front door
The first outlet after the calorifier and the last outlet on the loop
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Sentinels on a loop are the nearest outlet to the calorifier and the furthest one on the return.

n.0: Appearance is irrelevant to sentinel selection.
n.1: Sentinels are chosen by position, not randomly.
n.2: Distance from the door does not define a sentinel.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why is it important that a hot outlet reaches temperature within one minute rather than eventually?
o: To save water only
So the record card fits on one line
Because a slow rise suggests poor circulation where bacteria can grow
Because thermometers only read for one minute
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A hot outlet that is slow to heat points to dead legs or poor circulation where bacteria can establish.

n.0: Water saving is a benefit but not the safety reason.
n.3: Thermometers can read for longer than a minute.
n.1: The one minute is a control standard, not a paperwork limit.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: During a monthly sentinel check the furthest hot outlet reads 46°C after one minute. What action is correct?
o: Accept it as within the danger zone
Re-label it as a cold outlet
Turn down the calorifier to match
Record and report it as failing the 50°C minimum
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 46°C is below the 50°C outlet minimum, so it is recorded and reported for investigation.

n.0: Being within the danger zone is the problem, not an acceptance.
n.2: Lowering the calorifier would worsen the risk.
n.1: Relabelling does not correct the failure.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the main risk of water sitting in a rarely used outlet, sometimes called a dead leg?
o: The water becomes too cold to use
The pipe will freeze quickly
The tap will run faster
The water can warm into the danger zone and stagnate
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Little-used pipework lets water stagnate and drift into the 20 to 45°C growth range.

n.1: Dead legs are a stagnation risk, not primarily a freezing risk.
n.0: Stagnant water tends to warm, not become too cold.
n.2: Flow rate is not affected in the way described.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which thermometer or probe is suitable for recording an outlet water temperature quickly and accurately?
o: A domestic oven thermometer
A calibrated digital thermometer with a suitable probe
A hand held on the pipe
An unmarked mercury thermometer left in a drawer
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A calibrated digital thermometer with the correct probe gives a quick, reliable reading.

n.0: An oven thermometer is not designed for water outlet checks.
n.2: A bare hand cannot give an accurate recorded figure.
n.3: An uncalibrated, unmarked thermometer cannot be relied upon.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You take a hot tap reading and it reaches 51°C within one minute. What does this show?
o: The outlet meets the minimum hot water standard
The outlet is failing and must be reported
The water is too hot and must be cooled
The cold supply is faulty
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 51°C within one minute is at or above the 50°C minimum, so the outlet passes.

n.1: The reading meets the standard, so it is not failing.
n.2: 51°C is not excessively hot for a hot outlet.
n.3: The reading tells you nothing wrong about the cold supply.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why should hot and cold pipework not run close together or share the same insulation space?
o: Heat can transfer, warming the cold and cooling the hot
It makes the pipes heavier
It looks untidy
It uses more clips
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Adjacent hot and cold pipes can exchange heat, pushing the cold above 20°C and the hot below its target.

n.2: Appearance is not the control reason.
n.1: Weight is irrelevant to temperature control.
n.3: The number of fixings is not the issue.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A cold water storage tank reads 21°C during a routine check. What is the correct interpretation?
o: It should be ignored as tanks are exempt
It is above the 20°C limit and should be recorded and reported
It is acceptable as it is near 20°C
It is too cold and needs heating
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: At 21°C the stored cold water exceeds the 20°C limit and must be recorded and reported.

n.2: Near the limit is not the same as meeting it.
n.3: Cold water is not required to be heated.
n.0: Tanks are included in the monitoring, not exempt.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the purpose of allowing a set run time before recording an outlet temperature?
o: To let the temperature settle to a true, representative value
To cool the thermometer
To fill a record sheet faster
To waste time during the round
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The run time lets the reading stabilise so the recorded figure truly reflects the delivered water.

n.3: It is a technical requirement, not wasted time.
n.1: The aim is a stable water reading, not cooling the probe.
n.2: It does not speed up paperwork.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A calorifier flow reads 61°C but the return reads 44°C. What does the low return suggest?
o: The system is fine because flow is above 60°C
Poor circulation on the loop, allowing cooler water where bacteria can grow
The thermometer is reading in the wrong units
The cold tank is overfilled
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A return below 50°C indicates poor circulation, leaving parts of the loop in the growth range.

n.0: A good flow does not excuse a failing return.
n.2: 44°C is a plausible Celsius reading, not a unit error.
n.3: Cold tank level is unrelated to the hot return figure.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why should you not rely on touch alone to judge whether water is hot or cold enough?
o: Touch cannot give a recordable, accurate figure
Touch always reads too high
Water temperature does not matter
Hands are not allowed near taps
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Touch is subjective and cannot produce the accurate recorded figure the control scheme needs.

n.1: Touch is unreliable in both directions, not always high.
n.2: Water temperature is central to Legionella control.
n.3: There is no blanket rule against hands near taps.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You reach a little-used guest bathroom hot tap that reads only 40°C after a minute. What is the best action?
o: Record and report it, and consider whether the outlet needs regular flushing
Leave it as guests rarely use it
Turn up every calorifier on site
Cap the tap off yourself immediately
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 40°C fails the 50°C minimum, so it is recorded, reported, and infrequent use is flagged for flushing.

n.1: Rare use makes stagnation more likely, so it cannot be ignored.
n.3: Capping outlets is not an operative's decision to take alone.
n.2: Turning up all calorifiers is not a targeted or safe response.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What does keeping cold water below 20°C achieve in Legionella control?
o: It keeps the water below the temperature where the bacteria multiply readily
It makes the water taste better only
It sterilises the water
It removes the need for any hot water checks
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Below 20°C the water is too cool for Legionella to multiply readily.

n.2: Cool water does not sterilise; it only slows growth.
n.3: Hot water checks are still required separately.
n.1: Taste is not the control purpose.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which reading would pass a healthcare hot outlet check taken at one minute?
o: Any of the above
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Healthcare hot outlets should reach at least 55°C within one minute.

n.2: 49°C is below even the general 50°C minimum.
n.3: 53°C meets the general figure but not the healthcare 55°C.
n.0: Only 55°C meets the healthcare standard, so not all pass.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: How should a temperature monitoring record ideally be kept?
o: Only in the operative's memory
As a rough guess added at month end
In writing, dated, showing outlet, reading and any action taken
On a loose note thrown away after the visit
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Records should be written, dated and show the outlet, reading and any action, to prove control.

n.0: Memory is not an auditable record.
n.3: Discarded notes provide no evidence of monitoring.
n.1: Guessed retrospective figures are not valid records.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A hot outlet consistently fails to reach 50°C even after the calorifier is confirmed at 60°C. What is a likely cause to investigate?
o: The record sheet being too short
The thermometer being brand new
A long dead leg or heat loss between the calorifier and the tap
The cold water tank being too clean
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Heat loss or a long dead leg between storage and outlet commonly causes low delivered temperatures.

n.3: A clean cold tank does not lower hot outlet temperature.
n.0: Paperwork length has no effect on water temperature.
n.1: A new thermometer is not a cause of low readings.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why is monthly sentinel monitoring preferred over checking only once a year at those points?
o: It gives early warning if control at the extremes of the system is slipping
It is required by the tap manufacturer
It replaces the need for any other checks
It uses less water overall
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Monthly checks at the nearest and furthest outlets give early warning that system control is failing.

n.1: It is a water safety requirement, not a manufacturer rule.
n.3: Water use is not the reason for the interval.
n.2: Sentinel checks supplement, not replace, other monitoring.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You record a cold outlet at 19°C after two minutes. What does this indicate?
o: The water is dangerously cold
It fails and must be reported
The hot supply has failed
It meets the cold water control standard
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 19°C is below the 20°C limit within two minutes, so the cold outlet passes.

n.1: The reading is within limits, so it does not fail.
n.0: 19°C is normal cold water, not dangerous.
n.2: A cold pass says nothing about the hot supply failing.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What should be done if a thermometer used for monitoring is found to be out of calibration?
o: Only use it for cold outlets
Stop using it and have it recalibrated or replaced
Throw the record cards away
Keep using it and adjust readings by guesswork
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: An out-of-calibration thermometer gives unreliable readings and must be recalibrated or replaced.

n.3: Guessing corrections makes the records unreliable.
n.0: An inaccurate probe is no more valid on cold than hot.
n.2: Past records should be kept, not destroyed.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A tap fitted with a thermostatic mixing valve delivers water at about 42°C. Why is measuring the incoming hot temperature before the valve important?
o: Because the blended 42°C proves the supply is fine
To make the round take longer
To confirm the hot supply itself still reaches at least 50°C
Because valves never need checking
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The blended outlet is deliberately cooler, so the hot feed before the valve must be checked to prove it reaches 50°C.

n.0: The blended 42°C is intentional and does not confirm the hot feed.
n.3: Mixing valves do require periodic checking and servicing.
n.1: The check has a safety purpose, not to lengthen the round.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which of these is the correct sequence when a routine temperature check finds a reading out of range?
o: Ignore it and move on
Turn hot storage below 60°C to fix it
Record the reading, then report it to the responsible person
Adjust the reading to look acceptable
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: An out-of-range reading is recorded honestly and reported to the responsible person for action.

n.0: Ignoring a failure leaves a risk uncontrolled.
n.3: Falsifying records is never acceptable.
n.1: Lowering storage below 60°C increases the Legionella risk.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the significance of the figure 60°C in a hot water system?
o: It is the maximum temperature water may ever reach
It is the minimum safe storage temperature that controls Legionella
It is the outlet target at the tap
It is the cold water limit
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 60°C is the minimum storage temperature that keeps Legionella from multiplying in the calorifier.

n.0: It is a minimum, not a maximum limit.
n.3: The cold water limit is below 20°C.
n.2: The outlet target is 50°C, or 55°C in healthcare.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You are monitoring an outlet and unsure whether it is a hot or cold tap. Why does this matter for the reading?
o: It does not matter as the limit is the same
Cold taps have no limit
The pass limit differs: 50°C minimum hot, below 20°C cold
Hot taps have no limit
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Hot outlets must reach at least 50°C while cold outlets must stay below 20°C, so the correct limit must be applied.

n.0: The limits are very different for hot and cold.
n.1: Cold taps do have a control limit, below 20°C.
n.3: Hot taps have a defined minimum of 50°C.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: During an annual check, a mixed selection of outlets is tested. What is the value of checking outlets beyond the sentinels?
o: It confirms control is being achieved across the whole system, not just the extremes
It lets you skip the calorifier check
It replaces the monthly sentinel checks
It is only for decoration of the log book
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Testing a wider selection confirms temperature control across the whole distribution, not only the sentinel points.

n.2: It supplements the monthly checks, not replaces them.
