Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 recommends inspecting cold water storage tanks at least annually and cleaning/disinfecting them where the inspection shows it is needed, with results recorded.

n.3: Weekly inspection of the tank interior is impractical and not what the guidance requires.
n.2: Monthly is the sentinel temperature interval, not the tank inspection interval.
n.0: Five years relates to keeping records, not to how often the tank is inspected.

Monitoring & Records.q: During monthly checks an operative records a hot sentinel outlet at 44°C after running for one minute, below the expected level. What is the correct first response?
o: Leave the entry blank and re-test only at the next monthly visit
Record the reading as an action level, investigate and carry out remedial action, escalating as needed
Round the figure up to 50°C so the record shows a pass
Note it as acceptable because the water still felt warm at the tap
Monitoring & Records.w: An out-of-range reading is an action level: it must be recorded honestly, the cause investigated, remedial action taken and the responsible person informed, as required by ACOP L8 and HSG274.

n.2: Altering the figure to show a pass is falsification and leaves a real legionella risk uncontrolled.
n.0: Leaving it blank hides the failure and delays action for a month while risk persists.
n.3: Whether water 'feels warm' is not a valid criterion; 44°C is below the control level and needs action.

Monitoring & Records.q: A responsible person suggests replacing routine temperature monitoring with occasional legionella sampling to save time. Why is this not acceptable?
o: Sampling is only ever used in cooling towers, never in hot and cold systems
Sampling gives an instant result at the outlet, unlike temperature checks
Sampling supplements temperature control but does not replace it as the main routine measure
Sampling is cheaper, so it should always be the primary method
Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 is clear that microbiological sampling can supplement monitoring but is not a substitute for maintaining and checking temperature control, which remains the principal routine control.

n.3: Cost does not make sampling the primary method; it is a supplementary check, not a replacement.
n.1: Sampling results take days of laboratory culture, so they give no instant assurance at the tap.
n.0: Sampling can be used in domestic hot and cold systems too, but always as a supplement to temperature control.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why is it valuable to review monitoring readings as a trend over several months rather than judging each reading in isolation?
o: Trends remove the need to keep the individual monthly records
Trends allow individual poor readings to be averaged out and ignored
Trends are required only so the water supplier can set the tariff
A gradual drift can reveal a developing fault before it breaches an action level
Monitoring & Records.w: Reviewing trends can expose a slow deterioration, such as a storage temperature creeping down, allowing intervention before an outright failure occurs.

n.1: Trends are used to spot problems early, not to average away and dismiss poor readings.
n.0: Individual records must still be kept; trends are derived from them, not a substitute.
n.2: Trend analysis supports risk control, not supplier tariffs, which are unrelated.

Monitoring & Records.q: For how long should legionella monitoring, inspection and maintenance records generally be retained?
o: Until the next monthly check is completed
At least five years
Only while the current operative remains employed on site
Six months, then destroyed to save storage
Monitoring & Records.w: ACOP L8 and HSG274 advise keeping records of the risk assessment, control scheme and monitoring for a suitable period, commonly at least five years.

n.0: Overwriting or discarding records each month destroys the audit trail entirely.
n.3: Six months is well short of the recommended retention period and would not support an investigation.
n.2: Retention is tied to a defined period, not to the tenure of any individual staff member.

Monitoring & Records.q: Thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) appear on the maintenance schedule. Which of the following should be checked and recorded as part of their routine servicing?
o: That the blended outlet temperature is within the safe range and the fail-safe still shuts off
That the valve reduces the incoming mains pressure to a fixed value
That the valve carries the installer's business card in a nearby cupboard
That the valve body is painted the correct colour for the room
Monitoring & Records.w: TMV servicing checks the blended temperature is correct for the application and that the thermal shut-off operates, because a failed TMV can deliver water at a temperature favouring legionella or cause scalding.

n.3: The colour of the valve body has no bearing on temperature control or safety.
n.2: A nearby business card is not a functional or recordable safety check.
n.1: A TMV blends hot and cold to a safe temperature; pressure reduction is a separate device's function.

Monitoring & Records.q: Which check on a calorifier (hot water cylinder) should form part of the routine monitoring records?
o: The colour of the insulation jacket fitted around it
The flow and return temperatures, confirming storage at or above the required level
The postcode of the manufacturer stamped on the plate
The number of pipe brackets used to support the outlet
Monitoring & Records.w: Monitoring a calorifier includes recording flow and return temperatures to confirm water is stored at 60°C or above and returned at 50°C or more, plus periodic checks for debris at the drain.

n.0: The colour of insulation is irrelevant to whether the stored water reaches control temperature.
n.2: The manufacturer's postcode is administrative trivia, not a monitoring parameter.
n.3: The count of pipe brackets has no relevance to legionella temperature control.

Monitoring & Records.q: An operative is behind on flushing and considers signing the log to show outlets were flushed when they were not. Why must records never be falsified?
o: Because falsified records slow down the next operative's paperwork
Because false records hide real risk, mislead the duty holder and can lead to illness and prosecution
Because the ink used for corrections is expensive to buy
Because the water supplier audits every log entry each week
Monitoring & Records.w: Falsifying records conceals uncontrolled risk, prevents proper action, breaches the duty of honesty in ACOP L8 record-keeping, and can contribute to outbreaks and enforcement action.

n.0: The issue is uncontrolled legionella risk and legal duty, not inconvenience to colleagues.
n.3: Water suppliers do not audit internal legionella logs; the duty holder and HSE rely on their accuracy.
n.2: The cost of ink is irrelevant; the point is the safety and legal consequences of dishonesty.

Monitoring & Records.q: On a monitoring schedule, which outlets are chosen as the hot water 'sentinel' points?
o: The outlets closest to and furthest from each calorifier or loop
Only outlets fitted with a thermostatic mixing valve
Any two outlets picked at random each month
The two outlets that are used most heavily by occupants
Monitoring & Records.w: Sentinel outlets are the first (nearest) and last (furthest) on a hot water circuit, chosen because they represent the extremes of the temperature the system can deliver.

n.3: Heaviest-use outlets are not necessarily the temperature extremes the sentinels are meant to capture.
n.2: Random selection each month prevents consistent trend comparison and is not how sentinels are defined.
n.1: Blended TMV outlets are unsuitable as hot sentinels because the true hot temperature is masked by mixing.

Monitoring & Records.q: Once completed, monitoring records should be reviewed. Who is ultimately accountable for ensuring the records are checked and acted upon?
o: The occupant who last used the outlet in question
The thermometer's calibration laboratory
The responsible/duty holder person named in the written scheme
The most junior member of the maintenance team
Monitoring & Records.w: The duty holder appoints a responsible person who is accountable for the control scheme, including reviewing monitoring records and ensuring remedial actions are completed.

n.0: Building occupants have no accountability for reviewing the monitoring regime.
n.1: A calibration lab certifies instruments; it plays no part in reviewing site records.
n.3: Accountability rests with the named responsible person, not by default with the most junior operative.

Monitoring & Records.q: A cold sentinel outlet is recorded at 23°C after running for two minutes on a warm day. What does the record require next?
o: Nothing, because cold water temperature is not part of legionella control
Waiting six months to see whether winter lowers the reading
Logging it as out of range, investigating the cause and taking remedial action
Deleting the entry, as ambient warmth always explains a high reading
Monitoring & Records.w: Cold water should stay below 20°C within two minutes; a reading of 23°C is an action level requiring the cause to be found (for example warming from nearby hot pipes) and corrected, all recorded.

n.0: Cold water temperature is a key control; keeping it below 20°C limits legionella growth.
n.3: Assuming ambient warmth without investigation could miss a genuine fault such as poor pipe segregation.
n.1: Delaying six months leaves a raised temperature uncontrolled through the highest-risk period.

Monitoring & Records.q: A contractor descales the showers but leaves the site without completing the log. From a monitoring and records standpoint, what is the correct position?
o: The next site operative can invent plausible details to close the log
A verbal report to the caretaker is a sufficient permanent record
The task is only fully valid once it is recorded with date, outlet, result and who did it
No record is needed because the contractor is not directly employed
Monitoring & Records.w: Work is only demonstrably done when documented; the record must capture what was cleaned, when, the outcome and who performed it, regardless of employment status.

n.3: Contractor status does not remove the need to record safety-critical maintenance.
n.0: Inventing details is falsification and destroys the integrity of the record.
n.1: A verbal report is not a durable, auditable record and can be forgotten or disputed.

Monitoring & Records.q: A monitoring reading remains out of range after the operative's first remedial attempt. What should the records-and-reporting process require next?
o: Marking the outlet as decorative so it no longer needs checking
Closing the log entry and moving on to the next scheduled outlet
Reducing the monitoring frequency to avoid repeat failures on the log
Escalating to the responsible person so further action and resources can be arranged
Monitoring & Records.w: When first-line remedial action does not restore control, the failure must be escalated to the responsible person, who decides on further measures; the escalation itself is recorded.

n.1: Closing an unresolved failure leaves the risk uncontrolled and unrecorded for follow-up.
n.2: Cutting monitoring frequency hides recurring failures rather than resolving them.
n.0: Falsely reclassifying an outlet to dodge checks is dishonest and dangerous.

Monitoring & Records.q: In broad terms, what does an effective monitoring and records regime allow a duty holder to demonstrate?
o: That every occupant has read the water safety policy
That the building uses less energy than neighbouring premises
That the plumbing was installed by an approved manufacturer
That the control measures identified in the risk assessment are in place and working
Monitoring & Records.w: The central value of monitoring records is evidencing that the risk assessment's control measures are being implemented and remain effective over time.

n.1: Energy comparison is unrelated to legionella control evidence.
n.0: Occupant awareness is useful but is not what temperature/flushing records demonstrate.
n.2: Installer approval is a design matter and does not show ongoing control is maintained.

Monitoring & Records.q: When recording a hot sentinel temperature, what target should the water reach at the outlet, and within what time?
o: At least 50°C within one minute of running
Exactly 38°C at the moment the tap is opened
No higher than 20°C within two minutes of running
At least 43°C within five minutes of running
Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 states hot water should reach at least 50°C at the sentinel outlet within one minute of running (55°C in healthcare); the reading and time are recorded.

n.3: 43°C is a scald-risk/blended figure, not the hot sentinel control temperature.
n.2: 20°C in two minutes is the cold water target, not the hot sentinel target.
n.1: 38°C is a typical blended TMV delivery temperature, not the hot sentinel requirement.

Monitoring & Records.q: What is the recorded target for a cold water sentinel outlet?
o: Above 60°C to prevent stagnation
At least 50°C within one minute of running
Between 38°C and 46°C at all times
Below 20°C within two minutes of running
Monitoring & Records.w: Cold water should remain below 20°C, measured after running the outlet for up to two minutes, to keep temperatures outside the range that favours legionella growth.

n.1: 50°C in one minute is the hot sentinel target, not the cold requirement.
n.2: 38-46°C describes blended outlet temperatures, which would be dangerously warm for cold water.
n.0: Above 60°C applies to hot water storage, not cold supply.

Monitoring & Records.q: When monitoring a calorifier's return leg, what minimum temperature should the returning water record to keep the whole circuit protected?
o: Below 20°C
Around 38°C
Exactly 100°C
At least 50°C
Monitoring & Records.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above and circulate so that it returns to the calorifier at no less than 50°C, ensuring the loop stays above growth temperatures throughout.

n.0: Below 20°C is a cold water target; a hot return that cool would indicate serious failure.
n.1: Around 38°C sits within the legionella growth range and is far too low for the return leg.
n.2: 100°C is boiling and neither required nor safe for a distribution return.

Monitoring & Records.q: Reviewing the flushing log, the responsible person finds a three-week gap where a wing was closed for refurbishment. What is the correct records action before reopening those outlets?
o: Flush and, where the assessment requires, disinfect the affected outlets, recording the remedial work before use
Ignore the gap because the wing had no occupants at the time
Remove the wing's outlets from the monitoring schedule permanently
Backdate flushing entries to fill the gap so the log looks continuous
Monitoring & Records.w: Standing water during closure raises risk; the outlets should be flushed (and disinfected if the assessment requires) and that remedial work recorded before the wing is brought back into use.

n.3: Backdating entries is falsification and hides a genuine period of stagnation.
n.1: Lack of occupants during closure is exactly why the water stagnated and now needs managing.
n.2: Deleting the outlets from monitoring abandons control rather than restoring it safely.

Monitoring & Records.q: An enforcing inspector visits and asks to see how the water system is being managed. Which document set best demonstrates ongoing compliance?
o: The risk assessment, written scheme and up-to-date monitoring records
The manufacturer's brochure for the taps
A verbal assurance from the site caretaker
The original boiler purchase invoice on its own
Monitoring & Records.w: Compliance is evidenced by the current risk assessment, the written control scheme and complete, up-to-date monitoring and maintenance records showing the scheme is being followed.

n.3: A purchase invoice shows procurement, not ongoing control of the system.
n.2: Verbal assurance is not auditable evidence of a managed regime.
n.1: A product brochure describes equipment, not how risk is being controlled over time.

Monitoring & Records.q: When checking a TMV-served basin used by vulnerable people, which blended-outlet temperature would you expect to record as within the safe delivery range?
o: At least 60°C to match storage temperature
Below 20°C as for a cold outlet
Exactly 50°C, the hot sentinel figure
Around 41°C, within the typical safe blended range
Monitoring & Records.w: TMVs deliver a blended temperature typically around 38-46°C to prevent scalding of vulnerable users; a recorded value near 41°C sits within that safe range.

n.0: 60°C at the outlet would scald; that figure is the storage temperature, not the blended delivery.
n.1: Below 20°C is a cold sentinel target and would be far too cold for a blended washing outlet.
n.2: 50°C is the hot sentinel control temperature, above the safe blended delivery range for a TMV outlet.

Monitoring & Records.q: An entry shows a temperature reading but no operative's name or initials against it. Why does this weaken the record?
o: It stops the water supplier from issuing a certificate
There is no accountability or traceability for who took the reading and whether it can be relied upon
It makes the ink harder to read on the page
It prevents the reading from being converted to Fahrenheit
Monitoring & Records.w: Without identifying who took a reading, the record loses traceability and accountability, so its reliability cannot be assured during review or investigation.

n.2: Legibility of ink is unrelated to the missing accountability information.
n.3: Unit conversion is unaffected by whether a name is present.
n.0: Water suppliers do not issue certificates from these internal logs; the issue is traceability.

Monitoring & Records.q: Over four months a calorifier's stored temperature records read 62, 61, 60 and 58°C. What does this trend indicate and require?
o: A perfect result needing no attention because none has failed yet
That the thermometer should be thrown away as clearly faulty
A developing downward drift that should be investigated before it breaches control
That monitoring should now stop because the figures are close together
Monitoring & Records.w: Even though the latest figure is still near target, a steady decline signals a developing fault (such as a failing thermostat or scaling) that trend review lets you catch early.

n.0: A downward drift is a warning sign, not a result to be dismissed as perfect.
n.3: A concerning trend is a reason to maintain, not stop, monitoring.
n.1: A consistent gradual fall points to a system issue, not a random instrument fault to discard.

Monitoring & Records.q: After a failed reading is put right, what should the monitoring record show about the remedial action?
o: Only that a failure occurred, with the outcome left blank
The failure erased once the fix is complete
A note to 'see me' with no further detail
What action was taken, by whom, when, and confirmation that control was restored
Monitoring & Records.w: A complete record closes the loop: it states the corrective action, who did it, the date, and the follow-up reading confirming the outlet is back within its control limits.

n.0: Recording the failure but not the outcome leaves it unclear whether control was ever restored.
n.2: A vague 'see me' note is not an auditable account of what was done.
n.1: Erasing the failure destroys the evidence trail and hides that an action level occurred.

Monitoring & Records.q: During a quarterly clean an operative finds a showerhead heavily scaled and discoloured. Beyond cleaning it, what should the records reflect?
o: That cleaning frequency need never change regardless of scaling
Only the date, with the poor condition left unmentioned
That the head was hidden from view to avoid alarming occupants
The condition found, the descale/disinfection carried out, and any review of cleaning frequency
Monitoring & Records.w: The record should capture the condition observed, the remedial cleaning and disinfection performed, and prompt consideration of whether the cleaning interval needs shortening given the scaling rate.

n.2: Concealing a component is dishonest and does nothing to control the risk.
n.0: Heavy scaling is exactly the trigger to review and possibly increase cleaning frequency.
n.1: Omitting the poor condition loses the information needed to justify any frequency change.

Monitoring & Records.q: Two similar buildings have different monitoring frequencies for the same task. What most likely explains this legitimately?
o: One building simply has more spare staff time available
The colder building can safely skip monitoring altogether
Frequencies are chosen at random and any difference is meaningless
The monitoring frequency is set by each building's individual risk assessment
Monitoring & Records.w: Monitoring frequencies are risk-based: the site-specific assessment determines how often each task is done according to the system, its users and its history.

n.0: Available staff time does not set safety-critical monitoring intervals; risk does.
n.2: Frequencies are deliberately assessed, not chosen at random.
n.1: No building can lawfully skip monitoring entirely; temperature can rise in any system.

Monitoring & Records.q: As part of cold water monitoring, why is the incoming supply temperature also recorded where practicable?
o: To decide the colour coding of the cold pipework
To confirm the mains meets minimum drinking-water fluoride levels
To calculate the building's total water bill
To establish a baseline and reveal if the cold system is warming above the incoming value
Monitoring & Records.w: Recording the incoming cold temperature provides a baseline; a rise between the supply and outlets shows the system is picking up unwanted heat, which needs investigation.

n.2: Billing is unrelated to temperature monitoring for legionella control.
n.0: Pipe colour coding follows standards, not the measured incoming temperature.
n.1: Fluoride and drinking-water chemistry are separate from legionella temperature monitoring.

Monitoring & Records.q: A duty holder cannot produce any monitoring records when an outbreak is investigated. Why is this a serious position?
o: Because printing new records later is technically difficult
Because the thermometer warranty will be voided
Because without records there is no evidence controls were applied, which weakens the legal defence and hampers investigation
Because the water supplier will increase the standing charge
Monitoring & Records.w: Absent records, the duty holder cannot demonstrate that the required controls were carried out; this undermines any legal defence and deprives investigators of the data needed to trace the fault.

n.0: The difficulty of reprinting is trivial next to the loss of evidence and legal exposure.
n.3: Standing charges are unrelated to legionella record-keeping.
n.1: A thermometer warranty has no bearing on the compliance failure.

Monitoring & Records.q: Good practice is for someone to review and sign off the monitoring records periodically. What does this review primarily achieve?
o: It confirms readings are within limits, spots trends and ensures failures were actioned
It transfers all legal duty onto the person who signs
It replaces the need to carry out the checks in the first place
It increases the resale value of the building
Monitoring & Records.w: Periodic review verifies that readings sit within control limits, identifies adverse trends, and checks that any out-of-range results were investigated and resolved.

n.3: Resale value has nothing to do with the purpose of a records review.
n.2: Reviewing records does not replace actually performing the monitoring checks.
n.1: Signing a review does not shift the duty holder's overall legal responsibility onto the reviewer.

Monitoring & Records.q: At a non-TMV kitchen tap the operative records the hot water reaching 43°C after a minute and holding there. What does the record indicate?
o: A pass, because any warm water is acceptable at a kitchen tap
A failure to reach the 50°C hot control temperature, needing investigation and action
A cold outlet within its correct range
That the tap should be relabelled as a blended outlet
Monitoring & Records.w: A direct hot outlet should reach at least 50°C within a minute; 43°C sits within the legionella growth range and is an action level requiring the cause to be found and corrected.

n.0: 'Any warm water' is not the standard; the outlet is below its 50°C control temperature.
n.2: 43°C is far above the sub-20°C cold target, so it cannot be treated as an acceptable cold reading.
n.3: Relabelling a plain hot tap does not fix an undersupplied temperature and would mask the failure.

Monitoring & Records.q: What is the minimum stored-water temperature you would expect to confirm and record for a hot water calorifier serving a domestic system?
Monitoring & Records.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above so that legionella cannot multiply and is killed on contact; the monitoring record confirms this storage temperature.

n.1: 38°C is a blended delivery temperature and sits well inside the legionella growth range for storage.
n.3: 45°C is below the storage requirement and still within the range where legionella can grow.
n.2: 20°C is the cold water ceiling, not a hot storage target.

Monitoring & Records.q: A meeting room that was mothballed for two months is about to be brought back into use. What should the monitoring and records regime require for its outlets?
o: Flushing (and disinfection if the assessment requires) with the remedial work recorded before use
Permanent removal of the outlets from the flushing schedule
Only a note that the room reopened, with no physical action
Immediate normal use, because a short closure carries no risk
Monitoring & Records.w: Water standing for two months can allow growth; the outlets should be flushed, and disinfected where the assessment requires, with the action recorded before the room returns to use.

n.3: A two-month closure is ample time for stagnation and raised risk, so normal use without action is unsafe.
n.1: Removing the outlets from the schedule abandons control rather than restoring it.
n.2: A note without physical flushing leaves potentially stagnant water in service.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the main reason a cold water storage tank must have a close-fitting lid?
o: To keep out light, dust, insects, debris and vermin
To increase the water pressure in the building
To make the tank easier to lift and move
To stop the water inside from freezing in winter
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A close-fitting lid keeps out light, dust, insects, debris and birds or vermin that would contaminate the stored water and encourage bacterial growth.

n.1: A lid has no effect on pressure, which comes from the height of the tank above the outlets.
n.3: Insulation, not the lid, is used to protect against freezing.
n.2: A lid is a hygiene barrier, not a lifting aid, and tanks are fixed in position.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You lift a tank lid and find it does not seal down properly, leaving a gap around one edge. Why is this a problem?
o: The gap will lower the temperature of the stored water
It will make the ball valve close too quickly
The water will drain out of the tank through the gap
Light, insects and debris can get in and contaminate the water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A gap lets in light, insects, dust and vermin, all of which contaminate the water and promote microbial growth, so the lid must be refitted to seal fully.

n.2: Water sits in the base of the tank and cannot escape through a gap at the top rim.
n.0: A gap lets warm air and light in and tends to raise temperature, not lower it.
n.1: The ball valve operation is unaffected by the lid seal.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Keeping light out of a cold water storage tank is important mainly because light encourages the growth of:
o: Limescale on the tank walls
Air bubbles in the water
Rust on metal fittings
Algae and other micro-organisms
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Daylight promotes the growth of algae and other micro-organisms in stored water, so a light-tight lid helps keep the water safe.

n.0: Limescale is caused by hard water and heat, not by light.
n.2: Rust is caused by moisture and oxygen on unprotected metal, not by light.
n.1: Air bubbles are not caused by light entering the tank.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A tank lid is made of a translucent plastic that lets daylight pass through into the tank. What should be done?
o: Add more water so light cannot reach the bottom
Paint the inside of the tank black
Leave it, as some light keeps the water fresh
Fit a light-proof cover so daylight cannot reach the water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Daylight reaching the water encourages algae and microbial growth, so the tank needs a light-proof lid or cover.

n.2: Light never keeps water fresh; it encourages micro-organisms to grow.
n.1: Painting the inside introduces a coating that is not approved for contact with drinking water and does not stop light entering.
n.0: Extra water does not block light entering through a translucent lid and would still allow growth near the surface.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which of these does a properly fitting tank lid help to prevent?
o: Water hammer in the pipework
The pump from running dry
Birds, insects and vermin getting into the stored water
Loss of water pressure at the taps
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A close-fitting lid is a physical barrier that stops birds, insects and vermin entering and fouling the stored water.

n.1: Low-water protection for a pump is a separate control, not the lid's job.
n.0: Water hammer is caused by fast-closing valves, not by the tank lid.
n.3: Pressure depends on the tank height, not on whether the lid fits.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You open a tank and see droppings and feathers floating on the surface. What is the most likely cause?
o: Birds have been getting in through a missing or ill-fitting lid
The tank is too large for the building
The water has been chlorinated too heavily
The insulation has come loose inside the tank
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Droppings and feathers show birds have entered through a missing or poorly fitting lid, which is a serious contamination that needs cleaning and disinfection.

n.2: Chlorination does not produce droppings or feathers.
n.1: Tank size does not put droppings into the water.
n.3: Insulation is fitted on the outside of the tank and would not create droppings.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should the lid of a cold water storage tank be checked as part of a routine inspection?
o: To measure how much water is in the tank
To confirm it still fits closely and keeps contaminants out
To check the water pressure at the outlets
To see whether the tank needs repainting
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Checking the lid confirms it still fits closely and continues to exclude light, insects, dust and vermin from the stored water.

n.0: Water level is judged by the float valve setting, not by the lid.
n.2: Pressure checks are done at outlets, not by inspecting the lid.
n.3: Repainting is not part of a standard water-hygiene tank inspection.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Where should insect and vermin screens be fitted on a cold water storage tank?
o: Inside the tank on the float valve
On the overflow, warning pipe and any vent openings
On the outlet pipe feeding the building
Only across the tank inlet from the mains
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Screens are fitted on the overflow, warning pipe and vent openings because these are the routes through which insects and vermin could otherwise enter the tank.

n.3: The inlet comes from the mains under pressure and is not an entry route needing a screen.
n.2: The outlet carries water away and does not need an insect screen.
n.0: The float valve does not open to the outside, so it needs no screen.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You inspect a tank overflow pipe and find the mesh screen is torn. What is the risk?
o: The stored water will lose pressure
Insects and small animals can enter the tank through the overflow
The overflow will no longer carry excess water away
The tank will fill more slowly
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A torn screen lets insects and small animals travel up the overflow into the tank, so it must be repaired or replaced to keep them out.

n.2: A torn screen does not block the overflow; water can still flow out.
n.0: Screen condition has no effect on water pressure.
n.3: Fill rate is controlled by the float valve and inlet, not the overflow screen.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the purpose of a screen fitted to a tank's air vent?
o: To stop the water evaporating from the tank
To reduce the noise of water filling the tank
To filter limescale from the incoming mains water
To let air in and out while keeping insects and dust out
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A vent screen allows the tank to breathe as the level changes while preventing insects, dust and debris from entering through the vent.

n.2: Vent screens do not treat mains water or remove limescale.
n.1: A screen is a hygiene barrier, not a noise reducer.
n.0: A closed lid limits evaporation; the vent screen is about excluding contaminants.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An overflow (warning) pipe should be arranged so that:
o: It runs uphill from the tank to the roof
It is screened and turns down to discharge visibly to warn of a fault
It discharges directly into the nearest foul drain
It is left open and unscreened for maximum airflow
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A warning pipe is screened against insects and turns down to a visible discharge point so an overflow is noticed and does not become an entry route.

n.2: Connecting straight into a drain risks back-siphonage of contaminated water and hides the warning.
n.0: An overflow must fall away from the tank; it cannot run uphill and drain.
n.3: Leaving it open and unscreened invites insects and vermin into the tank.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You find a wasps' nest built inside a tank vent where no screen is fitted. What does this tell you?
o: The overflow pipe is working correctly
The tank is the correct size for the demand
The tank water is too cold for bacteria
The vent needs a screen fitted to stop insects entering the tank
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insects nesting in the vent show the opening is unprotected, so a screen must be fitted to keep insects out of the stored water.

n.2: An insect nest tells you nothing about water temperature.
n.0: An unscreened, nested vent is a fault, not evidence the overflow works.
n.1: Insect ingress is unrelated to whether the tank is correctly sized.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which statement about insect screens on a storage tank is correct?
o: They should be intact, correctly fitted and checked at inspections
They are only needed on tanks kept outdoors
They can be removed once the tank has been cleaned
They should be replaced with fine muslin cloth over the openings
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Screens must be intact, correctly fitted and checked at each inspection so they keep excluding insects and vermin throughout the tank's service.

n.2: Screens are a permanent barrier and must never be left off after cleaning.
n.1: Indoor tanks still have overflows and vents that insects can use, so screens are needed there too.
n.3: Loose cloth is not a durable approved screen and can rot, clog or fall in.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Screens on the overflow and vent of a tank mainly protect the water from:
o: Excessive water pressure
Dissolved limescale from hard water
High chlorine levels from the mains
Physical entry of insects, spiders and small vermin
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Screens are a physical barrier against insects, spiders and small vermin entering the tank through its openings.

n.1: Screens cannot remove dissolved limescale, which is a chemical property of the water.
n.2: Screens do not affect chlorine concentration.
n.0: Screens have nothing to do with controlling water pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why must cold water storage tanks and their pipework be insulated?
o: To help keep the stored cold water below 20°C
To reduce the weight the tank support must carry
To hold the water above 60°C for safety
To make the water flow faster to the taps
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulation helps keep stored cold water below 20°C, the temperature above which Legionella and other bacteria multiply more readily.

n.3: Insulation does not speed up flow, which depends on head and pipe size.
n.2: Cold water should stay cold and low; only hot water is held hot, and never in a cold tank.
n.1: Insulation adds a little weight and is not about reducing structural load.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Cold water should be stored and distributed below which temperature to limit bacterial growth?
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Keeping cold water below 20°C limits the growth of Legionella and other bacteria, which multiply fastest between roughly 20°C and 45°C.

n.0: 30°C is well inside the range where bacteria multiply readily.
n.2: 45°C is near the top of the growth range and far too warm for stored cold water.
n.3: 5°C is colder than required; the recognised control limit for cold water is below 20°C, not 5°C.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You measure the stored water in a tank at 24°C. What does this indicate?
o: The water is too warm and controls such as insulation should be reviewed
The float valve has failed shut
The tank is oversized and should be drained
The water is safely within the cold water limit
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: At 24°C the cold water is above the 20°C limit and in the bacterial growth range, so insulation, location and turnover should be reviewed to bring it down.

n.3: 24°C is above the 20°C cold water limit, so it is not safely within it.
n.2: A high temperature does not on its own prove the tank is oversized, and draining is not the direct fix.
n.1: A failed-shut float valve stops the tank filling; it does not raise the water temperature.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cold water tank is sited in a warm plant room next to hot pipes. Why is this a concern?
o: Heat gain can raise the stored water above 20°C
The tank will fill more quickly than normal
The overflow screen will corrode faster
The mains pressure will drop across the building
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Warm surroundings and nearby hot pipes transfer heat into the tank, raising the water above 20°C into the bacterial growth range, so insulation or relocation is needed.

n.1: Ambient heat does not change how fast the tank fills.
n.3: Room temperature does not affect mains supply pressure.
n.2: Heat gain warms the water; it is not primarily a corrosion issue for the screen.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which practice best helps keep stored cold water cool?
o: Wrapping the tank in a dark, heat-absorbing cover
Leaving the tank lid off to let heat escape
Placing the tank directly above the boiler
Insulating the tank and keeping it away from heat sources
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulating the tank and siting it away from heat sources keeps the stored water below 20°C and limits bacterial growth.

n.2: Placing a tank above a boiler adds heat and warms the water.
n.1: Removing the lid lets in light, insects and warm air and does not keep the water cool.
n.0: A dark, heat-absorbing cover would gain heat rather than keep the water cool.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Insulation on a cold water storage tank should be:
o: Removed in summer to let the tank cool naturally
Complete and in good condition, including the lid where appropriate
Made from any absorbent material to soak up condensation
Fitted only to the base of the tank
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulation should be complete and sound so the whole tank is protected from heat gain and stays below 20°C, including insulating the lid where appropriate.

n.0: Removing insulation in summer exposes the tank to warmer ambient air and heat gain.
n.3: Insulating only the base leaves the sides and top exposed to heat.
n.2: Absorbent material that stays damp encourages mould and is not suitable tank insulation.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why is the temperature range of about 20°C to 45°C important in water hygiene?
o: It is the range at which limescale dissolves fastest
It is the range at which water freezes
It is the range at which chlorine works best
It is the range in which Legionella bacteria multiply most readily
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Legionella and similar bacteria multiply most readily between about 20°C and 45°C, which is why cold water is kept below 20°C and hot water above 60°C.

n.0: Limescale forms more with heat but this range is defined by bacterial growth, not scale.
n.2: Chlorine effectiveness is not the reason this specific range is highlighted.
n.1: Water freezes at 0°C, nowhere near this range.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You find the insulation on a rooftop tank is missing on the sunny side. What is the likely effect?
o: The tank will overflow more often
Solar heat gain warms the stored water above 20°C
The float valve will stick open
The water pressure will increase
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: With insulation missing, sunshine heats that side of the tank and can push the stored water above 20°C into the bacterial growth range.

n.0: Missing insulation warms the water; it does not cause overflowing.
n.3: Insulation does not affect pressure.
n.2: A warm tank side does not make the float valve stick open.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which of the following is essential when keeping a cold water storage tank in good hygienic condition?
o: Leaving deposits in the base to seal small leaks
Keeping it free of scale, sludge, sediment, rust and debris
Adding a scoop of sand to help settle particles
Filling it with as much water as possible at all times
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A hygienic tank must be free of scale, sludge, sediment, rust, biofilm and debris, as these harbour and feed bacteria.

n.3: Overfilling has nothing to do with cleanliness and does not keep the tank hygienic.
n.2: Adding sand introduces contamination and material for bacteria to grow on.
n.0: Deposits are not a sealant; they foul the water and support bacterial growth.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You open a tank lid and see a layer of brown sludge and sediment across the bottom. What should happen?
o: The tank should be cleaned and disinfected to remove the contamination
The water level should simply be raised above the sludge
Nothing, as sediment always settles harmlessly at the bottom
A little bleach should be poured in and the lid closed
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Sludge and sediment harbour bacteria and biofilm, so the tank must be cleaned and disinfected to restore a hygienic condition.

n.2: Settled sludge is not harmless; it is a reservoir for bacterial growth.
n.1: Raising the level leaves the contamination in the tank feeding the water.
n.3: An unmeasured splash of bleach is not a controlled disinfection and leaves the sludge in place.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Biofilm inside a storage tank is a concern because it:
o: Acts as a useful protective coating for the tank
Improves the taste of the stored water
Shelters and feeds bacteria such as Legionella
Keeps the water below 20°C
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Biofilm is a slimy layer that shelters and provides nutrients for bacteria including Legionella, so it must be removed by cleaning and disinfection.

n.1: Biofilm degrades water quality; it does not improve taste.
n.0: Biofilm is harmful growth, not a protective coating.
n.3: Biofilm has no cooling effect and often signals warm, stagnant conditions.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A dead pigeon is found floating in a storage tank. What is the correct response?
o: Ignore it as the water will dilute any contamination
Remove it, then clean and disinfect the tank before returning it to use
Top the tank up so the body sinks out of sight
Scoop it out and carry on using the water straight away
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A dead animal is a gross contamination, so the carcass is removed and the tank cleaned and disinfected before the water is used again.

n.3: Removing the body alone leaves bacterial contamination behind in the water.
n.0: Dilution does not make contaminated water safe.
n.2: Hiding the body does nothing to remove the contamination and is unacceptable.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should debris and dead insects never be left inside a storage tank?
o: They increase the mains water pressure
They decompose and provide nutrients for bacterial growth
They lower the water temperature too far
They make the water taste of chlorine
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Decomposing debris and insects release nutrients that feed bacteria and support biofilm, so they must be removed by cleaning.

n.3: Debris does not create a chlorine taste.
n.2: Debris does not cool the water.
n.0: Material in the tank has no effect on mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: When a tank is cleaned, rust and corrosion on the internal surfaces should be:
o: Removed and the surface made good, using suitable approved materials
Left alone as rust protects the metal underneath
Painted over with ordinary gloss paint
Covered with a plastic sheet inside the tank
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Rust provides a rough surface for bacteria and biofilm, so it is removed and the surface made good with materials approved for contact with drinking water.

n.1: Rust is active corrosion, not a protective layer, and harbours growth.
n.2: Ordinary gloss paint is not approved for contact with wholesome water and can taint it.
n.3: A loose plastic sheet is not an approved lining and can trap debris and bacteria.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which finding inside a tank most clearly means it needs cleaning and disinfection?
o: Water sitting at 12°C
Intact insect screens on the overflow
A securely fitting, light-proof lid
Sediment, slime and debris covering the base
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Sediment, slime and debris are contamination that harbours bacteria, so the tank needs cleaning and disinfection.

n.0: Water at 12°C is safely below the 20°C limit and is a good sign, not a fault.
n.2: A secure, light-proof lid is correct and desirable.
n.1: Intact overflow screens are exactly what an inspection wants to find.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should a cold water storage tank not be much larger than the building actually needs?
o: A large tank lowers the mains water pressure
Bigger tanks cannot be fitted with a lid
Oversized tanks let water sit and warm, causing stagnation
Larger tanks always leak more than small ones
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: An oversized tank stores more water than is used, so it turns over slowly, sits longer, warms up and stagnates, which encourages bacterial growth.

n.3: Size does not determine whether a tank leaks; condition and installation do.
n.1: Large tanks can and should still have close-fitting lids.
n.0: Tank size does not reduce mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What does 'turnover' of stored water mean in a storage tank?
o: The number of times the lid is opened each year
The water changing colour over time
The stored water being used and replaced regularly with fresh water
The tank being physically turned over to empty it
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Turnover is the regular use and replacement of the stored water with fresh mains water, which keeps it from stagnating and warming.

n.3: Turnover refers to water exchange, not physically inverting the tank.
n.1: A colour change is a sign of a problem, not the meaning of turnover.
n.0: Lid openings are unrelated to water turnover.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A tank was sized for a large workforce that has since shrunk, so most of the water is rarely used. What is the risk?
o: The mains pressure will become dangerously high
The tank will run dry every day
The insulation will absorb the extra water
The water stagnates and warms, encouraging bacterial growth
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: With low demand the water sits for long periods, warms toward ambient and stagnates, giving bacteria time and conditions to multiply.

n.1: Low demand means the tank is used less, so running dry is unlikely.
n.0: Reduced demand does not raise mains pressure.
n.2: Insulation does not absorb water; it limits heat transfer.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Stagnant water in a storage system is a hazard mainly because:
o: It gives bacteria time to grow and lets any disinfectant residual fade
It raises the pressure in the pipework
It makes the water freeze more easily
It becomes too cold to use safely
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: When water stagnates it warms, the disinfectant residual decays and bacteria have time to multiply, increasing the risk of Legionella.

n.3: Stagnant water tends to warm toward ambient, not become dangerously cold.
n.1: Stagnation does not raise system pressure.
n.2: Stagnation is linked to warming and growth, not to freezing.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which action helps maintain good turnover and reduce stagnation in a storage tank?
o: Keeping the tank permanently brim full and unused
Fitting the largest tank that will physically fit
Sizing the tank to match real daily demand
Blocking off the outlet to save water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Matching tank size to genuine daily demand keeps the stored water moving and refreshed, reducing the time it sits and warms.

n.1: An over-large tank stores water that is not used and encourages stagnation.
n.0: A full, unused tank is the definition of stagnant storage.
n.3: Blocking the outlet stops turnover entirely and would let the water stagnate.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You notice a large storage tank that is divided so both halves stay in use. Why can this design help?
o: It keeps water moving through both sections and avoids a still, oversized volume
It doubles the mains pressure to the building
It removes the need for a lid on the tank
It stops the water ever needing to be tested
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Keeping both sections in flow avoids a large stagnant volume and helps maintain turnover so the water does not sit and warm.

n.1: A divided tank does not change mains pressure.
n.2: Every storage tank still needs a close-fitting lid regardless of design.
n.3: Good design reduces risk but does not remove the need for monitoring and testing.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An unused, capped section of an old oversized tank still holds standing water connected to the system. This is best described as a:
o: Method of keeping the water cool
Normal and acceptable storage arrangement
Useful reserve supply for busy periods
Dead leg or stagnant volume that should be removed
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Standing water in an unused section acts as a dead leg where water stagnates and bacteria grow, so it should be removed from the system.

n.2: Stagnant standing water is a hazard, not a safe reserve.
n.1: An unused connected volume that never turns over is not acceptable in water hygiene terms.
n.0: Still, unused water tends to warm and stagnate rather than stay cool.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: How often should a cold water storage tank typically be inspected as a minimum?
o: At least once a year
Once every five years
Once every ten years
Only when a fault is reported
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Storage tanks should be inspected at least annually to check condition, cleanliness, temperature and that the lid and screens are intact.

n.1: A five-year gap is far too long to spot contamination or damage in time.
n.3: Waiting for a reported fault means problems go unnoticed until they are serious.
n.2: A ten-year interval leaves the tank unchecked for a dangerously long period.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During a routine tank inspection, which of these should be checked?
o: Lid fit, screens, water clarity, temperature and material condition
Nothing internal, to avoid disturbing the water
Only the colour of the outside of the tank
Just the name of the plumber who fitted it
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A proper inspection covers the lid fit, insect screens, clarity of the water, temperature and the condition of the tank and its fittings.

n.2: External colour alone tells you nothing about the hygiene of the stored water.
n.3: Who fitted the tank is not a condition check.
n.1: The inside condition, clarity and temperature must be checked, carefully, not avoided.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You open a tank for inspection and cannot see the bottom because the water is cloudy. What does this suggest?
o: That the water is perfectly clean
That the tank is correctly insulated
That the lid is fitting well
Possible contamination or sediment that needs investigation and cleaning
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Cloudy water suggests suspended sediment or contamination, so the cause must be investigated and the tank cleaned and disinfected as needed.

n.0: Clean stored water should be clear, not cloudy.
n.1: Cloudiness is unrelated to whether the tank is insulated.
n.2: Water clarity is a separate check from lid fit and does not indicate a good lid.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why is it good practice to record the findings of each tank inspection?
o: To replace the need for a close-fitting lid
So the tank does not need cleaning again
To track the tank's condition over time and show checks are being done
Because the record increases the water pressure
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Written records show the tank is being monitored, track changes in condition over time and demonstrate that the required checks are carried out.

n.3: Records have no effect on water pressure.
n.1: Recording an inspection does not remove the need to clean a tank when it is dirty.
n.0: A record cannot substitute for the physical barrier of a lid.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: On inspection you find the tank temperature is fine but a screen is missing and there are dead flies inside. What should you do?
o: Record only the temperature and take no further action
Leave the screen off since the temperature is acceptable
Report it, clean and disinfect as needed, and refit the missing screen
Add more cold water to dilute the flies
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A missing screen and insect debris are faults that let contamination in, so they must be reported, the tank cleaned and disinfected as needed, and the screen refitted.

n.0: A good temperature does not cancel out the contamination and open entry route.
n.1: Leaving the screen off keeps the tank open to insects and vermin.
n.3: Dilution does not remove the flies or the contamination they cause.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Checking the stored water temperature during inspection is important because it confirms whether:
o: The paint on the tank is sound
The mains pressure is correct
The tank is exactly half full
The cold water is being kept below 20°C
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Measuring the temperature confirms whether the cold water is being kept below 20°C, the key control against bacterial growth.

n.2: Temperature does not indicate the water level.
n.1: Temperature readings do not measure mains pressure.
n.0: Paint condition is a separate visual check, not shown by temperature.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Who should carry out cleaning and disinfection of a storage tank found to be contaminated?
o: Nobody, as tanks clean themselves over time
A competent, trained person following a safe procedure
Any passer-by who is available at the time
The first person to notice, without any training
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Cleaning and disinfection must be done by a competent, trained person following a safe, controlled procedure so the work is effective and safe.

n.2: An untrained passer-by could do the job wrongly or unsafely.
n.0: Tanks do not self-clean; contamination remains until removed.
n.3: Noticing a problem does not make someone competent to carry out disinfection.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Materials used inside a cold water storage tank, such as the lining or float valve, should be:
o: Made of untreated absorbent material
Any spare parts that physically fit
Chosen only for the lowest price
WRAS-approved and suitable for contact with wholesome water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Components in contact with drinking water must be approved as suitable so they do not taint the water or support bacterial growth.

n.1: Parts that merely fit may not be approved and could contaminate the water.
n.2: Price alone does not ensure a material is safe for contact with drinking water.
n.0: Absorbent, untreated materials can leach substances and harbour bacteria.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the job of the ball (float) valve in a storage tank?
o: To filter debris out of the outgoing water
To hold the lid firmly in place
To heat the stored water to a safe temperature
To control the inflow and keep the water at the correct level
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The float valve opens and closes the inlet to maintain the correct water level, preventing both overflow and running dry.

n.2: The float valve does not heat water and cold water should not be heated.
n.0: It controls level, not filtration of the outgoing supply.
n.1: It has nothing to do with securing the lid.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You find water trickling from the overflow pipe continuously. What is the most likely cause?
o: The insect screen is too fine
The tank is too well insulated
The lid is fitting too tightly
The float valve is not shutting off properly
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A continuous overflow usually means the float valve is failing to shut off the inflow at the correct level, so it needs adjusting or replacing.

n.1: Insulation controls temperature and cannot cause a continuous overflow.
n.0: A fine screen restricts insects, not the water level control.
n.2: A tight-fitting lid is desirable and does not cause overflowing.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: After a storage tank has been cleaned and disinfected, before returning it to normal use you should:
o: Confirm the disinfection is complete and the water is safe to use
Leave the lid off for a week to air the tank
Remove the insect screens to speed up refilling
Immediately paint the outside of the tank
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The disinfection process must be properly completed and the water confirmed safe before the tank is brought back into normal service.

n.3: Painting the outside is unrelated to safely returning the tank to use.
n.2: Removing screens exposes the freshly cleaned tank to insects and vermin.
n.1: Leaving the lid off lets in light, dust and insects and undoes the cleaning.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A galvanised tank shows heavy rust and flaking on its inner walls. What does this indicate about the material?
o: The tank must be brand new
It is in ideal condition for storing water
It is corroding and provides surfaces where bacteria can grow
The rust makes the water safer to drink
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Rust and flaking show the material is corroding, creating rough surfaces and particles that harbour bacteria and biofilm, so the tank needs attention or replacement.

n.1: Heavy corrosion is the opposite of ideal condition.
n.3: Rust contaminates the water rather than making it safer.
n.0: Advanced rusting indicates an old or failing tank, not a new one.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which combination best describes a well-managed cold water storage tank?
o: Close-fitting lid, intact screens, insulated, clean and regularly inspected
Open top, no screens, warm location, cleaned once a decade
Translucent lid, torn screens, sited by the boiler
Oversized, always full, uninsulated, never inspected
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A well-managed tank has a close-fitting light-proof lid, intact insect screens, adequate insulation, clean water and regular inspection, all of which control bacterial growth.

n.1: An open top with no screens in a warm spot invites contamination and growth.
n.3: An oversized, always-full, uninsulated, uninspected tank stagnates and warms.
n.2: A translucent lid, torn screens and a hot location are all faults, not good practice.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should a cold water storage tank be kept solely for wholesome water and not connected to other uses?
o: To reduce the number of screens needed
To keep the stored water warmer
To make the tank fill up faster
To prevent contaminated water flowing back and fouling the stored supply
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Keeping the tank dedicated to wholesome water and protected against backflow stops contaminated water from other systems entering and fouling the supply.

n.2: Sharing the tank with other uses does not speed up filling and adds contamination risk.
n.1: Cold water should be kept cool, not warmed, so warming is never a goal.
n.0: Screens are still required on the overflow and vent regardless of what the tank feeds.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why must a cold water storage tank have a close-fitting lid or cover?
o: To make the tank easier to lift and move
To keep out light, insects, dust and debris
To raise the water temperature above 20°C
To increase the water pressure in the system
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A close-fitting lid keeps out light, insects, dust and debris that would encourage legionella growth and contamination.

n.2: Cold water should be kept below 20°C, not warmed above it.
n.3: A lid does not affect the pressure in the system.
n.0: Tanks are not designed to be lifted; the lid is about hygiene.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Cold water in a storage tank should be kept below which temperature to control legionella?
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Legionella multiplies between 20°C and 45°C, so stored cold water should be kept below 20°C.

n.2: 30°C is well inside the range where legionella multiplies.
n.3: 45°C is at the top of the danger zone, not a safe cold limit.
n.0: 60°C is the storage temperature for hot water, not cold.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is fitted to a cold water tank's overflow and vent pipes to stop pests getting in?
o: An insect or vermin screen
A pressure relief valve
A thermostatic mixing valve
A one-way check valve on the inlet
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A fine insect or vermin screen on the overflow and vent stops insects, birds and rodents entering and contaminating the water.

n.1: A pressure relief valve protects hot water systems, not against pests.
n.2: A mixing valve blends hot and cold water and does not screen pests.
n.3: A check valve prevents backflow, not the entry of insects or vermin.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should a cold water storage tank be insulated?
o: To speed up how fast the water heats up
To stop the tank overflowing
To increase how much water it holds
To help keep the stored water below 20°C
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulation keeps the stored cold water cool and below 20°C, out of the temperature range where legionella multiplies.

n.1: Overflow is controlled by the ball valve and overflow pipe, not insulation.
n.2: Insulation does not change the tank's capacity.
n.0: Cold water should be kept cool, not heated up.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: How often should the condition of a cold water storage tank normally be inspected as a minimum?
o: Once every five years
At least once a year
Once every ten years
Only when a fault is reported
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Tanks should be inspected at least annually to check for debris, corrosion, a secure lid, light ingress and water clarity and temperature.

n.0: Five yearly is far too infrequent for a stored water tank.
n.3: Waiting for a fault means problems go unnoticed until it is too late.
n.2: Ten yearly leaves the tank unchecked for a dangerously long time.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You open a cold water tank lid and find dead insects, silt and a film of algae on the water. What should you do?
o: Add extra insulation to the tank and move on
Put the lid back and leave it until the next yearly check
Skim off what you can see and take no further action
Report it and arrange for the tank to be cleaned and disinfected
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insects, silt and algae mean the tank is contaminated, so it must be reported and properly cleaned and disinfected.

n.1: Leaving known contamination in place lets legionella grow unchecked.
n.2: Skimming the surface leaves the underlying contamination and cause behind.
n.0: Insulation does not remove the contamination already in the tank.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During a tank inspection you notice daylight shining in through a gap in the lid. Why does this matter?
o: Light encourages algae and organisms that help legionella grow
Light has no effect and the gap can be ignored
Light increases the water pressure in the tank
Light makes the water freeze more quickly
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Light entering the tank encourages algae and other organisms that support legionella, so the lid must exclude light completely.

n.3: Light does not freeze water; if anything it warms it.
n.2: A gap in the lid does not raise water pressure.
n.1: Light ingress is a real hygiene problem and must be fixed.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cold water storage cistern is found with a loose-fitting timber board resting on top instead of a proper cover. Under HSG274 Part 2, why is this a significant Legionella risk?
o: It prevents the float valve from operating and starves the outlets of water
It allows light, dust, insects and debris to enter, promoting microbial and Legionella growth
A timber board improves insulation and lowers the stored water temperature below 20°C
It makes the cistern easier to inspect so no further action is needed
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A close-fitting, dust- and insect-proof lid is required to keep out light, dust, insects, debris and vermin. A loose board lets contaminants and light in, encouraging microbial and Legionella growth.

n.2: Bare timber is not effective insulation and does not seal the cistern; it can also shed contaminants into the water.
n.3: Ease of inspection does not offset the contamination the open gap allows; the cover must still be close-fitting.
n.0: A board on top does not affect float valve operation; the risk is contamination, not supply failure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the primary purpose of fitting an insect/vermin screen to the overflow and warning pipe of a cold water storage cistern?
o: To stop insects and vermin entering the cistern through the open pipe
To act as a backflow prevention device for the incoming main
To slow the flow so the overflow discharges more gently
To filter scale and sediment out of the stored water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Overflow, warning and vent pipes are potential entry points; fitting screens keeps insects and vermin from getting into the cistern.

n.2: Screens are not intended to regulate flow rate of an overflow discharge.
n.1: A screen is not a backflow prevention device; a suitable air gap and valve arrangement handle backflow.
n.3: Screens keep pests out; they do not remove scale or sediment already in the water.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During an inspection an operative measures the stored water in a loft cistern at 23°C. According to HSG274 Part 2, what does this indicate?
o: The water is at the ideal storage temperature and no action is needed
The float valve has failed and must be replaced immediately
The cistern is oversized and should be drained down permanently
The temperature is too high, favouring Legionella growth, so the cause should be investigated
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Stored cold water should be kept below 20°C. At 23°C it is within the range that favours Legionella proliferation, so the cause (e.g. poor insulation, warm surroundings) should be investigated and corrected.

n.0: Above 20°C is not ideal; it is a warning sign, not an acceptable condition.
n.2: Warmth may relate to oversizing or heat gain, but the immediate finding is a temperature exceedance to investigate, not an instruction to abandon the cistern.
n.1: A high temperature does not indicate a failed float valve; the two are unrelated.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should a cold water storage cistern be correctly sized for the building's actual demand rather than deliberately oversized?
o: Oversized cisterns need larger float valves that fail more often
Oversized cisterns increase mains water pressure at the outlets
Oversized cisterns hold water longer, causing stagnation and warming that promote Legionella
Oversized cisterns cost more to insulate and are harder to lift into a loft
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A cistern sized far above demand turns water over too slowly. The long residence time allows stagnation and warming, both of which encourage Legionella growth.

n.3: Cost and handling are practical issues but not the water-hygiene reason for correct sizing.
n.1: Cistern size does not raise mains pressure; the cistern feeds outlets by gravity or pumping.
n.0: Float valve reliability is not the hygiene rationale; the concern is stagnation from slow turnover.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern lid has a vent left uncovered so the cistern can 'breathe'. What is the correct arrangement under HSG274 Part 2?
o: The vent should be enlarged so more air can circulate over the water surface
The vent should be connected to the overflow so both discharge together
The vent should be fitted with an insect/vermin screen to keep contaminants out while allowing air movement
The vent should be sealed completely so no air can enter the cistern
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Vents are required for the cistern to equalise pressure as the level changes, but they must be screened so insects, vermin and debris cannot enter.

n.3: Fully sealing the vent can cause pressure problems as the water level rises and falls; screening is the correct control.
n.0: Enlarging the opening increases the contamination risk rather than reducing it.
n.1: A vent and an overflow serve different functions and should not be combined.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which combination of materials and finish is appropriate for a cold water storage cistern used for wholesome (potable) water?
o: Galvanised steel with an internal copper heating coil
Reclaimed timber lined with heavy-duty plastic sheeting
WRAS-approved, non-corroding materials suitable for potable water
Untreated mild steel with a bituminous internal coating
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Cisterns should be made from WRAS-approved, non-corroding materials suitable for contact with potable water, so they do not taint the water or shed corrosion products.

n.3: Untreated mild steel corrodes and shedding rust supports microbial growth; ad-hoc bituminous coatings are not suitable potable materials.
n.1: Improvised timber and sheeting are not approved potable-water materials and cannot be reliably cleaned.
n.0: A heating coil warms the stored water, which is the opposite of keeping cold water below 20°C.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative opens a cistern and finds a layer of brown sludge and scale on the base. What is the most appropriate action sequence?
o: Clean and, where required, disinfect the cistern, then identify why the sediment built up
Top up the cistern and record the level as satisfactory
Add more insulation to the outside of the cistern to cool the water
Increase the float valve setting so the cistern holds more water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Sludge, scale and sediment provide nutrients and shelter for Legionella. The cistern should be cleaned and disinfected as required, and the underlying cause investigated to prevent recurrence.

n.1: Recording it as satisfactory ignores a clear contamination finding that needs remedial cleaning.
n.2: External insulation does not remove existing sediment inside the cistern.
n.3: Raising the water level does not clean the cistern and can worsen slow turnover.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: How does keeping stored cold water below 20°C help control Legionella?
o: It sterilises the incoming mains water before it enters the cistern
It kills any Legionella already present within minutes
It keeps the water outside the temperature range in which Legionella multiplies readily
It removes the need to keep the cistern clean and covered
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Legionella proliferates roughly between 20°C and 45°C. Holding cold water below 20°C keeps it outside the range where the bacteria multiply readily.

n.1: Cold storage suppresses multiplication but does not rapidly kill Legionella; low temperature is a control, not a disinfection.
n.0: Temperature control in the cistern does not sterilise the incoming supply.
n.3: Temperature control works alongside cleanliness and covering, not instead of them.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern is installed directly against a hot water cylinder in a warm airing cupboard. Why is this location a concern?
o: The proximity reduces mains pressure feeding the cistern
The cylinder will draw cold water backwards into the cistern
Heat gain from the surroundings can raise the stored water above 20°C, encouraging Legionella
The warm air will dry out the float valve washer and cause leaks
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Storing cold water next to warm plant lets heat transfer into the cistern, pushing the temperature toward or above 20°C and favouring Legionella growth. Cisterns should be sited away from heat sources and insulated.

n.1: A hot cylinder does not siphon water back into a feed cistern; this is not the hazard.
n.3: Warm air is not the reason for float valve failure; the concern is stored water temperature.
n.0: Location beside a cylinder does not reduce incoming mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the main hygiene reason for insulating a cold water storage cistern and its associated pipework?
o: To reduce noise from water entering the cistern
To increase the volume of water the cistern can hold
To limit heat gain and keep the stored cold water below 20°C
To make the float valve operate more quietly
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulation limits heat gain from warm surroundings, helping keep the stored cold water below 20°C and out of the Legionella growth range.

n.0: Noise reduction is not the water-hygiene purpose of insulation.
n.1: Insulation does not change the cistern's capacity.
n.3: Float valve noise is unrelated to the hygiene reason for insulation.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: How often should cold water storage cisterns typically be inspected as part of a Legionella control scheme?
o: At least annually, or more frequently where conditions require
Once every ten years at major refurbishment
Only during commissioning and never again
Only when a fault is reported by building occupants
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Cisterns should be inspected on a regular, scheduled basis, commonly at least annually, with more frequent checks where the risk assessment or conditions indicate.

n.3: Waiting for occupant complaints is reactive and misses developing contamination.
n.1: Ten-yearly intervals are far too long for a Legionella control scheme.
n.2: Commissioning checks alone do not maintain ongoing control.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During a routine visit an operative notices the cistern lid is present but has a gap around a pipe penetration where daylight is visible. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Daylight helps the operative see the water level so the gap is acceptable
The gap provides necessary ventilation and must be left open
The gap allows light and contaminants in and should be sealed to restore a close-fitting cover
The gap shows the cistern is correctly sized and needs no action
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The cover must be close-fitting and light-excluding. A gap at a pipe penetration lets in light, dust and insects and must be sealed while still allowing screened venting.

n.0: Admitting daylight encourages microbial growth; the gap is a defect, not a convenience.
n.1: Ventilation is provided by a screened vent, not by an unsealed gap around a pipe.
n.3: A gap in the cover has nothing to do with correct sizing.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why are dead insects, leaves and other debris found floating in a cistern considered a Legionella control problem?
o: They lower the water temperature below the safe range
They provide nutrients that support microbial and Legionella growth
They improve the taste of the stored water
They increase the mains pressure entering the cistern
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Organic debris supplies nutrients for biofilm and micro-organisms, supporting Legionella growth. Their presence also shows the cover or screens are failing to keep contaminants out.

n.0: Debris does not cool the water; if anything it signals failed protection.
n.2: Contaminants degrade water quality; they do not improve it.
n.3: Floating debris has no effect on incoming mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A building has two cisterns supplying the same system, but valves are set so nearly all draw-off comes from one cistern. What is the water-hygiene concern?
o: The heavily used cistern will run permanently dry
The arrangement guarantees the water stays below 20°C
The little-used cistern stagnates and warms, becoming a Legionella reservoir
Two cisterns always double the mains pressure available
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Where flow is not balanced, the little-used cistern experiences low turnover, stagnation and warming, allowing it to become a reservoir for Legionella. Turnover across storage should be maintained.

n.0: The heavily used cistern is fed by its float valve and refills; it does not run permanently dry.
n.3: Multiple cisterns do not increase mains pressure.
n.1: Poor turnover tends to raise, not guarantee low, stored water temperature.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the correct function of the warning pipe (as distinct from the overflow) on a cold water storage cistern?
o: To vent air displaced as the cistern fills
To drain the cistern completely for cleaning
To supply water to the lowest outlet in the building
To give a visible signal that the float valve is passing and the water level is too high
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The warning pipe discharges in a visible position to warn that the level has risen above normal, indicating a passing or failed float valve, before the higher overflow is reached. It must be screened against pests.

n.2: The warning pipe is not a supply pipe to outlets.
n.0: Venting is provided by a screened vent, not the warning pipe.
n.1: Draining for cleaning is done via a drain-down point, not the warning pipe.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A float (ball) valve is found dripping continuously so the cistern overflows intermittently. Beyond wasting water, why does this matter for Legionella control?
o: A passing valve proves the cistern is correctly sized
Continuous overflow keeps the water permanently below 20°C
A faulty valve and open overflow can let pests in and signals loss of level control that should be repaired
Overflowing raises the mains pressure to the whole building
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A passing float valve causes discharge through the overflow, and a running overflow with a compromised screen is an entry route for insects and vermin. The valve should be repaired to restore proper level control.

n.1: Overflowing does not reliably control temperature and is a fault to fix.
n.0: A leaking valve indicates a defect, not correct cistern sizing.
n.3: An overflowing cistern does not raise mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which statement best describes how sediment at the bottom of a cistern and biofilm on its walls relate to Legionella?
o: They keep the water cool and therefore reduce risk
They only matter in hot water systems, not cold cisterns
They are harmless as long as the lid is fitted
