They shelter and feed micro-organisms, protecting Legionella from control measures
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Sediment and biofilm provide nutrients and physical shelter, protecting Legionella and other organisms and making temperature or biocide control less effective. Cisterns must be kept clean.

n.2: A fitted lid helps keep contaminants out but does not neutralise sediment and biofilm already present.
n.1: Sediment and biofilm are a recognised cold-water storage problem, not just a hot-water issue.
n.0: They do not cool the water; they increase risk.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative is asked to disinfect a cistern found heavily contaminated. What is the correct principle before returning it to service?
o: Leave the sediment in place so the disinfectant has something to work on
Disinfect first, then clean out the debris afterwards
Simply refill with fresh mains water without cleaning or disinfecting
Clean out debris and sludge, then disinfect, so the disinfectant can act on clean surfaces
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Physical cleaning to remove sludge and debris should precede disinfection, because organic matter consumes and shields against biocide. Cleaning then disinfection lets the biocide act effectively on clean surfaces.

n.1: Disinfecting over a layer of debris wastes biocide and leaves shielded organisms; cleaning comes first.
n.0: Sediment protects micro-organisms from disinfectant rather than helping it work.
n.2: Refilling without cleaning or disinfecting leaves a contaminated cistern in service.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should the cold water storage cistern feed the system so that water is drawn off and replaced regularly (good turnover)?
o: So fresh, cooler mains water regularly replaces stored water, limiting stagnation and warming
So the cistern can be left uncovered without risk
So scale forms faster and coats the base protectively
So the float valve can be smaller and cheaper
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Regular turnover means stored water is frequently replaced with fresh, cooler mains water, reducing residence time, stagnation and the temperature rise that favour Legionella.

n.3: Turnover is about water quality, not float valve cost or size.
n.1: Good turnover does not remove the need for a close-fitting cover.
n.2: Scale is a contaminant to be prevented and removed, not encouraged.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: On a hot summer visit an operative records the incoming mains at 15°C but the top of the stored water at 24°C. What is the most likely cause to investigate?
o: The overflow screen is too fine and is heating the water
The mains supply is contaminated and should be shut off
The float valve is oversized for the cistern
Heat gain and stratification from warm surroundings and poor insulation warming the stored water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A large gap between incoming mains and stored temperature, with the surface warmest, points to heat gain from warm surroundings and inadequate insulation. Insulation, siting and turnover should be reviewed.

n.1: Cool incoming mains at 15°C is normal and gives no basis to declare the supply contaminated.
n.2: Float valve size does not warm the stored water.
n.0: A screen mesh does not heat water; the temperature rise comes from heat gain.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which of the following is the correct reason a cold water storage cistern must be provided with a properly fitting, light-tight cover?
o: A cover raises the stored water temperature to aid disinfection
Light and airborne contaminants promote algal and microbial growth in the stored water
A cover removes the need for insulation
A cover increases the flow rate to the taps
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Excluding light discourages algae, and a close-fitting light-tight cover keeps out dust, insects, debris and vermin that would otherwise support microbial and Legionella growth.

n.3: A cover has no effect on the flow rate delivered to outlets.
n.2: A cover and insulation address different risks; one does not replace the other.
n.0: Cold storage should stay below 20°C; a cover is not meant to warm the water.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A newly installed plastic cistern has a screened vent, screened overflow and close-fitting lid, but the lid is a light translucent colour that lets daylight through. What should be done?
o: Remove the screens so the translucent lid can ventilate the cistern
Nothing, because the lid is close-fitting and that is all that matters
Replace or over-cover the lid so it excludes light, preventing algal and microbial growth
Paint the inside of the cistern black to absorb the light
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A cover must exclude light as well as fit closely. A translucent lid admits daylight that encourages algae and microbial growth, so it should be replaced or over-covered with a light-excluding cover.

n.1: Close fit alone is not enough; light exclusion is also required.
n.0: Removing pest screens introduces a contamination route and does not solve the light problem.
n.3: Painting the interior introduces non-approved materials in contact with potable water and does not address the translucent lid correctly.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the correct arrangement of the cold feed (outlet) and the inlet on a storage cistern to encourage good mixing and turnover?
o: Inlet and outlet positioned so incoming water flows across the cistern to the draw-off, avoiding short-circuiting and dead zones
Inlet and outlet both fitted at the base so no fresh water reaches the surface
Inlet and outlet placed immediately next to each other on the same side
Outlet fitted at the very top so only the warmest surface water is drawn off
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Positioning the inlet and outlet so water flows across the cistern promotes turnover and mixing, avoiding short-circuiting and stagnant dead zones where Legionella can develop.

n.2: Adjacent inlet and outlet short-circuit the flow, leaving most of the stored water stagnant.
n.3: Drawing only warm surface water leaves cooler water below stagnant and is poor practice.
n.1: Poor placement creating dead zones increases stagnation risk rather than reducing it.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative finds rust staining and flaking on the interior of an old galvanised cistern. Why is corrosion a water-hygiene concern?
o: Rust lowers the water temperature and improves quality
Rust particles and rough corroded surfaces harbour sediment and biofilm that support microbial growth
Corrosion increases the mains pressure to the outlets
Rust proves the cistern is made from WRAS-approved material
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Corrosion products create sediment and rough surfaces that trap debris and biofilm, providing nutrients and shelter for micro-organisms including Legionella. Non-corroding, approved materials are required.

n.0: Rust does not cool the water and degrades, not improves, its quality.
n.2: Corrosion has no effect on mains pressure.
n.3: Visible corrosion indicates unsuitable or degraded material, the opposite of approved non-corroding material.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern in a seldom-used wing shows very low turnover on the risk assessment. Which control is most appropriate to reduce Legionella risk?
o: Raise the stored water temperature deliberately to try to pasteurise the whole cistern
Leave it exactly as found, since low use must always mean low demand and low risk
Remove the cistern lid to let it cool naturally
Restore regular turnover and keep the cistern clean, cool, covered and correctly sized
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Low turnover leads to stagnation and warming. The control is to restore regular use or flushing, right-size storage where possible, and maintain cleanliness, temperature and covering.

n.0: Warming stored cold water is the opposite of the required control and increases risk.
n.2: Removing the lid exposes the water to light and contaminants, worsening risk.
n.1: Low use actually raises stagnation risk; it must be actively managed, not ignored.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the correct purpose of maintaining a suitable air gap where the mains inlet discharges into a storage cistern?
o: To filter sediment out of the incoming supply
To provide backflow protection preventing stored water being drawn back into the mains
To warm the incoming water before storage
To increase the noise so a passing valve is easier to hear
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A suitable air gap between the inlet and the water level provides backflow prevention, stopping potentially contaminated stored water from siphoning back into the wholesome mains.

n.2: An air gap does not warm the water; the aim is cold storage.
n.0: The gap is a backflow safeguard, not a sediment filter.
n.3: Its purpose is contamination prevention, not making noise.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During cleaning, an operative removes the lid and rests tools and a jacket on the open cistern rim. Why is this poor practice?
o: It increases the mains pressure while the lid is off
It causes the float valve to close permanently
It risks introducing dirt, contaminants and micro-organisms into the open cistern
It could lower the water temperature too far
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: With the cover off, the water is exposed. Placing dirty items over or near the opening risks dropping dirt, debris and micro-organisms into the water. Good hygiene discipline is essential during any cistern work.

n.3: Tools on the rim do not meaningfully cool the water, and cooling is not the hazard here.
n.0: Removing the lid does not change mains pressure.
n.1: Items on the rim do not lock the float valve closed.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which record is most important to keep after inspecting or cleaning a cold water storage cistern under a Legionella control scheme?
o: A dated record of the condition found, temperatures, actions taken and any remedial work
Only the brand of disinfectant, with no dates or findings
A note of who was on site but nothing about the cistern's condition
No record is needed if the cistern looked acceptable
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Control schemes require documented evidence: dated records of condition, temperatures, cleaning or disinfection carried out and remedial actions support monitoring and demonstrate control.

n.1: The disinfectant brand alone, without dates or findings, does not evidence control.
n.2: Attendance without condition data fails to record the state of the cistern.
n.3: Records are required even when conditions look acceptable, to show ongoing monitoring.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern's insect screen on the overflow is found torn. Why should it be repaired or replaced promptly?
o: A torn screen lowers the stored water temperature
A torn screen leaves an open route for insects and vermin to enter the cistern
A torn screen slows the overflow discharge dangerously
A torn screen increases the mains pressure to the building
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The screen's job is to block pests at an opening in the cistern. Once torn, insects and vermin can enter, contaminating the water, so it must be repaired or replaced without delay.

n.2: Overflow discharge speed is not the safety concern; contamination entry is.
n.0: A screen has no role in controlling water temperature.
n.3: A damaged screen does not affect mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why is a very large single cistern often replaced or subdivided into smaller cisterns in modern Legionella-conscious design?
o: Larger cisterns always keep water cooler and are preferred
Smaller cisterns remove the need for covers and screens
Right-sized or divided storage improves turnover and allows one section to be cleaned while the other stays in service
Smaller cisterns hold water long enough to warm up naturally
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Matching storage to demand improves turnover and reduces stagnation; dividing storage lets one part be isolated and cleaned while supply continues, aiding both hygiene and maintenance.

n.3: Allowing water to warm through long residence is undesirable, not a design aim.
n.1: Smaller cisterns still require covers and screens.
n.0: Oversized storage tends to stagnate and warm rather than stay cool.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative is asked why cold water storage temperature is checked at the ball valve inlet and at the cistern outlet. What does comparing these readings help reveal?
o: Whether the float valve is the correct colour
Whether the overflow is discharging into the correct drain
Whether the mains water is being over-chlorinated at source
Whether the stored water is warming above the incoming supply and approaching the Legionella growth range
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Comparing incoming and stored/outgoing temperatures shows any heat gain within the cistern. A significant rise toward 20°C flags stagnation or heat gain needing attention.

n.2: These temperature checks do not measure chlorine levels at source.
n.0: Float valve colour is irrelevant to temperature monitoring.
n.1: Overflow routing is a separate check from stored water temperature.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern serving a healthcare ward is found with a poorly fitting lid and warm, discoloured water. Given the vulnerable occupants, what is the appropriate response?
o: Ignore the finding entirely because the ward taps happen to be used fairly often
Delay any action until the next annual service is due
Simply top the cistern up with fresh water and loosely refit the ill-fitting lid
Treat it as a priority: report, investigate, clean, disinfect and correct the defects
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Warm, discoloured water with a failed cover in a setting with vulnerable people is high priority. It should be reported and remediated promptly: cleaning/disinfection as required plus correcting the cover, temperature and turnover.

n.1: Vulnerable occupants make delay to the next annual service unacceptable.
n.0: Frequent use does not excuse contaminated, warm stored water feeding at-risk patients.
n.2: Topping up and refitting a loose lid does not clean the water or restore a proper cover.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which statement about the relationship between cleanliness and temperature control in cold water storage is correct?
o: Cleanliness and keeping water below 20°C are complementary controls that should both be maintained
A clean cistern can safely store water at any temperature
Temperature control only applies to hot water, not cold storage
Keeping water below 20°C means cleanliness no longer matters
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Legionella control relies on multiple barriers. Keeping the cistern clean and keeping stored water below 20°C work together; neither on its own removes the need for the other.

n.3: Low temperature suppresses growth but sediment and biofilm still create risk, so cleanliness still matters.
n.1: Even a clean cistern must keep cold water below 20°C.
n.2: Keeping cold water below 20°C is a specific requirement for cold storage, not only hot systems.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative finds a cistern where the overflow and warning pipe have been joined into a single pipe with no screen at the open end. What is the correct assessment?
o: The open end must be fitted with an insect/vermin screen to prevent pests entering the cistern
The pipe should be sealed shut to stop any discharge
Acceptable, because an unscreened open end lets the cistern breathe
Acceptable, because combining pipes saves material
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Any pipe open to the cistern interior is a pest entry route and must be screened. The open discharge end requires an insect/vermin screen while still allowing the pipe to discharge.

n.3: Saving material does not justify an unscreened open route for pests into the cistern.
n.2: Venting is provided by a screened vent; an unscreened open pipe is a contamination risk, not acceptable breathing.
n.1: Sealing an overflow/warning pipe would stop it protecting against high water level; it must discharge but be screened.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: After cleaning and disinfecting a contaminated cistern, what is the correct final step before returning it to normal use?
o: Return it to use immediately at full disinfectant concentration
Leave the disinfectant in the stored water permanently for ongoing protection
Thoroughly flush/rinse out the disinfectant to acceptable levels, then refill with wholesome water before use
Drain it and leave it empty to prevent any future growth
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: After disinfection the cistern and system must be flushed/rinsed so residual disinfectant is reduced to acceptable levels, then refilled with wholesome water before being returned to service.

n.1: High-concentration disinfectant is not left in potable stored water; it must be flushed to acceptable levels.
n.0: Supplying water at full disinfection concentration is unsafe for use.
n.3: Leaving the cistern empty removes the supply and does not return it to safe service.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is a calorifier?
o: A pump that circulates cold water around a building
A filter fitted to remove sediment from mains water
A vessel that stores and heats water for the hot water system
A tank that stores cold water before it reaches the taps
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A calorifier is a storage vessel that heats and holds hot water ready for use in the building.

n.0: A calorifier stores and heats water; it is not a circulating pump.
n.1: A calorifier is a heated storage vessel, not a sediment filter.
n.3: Cold water storage is a separate cistern or tank, not a calorifier.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: At what temperature should the water stored in a hot water calorifier be kept?
o: At or above 60°C
Between 45°C and 50°C
At or above 40°C
Between 20°C and 45°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Storing hot water at 60°C or above controls legionella because the bacteria do not survive well at that temperature.

n.3: 20°C to 45°C is the range where legionella multiply, so it is unsafe for storage.
n.2: 40°C is too low and sits within the range that lets legionella grow.
n.1: 45°C to 50°C is still within or near the growth range and is too low for safe storage.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is hot water stored at 60°C or above rather than at a lower, more energy-saving temperature?
o: Because it reduces the water pressure at the taps
Because it makes the water taste better
Because legionella bacteria are killed off at that temperature
Because it stops the pipes rusting
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: At 60°C and above legionella bacteria are killed, so keeping storage hot is the main control measure.

n.1: Taste is not the reason; the temperature is set to control bacteria.
n.3: Temperature is chosen to kill legionella, not to prevent pipe corrosion.
n.0: Storage temperature is about killing bacteria, not about controlling pressure.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: The temperature range in which legionella bacteria multiply most readily is generally given as:
o: 20°C to 45°C
60°C to 80°C
0°C to 10°C
50°C to 60°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Legionella multiply readily between about 20°C and 45°C, which is why hot storage is kept above this band.

n.2: Below 20°C the bacteria stay dormant rather than multiplying readily.
n.1: Above 60°C the bacteria are killed, not multiplying.
n.3: 50°C to 60°C is above the main growth band and is used to hold water safe.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier is best described as which part of the hot water system?
o: The thermostatic mixing valve at the tap
The expansion vessel on the heating circuit
The cold feed cistern in the roof space
The heated storage vessel that supplies hot water to the outlets
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The calorifier is the heated store that feeds hot water out to the taps and other outlets.

n.2: The cold feed cistern supplies cold water in, not the heated store.
n.0: A thermostatic mixing valve blends water at the outlet; it does not store it.
n.1: An expansion vessel absorbs pressure changes and does not store the hot supply.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Keeping a calorifier at the correct hot temperature is described in water hygiene guidance as:
o: Something only required in swimming pools
A measure that increases the risk of legionella
A key control measure against legionella
An optional step only needed in summer
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Maintaining correct storage temperature is one of the main control measures for legionella in hot water systems.

n.3: Temperature control is needed year round, not only in summer.
n.0: It applies to hot water systems in all types of building, not only pools.
n.1: Correct hot temperature reduces the risk; it does not increase it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which statement about a hot water calorifier is correct?
o: It should be run cold to prevent any risk of scalding
It should keep the water lukewarm to save on fuel
It should heat the stored water so it is delivered hot to the system
It is only used to store cold drinking water
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A calorifier's job is to heat and store water so it reaches the outlets hot enough to control bacteria.

n.1: Lukewarm water sits in the growth range and is unsafe.
n.3: A calorifier stores hot water, not cold drinking water.
n.0: Running it cold would encourage bacteria; scalding is controlled by mixing valves, not by cooling storage.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Where in a calorifier does sludge and sediment tend to collect?
o: Only in the flow pipe leaving the vessel
Evenly spread through the whole vessel
At the very top of the vessel
At the base of the vessel
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge and sediment settle and collect at the base of the calorifier under gravity.

n.2: Sediment settles downward, so it does not gather at the top.
n.0: Debris settles inside the vessel rather than collecting only in the outgoing flow pipe.
n.1: It does not stay evenly spread; it settles to the bottom.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is sludge at the base of a calorifier a particular concern for legionella control?
o: It can shelter legionella and provide nutrients for them
It improves the flow of hot water to the taps
It makes the water hotter than intended
It has no effect on legionella at all
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge and sediment shelter legionella and provide nutrients, protecting the bacteria from heat.

n.2: Sludge does not raise the water temperature; it can insulate cooler pockets.
n.1: Sludge restricts and fouls the system rather than improving flow.
n.3: Sludge is a recognised concern because it harbours bacteria, so it does have an effect.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What should be done about the sludge that collects in the base of a calorifier?
o: It should be drained off and the base de-sludged periodically
It should be left in place as it protects the metal
It should be topped up with extra sediment
It should be heated to a higher temperature and ignored
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The base is drained and de-sludged periodically so bacteria have nowhere to shelter.

n.1: Leaving sludge in place lets it shelter legionella, so it must be removed.
n.2: Adding sediment increases the risk; the aim is to remove it.
n.3: Heating alone does not clear the sludge, which still shelters bacteria and must be drained out.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: During calorifier inspection, why is a drain valve at the lowest point of the vessel important?
o: It measures the flow temperature of the water
It vents air out of the top of the vessel
It mixes cold water in to prevent scalding
It lets sediment and sludge be drained from the base
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A low-level drain valve allows the settled sludge at the base to be flushed out during maintenance.

n.0: Temperature is read with a thermometer or sensor, not a drain valve.
n.2: Scald protection is provided by mixing valves, not by the drain point.
n.1: Air is vented at the top; the base drain is for removing sludge.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier is opened for inspection and a layer of soft brown sludge is found in the base. What does this indicate?
o: That the water is being stored too hot
That the vessel is working perfectly and needs no action
A build-up that can harbour legionella and should be removed
That the drain valve is fitted at the wrong height
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge in the base is a build-up that can shelter legionella and must be drained and cleaned out.

n.1: Sludge build-up is a fault to correct, not a sign of perfect operation.
n.0: Sludge relates to settled debris, not to the water being too hot.
n.3: The presence of sludge does not tell you the drain height is wrong; it tells you the base needs de-sludging.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which of these best explains how sediment protects legionella from heat inside a calorifier?
o: It circulates the bacteria out to the drain
It insulates and shelters the bacteria in cooler pockets at the base
It removes the nutrients the bacteria need
It raises the whole vessel above 60°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sediment insulates and shelters bacteria in cooler pockets, protecting them from the hot stored water.

n.3: Sediment does not heat the vessel; it shields cooler areas.
n.2: Sediment supplies nutrients and debris rather than removing them.
n.0: Sediment settles and stays put; it does not flush bacteria away.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: De-sludging a calorifier as part of routine control is mainly carried out to:
o: Remove settled deposits that can support bacterial growth
Increase the storage temperature above 80°C
Reduce the flow rate to the outlets
Add fresh nutrients to the stored water
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: De-sludging removes the settled deposits that would otherwise support and shelter bacterial growth.

n.1: De-sludging clears deposits; it does not set the storage temperature.
n.2: It is not done to reduce flow; it keeps the vessel clean.
n.3: The aim is to remove nutrient-rich debris, not to add nutrients.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which practice helps keep the base of a calorifier free from harmful sediment?
o: Never opening the vessel once it is installed
Keeping the drain valve permanently sealed
Regular draining and inspection of the base
Lowering the storage temperature below 50°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Regular draining and inspection of the base removes sediment before it can shelter bacteria.

n.0: Never opening the vessel lets sludge build up unchecked.
n.1: A permanently sealed drain prevents the base being cleared of sludge.
n.3: Lowering the temperature encourages bacterial growth rather than controlling it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is meant by 'stratification' inside a hot water calorifier?
o: Sludge dissolving evenly into the stored water
The water being the same temperature throughout the vessel
Air becoming trapped in the flow pipe
Hot water sitting on top of cooler layers, so temperature varies with height
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Stratification is layering, where hotter water rises to the top and cooler water sits below, so temperature varies with depth.

n.1: Even temperature throughout is the opposite of stratification.
n.0: Stratification refers to temperature layers, not to sludge dissolving.
n.2: Trapped air in a pipe is a separate issue from temperature layering in the store.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Because of stratification, which part of a calorifier is most likely to be cooler than the rest?
o: The top of the vessel
The outgoing flow connection
The base of the vessel
The insulation on the outside
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Cooler water settles low, so the base of the calorifier is most likely to be below the target temperature.

n.0: Hot water rises, so the top is usually the hottest part.
n.1: The flow leaves from the hotter upper region, not the cool zone.
n.3: External insulation is not part of the stored water's temperature layering.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why does the whole volume of water in a calorifier need to reach the control temperature, not just the top?
o: Because the flow pipe draws from the coldest layer
Because cooler layers, especially at the base, can let legionella survive
Because only the base water reaches the taps
Because the top layer cools down fastest
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: If cooler layers remain, particularly at the base, legionella can survive there, so the whole volume must reach temperature.

n.3: The concern is the cool base surviving, not the top cooling fastest.
n.2: Water is drawn from the hotter upper region, but any surviving bacteria at the base can still spread through the system.
n.0: The flow normally draws from the hotter top, which is why the neglected base is the risk.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A thermometer at the top of a calorifier reads 62°C, but a check at the base reads 41°C. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The vessel is stratified and the base is not reaching temperature
The base thermometer is reading too high
The whole vessel is safely above 60°C
Hot water has collected at the base
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A hot top and cool base is classic stratification, showing the base is not reaching the control temperature.

n.2: A base reading of 41°C means the vessel is not safely above 60°C throughout.
n.1: 41°C is a low reading, not a falsely high one.
n.3: Hot water rises to the top; it is cooler water, not hot, that has collected at the base.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Stratification in a calorifier is a hygiene concern mainly because:
o: It makes the water at the taps too hot to use
It can leave a cool zone at the base within the legionella growth range
It removes sludge from the base
It increases the storage capacity of the vessel
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Stratification can leave the base in the 20°C to 45°C growth range, allowing legionella to multiply.

n.0: Stratification leaves a cool base; it does not overheat the tap water.
n.2: Stratification does not clear sludge; cool bases and sludge often occur together.
n.3: It does not change the vessel's capacity; it changes the temperature distribution.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: To overcome stratification and make sure the base heats up, a calorifier may be fitted with or checked for:
o: A cold water bypass to cool the base
Adequate heat input and, where used, a shunt pump to mix the contents
Extra sludge to hold the heat in
A reduced storage temperature setting
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Enough heat input, sometimes with a shunt pump to circulate the contents, helps bring the whole volume including the base up to temperature.

n.0: Cooling the base with a bypass would make the problem worse.
n.2: Sludge insulates cool pockets and shelters bacteria; it is removed, not added.
n.3: Lowering the setting would leave more of the vessel too cool.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which reading pattern in a calorifier would suggest the whole volume is safely up to temperature?
o: Top and base both at or above 60°C
Top at 60°C and base at 35°C
Top at 45°C and base at 60°C
Top at 55°C and base at 40°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: When both the top and the base sit at or above 60°C, the whole volume has reached the control temperature.

n.1: A base at 35°C shows a cool zone in the growth range, so it is not safe throughout.
n.2: A top at 45°C is below the safe storage value.
n.3: A base at 40°C is within the growth range and not up to temperature.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which of these is the correct way to think about a calorifier's stored temperature?
o: The average of the top and base is all that counts
Only the hottest layer at the top matters
The coolest part of the volume, not just the hottest, must be controlled
Only the temperature of the incoming cold feed matters
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Control depends on the coolest part of the stored water reaching temperature, because that is where bacteria could survive.

n.1: The hot top can mask a dangerously cool base, so the top alone is not enough.
n.3: The cold feed temperature does not tell you whether the store has been heated through.
n.0: An average can hide a cool base that is still in the growth range.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: On a hot water calorifier, which two temperatures are routinely monitored to check the system is working?
o: The flow temperature and the return temperature
The drain water and the outside air
The insulation surface and the floor
The cold feed and the room temperature
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The flow leaving the calorifier and the return coming back are the two temperatures routinely monitored to confirm hot water is maintained.

n.3: Room and cold feed temperatures do not confirm the hot circuit is holding heat.
n.1: Drain water and outside air are not the routine monitoring points for the hot circuit.
n.2: Surface and floor temperatures are not the hot water flow and return.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: The flow temperature from a hot water calorifier should normally be at least:
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Hot water should leave the calorifier at 60°C or above so it stays hot as it travels round the system.

n.3: 45°C is too low; it sits near the top of the growth range.
n.0: 40°C is within the growth range and unsafe as a flow temperature.
n.2: 30°C is well within the growth range and far too low.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: The return temperature of a hot water circuit coming back to the calorifier should commonly be kept at least:
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The return should stay at 50°C or above so that no part of the circulating loop drops into the growth range.

n.1: 30°C is within the growth range and shows the loop has cooled too far.
n.3: 20°C is far too low and well inside the growth range.
n.2: 10°C would mean the hot loop has effectively gone cold.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier flow reads 60°C but the return reads 43°C. What does the low return most likely mean?
o: The system is performing exactly as intended
The thermometer on the return is reading too high
The stored water is too hot and must be reduced
Hot water is cooling too much in the circulation loop
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A return well below the recommended value shows the water is losing too much heat around the loop, allowing cool zones to form.

n.2: A low return points to heat loss, not to the store being too hot.
n.1: 43°C is a low reading, not a falsely high one.
n.0: A return in the growth range is a fault to investigate, not intended performance.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is monitoring the return temperature as well as the flow temperature important?
o: Only the return water reaches the taps
The flow temperature cannot be measured directly
It confirms the far ends of the loop are staying hot, not just the outlet
The return temperature is always higher than the flow
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Checking the return confirms that water is still hot after travelling round the building, so no cool zones have developed.

n.3: The return is normally slightly cooler than the flow, not higher.
n.0: Water is drawn from the flow side to the taps; the return brings unused water back.
n.1: The flow temperature can be and is measured directly at the calorifier.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: If routine monitoring shows the calorifier return temperature has been steadily falling over several weeks, the appropriate response is to:
o: Ignore it, as the return temperature does not matter
Seal the return pipe so no water comes back
Lower the flow temperature to match the return
Investigate the cause, as heat loss in the loop may be creating cool zones
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A falling return should be investigated because heat loss in the circulation loop can create cool zones where legionella grow.

n.0: The return temperature is a key monitoring value and must not be ignored.
n.2: Lowering the flow to match a poor return spreads the problem instead of fixing it.
n.1: Sealing the return would stop circulation and make the risk worse.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Recording flow and return temperatures on a regular schedule is an example of:
o: A task that replaces the need to keep water hot
A one-off check needed only at installation
An optional extra with no hygiene value
Routine monitoring that shows the control scheme is working
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Regular flow and return records are routine monitoring that demonstrates the temperature control scheme is being maintained.

n.1: Monitoring is ongoing, not a single check at installation.
n.0: Monitoring confirms the water is hot; it does not remove the need to keep it hot.
n.2: It has clear hygiene value as evidence that control is being kept.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is the purpose of a secondary circulation (secondary return) on a hot water system?
o: To filter sediment out of the hot water
To store extra hot water for peak demand
To keep hot water moving so it stays hot throughout the building
To supply cold water to the drinking taps
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A secondary return continuously circulates hot water so it stays hot in the pipework and does not cool in long runs.

n.3: The secondary return handles hot water, not the cold drinking supply.
n.1: Storage is the calorifier's job; the secondary loop keeps water moving.
n.0: Sediment removal is done by draining and cleaning, not by the return loop.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Without a working secondary return, what tends to happen to hot water in long pipe runs?
o: It gets hotter the further it travels
It is filtered clean of all bacteria
It turns into cold drinking water
It cools down and can drop into the legionella growth range
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: In long dead legs or runs without circulation, stationary hot water cools into the range where legionella multiply.

n.0: Water loses heat as it sits in pipes; it does not get hotter.
n.2: It becomes tepid rather than a safe cold supply.
n.1: Cooling in the pipe does not remove bacteria; it encourages their growth.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A secondary circulating pump on the hot water system helps control legionella by:
o: Adding fresh nutrients to the returning water
Storing sludge until the next service
Keeping the water in the loop moving and above the control temperature
Cooling the water down to save energy
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The circulating pump keeps water moving so the whole loop stays above the control temperature and does not stagnate.

n.3: The pump keeps water hot; it is not there to cool it.
n.0: It moves water, it does not add nutrients.
n.1: Sludge is drained from the calorifier base, not stored by the pump.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Outlets sited a long way from the calorifier are best kept safe by:
o: Fitting a cold water cistern nearby
A secondary return loop that circulates hot water close to them
Reducing the calorifier storage temperature
Leaving the taps unused for long periods
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A secondary return brings circulating hot water close to distant outlets so the water reaching them stays hot.

n.3: Leaving taps unused causes stagnation, increasing the risk.
n.2: Reducing storage temperature lets more of the system fall into the growth range.
n.0: A cold cistern does not address keeping the hot supply hot at distant outlets.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: At a large site, taps at the far end of a wing run only warm even after running for a while, while taps near the plant room run hot quickly. This most likely points to:
o: The calorifier being stored far too hot
The cold water supply being switched off
A problem with the secondary circulation reaching that wing
Too much sludge in the tap spouts
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Distant outlets that never get properly hot suggest the secondary circulation is not maintaining temperature to that part of the building.

n.0: If storage were too hot, distant taps would tend to run hotter, not cooler.
n.3: Warm-not-hot water across a whole wing points to circulation, not sludge in individual spouts.
n.1: A cold supply being off would affect cold water, not the warmth of the hot outlets.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which statement about the secondary return temperature is correct?
o: It is expected to be cold when it reaches the calorifier
It should be allowed to fall to room temperature overnight
It should be kept hot, commonly at 50°C or above, all the way round the loop
It only matters on cold water systems
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The secondary return should stay hot, commonly at least 50°C, so the whole loop remains above the growth range.

n.0: A cold return would mean the loop has stagnated and cooled dangerously.
n.3: The secondary return is a feature of the hot water system, not the cold.
n.1: Letting it fall to room temperature overnight would allow bacteria to multiply.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: How does a point-of-use (instantaneous) water heater differ from a calorifier in terms of legionella risk?
o: It stores a much larger volume of warm water
It always runs cooler than a calorifier and is more dangerous
It removes the need to keep any water hot anywhere
It heats water on demand and stores little or none, giving lower storage risk
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Instantaneous heaters heat water only as it is drawn, so with little or no stored warm water the storage risk is lower.

n.0: A point-of-use heater stores little or no water, unlike a large calorifier.
n.1: Its lower stored volume gives lower, not higher, storage risk.
n.2: Other parts of a system, and scald control, still need managing; the heater does not remove all requirements.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is a point-of-use heater serving a single tap generally considered lower risk for legionella storage?
o: It stores water for several days before use
It runs at a much lower temperature than a calorifier
There is little or no stored water sitting in the growth range
It has a large sludge trap at its base
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: With little or no standing warm water, there is far less opportunity for legionella to multiply in storage.

n.1: Lower risk comes from little stored water, not from running cooler.
n.3: Point-of-use heaters are small and generally have no large sludge trap.
n.0: They heat on demand rather than holding water for days.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A small unvented hot water cylinder differs from an open-vented calorifier mainly in that it:
o: Cannot store water above 45°C
Never needs its temperature checked
Has no need for any hygiene controls
Is a sealed, pressurised store fed directly from the mains
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: An unvented cylinder is a sealed, pressurised vessel supplied directly from the mains rather than from an open cistern.

n.1: It still stores hot water and its temperature must be checked.
n.0: It is designed to store water hot, typically at 60°C or above.
n.2: Being sealed does not remove the need for temperature and hygiene controls.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Even where instantaneous heaters reduce storage risk, what consideration still applies at the outlet?
o: The water must be kept below 20°C at the tap
There is no risk of any kind at the outlet
The heater must store water for a week first
Scald risk, because water delivered hot can burn without temperature control at the tap
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Hot water delivered to an outlet can scald, so scald control at the tap remains a consideration even with low storage risk.

n.1: Scalding is a genuine risk at hot outlets, so it is not risk-free.
n.0: Hot outlets are not kept cold; scald is managed by mixing, not by cooling the supply.
n.2: Instantaneous heaters heat on demand and do not store water for a week.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which of these hot water arrangements stores the largest volume of warm water and so needs the most storage-related control?
o: A single point-of-use heater at one basin
A sealed kettle in the staff kitchen
A small instantaneous shower heater
A central calorifier serving the whole building
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A central calorifier holds a large stored volume, so it carries the greatest storage-related legionella control requirement.

n.0: A single point-of-use heater stores little or no water.
n.2: An instantaneous shower heater heats on demand with minimal storage.
n.1: A kettle is boiled and emptied in use and is not part of the stored hot water system.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A washroom is fed by a small local instantaneous heater rather than the main calorifier. What is the correct view of its legionella risk?
o: Storage risk is lower, but the outlet and any short pipe still need managing
It needs no attention of any kind
It carries exactly the same storage risk as the main calorifier
It is more dangerous than the calorifier because it is smaller
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Little stored water lowers the storage risk, but the outlet and any pipework to it still need managing.

n.2: With little stored water its storage risk is lower than the large calorifier's.
n.1: Even low-risk fittings need basic management such as regular use and scald control.
n.3: Smaller stored volume makes it lower risk for storage, not more dangerous.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier is taken out of service for internal inspection and cleaning. Before opening it, the operative should first:
o: Add sludge to protect the internal surfaces
Open the vessel while it is still full and hot
Turn the storage temperature up to 90°C
Isolate and safely drain the vessel following the correct procedure
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The calorifier must be isolated and safely drained down following the correct procedure before it can be opened for inspection.

n.2: Raising the temperature does not prepare the vessel for opening and adds a burn hazard.
n.0: Sludge is removed during cleaning, never added.
n.1: Opening a full, hot vessel is unsafe and risks scalding.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Internal inspection and cleaning of a calorifier is carried out mainly to:
o: Add a new nutrient supply for the water
Increase the pressure in the hot water mains
Lower the storage temperature permanently
Remove scale, sludge and debris that can harbour bacteria
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Cleaning removes the scale, sludge and debris that provide shelter and nutrients for bacteria.

n.1: Cleaning is about hygiene, not raising mains pressure.
n.2: Cleaning does not aim to lower the storage temperature; the water is still kept hot.
n.0: The purpose is to remove nutrient sources, not to add them.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: To save energy, a site manager suggests turning the calorifier down so the stored water sits at 50°C. Why is this the wrong decision for water hygiene?
o: 50°C is hot enough to sterilise the whole system
Storage below 60°C lets legionella survive and multiply in the vessel
Lower storage always removes sludge from the base
It would make the return temperature too high
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Dropping storage below 60°C moves the vessel toward the growth range, letting legionella survive and multiply.

n.0: 50°C does not reliably kill legionella; storage is kept at 60°C or above for that reason.
n.2: Lowering the temperature does nothing to remove sludge; it encourages growth.
n.3: Lower storage would tend to lower the return, not raise it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Staff are worried about scalding from hot taps. What is the correct way to control scald risk without lowering the calorifier storage temperature?
o: Remove the hot supply from the building
Turn the calorifier off between uses
Store the water at 40°C in the calorifier
Fit thermostatic mixing valves at the outlets to blend the water down
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Thermostatic mixing valves blend hot and cold at the point of use, controlling scald risk while storage stays safely hot.

n.2: Storing at 40°C would create ideal conditions for legionella.
n.1: Switching the calorifier off between uses lets the water cool into the growth range.
n.0: Removing the hot supply is not a practical or safe control for a working building.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which statement about scald control and storage temperature is correct?
o: Lower storage to prevent scalding and accept the legionella risk
Keep storage at 60°C or above and control scalding at the tap with a TMV
Scald risk means hot water should never be stored above 45°C
A TMV replaces the need to store water hot
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The safe approach is to store water hot at 60°C or above for legionella control and use a thermostatic mixing valve to limit the temperature at the tap.

n.0: Lowering storage to stop scalds trades one hazard for a worse one; both must be managed correctly.
n.2: Storing at 45°C or below invites legionella growth.
n.3: A TMV controls delivery temperature but does not remove the need to store water hot.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: After a calorifier has been cleaned and refilled, a sensible check before returning it to normal use is to:
o: Confirm it heats through and the flow and return reach the control temperatures
Leave it cold overnight to settle
Skip temperature checks as it has just been cleaned
Add sediment back to protect the base
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Confirming the vessel heats through and that flow and return reach the correct temperatures shows control has been restored after cleaning.

n.1: Leaving it cold overnight lets the fresh fill cool into the growth range.
n.2: Cleaning does not guarantee correct temperatures, so checks are still needed.
n.3: Sediment is what was removed; adding it back would defeat the cleaning.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: An operative finds a calorifier has been left running at 52°C 'to prevent scalding'. The correct action is to:
o: Turn it down further to 45°C
Leave it as it is because 52°C feels safe
Drain the vessel and leave it empty
Report it and have storage restored to 60°C or above, with TMVs for scald control
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Storage should be restored to 60°C or above, with scald risk managed by thermostatic mixing valves at the outlets.

n.1: 52°C is within reach of the growth range and is not a safe storage temperature.
n.0: Lowering it to 45°C makes conditions even better for legionella.
n.2: Draining and leaving it empty does not provide the building with safe hot water and is not the required fix.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: During a monthly check an operative finds the calorifier base drain has never been opened and heavy sediment is suspected. What is the appropriate response?
o: Record it and take no further action
Raise the storage temperature to 90°C instead
Arrange for the base to be drained and de-sludged as part of maintenance
Weld the drain valve shut to stop leaks
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A base that has never been drained should be de-sludged as part of maintenance so bacteria have nowhere to shelter.

n.3: Sealing the drain shut prevents the base ever being cleared of sludge.
n.1: Overheating the store does not remove the settled sludge, which still shelters bacteria.
n.0: Recording without acting leaves the sludge in place and the risk uncontrolled.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: At what temperature should a calorifier store hot water to control legionella?
o: Below 20°C
60°C or above
About 45°C
Between 20°C and 30°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above, a temperature at which legionella cannot survive.

n.3: 20–30°C is within the range where legionella actively multiplies.
n.2: 45°C is at the top of the danger zone and does not kill legionella.
n.0: Below 20°C is the target for cold water, not hot storage.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is sludge and sediment at the base of a calorifier a concern?
o: It makes the water heat up too quickly
It improves the flow and return balance
It raises the storage temperature above 60°C
It shelters legionella from the hot water above it
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge and sediment settling at the base protect legionella and other bacteria from the heat of the stored water, so the base must be drained and de-sludged.

n.0: Sludge insulates and slows heat reaching the base, it does not speed heating.
n.2: Sludge does not raise the storage temperature; it creates cool, sheltered layers.
n.1: Sludge worsens performance and hygiene, it does not improve flow balance.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What does stratification inside a calorifier mean, and why is it a problem?
o: The tank overflows because it is overfilled
The flow and return pipes are the same temperature
Cooler layers form so not all the water reaches safe temperature
The water is heated far above 60°C and wastes energy
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Stratification is where cooler layers form in the cylinder so part of the water sits in the danger zone below 60°C rather than reaching safe temperature.

n.3: The problem is cool layers, not overheating or wasted energy.
n.0: Stratification is about temperature layers, not overfilling or overflow.
n.1: Equal flow and return temperatures would indicate good, not poor, heating.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which temperatures are checked on a calorifier to confirm it is working correctly?
o: The room and outdoor air temperatures
The flow and return temperatures
The overflow and vent temperatures
The cold feed and float valve temperatures
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The flow (outgoing) and return temperatures are checked to confirm the whole cylinder is reaching and holding a safe temperature.

n.2: Overflow and vent pipes are features of cold tanks, not calorifier performance checks.
n.3: Cold feed and float valve temperatures relate to the cold supply, not hot storage output.
n.0: Room and outdoor air temperatures do not tell you about the stored hot water.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: You take a calorifier's flow temperature at 62°C but the return is only 48°C. What does this most likely indicate?
o: The cylinder is running too hot and should be turned down
Cool layering or sludge, so it needs draining and further checks
Everything is fine and no action is needed
The cold water tank lid is missing
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A return well below the flow suggests cool layers or sludge at the base, so the calorifier should be drained, de-sludged and re-checked.

n.0: The problem is a low return in the danger zone, not overheating.
n.2: A 48°C return sits in the danger zone and must not be ignored.
n.3: These readings are about the calorifier, not the cold tank lid.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: You open a calorifier's drain point during service and a large amount of brown sludge runs out. What should you do?
o: Drain and de-sludge the base fully, then record and report it
Close the drain quickly to avoid losing hot water
Ignore it because sludge is normal and harmless
Lower the storage temperature below 60°C to settle it
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Brown sludge shelters bacteria, so the base should be drained and de-sludged fully, with the finding recorded and reported.

n.1: Stopping early leaves the sludge and its bacteria in place.
n.2: Sludge is not harmless; it protects legionella from the heat.
n.3: Dropping below 60°C would make the problem worse, not settle it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is hot water stored at 60°C or above rather than at a warm 40°C?
o: 40°C water is too hot and would scald users at the tap
40°C water damages the calorifier over time
60°C uses less energy than storing at 40°C
Legionella is killed at 60°C but thrives at around 40°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: At 60°C legionella is killed, whereas around 40°C sits in the range where the bacteria multiply readily.

n.0: 40°C is a warm, comfortable temperature, not a scalding one.
n.2: Storing hotter uses more energy, not less; safety is the reason.
n.1: It is legionella growth, not tank damage, that rules out 40°C storage.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: To confirm a calorifier is not stratified, what should be true of the stored water?
o: The whole cylinder, top to bottom, reaches safe temperature
The water should be cooler at the outlet than the base
Only the base needs to be hot where the sludge sits
Only the top of the cylinder needs to be hot
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Avoiding stratification means the entire cylinder from top to bottom reaches a safe temperature, leaving no cool layers.

n.3: A hot top with a cool base is exactly the stratification to be avoided.
n.2: A cool top over a hot base is still stratified and unsafe.
n.1: The outlet should not be cooler; cool layers are the hazard.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier stores hot water for distribution around a building. To control legionella, at what minimum temperature should the stored water be held?
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: ACOP L8 / HSG274 Part 2 require hot water in a calorifier to be stored at 60°C or above, which is hot enough to kill legionella bacteria over time.

n.1: 50°C is the minimum for water reaching outlets, not for stored water; legionella can still survive at 50°C in storage.
n.3: 55°C is below the storage standard and allows legionella to persist in the vessel.
n.2: 65°C exceeds the requirement; the standard minimum for storage is 60°C, not 65°C.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: During a monthly check you record the calorifier flow at 61°C but the return leg at only 44°C. What does the low return reading most likely indicate?
o: Normal operation that needs no action
Cooling in the circulation loop, so parts of the system fall into the legionella growth range
The whole system is over-heated and should be turned down
A faulty thermometer that can be ignored
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The return should be at least 50°C. A return of 44°C shows the water has cooled below the control temperature as it circulates, allowing legionella to multiply in the cooler parts of the loop; the cause must be investigated and corrected.

n.2: A 44°C return is too cold, not too hot; turning the system down would worsen the problem.
n.3: A reading this far below standard must be acted on, not dismissed as instrument error without checking.
n.0: A return below 50°C is outside the required standard and is not acceptable normal operation.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why does sludge and sediment collecting at the base of a calorifier present a particular legionella risk?
o: It raises the stored water temperature above safe limits
It improves circulation through the vessel
It insulates the base and shelters bacteria in cooler debris where they can multiply
It makes the water discolour but is otherwise harmless
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge and scale settle at the base, where the water is often coolest. The debris provides nutrients and shelters legionella from the heat, so the base must be checked and periodically drained/de-sludged.

n.3: Sediment is not merely cosmetic; it harbours bacteria and biofilm and is a genuine health risk.
n.0: Debris tends to keep the base cooler, not hotter; it does not raise temperature above safe limits.
n.1: Sediment obstructs and stagnates flow at the base rather than improving circulation.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: 'Stratification' inside a hot water calorifier refers to which of the following?
o: The vessel operating above its rated pressure
A protective scale layer forming on the vessel walls
Layers of water at different temperatures forming, with cooler water settling at the base
Hot water flowing too quickly through the outlets
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Stratification is the layering of water by temperature. Cooler water settles to the bottom while hotter water rises, so the base can sit in the legionella growth range even when the top of the vessel is hot.

n.1: Stratification describes temperature layering of the water, not a scale coating on the walls.
n.0: It is a thermal layering effect, unrelated to the vessel's operating pressure.
n.3: It concerns temperature distribution inside the store, not the flow rate at outlets.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is the correct purpose of a secondary circulation (hot water return) system on a large building?
o: To store additional hot water away from the calorifier
To keep hot water circulating so it stays above 50°C throughout long pipe runs
To lower the flow temperature and save energy
To reduce the amount of cold water entering the calorifier
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A secondary return keeps hot water constantly moving around long distribution runs so temperature does not drop; the return to the calorifier should be at least 50°C, preventing cool stagnant legs where legionella grows.

n.3: The secondary loop circulates hot water; it does not regulate cold water entering the vessel.
n.2: Its purpose is to maintain, not lower, temperature; the hot water must stay hot, not be cooled to save energy.
n.0: It is a circulation loop, not additional storage capacity.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A site manager proposes lowering the calorifier storage temperature from 60°C to 52°C to cut energy bills and reduce scald risk. Under ACOP L8, is this acceptable?
o: Yes, provided the outlets still reach 45°C
Yes, if a chemical dosing system is added at the same time
Yes, because 52°C is warm enough to prevent bacterial growth
No; storage must stay at 60°C, and scalding is controlled separately using TMVs
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Storage must be kept at 60°C or above for legionella control; it must never be reduced to save energy or manage scalding. Scald risk is controlled at the point of use with thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs), not by lowering stored temperature.

n.0: Reducing storage to 52°C breaches the control standard regardless of outlet temperature; 45°C outlets do not justify it.
n.2: 52°C is within the range where legionella can survive in storage and is not a safe storage temperature.
n.1: Chemical dosing does not permit abandoning the 60°C storage standard; temperature control remains the primary requirement.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Hot water reaching outlets should achieve at least what temperature within one minute of running?
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: HSG274 Part 2 requires hot water to reach the outlet at 50°C or above within one minute of running, confirming hot water is being delivered throughout the system.

n.0: 60°C is the storage standard for the calorifier, not the minimum delivery temperature at outlets.
n.2: 55°C applies to healthcare premises; the general standard at outlets is 50°C.
n.1: 45°C is a mixed-water target after a TMV, not the hot supply temperature at the outlet.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: When checking a calorifier for temperature control, why is the reading taken at the base of the vessel especially important?
o: The base is the coolest point, so it confirms the whole volume has reached temperature
The base is always the hottest point in the vessel
The base reading is only needed to check water pressure
The base is where the safety valve is fitted
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Because cooler water and sediment settle at the bottom, the base is typically the coldest point. Confirming it is at temperature verifies the entire stored volume, not just the hot upper layer, is being controlled.

n.3: The base check is about temperature of the coolest water, not the location of the safety valve.
n.1: The base is normally the coolest point due to stratification, not the hottest.
n.2: The base temperature check monitors thermal control against legionella, not water pressure.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Point-of-use (instantaneous) water heaters are sometimes preferred for infrequently used outlets. What is their main legionella advantage?
o: They heat water only when needed, so there is little or no stored water to stagnate
They store large volumes of warm water close to the tap
They remove the need to monitor any temperatures
They allow the temperature to be run below 60°C safely
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Instantaneous heaters warm water on demand and hold little or no stored volume, so there is minimal opportunity for water to sit warm and stagnate, reducing the legionella risk associated with storage.

n.1: Their advantage is the opposite: they hold little or no stored volume, not large warm reserves.
n.3: They do not license running below control temperatures; scald control is still via TMVs where fitted.
n.2: Monitoring is still required; the outlet and heater performance must be checked as part of the scheme.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Before a calorifier can be internally inspected and cleaned, which step is essential?
o: Raise the storage temperature to 70°C for an hour
Add extra cold water to dilute any sediment
Drain the vessel down and isolate it safely so the interior can be accessed
Increase circulation to flush debris out through the outlets
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Internal inspection and cleaning require the calorifier to be drained down and safely isolated so the interior, particularly the base, can be examined and any sludge removed.

n.0: Raising the temperature does not remove accumulated sludge or allow physical inspection of the interior.
n.1: Adding cold water dilutes nothing usefully and would only cool the store; it does not enable inspection.
n.3: Circulation cannot flush settled sludge out through outlets; the vessel must be drained and cleaned.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: On a healthcare premises, at what minimum temperature should hot water reach the outlets, reflecting the higher-risk population?
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: In healthcare settings serving vulnerable people, HSG274 Part 2 sets the higher outlet standard of 55°C within one minute, above the general 50°C, to give an added margin of protection.

n.3: 50°C is the general premises standard; healthcare adopts the stricter 55°C figure.
n.2: 45°C is a blended-water figure after a TMV, not the hot delivery temperature.
n.1: 43°C is around the maximum safe mixed temperature at a bath/shower, not a hot supply standard.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A duty-holder wants to protect users from scalding at wash-hand basins in a care home without lowering the stored hot water temperature. What is the correct approach?
o: Fit thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) at the outlets to blend the hot water down
Remove the hot supply from the basins entirely
Reduce the calorifier to 48°C at night only
Insulate the pipework to cool the water before the tap
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Scald protection is delivered at the point of use with TMVs, which blend stored 60°C water down to a safe temperature at the tap while storage and distribution stay hot for legionella control.

n.2: Dropping the calorifier to 48°C, even at night, breaches the storage standard and risks legionella growth.
n.1: Removing the hot supply is impractical for a care home and does not address safe warm-water delivery.
n.3: Insulation keeps water hot; it does not cool it, and deliberately cooling pipework would create risk.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: The temperature range within which legionella bacteria multiply most readily is approximately:
o: 50°C to 60°C
20°C to 45°C
0°C to 15°C
60°C to 70°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Legionella multiplies in the approximate range of 20°C to 45°C. Storing hot water at 60°C and keeping cold water below 20°C both keep water out of this growth band.

n.2: Below about 20°C legionella survives but does not readily multiply; growth is slow, not optimal.
n.0: At 50°C to 60°C legionella is being killed off, not multiplying.
n.3: Above 60°C legionella is rapidly destroyed, so this is not a growth range.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier's flow temperature reads a healthy 62°C, yet a distant outlet on the same system only reaches 47°C after two minutes. What is the most likely underlying issue?
o: The calorifier thermostat is set too high
The cold water supply is contaminating the hot outlet
The outlet thermometer is reading too low and should be replaced
Poor secondary circulation or a stagnant leg allowing the hot water to cool before it reaches the outlet
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Hot water leaving at 62°C but arriving at 47°C shows heat loss on the way, typically from inadequate secondary circulation or a long dead-leg where water sits and cools, dropping into the growth range.

n.0: A high flow temperature is not the fault; the problem is heat lost between the calorifier and the outlet.
n.1: Cold-water contamination would suggest a faulty valve, but the pattern here points to distribution heat loss and poor circulation.
n.2: Assuming instrument error without investigating the circulation would leave a genuine legionella risk unaddressed.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why should the whole stored volume of a calorifier reach the control temperature rather than just the water near the outlet?
o: To prevent the safety valve from operating too often
To reduce the building's energy consumption
To speed up the delivery of hot water to taps
Because cooler zones, especially at the base, can allow legionella to grow and seed the system
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: If only the upper part of the vessel is hot, cooler water at the base sits in the growth range and can contaminate the whole system. The entire volume must reach 60°C so no reservoir of bacteria remains.

n.1: Heating the full volume is a control measure, not an energy-saving one.
n.2: It concerns eliminating cool zones for safety, not the speed of hot water delivery.
n.0: It is about bacterial control across the stored volume, not safety-valve operation.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Small unvented hot water cylinders are increasingly common in smaller premises. Compared with a large stored calorifier system, what is generally true?
o: They present a lower storage risk but scald protection still needs attention at outlets
They must always be run below 60°C to avoid over-pressure
They eliminate the need for any temperature checks
They are exempt from legionella control because they are sealed
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A small unvented cylinder holds far less water than a large calorifier, so the storage risk is lower, but it still stores hot water and must be kept at 60°C, with scalding controlled at outlets by TMVs where needed.

n.2: Temperature monitoring is still needed to confirm the cylinder and outlets meet the standards.
n.3: Being sealed does not exempt a cylinder from legionella control; it still stores hot water.
n.1: Unvented cylinders are designed to run at 60°C safely; they are not required to run cooler.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: As part of the routine scheme, how often are calorifier flow and return temperatures typically checked?
o: Annually
Only when a fault is reported
Monthly
Once every three years
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: HSG274 Part 2 recommends checking calorifier flow and return temperatures monthly to confirm the system is holding 60°C flow and 50°C return.

n.3: A three-yearly interval is far too infrequent to detect a temperature fault before risk develops.
n.1: Checks are planned and routine, not left until a problem is reported.
n.0: Annual is too infrequent for flow/return; the annual task is typically the more detailed base inspection.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier has a drain valve at its base. As part of legionella control this valve is used to:
o: Regulate the incoming cold water pressure
Bleed air from the top of the vessel
Draw off and check water from the base, and periodically remove settled sludge
Increase the flow temperature during high demand
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The base drain lets the operator draw off water from the coolest point to check its temperature and clarity, and to de-sludge the vessel by flushing out settled sediment.

n.1: Air is vented from the top of a vessel, not drained from the base valve.
n.3: A drain valve does not raise flow temperature; that is set by the heat source and thermostat.
n.0: Incoming cold water pressure is managed by supply valves, not the calorifier base drain.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A large calorifier serves a hotel. To confirm the full volume is being heated, an operative draws water from the base drain and measures 51°C, while the flow reads 61°C. What does this suggest?
o: The system is fully compliant and needs no action
The building has no legionella risk at all
Stratification is occurring, with a cooler layer at the base that needs investigation
The flow thermometer is faulty
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A base reading of 51°C against a 61°C flow shows the bottom of the vessel is significantly cooler, a sign of stratification. The cooler base layer sits nearer the growth range and must be investigated and corrected.

n.0: A 10°C difference with a base near the growth range is not full compliance; the base should also be at 60°C.
n.3: Both readings are plausible; the issue is a genuine cool layer at the base, not a faulty flow gauge.
n.1: A cooler base layer is exactly the kind of condition that can allow legionella, so risk is not absent.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is it important that hot water pipework, including the secondary return, is adequately insulated?
o: To minimise heat loss so water stays above 50°C and out of the growth range
To increase the water pressure at the outlets
To reduce noise from the flowing water
To allow the storage temperature to be safely reduced
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Insulation reduces heat loss along the pipes, helping keep circulating hot water above 50°C so it does not cool into the 20-45°C growth range between the calorifier and the outlets.

n.2: Noise reduction is not the reason; the aim is thermal control for legionella.
n.1: Insulation conserves heat; it does not raise water pressure.
n.3: Good insulation supports maintaining 60°C storage, not reducing it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: During an annual inspection the base of a calorifier is found to hold a thick layer of brown sludge. What is the correct response?
o: Leave it, as sludge protects the vessel from corrosion
Raise the storage temperature permanently to burn the sludge off
Add more cold water to dilute and settle the sludge
Drain, clean and de-sludge the vessel, then confirm temperatures on refilling
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Settled sludge harbours legionella and biofilm, so the vessel must be drained, physically cleaned and de-sludged. On refilling, temperatures are confirmed to ensure the whole volume reaches 60°C.

n.0: Sludge shelters bacteria and provides nutrients; it is a hazard, not a protective layer to be left.
n.1: Heat alone does not remove accumulated sludge from the base; physical cleaning is required.
n.2: Adding cold water increases sediment and cools the store; it does not resolve the contamination.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is the correct minimum temperature for hot water returning to the calorifier through the secondary circulation loop?
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The secondary return should be at least 50°C when it reaches the calorifier, confirming the circulating hot water has stayed hot throughout the loop and not fallen into the growth range.

n.2: 45°C is below the return standard and sits within the legionella growth range.
n.3: 48°C is still below the 50°C minimum required for the return.
n.0: 55°C is higher than required; the minimum return standard is 50°C, though a higher figure is not a fault.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Two calorifiers are installed in parallel with a shared pipework arrangement, but one is kept on standby and rarely used. What is the legionella concern?
o: The standby vessel uses too much energy
Parallel calorifiers cannot be temperature controlled
Water in the idle standby calorifier can stagnate and cool, becoming a reservoir for legionella
The duty calorifier will overheat to compensate
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A rarely used standby vessel can hold stagnant water that cools into the growth range, acting as a reservoir that seeds the system when it is brought into use; standby units should be kept hot or regularly cycled and monitored.

n.0: The concern is stagnation and bacterial growth, not the energy an idle vessel uses.
n.1: Parallel calorifiers can be temperature controlled; the issue is stagnation in the idle unit.
n.3: The duty calorifier does not overheat to compensate; the risk lies in the stagnant standby vessel.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A thermometer pocket (test point) is fitted to the flow and return of a calorifier primarily to:
o: Allow accurate temperature readings to be taken without opening the system
Provide a point to add biocide chemicals
Let air escape from the circulation loop
Reduce the pressure in the return pipe
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Thermometer pockets let an operative insert a probe and take accurate flow and return readings quickly and safely, without breaking into the pipework, supporting routine monthly monitoring.

n.1: Test pockets are for temperature measurement, not for dosing chemicals into the system.
n.2: Air is vented through dedicated vents, not through a thermometer pocket.
n.3: A thermometer pocket does not regulate or reduce pressure in the return.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Following a period when a building was closed and the hot water system stood idle, what should be done to the calorifier and distribution before reoccupation?
o: Bring the system up to temperature and flush all outlets to clear stagnant water
Nothing, provided the calorifier was left switched on
Drain the system permanently and rely on point-of-use heaters
Simply lower the temperature to save energy until occupants return
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: After a shutdown, stagnant water may have cooled into the growth range, so the calorifier is brought back up to 60°C and every outlet is flushed through to clear stagnant water before people use the system.

n.1: Even if left on, distant legs and outlets may have stagnated and must be flushed before reoccupation.
n.3: Lowering the temperature after a shutdown increases risk; the system must be hot and flushed.
n.2: Permanent draining is not the standard response; the system is recommissioned by heating and flushing.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which statement best explains why running a calorifier below 60°C 'to save energy' is not permitted for legionella control?
o: It increases the building's water pressure unsafely
It moves stored water towards the 20-45°C range where legionella multiplies
It makes the outlets deliver water too quickly
It causes the vessel to corrode more quickly
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Lowering storage below 60°C brings the stored water closer to the 20-45°C growth range, allowing legionella to multiply. Temperature control is the primary safeguard and must not be relaxed to save energy.

n.3: Corrosion is a maintenance concern but is not the legionella reason storage must stay at 60°C.
n.2: Storage temperature does not control how quickly outlets deliver water.
n.0: Storage temperature has no meaningful effect on the building's water pressure.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier's incoming cold feed is measured at 24°C on a warm day. Why is this relevant to the hot water system's legionella risk?
o: Warm feed water is already within the growth range and adds thermal load, so the calorifier must still reach 60°C throughout
Warmer incoming water reduces the heat needed, so it is beneficial
It means the calorifier can be safely run cooler
It has no bearing on hot water safety
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Cold water above 20°C is already in the growth range and gives the calorifier a warmer, higher-risk starting point. The vessel must still bring the entire volume to 60°C, and the cold-side warming should also be investigated.

n.1: Warmer feed water is a risk factor, not a benefit; it is closer to the growth range.
n.3: The temperature of the feed water directly affects risk and the heating duty of the calorifier.
n.2: A warm feed is a reason for vigilance, not for running the calorifier cooler.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Sentinel outlets on a hot water system are best described as:
o: Any three outlets chosen at random each month
Only the outlets fitted with thermostatic mixing valves
The outlets that are never used
