The outlets nearest to and furthest from the calorifier, chosen to represent the system
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sentinel outlets are the first and last (nearest and furthest) on each loop. Monitoring them monthly gives a representative picture of temperatures across the whole hot water distribution.

n.1: Sentinel status is about position on the system, not whether a TMV is fitted.
n.2: Unused outlets are a separate stagnation concern; sentinels are chosen for their representative position.
n.0: Sentinels are fixed representative points, not random each month, so trends can be tracked.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: On a hospital ward, a TMV-served shower reads a mixed 41°C while the hot supply feeding the TMV reads 58°C. How should this be interpreted?
o: The hot supply is too cold and must be raised
The whole system must be shut down immediately
The mixed temperature is dangerously high and the TMV has failed
The TMV is blending 58°C hot water down to a safe 41°C, which is acceptable for the outlet
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The 58°C hot supply meets the healthcare standard, and the TMV is correctly blending it to a safe 41°C at the shower to prevent scalding, while storage and distribution stay hot for legionella control.

n.0: 58°C meets the healthcare hot supply standard, so the hot feed is not too cold.
n.2: 41°C is a safe blended shower temperature, not dangerously high; the TMV is working correctly.
n.1: The readings show correct operation, so an immediate shutdown is not warranted.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why should thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) be positioned as close as possible to the outlet they serve?
o: To keep the length of cooled, blended-temperature pipework to a minimum
To allow the hot supply to be run below 50°C
To make the valve easier to reach for cleaning
To increase the flow rate at the tap
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Blended water leaving a TMV is in the legionella growth range, so the pipe between the valve and outlet should be as short as possible to limit the volume of warm water that could support bacterial growth.

n.2: Ease of access is a minor benefit, not the control reason for close positioning.
n.3: Position relative to the outlet does not increase the flow rate at the tap.
n.1: The hot supply to the TMV must still meet its temperature standard; close mounting does not permit a cooler hot supply.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier is described as having 'inadequate turnover'. What does this mean for legionella risk?
o: The stored water is replaced too slowly, so it can sit warm and stagnate
The vessel is heated well above 60°C
The circulation pump is running continuously
Hot water is used up faster than it can be heated
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Poor turnover means water sits in the vessel for long periods. If any part is below 60°C, stagnant warm water can allow legionella to grow, so vessel sizing and demand should suit actual usage.

n.3: That describes excessive demand outstripping heating, which is a different issue from low turnover.
n.1: Overheating above 60°C is not what inadequate turnover means; the concern is stagnant warm water.
n.2: Continuous pump operation actually improves circulation rather than causing poor turnover.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: An operative is asked to record calorifier readings in the site log. Which set of values would indicate the system is meeting the standard?
o: Flow 55°C, return 45°C
Flow 61°C, return 52°C
Flow 58°C, return 47°C
Flow 60°C, return 43°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Flow must be at least 60°C and return at least 50°C. Flow 61°C with return 52°C satisfies both, showing the water is stored hot and stays hot around the loop.

n.2: A 58°C flow is below the 60°C standard and a 47°C return is below 50°C, so both fail.
n.0: Flow 55°C and return 45°C are both below their minimums and sit near the growth range.
n.3: The 60°C flow just meets the standard but the 43°C return is well below 50°C and within the growth range.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A single-feed 'combination' style calorifier serving both storage and demand is found running with the base at 40°C. What is the priority action?
o: Treat it as a control failure: investigate, restore full-volume heating and check for sludge
Reduce demand on the vessel and monitor next month
Record it as satisfactory because the top is hot
Increase the outlet flow rate to mix the layers
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A base at 40°C sits squarely in the growth range and is a temperature-control failure. The cause (stratification, poor heating, sludge) must be investigated and the whole volume restored to 60°C, with the base checked and cleaned.

n.2: A hot top with a 40°C base is not satisfactory; the cool base is a legionella reservoir.
n.1: A base in the growth range needs prompt corrective action, not a month's further monitoring.
n.3: Raising outlet flow does not reliably heat the base; the heating fault and any sludge must be addressed.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Where a calorifier cannot practically achieve 60°C throughout because of its design, what is the correct course of action?
o: Seek expert advice and apply additional control measures, because temperature alone is now insufficient
Switch the vessel off between uses
Ignore the base temperature and monitor only the flow
Accept a lower storage temperature as normal
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: If temperature control cannot be fully achieved, the risk assessment must be reviewed and competent/expert advice sought so that supplementary control measures are put in place; the shortfall is never simply accepted.

n.3: A lower storage temperature must not be accepted as normal; the control gap has to be addressed.
n.1: Switching the vessel off between uses creates stagnation and cooling, increasing risk.
n.2: Ignoring the base leaves the coolest, highest-risk zone unmonitored, which is unsafe.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is the main reason records of calorifier temperatures and cleaning should be kept as part of the water safety scheme?
o: Only to satisfy the water supplier's billing
To demonstrate the control scheme is being followed and to reveal trends before they become failures
To decide when to replace the outlet taps
To calculate the building's energy bills
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Records provide evidence that monitoring and cleaning are being carried out as required, and reviewing them reveals adverse trends, such as a slowly falling return temperature, so action can be taken before a control failure occurs.

n.3: Records support legionella control and compliance, not energy bill calculation.
n.0: They exist for the water safety scheme and legal duty of care, not for the water supplier's billing.
n.2: Tap replacement is a maintenance decision, not the purpose of temperature and cleaning records.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is a 'dead leg' on a water system?
o: A length of pipe closed at one end that water is not regularly drawn through
A pipe that carries water at high pressure to a tap
A pipe fitted with a working outlet used every day
The main incoming supply pipe from the street
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A dead leg is a section of pipe, often closed off at one end, where water is not drawn through and so sits and stagnates.

n.1: A pressurised pipe in daily use keeps water moving, which is the opposite of a dead leg.
n.3: The incoming main is a live, flowing supply, not a stagnant dead end.
n.2: A pipe with an outlet used every day has good turnover and is not a dead leg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does water sitting in a blind end or dead leg become a legionella risk?
o: It stays still and warms up, letting bacteria and biofilm multiply
It is under too much pressure for bacteria to survive
It is constantly refreshed with cold mains water
It is chlorinated more heavily than the rest of the system
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Still, warming water in a dead leg gives legionella the stagnation, warmth and biofilm it needs to grow.

n.1: Dead legs are typically low or no pressure, and pressure does not kill legionella anyway.
n.2: A dead leg is not refreshed; that lack of turnover is exactly the problem.
n.3: Trapped water in a dead leg loses any disinfectant residual over time rather than gaining it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: In a dead leg with no through-flow, how does any fresh water reach the closed end?
o: Only very slowly by diffusion, so the water effectively stagnates
Quickly, because pressure pushes it through the closed end
It is pumped through on a timed cycle automatically
It cannot warm up because no water reaches it at all
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: With no outlet drawing water through, the closed end is refreshed only by slow diffusion, so it stagnates.

n.1: A closed end has no exit, so pressure cannot push a flow through it.
n.2: There is no automatic timed cycle on an ordinary dead leg.
n.3: Water does reach it and sits there warming to the surrounding temperature.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which best describes why a blind-ended pipe helps legionella grow?
o: The fast flow scours away any bacteria present
Ultraviolet light inside the pipe kills the bacteria
The cold temperature freezes any bacteria
Stagnant, warm water and biofilm collect there undisturbed
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A blind end holds undisturbed warm water and biofilm, the ideal conditions for legionella to multiply.

n.0: There is no fast flow in a blind end; the water is static.
n.2: Water in a blind end tends to reach room temperature, not freeze.
n.1: There is no UV light inside ordinary pipework.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What tends to happen to the temperature of water trapped in a long dead leg?
o: It drifts towards the surrounding room temperature, often into the growth range
It always stays below 20 degrees C
It always stays above 60 degrees C
It stays exactly at the temperature of the live main
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Trapped water loses or gains heat towards the ambient temperature, frequently landing in the 20-45 degrees C growth range.

n.3: Because it is not flowing, it drifts away from the main's temperature towards ambient.
n.1: It only stays cold if the surroundings are cold, which is often not the case.
n.2: It only stays hot if kept hot; a dead leg normally cools down.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A dead leg is a concern mainly because it combines which conditions?
o: Stagnation, warmth and nutrients from biofilm
Freezing temperatures and constant movement
High pressure and daily flushing
High flow, cold water and fresh disinfectant
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Stagnation, warmth and biofilm nutrients together are the recipe for legionella growth in a dead leg.

n.3: High flow, cold and fresh disinfectant are protective, not a risk.
n.1: Freezing and constant movement would suppress growth, not encourage it.
n.2: High pressure and daily flushing would keep the section safe.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: How does a live, regularly used pipe differ from a dead leg in legionella terms?
o: The live pipe has water moving through it, so it is far less likely to stagnate
The live pipe has no water in it between uses
The live pipe holds warmer water so it is more dangerous
There is no real difference between the two
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Regular flow through a live pipe keeps water moving and turned over, unlike the static water in a dead leg.

n.2: A live cold pipe is normally kept cool, and flow reduces risk rather than raising it.
n.1: A live pipe stays full and pressurised between uses; it does not empty.
n.3: There is a large difference: flow versus stagnation is central to legionella control.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: When a run of pipework is no longer used, what is the correct way to remove the risk?
o: Paint the pipe so it is easy to identify
Fit an extra valve and close it
Cap the end and leave the pipe in place
Cut it out back to the live main so no stub is left to stagnate
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Removing redundant pipe right back to the live main leaves no stub of standing water to stagnate.

n.2: A capped pipe still holds a length of stagnant water and remains a dead leg.
n.1: A closed valve still leaves standing water beyond it that stagnates.
n.0: Painting the pipe identifies it but does nothing about the stagnant water inside.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why is simply capping off a disused pipe not good enough?
o: The capped length still holds standing water that stagnates and can grow legionella
Caps are illegal on water systems
A cap always leaks within a few days
Capping raises the water pressure dangerously
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A cap seals the end but the water trapped behind it becomes a stagnant dead leg.

n.1: Caps are commonly used fittings and are not illegal.
n.3: Capping a short branch does not create a dangerous pressure rise.
n.2: A properly fitted cap does not necessarily leak; the issue is the stagnant water it traps.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A sink has been removed but the pipe that fed it has been capped just below the old tap position. What should be done?
o: Insulate the capped pipe and take no further action
Leave the capped pipe as it is
Cut the redundant pipe back to the live main and cap it there
Open the cap once a month to let air in
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The disused branch should be removed back to the live main so no stagnant dead leg is left.

n.1: Leaving the long capped stub leaves stagnant water that can grow legionella.
n.3: Letting air in does not refresh the water and does not fix the dead leg.
n.0: Insulation alone does not remove the stagnant water inside the redundant pipe.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: When cutting back a redundant pipe, how close to the live main should the cut be made?
o: About one metre away from the main is close enough
Halfway along the old branch
Right at the old outlet position only
As close as practicable to the live pipe so almost no dead length remains
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Cutting back close to the live main leaves the shortest possible stub, minimising standing water.

n.0: A metre of pipe left on the main is still a dead leg holding stagnant water.
n.1: Cutting halfway leaves a long stagnant stub still connected.
n.2: Cutting at the old outlet removes nothing useful and leaves the whole branch as a dead leg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A shower in a rarely used changing room has been taken out, and the supply pipe left capped at full length behind the wall. What is the best action?
o: Fit a longer cap to seal it better
Record it on the plan and leave it capped
Flush the capped pipe from the mains end once a year
Remove the redundant pipework back to the live supply
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The capped full-length branch is a dead leg and should be removed back to the live supply.

n.2: A capped pipe has no outlet, so it cannot be flushed through from the mains.
n.0: A better cap still traps the same stagnant water.
n.1: Recording it does not remove the stagnation risk it poses.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: An old water heater has been removed and its feed pipe capped where the heater used to stand. Why is this a problem?
o: The cap will make the remaining hot water too hot
There is no problem once the heater is gone
The capped feed is now a dead leg full of standing water
The capped pipe will freeze the rest of the system
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The capped feed pipe holds standing water with no turnover, forming a dead leg where legionella can grow.

n.0: A cap on a redundant feed does not raise the temperature of live water elsewhere.
n.3: A capped branch does not freeze the working system.
n.1: There is a problem: the redundant capped pipe stagnates and should be removed to the main.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why is closing an isolation valve, rather than removing the pipe, an unsatisfactory way to deal with a disused branch?
o: Isolation valves are not allowed on cold water systems
The standing water beyond the closed valve still stagnates
The valve will always seize open
A closed valve increases the water temperature
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Water trapped beyond a closed valve has no turnover and stagnates just like any other dead leg.

n.0: Isolation valves are normal and permitted components of water systems.
n.3: Closing a valve does not heat the water beyond it.
n.2: The concern is the stagnant water, not the valve seizing open.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the recommended action for an outlet, such as a tap, that is only used occasionally?
o: Flush it regularly, at least weekly, to keep water turning over
Turn up the water pressure to it
Cap it off permanently between uses
Leave it, because occasional use is enough
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Little-used outlets should be flushed regularly, at least weekly, to move fresh water through and prevent stagnation.

n.2: Capping it turns a usable outlet into a dead leg; if truly not needed it should be removed, not capped.
n.1: Raising pressure does not move water through an outlet that is not being opened.
n.3: Occasional use is often not frequent enough to prevent stagnation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does an oversized pipe or storage vessel increase legionella risk?
o: Bigger vessels are automatically self-cleaning
Large pipes always run at very high velocity
The extra volume keeps all the water below 20 degrees C
Water turns over slowly, so it sits longer and can stagnate
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Oversized pipes and tanks hold more water than is used, so turnover is poor and water stagnates.

n.2: A large volume does not by itself keep water cold; slow turnover often lets it warm.
n.1: Oversizing lowers velocity, it does not raise it.
n.0: Large vessels are not self-cleaning; sediment and biofilm can build up in them.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What does 'low turnover' of water in part of a system mean for legionella control?
o: Water is replaced so fast that bacteria cannot settle
The disinfectant residual is automatically boosted
Water sits for long periods, giving bacteria time to multiply
The water is kept permanently above 60 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Low turnover means water lingers, giving legionella the standing time it needs to grow.

n.0: That describes high turnover, which is protective, not low turnover.
n.3: Low turnover does not keep water hot; it usually drifts into the warm growth range.
n.1: Standing water tends to lose disinfectant residual, not gain it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cold water storage tank is far larger than the building actually needs. Why is this a concern?
o: The stored water turns over slowly and can warm up and stagnate
It uses less energy so there is no downside
The water will be too cold to use
The tank will overflow constantly
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: An oversized tank holds more water than is drawn each day, so turnover is poor and the water can warm and stagnate.

n.3: Tank size does not by itself cause constant overflowing; a float valve controls the level.
n.2: Slow turnover tends to let cold water warm, not make it colder.
n.1: There is a clear downside: poor turnover and stagnation risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A hotel bedroom is only used a few times a year, so its basin and shower are rarely run. What is the sensible control measure?
o: Increase the hot water temperature for that room only
Do nothing, as the room is rarely occupied
Include the outlets in a regular flushing routine
Disconnect the water and cap the pipes at the outlets
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Rarely used outlets should be flushed regularly so fresh water moves through and does not stagnate.

n.3: Capping at the outlets turns them into dead legs; unused pipework should be removed, not capped.
n.0: Raising temperature for one room does not move water through unused outlets.
n.1: Doing nothing lets the standing water stagnate between the infrequent uses.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: How often, as a minimum, should seldom-used outlets generally be flushed to control stagnation?
o: Once a year at the annual service
Once every six months
At least weekly
Only when the water looks discoloured
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Guidance is to flush little-used outlets at least weekly to keep water moving and prevent stagnation.

n.1: Six-monthly is far too infrequent to prevent stagnation.
n.3: Waiting for visible discolouration means the problem has already developed.
n.0: An annual flush leaves long periods for stagnation to occur.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which situation is most likely to cause stagnation in a water system?
o: A short pipe run in constant use
A branch of pipework that is hardly ever used
A well-sized pipe carrying water at normal flow
A tap that is opened many times every day
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A branch that is hardly ever used has poor turnover, so water sits and stagnates.

n.3: A tap used many times a day keeps water moving and turned over.
n.0: A short pipe in constant use has good turnover and low stagnation risk.
n.2: A correctly sized pipe at normal flow keeps water moving well.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Legionella multiplies most readily within which temperature range?
o: Between 0 and 5 degrees C
Below freezing point
Between about 20 and 45 degrees C
Between 60 and 70 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The 20 to 45 degrees C range is where legionella grows fastest, so systems aim to keep water outside it.

n.0: At 0 to 5 degrees C bacteria are dormant, not multiplying rapidly.
n.3: At 60 to 70 degrees C legionella is killed, not growing.
n.1: Below freezing the bacteria do not multiply.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A long cold water pipe runs through a warm building before reaching the tap. What is the risk?
o: The cold water warms up towards the growth range on its way
The cold water gets colder as it travels
The water becomes over-chlorinated
The pipe cannot carry cold water at all
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A long run through warm surroundings lets cold water pick up heat and drift into the 20-45 degrees C range.

n.1: Passing through warm areas warms the water rather than cooling it.
n.3: The pipe carries cold water fine; the issue is it warming up along the way.
n.2: Standing in a warm pipe does not add chlorine to the water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Cold water should be kept below what temperature to hold down legionella growth?
o: 60 degrees C
20 degrees C
45 degrees C
55 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Cold water is kept below 20 degrees C so it stays out of the temperature range where legionella multiplies.

n.2: 45 degrees C is well inside the growth range, not a safe cold target.
n.3: 55 degrees C is a hot water distribution target, not a cold one.
n.0: 60 degrees C is a hot storage target, far too warm for cold water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Hot water is normally stored and distributed at which temperatures to control legionella?
o: Stored at 45 degrees C and distributed at 40 degrees C
Stored at 20 degrees C and distributed at 15 degrees C
Stored at 60 degrees C and distributed so it reaches outlets at 50 degrees C or above
Stored at 30 degrees C and distributed at 25 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Storing hot water at 60 degrees C and delivering it at 50 degrees C or above keeps it out of the growth range and controls legionella.

n.3: 30 and 25 degrees C sit right inside the growth range and would encourage legionella.
n.0: 45 and 40 degrees C are within the growth range, not a safe hot regime.
n.1: 20 and 15 degrees C are cold-water figures, far too low for hot water control.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does a long hot water pipe run to a distant outlet raise legionella risk?
o: The hot water gets hotter and scalds the pipe
Long runs always keep water above 60 degrees C
Long runs remove all bacteria by the time water arrives
The hot water cools as it travels and can fall into the growth range before reaching the tap
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Over a long run, hot water loses heat and can drop into the 20-45 degrees C range where legionella grows.

n.0: Hot water loses heat over distance; it does not gain it.
n.1: Long runs tend to let hot water cool below target, not stay above 60 degrees C.
n.2: Cooling in a long run does not sterilise the water; it can make matters worse.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A tap in an outbuilding is fed by a very long pipe from the main building. What temperature problem is likely?
o: Both hot and cold arrive far colder than intended
The temperatures are unaffected by the pipe length
Both hot and cold arrive far hotter than intended
Cold water arrives warmer and hot water arrives cooler than intended
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Over a long run the cold gains heat and the hot loses it, so both can drift towards the growth range.

n.0: The cold does not get colder over a long run; it warms up.
n.2: The hot does not get hotter; it cools down over distance.
n.1: Long runs clearly do affect the delivered temperatures.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: When a hot tap is opened, roughly how quickly should the water reach its proper hot temperature?
o: Within about one minute of running the tap
Only after half an hour of running
Within about ten minutes of running the tap
It does not matter how long it takes
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Hot water should reach at least 50 degrees C at the outlet within about one minute; longer means the run is too long or poorly insulated.

n.2: Ten minutes indicates a badly designed or uninsulated run holding cooling water.
n.1: Half an hour would mean a very large volume of cooled water sitting in the pipe.
n.3: It does matter: slow-to-heat outlets signal cooled, higher-risk water in the pipe.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should cold water pipes be insulated (lagged)?
o: Only to stop the pipe looking untidy
To make the water flow faster
To help keep the water below 20 degrees C by shielding it from warmth
To raise the water temperature above 20 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Insulating cold pipes shields them from surrounding heat so the water stays below 20 degrees C.

n.1: Insulation does not change flow rate.
n.3: The aim is to keep cold water cool, not to warm it up.
n.0: Appearance is not the reason; temperature control is.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why are hot water pipes insulated?
o: To help hold the water hot and reduce heat loss along the run
To cool the water down to the growth range
Purely to save the cost of the pipe
To allow the pipe to be run next to cold pipes safely
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Lagging hot pipes reduces heat loss so the water stays above the growth range all the way to the outlet.

n.1: Insulation keeps hot water hot, it does not cool it into the growth range.
n.3: Insulating a hot pipe does not make it safe to sit against a cold pipe; separation is still needed.
n.2: The purpose is temperature control and energy saving, not the pipe cost.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What can happen if a cold water pipe is run right next to a hot water pipe?
o: The cold pipe cools the hot water to a safe level
Nothing, because pipes never affect each other
The cold water automatically stays below 20 degrees C
Heat transfers across and warms the cold water towards the growth range
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A hot pipe alongside a cold pipe warms it by conduction and radiation, pushing the cold water into the growth range.

n.0: The much larger heat in the hot pipe warms the cold, not the other way to a safe state.
n.1: Adjacent pipes clearly do affect each other's temperature.
n.2: Sitting next to a heat source is exactly what stops it staying below 20 degrees C.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Besides insulating pipes, what else helps keep cold water below 20 degrees C?
o: Leaving cold pipes uninsulated so they lose heat
Routing cold pipes away from hot pipes and other heat sources
Bundling cold and hot pipes tightly together
Running cold pipes through the boiler house for convenience
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Keeping cold pipes clear of hot pipes, heaters and other heat sources stops the cold water from warming up.

n.3: A boiler house is a warm place that would heat the cold water.
n.2: Bundling hot and cold together transfers heat into the cold pipe.
n.0: Cold water does not lose heat to a warm room; it gains it, so it needs insulation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: In a service duct, the cold water pipe runs tight against an uninsulated hot flow pipe. What should be done?
o: Move only the cold pipe closer to the hot pipe
Wrap both pipes together in one sleeve
Leave them together as it saves duct space
Separate them and insulate the pipes so the cold stays below 20 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The pipes should be separated and insulated so heat from the hot pipe cannot warm the cold water into the growth range.

n.2: Saving space at the cost of warming the cold water is not acceptable for legionella control.
n.1: One sleeve around both still lets heat pass from hot to cold.
n.0: Moving the cold pipe closer makes the heating worse, not better.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the main purpose of insulating water pipes in legionella control?
o: To keep hot water hot and cold water cold, holding both out of the growth range
To make the water taste better
To increase the water pressure at the taps
To reduce the noise of flowing water only
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Insulation maintains temperatures, keeping hot water above and cold water below the legionella growth range.

n.2: Insulation does not raise water pressure.
n.1: Insulation does not change the taste of the water.
n.3: Noise reduction is not the purpose; temperature control is.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cold water pipe passes through a warm plant room with no lagging. Why is this a risk?
o: The pipe will burst from the warmth
The warm room heats the unlagged cold water towards the growth range
The plant room keeps the cold water below 20 degrees C
There is no risk if the water is moving occasionally
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: An unlagged cold pipe in a warm plant room absorbs heat and can rise into the 20-45 degrees C range.

n.2: A warm room heats the water; it does not keep it cold.
n.0: Warmth does not burst a pipe; the concern is the temperature of the water.
n.3: Occasional movement does not overcome constant heating; lagging and separation are needed.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should pipes, fittings and materials in a water system be WRAS-approved (approved for use with drinking water)?
o: They change the colour of the water for identification
They make the water flow faster
They are always the cheapest option available
They are tested not to encourage bacterial growth or contaminate the water
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: WRAS-approved materials are tested to be suitable for potable water and not to support microbial growth or leach contaminants.

n.2: Approval is about safety and suitability, not being the cheapest.
n.1: Approved materials do not speed up flow.
n.0: Approved materials do not colour the water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why do flexible hoses and rubber components carry extra legionella risk?
o: They are made of stainless steel that never corrodes
They cannot hold any water inside them
They always run at over 60 degrees C
Materials such as EPDM can provide nutrients and support biofilm and legionella growth
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Flexible hoses and rubber parts like EPDM can release nutrients and harbour biofilm, feeding legionella growth.

n.2: Flexible hoses are not kept permanently above 60 degrees C.
n.1: They hold water like any other pipe, which is part of the problem.
n.0: They are typically rubber-based, not stainless steel.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the concern with certain rubber washers, seals and hoses in a water system?
o: They make water permanently sterile
They have no effect on water quality at all
They can release nutrients that feed bacteria and support biofilm
They keep water above the growth range
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Some rubber and elastomer components leach nutrients and hold biofilm, which supports legionella growth.

n.0: They do not sterilise water; they can do the opposite.
n.3: They do not keep water hot.
n.1: They can clearly affect water quality by supporting growth.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should materials that support biofilm be avoided in water systems?
o: Biofilm makes the water flow more smoothly
Biofilm shelters and feeds legionella, protecting it from disinfectant
Biofilm keeps the water permanently cold
Biofilm has no link to legionella
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Biofilm harbours legionella and other bacteria and shields them from temperature and chemical control.

n.0: Biofilm roughens surfaces and can restrict flow, not smooth it.
n.2: Biofilm does not control temperature.
n.3: Biofilm is strongly linked to legionella survival and growth.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why are corrosion-resistant materials preferred in water pipework?
o: Rusty surfaces kill legionella on contact
Corroded pipes carry water at a safer temperature
Corrosion has no bearing on legionella risk
Corrosion products and rough surfaces give biofilm and bacteria somewhere to build up
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Corrosion creates rough, scaled surfaces and sediment that shelter biofilm and bacteria, so corrosion-resistant materials are preferred.

n.1: Corrosion does not control water temperature.
n.0: Rust does not kill legionella; it can shelter it.
n.2: Corrosion is relevant because it fosters biofilm and sediment.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A flexible braided hose has been fitted to connect a tap, and the outlet is used only now and then. Why is this a raised risk?
o: The hose cannot hold any standing water
Braided hoses are always WRAS-approved and risk-free
The hose material can support biofilm and the low use lets water stagnate in it
The hose keeps the water above 60 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A flexible hose can harbour biofilm, and infrequent use leaves standing water in it, combining two risks.

n.3: The hose does not keep water hot.
n.0: The hose holds standing water, which is part of the problem.
n.1: Not all braided hoses are approved, and even approved ones still need good turnover.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should non-approved or unsuitable fittings not be used on a water system?
o: They guarantee the water stays below 20 degrees C
They may leach substances or support growth, contaminating the water
They always cost more than approved fittings
They make the water flow too quickly
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Unsuitable fittings can leach materials into the water or support bacterial growth, so only approved fittings should be used.

n.2: Cost is not the reason; suitability for potable water is.
n.3: Fittings do not generally speed up flow to a dangerous level.
n.0: A fitting does not control water temperature.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which design principle helps reduce legionella risk in pipework?
o: Add extra spare branches for future use
Store as much water as the tank will hold
Make pipes as long and as wide as possible
Keep pipe runs and stored water to the minimum needed
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Minimising pipe length and stored water improves turnover and reduces where stagnant water can sit.

n.2: Long, wide pipes hold more standing water and lower velocity, raising risk.
n.1: Storing excess water reduces turnover and encourages stagnation.
n.0: Spare branches left in place become dead legs.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is a key aim when designing or running a water system to control legionella?
o: Keep as many unused branches as possible
Store water for as long as possible before use
Keep the water moving and turned over throughout the system
Let water sit still so sediment settles out
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Keeping water moving and turned over stops it stagnating and drifting into the growth range.

n.3: Letting water sit still is exactly what encourages legionella.
n.0: Unused branches become dead legs and should be removed.
n.1: Long storage lowers turnover and raises risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should low-flow or no-flow branches be avoided in system design?
o: Water sits in them and stagnates, encouraging legionella
They use too much disinfectant
They keep the whole system too cold
They carry water too fast to be safe
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Branches with little or no flow hold standing water that stagnates, so good design avoids them.

n.3: The problem is too little flow, not too much.
n.2: Low-flow branches tend to warm up, not keep the system cold.
n.1: Stagnant branches tend to lose disinfectant, not consume the system's supply.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: If a section of pipework must be kept for possible future use, what should be done in the meantime?
o: Drain it and leave it empty and open
Raise the pressure in it and leave it closed
Cap it and forget about it until needed
Flush it regularly so water does not stagnate in it
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A section that must be retained should be flushed regularly to keep water moving until it is brought back into use.

n.2: Capping and forgetting it lets the water stagnate as a dead leg.
n.0: Leaving it drained and open invites contamination and does not control the risk when refilled.
n.1: Raising pressure without flow does not move fresh water through it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A branch is being left in place because a new sink may be fitted there next year. What is the correct interim control?
o: Insulate the branch and leave it capped
Cap the branch and take no further action
Include the branch in the weekly flushing regime
Close a valve on the branch and leave it
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: While retained for future use, the branch should be flushed regularly so the water in it does not stagnate.

n.1: A capped branch with no flushing is a dead leg that stagnates.
n.0: Insulation does not stop stagnation of the standing water inside.
n.3: A closed valve still leaves standing water beyond it that stagnates.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should a water system be designed to avoid dead legs wherever possible?
o: Dead legs keep the water permanently sterile
Dead legs make the water flow too fast
Dead legs raise the water pressure too high
Dead legs hold stagnant water that lets legionella multiply
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Dead legs trap standing water where legionella can grow, so designs aim to eliminate them.

n.2: Dead legs do not raise system pressure.
n.1: Dead legs have little or no flow, not fast flow.
n.0: Dead legs harbour bacteria rather than keeping water sterile.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cafe kitchen has a rarely used pot-filling tap on a long branch. Which design improvement best reduces the risk?
o: Remove the tap and its branch back to the live main if it is not needed
Add a second dead-ended branch alongside it
Widen the branch pipe to hold more water
Leave it and rely on the annual service
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: If the outlet is genuinely not needed, removing it and its branch back to the live main eliminates the dead leg.

n.1: Adding another dead-ended branch creates a second stagnation point.
n.2: Widening the pipe increases the standing volume and worsens turnover.
n.3: Relying on an annual service leaves long periods for stagnation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Overall, which set of actions best keeps pipework free of legionella growth?
o: Fit extra flexible hoses and use non-approved fittings
Cap unused pipes, store plenty of water, and let it sit
Remove dead legs, keep water moving, and hold correct temperatures
Run cold pipes beside hot pipes and skip insulation
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Removing dead legs, maintaining flow and holding hot and cold temperatures out of the growth range are the core controls.

n.1: Capping and storing water that then sits encourages stagnation and growth.
n.3: Running cold beside hot and skipping insulation warms the cold water into the growth range.
n.0: Extra flexible hoses and non-approved fittings add nutrients and biofilm sites.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is a 'deadleg' in a water system?
o: A length of pipe with little or no flow where water stagnates
A pipe that carries only hot water to the taps
The main incoming supply pipe to the building
A pipe fitted with an insect screen on the end
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A deadleg is a section of pipe with little or no throughflow, so water sits and stagnates, letting legionella grow.

n.1: A busy hot water pipe with regular flow is not a deadleg.
n.2: The live incoming main has constant flow and is not a deadleg.
n.3: An insect screen is a tank fitting and does not define a deadleg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does stagnant water in pipework increase the legionella risk?
o: Moving water encourages more bacteria than still water
Still water is always colder than moving water
Still, warm water lets legionella multiply undisturbed
Stagnant water raises the mains pressure too high
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Where water is stagnant it can warm into the danger zone and sit undisturbed, giving legionella the conditions to multiply.

n.1: Stagnant water tends to drift toward room temperature, not stay colder.
n.3: Stagnation does not increase mains pressure.
n.0: Regular flow and turnover reduce bacterial growth, they do not encourage it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: When a length of pipework is taken out of use, what is the correct way to deal with it?
o: Remove it back to the live main, not just cap the end
Cap the end and leave the rest of the pipe in place
Insulate the pipe and leave it connected
Fit a valve and turn it off but leave the pipe full
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Disused pipework should be removed right back to the live main so no stagnant deadleg is left behind.

n.1: Capping the end still leaves a stagnant deadleg full of standing water.
n.3: A closed valve leaves the branch full of water that will stagnate.
n.2: Insulating a still-connected disused pipe does not stop the water stagnating.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should hot and cold water pipes be kept apart and properly insulated where they run together?
o: To stop cold pipes warming and hot pipes cooling into the danger zone
To make the pipes easier to paint different colours
To allow the pipes to share a single support bracket
To increase the flow rate through both pipes
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Keeping them apart and insulated stops the cold pipe warming above 20°C and the hot pipe cooling below 60°C into the danger zone.

n.1: Colour coding is a labelling matter, not the reason for separation.
n.3: Separation and lagging control temperature, they do not raise flow rate.
n.2: Sharing a bracket is not a water hygiene reason to separate the pipes.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why do long runs of pipework increase the legionella risk?
o: Long pipes cannot be insulated at all
Long pipes raise the storage temperature of the calorifier
Hot water cools and cold water warms toward the danger zone along the run
Long pipes always leak more than short pipes
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Over a long run, hot water loses heat and cold water gains heat, drifting into the 20–45°C danger zone where legionella grows.

n.3: Length does not by itself make a pipe leak more.
n.0: Long pipes can and should be insulated to hold temperature.
n.1: Pipe length does not change the calorifier's storage temperature.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: You find a capped, disused pipe branch that stays warm to the touch and is full of standing water. What should you do?
o: Open the cap to let the standing water drain onto the floor
Leave it as it is because it already has a cap on the end
Report it and arrange for the deadleg to be removed back to the main
Add more lagging to the branch and take no other action
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A warm, water-filled capped branch is a stagnant deadleg, so it should be reported and removed back to the live main.

n.1: A cap does not fix the problem; the stagnant water remains inside.
n.3: Lagging alone leaves the stagnant water and deadleg in place.
n.0: Draining onto the floor is unsafe and does not remove the deadleg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: During a survey you find a little-used outlet at the end of a long branch that is rarely turned on. What is the best control?
o: Cap the outlet off and leave the branch full of water
Flush it regularly, or remove the branch if it is genuinely not needed
Ignore it as one unused outlet cannot cause a problem
Turn up the calorifier temperature to compensate
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Little-used outlets are managed by regular flushing to keep water turning over, or by removing the branch entirely if it is not needed.

n.0: Capping it leaves a stagnant deadleg of standing water behind.
n.3: Raising the calorifier temperature does not move the stagnant water in the branch.
n.2: A single stagnant outlet can seed legionella into the wider system.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A dead leg is a length of pipework in which water is retained and rarely, if ever, drawn off. Why is a dead leg a specific legionella concern under HSG274 Part 2?
o: The pipe wall cools the water below 20 degrees C, which sterilises the section
The retained, stagnant water can warm into the growth range and support biofilm and legionella multiplication
The retained water is kept moving fast enough to strip protective scale from the pipe wall
Dead legs raise system pressure, which forces bacteria out of the outlet
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: HSG274 Part 2 identifies dead legs as areas where water stagnates, warms towards 20-45 degrees C and allows biofilm and legionella to proliferate because there is little or no turnover.

n.2: Stagnant water in a dead leg is not moving at all; scale stripping is not the mechanism of concern.
n.0: Stagnant retained water tends to drift towards ambient/warm temperatures, not sterile cold conditions.
n.3: A dead leg does not raise system pressure, and pressure does not expel bacteria.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: During a survey you find an old branch pipe that once fed a demolished sink; it is capped about 600 mm from the live main and never used. What is the correct remedial action under HSG274 Part 2?
o: Remove the redundant pipework right back to the live main so no stub remains
Leave the capped stub in place because the cap already isolates the stagnant water
Fit a second cap on the end to double-seal the retained water
Insulate the capped stub so the retained water cannot warm up
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Capping does not solve the problem; the capped section still holds stagnant water. HSG274 Part 2 requires redundant pipework to be removed back to the point of connection with the live/circulating main.

n.1: A cap still leaves a stagnant, warming volume of water connected to the system; it is not a solution.
n.2: A second cap adds nothing; the retained water still stagnates and can grow legionella.
n.3: Insulation slows temperature change but the stagnant retained water remains a colonisation risk; the stub must be removed.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which of the following best describes why oversized pipework increases legionella risk?
o: Larger bore holds more water with lower flow velocity and turnover, so water stagnates and warms
Larger bore reduces the surface area available for biofilm per litre of water
Larger bore increases velocity so much that biofilm cannot form anywhere
Larger bore always keeps water colder than the surrounding room air
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Oversized pipes carry a greater volume at reduced velocity, so turnover falls and water dwells longer, allowing it to reach growth temperatures and support biofilm.

n.3: Oversizing does not keep water cold; slow turnover lets it drift towards ambient temperature.
n.2: Oversizing lowers velocity, it does not raise it, and biofilm forms readily on wetted surfaces.
n.1: Larger bore increases wetted surface and dwell time, worsening biofilm potential rather than reducing it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cold water pipe runs for several metres alongside an uninsulated hot water flow pipe in a warm plant room. What is the main risk to the cold supply?
o: The cold water will freeze because of the proximity to the hot pipe
The cold water will become over-chlorinated by heat from the hot pipe
The cold pipe will lose pressure to the hot pipe through the shared bracket
Heat gain warms the cold water above 20 degrees C, entering the legionella growth range
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Cold pipes routed near hot pipes or heat sources pick up heat; if the cold water rises above 20 degrees C it enters the 20-45 degrees C range where legionella multiplies. Cold pipes should be kept away from heat and lagged.

n.0: Proximity to a hot pipe warms the cold water, it does not freeze it.
n.2: Pressure is not transferred between separate pipes through a bracket.
n.1: Heat does not add chlorine; if anything, warming and stagnation help disinfectant decay.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: An infrequently used outlet at the end of a long branch is identified as a stagnation risk but cannot yet be removed. What interim control does HSG274 Part 2 recommend?
o: Fit a longer run of pipe to increase the stored volume at the outlet
Flush the outlet regularly, typically weekly, to draw fresh water through and prevent stagnation
Raise the cold water temperature at the outlet to above 25 degrees C
Close the branch isolation valve and leave the water standing until removal
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Where little-used sections cannot be removed, the recommended interim control is regular flushing (commonly weekly) to move fresh water through and stop stagnation, until the redundant length can be removed.

n.3: Isolating and leaving water standing makes stagnation worse, not better.
n.2: Warming cold water into the low-20s pushes it towards the growth range, the opposite of what is wanted.
n.0: Adding pipe increases stored volume and dwell time, worsening stagnation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which pipework material choice is most consistent with HSG274 Part 2 guidance for minimising microbial risk in a water system?
o: Any material to hand, provided it is cheap and easy to fit
Natural rubber hoses because they flex and are quick to install
Materials that leach nutrients to encourage a stable biofilm
WRAS-approved materials that resist corrosion and do not support microbial growth
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: HSG274 Part 2 and the Water Fittings Regulations require materials in contact with wholesome water to be WRAS-approved (or equivalent), resisting corrosion and not providing nutrients that support microbial growth.

n.0: Suitability for potable water and approval status matter far more than cost or ease of fitting.
n.1: Natural rubber components can leach nutrients and harbour biofilm and legionella and are discouraged.
n.2: Encouraging biofilm is exactly what should be avoided; nutrient-leaching materials are unsuitable.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why are flexible flexible-hose connectors (such as those under taps or to appliances) flagged as a specific risk in HSG274 Part 2?
o: The EPDM/rubber lining can degrade and provide nutrients and surfaces that harbour biofilm and legionella
They contain chlorine reservoirs that over-dose the outlet
They cannot be connected to WRAS-approved fittings at all
They are always undersized and therefore raise water velocity too high
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Flexible hoses often use EPDM or similar elastomers that can degrade, shed nutrients and support biofilm and legionella growth; their use should be minimised and approved low-risk types selected.

n.3: The concern is the lining material and biofilm, not excessive velocity.
n.1: They do not store or over-dose chlorine.
n.2: They can be connected to approved fittings; the issue is the hose lining material itself.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A designer wants to reduce stagnation risk in a new washroom. Which design principle aligns with HSG274 Part 2?
o: Minimise pipe run lengths and stored volume so water is turned over quickly
Route long individual branches to each outlet for future flexibility
Provide generous spare capacity by oversizing pipes for possible future demand
Add several capped spur connections for future appliances
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Good design minimises pipe length, dead legs and stored volume so that water is used and replaced frequently, keeping it moving and reducing the chance of it reaching growth temperatures.

n.2: Oversizing lowers turnover and promotes stagnation and warming.
n.1: Long individual branches create low-turnover legs that stagnate.
n.3: Capped spurs are dead legs in waiting and should be avoided, not designed in.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the essential difference between a 'dead leg' and a 'blind end' in system terminology used in HSG274 Part 2?
o: A dead leg is always hot pipework and a blind end is always cold pipework
A dead leg is a rarely-used length still feeding an outlet, while a blind end is capped pipework feeding nothing
A blind end circulates continuously while a dead leg never holds water
There is no practical difference; both terms mean continuously flushed pipework
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A dead leg is a pipe leading to an outlet that is used infrequently; a blind end (or dead end) is pipework that is capped and no longer serves any outlet. Both retain stagnant water and are colonisation risks.

n.0: The distinction is about use and termination, not whether the pipe is hot or cold.
n.2: Neither circulates continuously; both are low- or no-turnover sections.
n.3: There is a difference, and neither is continuously flushed pipework.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A ward is temporarily closed and its outlets will not be used for six weeks. To manage the pipework stagnation risk, the safest approach is to:
o: Do nothing, as closed rooms present no water risk
Drain the system fully and leave it empty and open to the air
Isolate the branch and rely on residual disinfectant to hold for six weeks
Flush the outlets regularly during the closure, or drain down and disinfect before reuse
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: For temporarily unused outlets, HSG274 Part 2 advises maintaining regular flushing to keep water fresh, or draining down; before bringing outlets back into use after prolonged inactivity, disinfection/flushing is needed.

n.0: Stagnant water in unused outlets is a well-recognised risk and cannot be ignored.
n.1: Leaving pipework empty and open invites contamination and does not by itself make reuse safe.
n.2: Residual disinfectant decays; six weeks of standing water will stagnate and colonise.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which statement about biofilm in pipework is correct according to HSG274 Part 2 principles?
o: Biofilm is only a concern in outdoor cooling towers, not in domestic pipework
Biofilm dissolves harmlessly whenever water flows past it
Biofilm forms only in hot water above 60 degrees C
Biofilm develops on wetted pipe surfaces and can shelter legionella from disinfectant, especially in stagnant areas
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Biofilm forms on the wetted internal surfaces of pipework and equipment; it provides nutrients and shelter for legionella and other organisms and can protect them from disinfectant, and it is worst where water stagnates.

n.2: Biofilm forms across a wide temperature range; sustained temperatures above 60 degrees C suppress legionella but biofilm is not limited to hot systems.
n.0: Biofilm is a concern throughout hot and cold water systems, not only cooling towers.
n.1: Flow does not simply dissolve established biofilm; it can, however, shed organisms into the water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A maintenance operative removes a redundant length of pipe but leaves a short tee stub about 400 mm long projecting from the live pipe. Why is this still a problem?
o: The stub raises the mains pressure and can burst the fitting
The stub is a residual dead leg holding stagnant water that can warm and colonise
The stub increases flow velocity and erodes the tee joint
The stub reduces the volume of stored water and starves outlets
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Any length of pipe left projecting from the live main forms a residual dead leg that retains stagnant water, warms towards growth temperatures and can seed the live water with legionella. Removal should be flush to the live pipe.

n.2: A short dead stub carries little or no flow; velocity and erosion are not the issue.
n.0: The stub does not raise mains pressure.
n.3: The concern is stagnation in the stub, not any reduction in stored volume.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: In a cold water system, which condition most directly pushes stored or standing water into the legionella growth range?
o: Cold water warming above 20 degrees C in stagnant, poorly insulated pipework near heat sources
Cold water held below 20 degrees C in well-insulated, frequently used pipework
Continuous high-velocity flow through short, direct pipe runs
Rapid turnover of water in a correctly sized storage cistern
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Legionella multiplies between roughly 20 and 45 degrees C. Cold water that warms above 20 degrees C, especially where it stagnates in uninsulated pipe near heat, is at greatest risk.

n.1: Cold water kept below 20 degrees C and moving is exactly the safe condition, not the risk.
n.2: High turnover through short runs keeps water fresh and cool, reducing risk.
n.3: Rapid turnover in correctly sized storage limits warming and stagnation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does HSG274 Part 2 recommend lagging (insulating) cold water pipework as well as hot?
o: To reduce heat gain that would warm cold water into the growth range and to keep hot water hot
Only to reduce the noise of water flowing through the pipes
Only to prevent condensation dripping onto floors below
To slow the flow of water so that outlets are quieter in use
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Insulation on cold pipes limits heat gain so the water stays below 20 degrees C, and insulation on hot pipes limits heat loss so the water stays hot; both help keep water outside the 20-45 degrees C growth range.

n.2: Condensation control is a secondary benefit, not the primary legionella-control reason.
n.1: Noise reduction is not the guidance's purpose for lagging.
n.3: Lagging does not slow flow, and slowing flow would increase stagnation risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A hotel installs a bank of eight guest showers but typically only two are ever used. From a stagnation perspective, the best control is to:
o: Cap the pipes to the six unused showers close to the shower head
Turn up the cold water pressure to the whole shower bank
Rationalise the installation to the number actually needed, or ensure all heads are used or flushed on a rota
Leave the six unused showers plumbed and simply not use them
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Provision far in excess of demand creates low-turnover branches. HSG274 Part 2 favours matching provision to need, or, where outlets are retained, rotating use/flushing so every branch turns over regularly.

n.3: Unused but plumbed showers become dead legs that stagnate.
n.0: Capping at the head still leaves a stagnant branch feeding the cap; it does not remove the risk.
n.1: Raising pressure does not address the stagnant water in unused branches.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which of the following would a competent surveyor most likely record as a dead leg on a schematic?
o: A circulating hot water return pipe kept above 50 degrees C
A rising main feeding the whole building continuously
A frequently used kitchen tap on a short direct branch
A capped pipe left in place after a urinal was removed
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A capped pipe left after equipment removal serves no outlet and retains stagnant water; it is a classic dead leg / blind end that should be removed back to the live main.

n.2: A frequently used tap on a short branch turns over regularly and is not a dead leg.
n.0: A hot circulating return is continuously moving water, not a dead leg.
n.1: A continuously used rising main is live, high-turnover pipework.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A little-used tap is flushed weekly for control. What is the correct way to carry out the flush to gain the benefit?
o: Open the tap for one second so a small amount of water passes
Only flush the hot side and leave the cold side untouched
Flush at maximum spray to create as much aerosol as possible
Run the tap until the water has fully turned over and reached the incoming supply temperature, minimising aerosol
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A flush must draw fresh water through the whole retained length, so it should run until the standing water is displaced and the temperature reaches that of the incoming supply; aerosol should be minimised during flushing.

n.0: A one-second flush does not displace the standing water in the branch, so it achieves little.
n.1: Both hot and cold sides retain standing water and both need flushing.
n.2: Maximising aerosol increases inhalation risk; aerosol should be minimised while flushing.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why is proximity of stored or standing water to heat sources such as boilers, plant, or south-facing walls specifically noted in stagnation risk assessment?
o: Local heating raises the water above 20 degrees C into the legionella growth range
Heat sources have no measurable effect on water temperature in pipes
Heat sources chlorinate the nearby water automatically
Heat sources cool nearby pipework and freeze the water
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Local heat from plant, boilers or solar gain warms adjacent cold pipework and stored water; combined with stagnation this pushes the temperature into the 20-45 degrees C growth range.

n.2: Heat does not add disinfectant to the water.
n.3: Heat sources warm rather than cool and freeze the water.
n.1: Adjacent heat sources measurably warm pipework and are a recognised risk factor.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A site has a large storage cistern sized for a demand that no longer exists, so the water sits for days. Which control best addresses the stagnation this causes?
o: Raise the storage water temperature to 30 degrees C to discourage growth
Right-size the storage or reduce stored volume so turnover matches actual demand
Increase the cistern size further to add buffer capacity
Seal the cistern lid permanently and stop inspecting it
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Storage should be matched to demand so water is turned over roughly daily; oversized storage lets water dwell and warm. Reducing stored volume to suit real demand restores turnover.

n.2: Adding capacity worsens dwell time and stagnation.
n.3: Sealing the lid and stopping inspection removes control and does not address turnover.
n.0: Warming stored water to 30 degrees C puts it squarely in the growth range.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which of these is the strongest reason to remove rather than merely isolate a redundant pipe branch with a valve?
o: Isolation valves are more expensive than removing the pipe
Valves always leak and cause flooding within days
An isolated branch increases the flow rate to all other outlets
An isolated branch still holds standing water beyond the valve that stagnates and can be reopened into the system
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Closing a valve leaves a stagnant, water-filled length beyond it. If the valve is later opened, or leaks by, that colonised water can enter the live system. Removal back to the live main eliminates the retained volume.

n.0: Cost is not the guidance reason; the retained stagnant water is.
n.1: Valves do not always leak within days; this is not the rationale.
n.2: Isolating a branch does not meaningfully raise flow to other outlets.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: On a schematic review you notice a shower fed by a long, small-bore hot branch that is used once a fortnight. Which two factors combine to make this a high stagnation risk?
o: High turnover and cold-only supply
Long, low-turnover run and infrequent use allowing water to sit and reach growth temperatures
Frequent use and oversized bore keeping water cold
Short run length and continuous use
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A long branch used only occasionally means water sits for extended periods; in that time hot water cools and cold water warms towards the 20-45 degrees C range, and stagnation supports biofilm and legionella.

n.3: Short runs with continuous use are low risk, the opposite of this situation.
n.0: High turnover is protective; the branch here has low turnover.
n.2: The branch is used infrequently, not frequently, and small-bore, not oversized.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the recommended approach to a strainer, filter or expansion vessel that creates a low-flow or dead volume in the pipework?
o: Warm them deliberately to keep the water above 25 degrees C
Remove all strainers and filters from every water system permanently
Ignore them, as small components hold too little water to matter
Assess them as potential stagnation points and include them in cleaning, flushing or flow-through maintenance
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Components such as strainers, filters and expansion vessels can create localised low-flow or dead volumes where water stagnates; they should be identified in the risk assessment and managed by suitable maintenance, flow-through or flushing.

n.2: Even small dead volumes can harbour biofilm and legionella and seed the system.
n.1: Filters and strainers have legitimate functions; the answer is to manage them, not blanket-remove them.
n.0: Warming them into the growth range is the opposite of good control.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A new extension is plumbed and left filled with water but not commissioned or used for three months before occupation. What is the key stagnation control before hand-over?
o: Nothing, because new pipework is sterile and cannot support growth
Keep the system flushed during the delay, or disinfect and flush before it is brought into use
Leave the water standing so any disinfectant residual builds up
Simply run the taps once on the day of occupation
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Filled but unused new pipework stagnates just like existing pipework. It should be kept flushed through the delay or, where that has not happened, disinfected and thoroughly flushed before occupation.

n.0: New pipework is not sterile; it wets, forms biofilm and can support growth once water stands.
n.3: A single run on the day does not overcome three months of stagnation throughout the system.
n.2: Standing water depletes rather than builds disinfectant residual and stagnates.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which practice most reduces the length of dead legs at the design stage of a hot and cold water installation?
o: Placing infrequently used outlets closest to the circulating or frequently used pipework to keep dead legs short
Adding extra spare tee connections for possible future outlets
Connecting infrequently used outlets as far as possible from the main circulation
Running each outlet on its own long individual supply from the plant room
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Keeping infrequently used outlets close to the circulating loop or a busy branch keeps the low-turnover length short, minimising the dead-leg volume that can stagnate.

n.2: Placing them far from circulation lengthens the low-turnover run and worsens stagnation.
n.1: Spare tees are dead legs in waiting and should be avoided.
n.3: Long individual supplies to each outlet maximise dead-leg length.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Standing water in a poorly used section of pipe has been found at 32 degrees C. What does this reading indicate for legionella control?
o: It sits within the 20-45 degrees C range that favours legionella multiplication and needs control
It is safely below the growth range and needs no action
It is above the range, so legionella is being killed
The temperature is irrelevant provided the water looks clear
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: 32 degrees C is well within the 20-45 degrees C band in which legionella multiplies most readily; the stagnation and temperature together indicate a real risk requiring flushing, temperature control or removal of the section.

n.1: 32 degrees C is inside, not below, the growth range.
n.2: Legionella is not killed until sustained temperatures well above 50 degrees C; 32 degrees C encourages growth.
n.3: Clear-looking water can still be heavily colonised; temperature is a key control parameter.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should the number of joints, tees and fittings in a water system be kept to the minimum necessary?
o: Because copper fittings sterilise the water and should be avoided
Because fittings and tees create potential low-flow zones and surfaces where biofilm and stagnation can develop
Because every fitting adds cost that must be recovered from users
Because fittings always reduce the pressure below usable levels
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Each additional tee or fitting introduces potential dead volumes, turbulence-free pockets and extra wetted surface where biofilm forms; minimising them supports smoother flow and reduces stagnation opportunities.

n.2: Cost is not the microbial-control reason for minimising fittings.
n.3: Fittings do not automatically drop pressure below usable levels.
n.0: Copper does not sterilise water; this is not a reason to avoid fittings.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A facilities team proposes leaving a decommissioned wing's pipework full of water 'in case the wing reopens'. What should the risk assessment conclude?
o: Acceptable, provided the doors to the wing are kept locked
The full, unused pipework is a large dead leg that will stagnate and should be drained and isolated or removed, with controls before any reuse
Acceptable, because unused water slowly self-disinfects over time
Acceptable, as full pipes are always safer than empty ones
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: An entire wing of unused, water-filled pipework is effectively a very large dead leg. It will stagnate; the safe options are to drain down and physically disconnect, or maintain flushing, with disinfection and flushing before any reuse.

n.3: Full pipes that never turn over stagnate; 'full is always safer' is incorrect.
n.0: Locking doors does nothing about the stagnating water inside the pipes.
n.2: Water does not self-disinfect; disinfectant residual decays and organisms multiply.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: During refurbishment, a plumber tees off the live cold main to feed a temporary standpipe that will be used for a few weeks. What ongoing control does the stagnation risk demand while it is in place?
o: Use it daily or flush it regularly, and remove it back to the main promptly once it is no longer needed
Cap it at the standpipe end when the works finish and leave the tee
Insulate only the tee connection and take no other action
Leave it connected indefinitely after the works in case it is useful
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A temporary connection is a dead leg unless it turns over; it should be used or flushed regularly while needed and then removed back to the live main promptly, not capped and abandoned.

n.3: Leaving it indefinitely creates a permanent, unused dead leg.
n.1: Capping the end leaves a stagnant branch on the tee; the whole connection should be removed.
n.2: Insulating the tee does not address the stagnant water; regular use/flushing and removal are needed.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which combination of factors does HSG274 Part 2 associate with the greatest risk of legionella proliferation in pipework?
o: High disinfectant residual and rapid turnover
Frequent use, short runs and water held below 20 degrees C
Continuous circulation and hot water held above 55 degrees C
Stagnation, water at 20-45 degrees C, biofilm and suitable nutrients present together
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Proliferation is favoured when several conditions coincide: stagnant or low-flow water, temperatures of 20-45 degrees C, established biofilm and a source of nutrients. Control aims to remove one or more of these.

n.1: Frequent use, short runs and sub-20 degrees C water is the low-risk, well-controlled scenario.
n.2: Circulation and hot water above 55 degrees C suppresses legionella rather than promoting it.
n.0: High residual and rapid turnover are protective, not high-risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: An operative is asked to record 'sentinel' outlets for temperature monitoring. In relation to stagnation, which outlets are typically most useful to include?
o: Only the outlet nearest the incoming main, regardless of use
Only outlets that are used continuously all day
Any three outlets chosen at random each month
The outlets furthest from, and nearest to, the source, plus known low-use or long-branch outlets most at risk of stagnation
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Sentinel outlets are usually the nearest and furthest points on a system, chosen to represent temperature control across it; including known low-use or long-branch outlets targets the places where stagnation and temperature drift are most likely.

n.0: A single near outlet does not represent the far, higher-risk parts of the system.
n.2: Random monthly selection undermines trend monitoring and may miss high-risk points.
n.1: Continuously used outlets are least likely to stagnate and are not the priority to catch problems.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why is simply capping a redundant pipe considered an inadequate control, even though it stops water escaping?
o: Capping raises the pressure in the retained pipe until it bursts
Capping cools the retained water below the growth range permanently
The capped length still retains stagnant water connected to the live system, where it warms and can colonise
Capping is only inadequate if the cap is made of plastic
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A cap seals the end but the pipe behind it still holds water that no longer turns over; connected to the live system, this stagnant volume warms and supports growth, and can seed the live water. That is why removal to the live main is required.

n.0: A capped dead length does not build pressure to bursting.
n.1: Capping does not cool the water; stagnant water tends to drift towards ambient/warm.
n.3: The material of the cap is not the point; the retained stagnant water is.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cold water branch reads 22 degrees C at the sentinel outlet, above the target. Which investigation best addresses a likely pipework cause?
o: Increase the outlet flow restrictor to slow the water down
Check for heat gain from adjacent hot pipes or plant, missing/poor insulation, and low turnover or dead legs on the branch
Immediately raise the storage temperature to compensate
Assume the thermometer is faulty and record the target value instead
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A cold outlet above about 20 degrees C points to heat gain and/or low turnover. The pipework investigation looks for adjacent heat sources, inadequate lagging and stagnant or dead-leg sections, then corrects them.

n.3: Falsifying records hides a genuine control failure and is unacceptable.
n.2: Raising storage temperature does not fix a warm cold-water branch and may worsen scald risk.
n.0: Slowing the flow increases dwell time and warming, making the problem worse.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: In relation to pipework layout, what does 'keeping water moving' primarily achieve for legionella control?
o: It ensures water is used and replaced before it can warm and stagnate, and helps maintain disinfectant residual
It erodes the pipe walls so biofilm cannot attach anywhere
It removes the need to control temperature at all
It heats the water through friction to a safe temperature
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Regular turnover means water does not dwell long enough to warm into the growth range or lose its disinfectant residual, and it disrupts the conditions biofilm needs to build up; it is a core stagnation control.

n.1: Normal flow does not erode pipe walls, and biofilm still forms; erosion is not the mechanism.
n.3: Friction does not usefully heat the water; the benefit is turnover, not warming.
n.2: Movement supports but does not replace temperature control; both are needed.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A drinking water dispenser is fed by a 4-metre small-bore pipe that only delivers a few litres a day. Which description and control are correct?
o: It is a low-turnover branch at stagnation risk; keep the run as short as practicable, insulate it and ensure regular use or flushing
It should be fed by an even longer pipe to increase stored volume
It is a high-turnover run needing no specific stagnation control
It is safe as long as the dispenser is a branded unit
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A long, low-draw branch turns over slowly and can warm and stagnate. Controls are to minimise the branch length, keep it cool with insulation and away from heat, and ensure regular turnover or flushing.

n.2: A few litres a day through 4 metres is low turnover, not high; it does need control.
n.3: The brand of the dispenser does not remove the pipework stagnation risk.
n.1: Lengthening the pipe increases dwell time and stagnation, the opposite of the aim.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which record-keeping action best supports ongoing management of dead legs and stagnation identified in a risk assessment?
o: Recording only the outlets that passed temperature checks
Keeping a schematic and asset register that identifies dead legs, little-used outlets and flushing regimes, and logging the flushing and remedial removals carried out
Discarding old schematics once a single survey is complete
Relying on operatives' memory rather than written flushing records
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: An up-to-date schematic/asset register that marks dead legs and low-use outlets, together with logs of flushing and of redundant pipework removed, lets the responsible person track and demonstrate that stagnation risks are being controlled over time.

n.0: Recording only passes hides the at-risk outlets that most need action.
n.2: Discarding schematics loses the baseline needed to manage change and dead legs.
n.3: Memory is not auditable or reliable; written records are required to demonstrate control.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What does a thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) do?
o: Cools the whole hot water system down to a safe temperature
Stores a reserve of tepid water ready for use
Heats stored water to a higher temperature to kill legionella
Blends hot and cold water at the point of use to give safe, non-scalding water
