TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV mixes stored hot water with cold water so the water leaving the outlet is warm but not scalding.

n.2: A TMV does not heat water; it only blends hot and cold.
n.0: It does not cool the system; storage stays hot and only the outlet water is tempered.
n.1: It has no storage; it blends on demand as water is drawn.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A TMV allows a building to protect people from scalding WITHOUT doing what?
o: Lowering the hot water storage temperature below 60°C
Fitting it close to the outlet
Servicing the valve regularly
Using cold water in the blend
TMVs & Scalding.w: The point of a TMV is to control scald risk while the stored water stays at 60°C or above for legionella control.

n.1: TMVs should be fitted close to the outlet, so this is not something avoided.
n.2: Regular servicing is required, not avoided.
n.3: A TMV must draw cold water to blend, so this is essential, not avoided.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why must hot water storage NOT be turned down below 60°C to stop scalding?
o: It would use more energy over time
It would damage the storage cylinder
It would make the water taste unpleasant
Lower storage temperatures let legionella grow in the stored water
TMVs & Scalding.w: Storing hot water below 60°C brings it into the range where legionella can multiply, so scalding is controlled with a TMV instead.

n.2: Taste is not the safety concern; legionella growth is.
n.0: Lower temperatures generally use less energy, and energy is not the safety issue.
n.1: Lower temperatures do not damage the cylinder; the risk is bacterial growth.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Where should a TMV be sited in relation to the outlet it serves?
o: As close to the outlet as practicable
At the incoming cold water main
Halfway along the distribution pipe
As close to the storage cylinder as possible
TMVs & Scalding.w: Siting the TMV close to the outlet keeps the length of blended tepid water short, limiting where legionella could grow.

n.3: Near the cylinder would leave a long run of tepid blended water in the growth range.
n.1: The cold main is not where blending needs to happen.
n.2: Halfway along still leaves a long section of warm blended water.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A care home manager asks an operative to turn the hot water cylinder down to 45°C so frail residents cannot be scalded. What is the correct response?
o: Switch the hot water off during the day
Turn the cylinder down to 50°C as a compromise
Turn the cylinder down to 45°C as requested
Keep storage at 60°C or above and fit TMVs to the residents' outlets
TMVs & Scalding.w: Storage must stay at 60°C or above for legionella control, and scalding is prevented with TMVs at the outlets.

n.2: Storing at 45°C sits in the legionella growth range and is unsafe.
n.1: 50°C storage is still below the 60°C needed to control legionella.
n.0: Switching hot water off does not control legionella and disrupts the water supply.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why is the blended water leaving a TMV itself a legionella risk?
o: It comes only from the cold supply
It has had all the chlorine removed by the valve
It is warm and sits in the temperature range where legionella can grow
It is stored for long periods before use
TMVs & Scalding.w: The tepid blended water and the valve internals sit in the bacterial growth range, so TMVs need regular cleaning and servicing.

n.1: A TMV does not strip chlorine from the water.
n.3: The blended water is made on demand, not stored.
n.0: Blended water is a mix of hot and cold, not cold only.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What is a typical safe delivery temperature for a TMV-served bath or shower used by vulnerable people?
o: Around 55°C
Around 20°C
Around 41°C
Around 60°C
TMVs & Scalding.w: Blended delivery of roughly 41°C gives a warm, usable temperature that is well below the scalding threshold.

n.3: 60°C is the storage temperature and would scald.
n.1: 20°C is cold water territory, not a usable bath or shower temperature.
n.0: 55°C is close to the distribution temperature and would present a scald risk.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which of these is a reason a TMV needs regular servicing?
o: Scale and debris can affect the valve and let the delivery temperature drift
It runs out of stored cold water
It gradually loses its colour coding
The valve wears out and starts heating the water
TMVs & Scalding.w: Scale, debris and wear can stop the TMV holding its set temperature, so servicing, descaling and temperature checks are needed.

Only on cold water outlets
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs are fitted only where they are needed to protect against scalding, because each valve adds a legionella risk that must be managed.

n.1: Fitting TMVs everywhere adds unnecessary legionella breeding points that all need servicing.
n.3: TMVs blend hot with cold; they are not fitted to cold-only outlets.
n.0: TMVs are essential for scald protection where needed; the risk is managed by maintenance, not by banning them.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A care-home manager asks you to turn the hot water calorifier down to 45°C so residents cannot be scalded. What should you do?
o: Turn it down and add extra cold water to the tank
Turn it down to 50°C as a compromise
Turn it down to 45°C as requested straight away
Explain that storage must stay at 60°C or above and recommend TMVs for scald control
TMVs & Scalding.w: Storing hot water below 60°C allows legionella to grow, so the safe answer is to keep it hot and control scalding with TMVs.

n.2: 45°C storage is squarely in the legionella growth range and is unsafe.
n.1: 50°C storage is still below the 60°C control temperature and allows legionella to multiply.
n.0: Adding cold and lowering the temperature creates the same legionella risk.

TMVs & Scalding.q: During a TMV service you find the valve is heavily scaled and will not hold temperature. What is the correct action?
o: Descale, clean and disinfect it, and report the fault to the responsible person
Leave it and note it can be looked at next year
Turn off the cold feed so only hot water comes out
Wrap it in insulation to keep it warm
TMVs & Scalding.w: A faulty scaled TMV should be descaled, cleaned, disinfected and the fault recorded and reported so it can be put right.

n.1: Leaving a TMV that cannot hold temperature is both a scalding and a legionella risk.
n.3: Insulation does not fix scale and does not restore temperature control.
n.2: Turning off the cold feed removes scald protection and delivers dangerously hot water.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What temperature range should a correctly set TMV deliver at the outlet to prevent scalding?
o: A cold 20°C or below
Whatever temperature the user turns the tap to
A safe blended temperature, typically around 38–43°C depending on use
A hot 60°C to match the storage temperature
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV delivers a controlled blended temperature (typically about 38–43°C) that is warm enough to use but not hot enough to scald.

n.3: Delivering 60°C at the tap would scald the user; that is the storage temperature, not the outlet temperature.
n.0: A TMV supplies usable warm water for washing, not a cold supply.
n.1: A TMV controls the maximum blended temperature rather than leaving it to the user.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) controls scalding risk primarily by doing what?
o: Blending hot and cold water at the outlet to deliver water at a safe temperature
Recirculating stored hot water more quickly to even out its temperature
Sterilising the water with a chemical dose as it passes to the tap or shower
Holding the hot water storage cylinder at a reduced temperature of around 44°C
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV mixes hot and cold supplies at (or very near) the point of use so the delivered water is at a safe, non-scalding temperature, while storage and distribution remain hot enough to control legionella.

n.3: The cylinder must stay hot (≥60°C); a TMV does not and must not reduce storage temperature to control scalding.
n.1: Recirculation maintains distribution temperature; it does not blend water to a safe outlet temperature.
n.2: A TMV blends by temperature only; it does not chemically treat or sterilise the water.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A care-home manager suggests turning the calorifier thermostat down to 45°C so residents cannot be scalded at the basins. What is the correct response?
o: Reject the change and fit TMVs at the at-risk outlets, keeping storage at ≥60°C
Reduce storage to 45°C only during the day and raise it again overnight
Accept it, because 45°C is warm enough to kill legionella in the cylinder
Accept it only if the water is flushed weekly to compensate for the lower heat
TMVs & Scalding.w: Scald protection must never be achieved by lowering hot storage below 60°C, as that creates a legionella risk. The correct measure is a TMV at the point of use while storage stays hot.

n.2: 45°C is within the legionella growth range and will not disinfect stored water.
n.3: Flushing cannot compensate for storing water at a temperature that allows legionella to proliferate.
n.1: Cycling storage between low and high temperatures still allows growth during the warm periods and is not an accepted control.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why should a TMV be fitted as close as reasonably practicable to the outlet it serves?
o: To make the valve easier to reach for reading its serial number
To minimise the length of pipework holding tepid blended water where legionella can grow
To reduce the pressure the outlet fittings must withstand
To allow the blended supply to be shared between several buildings
TMVs & Scalding.w: Blended water sits in the legionella growth range, so the run of pipe carrying it must be kept as short as possible; siting the TMV close to the outlet minimises this dead-leg of tepid water.

n.0: Ease of reading a serial number is not the reason for close siting.
n.2: TMV positioning is about temperature and dead-legs, not reducing outlet pressure ratings.
n.3: Blended supplies should serve only nearby outlets, not be distributed widely, which would create long tepid runs.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which statement about a TMV and legionella risk is correct?
o: A TMV is itself a legionella risk and needs regular maintenance and checks
A TMV only poses a risk if it is fitted more than 2 metres from the outlet
A TMV removes legionella risk because the blended water is cooler
A TMV eliminates the need to keep hot storage above 60°C
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV holds water in the growth range and has internal components that can harbour bacteria and scale, so it requires routine servicing, cleaning, descaling, disinfection and temperature checks.

n.2: Cooling water into the tepid range increases legionella risk rather than removing it.
n.1: The valve is a risk regardless of distance; close siting reduces the dead-leg but the valve still needs maintenance.
n.3: Storage must still be kept ≥60°C; the TMV does not change that requirement.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A TMV serving a nursery washbasin is found to be delivering water at 41°C. How should this be regarded?
o: Too cold – the blended supply should always reach at least 50°C
Too hot – the valve has failed and must be shut off immediately
Acceptable only if the cold supply is below 15°C at the time
Within the expected safe blended range for a basin
TMVs & Scalding.w: A typical safe blended delivery for basins is around 41°C, so this reading is within the expected range and does not indicate a fault.

n.1: 41°C is not too hot; it sits within the recognised safe delivery range for a basin.
n.0: Blended water is deliberately kept tepid to prevent scalding; 50°C would present a scald risk.
n.2: A correct blended temperature does not depend on the cold feed being below 15°C.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which group of outlets is most likely to be prioritised for TMV fitting?
o: Plant-room drain-down points used during maintenance only
Cleaners' sinks and outside taps used only for filling buckets
Kitchen boiling-water taps used for making hot drinks
Baths and showers used by vulnerable people such as the elderly or young children
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs are targeted where a genuine scald risk exists, particularly baths and showers for at-risk users such as the elderly, very young and those unable to react to hot water.

n.1: Cleaners' sinks and external taps generally carry no scald risk to vulnerable users and are not priority TMV locations.
n.2: Boiling-water taps deliver near-boiling water by design and are not fitted with blending TMVs.
n.0: Drain-down points are not user outlets and present no scald risk requiring a TMV.

TMVs & Scalding.q: During a survey you find a TMV serving an outlet that has been permanently capped and is no longer used. What is the recommended action?
o: Increase the servicing frequency of the redundant TMV to compensate
Turn the blended temperature up so the short pipe stays warm
Remove the redundant TMV and outlet to eliminate the dead-leg
Leave the TMV in place in case the outlet is reinstated later
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV and outlet no longer in use form a stagnant dead-leg of tepid water; the correct control is to remove the redundant valve and pipework back to the live main.

n.3: Retaining unused equipment 'just in case' leaves a stagnant dead-leg and is poor practice.
n.0: More frequent servicing does not address the underlying stagnation of an unused leg.
n.1: Raising the temperature does not resolve stagnation and is not how a redundant leg is dealt with.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What is the purpose of the fail-safe (thermal shut-off) feature built into a TMV?
o: To divert unused blended water back into the cold main
To keep delivering water at the set temperature if the hot supply fails
To shut the water off if the cold supply fails, preventing a scald
To boost flow automatically when several outlets open at once
TMVs & Scalding.w: If the cold feed fails, the valve would otherwise pass full-temperature hot water to the outlet; the fail-safe shuts off the flow to prevent a scalding delivery.

n.3: The fail-safe is a safety cut-off, not a flow booster.
n.1: It cannot maintain a blended temperature without a working cold supply; instead it shuts off.
n.0: The fail-safe does not divert water into the cold main.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which routine check best confirms that a TMV's fail-safe is working?
o: Recording the flow rate of the outlet in litres per minute
Checking the paintwork and labelling on the valve body
Measuring the storage cylinder temperature at the calorifier
Isolating the cold supply and confirming the flow shuts off quickly
TMVs & Scalding.w: The recognised fail-safe test is to shut off the cold feed and confirm the valve rapidly stops the flow, proving it will not deliver scalding hot water if the cold supply is lost.

n.2: Storage temperature confirms disinfection control, not the TMV's fail-safe operation.
n.0: Flow rate alone says nothing about the fail-safe cut-off function.
n.1: Visual condition checks are useful but do not test the fail-safe mechanism.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why is a strainer or filter commonly fitted on the inlets of a TMV?
o: To increase the delivery temperature during periods of low demand
To chemically soften the incoming water before it is blended
To store a reserve of hot water for peak times
To catch debris and scale that could jam the valve and cause it to fail
TMVs & Scalding.w: Inlet strainers trap grit, scale and debris that could otherwise foul the valve's moving parts and lead to failure; they must themselves be cleaned during servicing.

n.1: A strainer is a mechanical filter, not a water softener, and does not chemically treat the water.
n.0: Strainers do not raise delivery temperature.
n.2: A TMV strainer does not store water; it filters the inlet flow.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why do TMVs incorporate check (non-return) valves on their inlets?
o: To allow the hot and cold supplies to share a single feed pipe
To silence water hammer generated by the outlet fittings
To raise the blended delivery temperature above 44°C when needed
To stop hot water crossing into the cold supply, or vice versa
TMVs & Scalding.w: Non-return checks prevent cross-flow between the hot and cold feeds, which would otherwise let hot migrate into the cold pipework (warming it into the growth range) or cold into the hot.

n.2: Check valves prevent backflow; they do not raise delivery temperature.
n.0: The hot and cold supplies remain separate feeds; the checks stop them mixing back through the valve.
n.1: Non-return valves address cross-flow, not primarily water hammer.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A maintenance record shows a healthcare TMV has not been serviced, descaled or checked for over two years. Why is this a significant concern?
o: The blended temperature will have dropped to match the incoming cold supply
The valve will have raised the storage temperature above safe limits
Scale and fouling may have degraded blending and the fail-safe, and the valve can harbour legionella
The check valves will have permanently welded the hot and cold feeds together
TMVs & Scalding.w: Without regular servicing, scale and biofilm build up inside the valve, which can impair accurate blending and the fail-safe and allow legionella to establish in the tepid internals – especially serious for vulnerable healthcare users.

n.1: A TMV does not control or raise storage temperature, so neglect does not push the cylinder above limits.
n.3: Fouling does not weld the feeds together; the concern is impaired function and bacterial growth.
n.0: A neglected valve does not simply track the cold feed; the risk is unreliable blending and contamination.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A TMV-fed shower that previously delivered 41°C now runs noticeably hotter over several visits. What does this most likely indicate?
o: The cold feed has been isolated deliberately for maintenance
The valve is drifting or failing and needs servicing or recalibration
The outlet has become a dead-leg and needs removing
The storage cylinder has been correctly raised to 60°C
TMVs & Scalding.w: A rising blended temperature over time points to the valve losing calibration or beginning to fail, which is a scald risk and calls for servicing, recalibration or replacement.

n.0: A deliberately isolated cold feed would trip the fail-safe and stop flow, not simply warm the delivery.
n.2: A shower in regular use is not a dead-leg; the symptom points to valve drift.
n.3: Correct storage temperature does not by itself change the delivered blended temperature at the outlet.

TMVs & Scalding.q: When a TMV is serviced, what must be done to its internal components as part of controlling legionella?
o: Leave the internals sealed and replace only the external pipework
Raise the set blended temperature by a few degrees to flush bacteria
Clean, descale and disinfect the internals, and clean the inlet strainers
Paint the valve body and renew the identification label only
TMVs & Scalding.w: Servicing includes dismantling as required to clean, descale and disinfect the internal parts and clean the strainers, removing scale and biofilm that harbour bacteria and impair operation.

n.3: Cosmetic attention to the body and label does not address the internal contamination and scaling.
n.1: Raising the temperature is not a substitute for cleaning and would compromise scald protection.
n.0: The internals are exactly where contamination gathers; they must be opened up and cleaned, not left sealed.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A new washroom is being designed for able-bodied office staff with no vulnerable users. How should TMV provision be decided?
o: Store hot water at 45°C instead so no TMVs are needed anywhere
Remove all hot water from the washroom to avoid any scald risk
Fit TMVs only where a scald risk assessment shows they are justified
Fit TMVs on every outlet as standard regardless of who uses them
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs should be provided on the basis of scald risk, targeting outlets and users where a real risk exists, rather than being fitted indiscriminately, as each valve adds a legionella maintenance burden.

n.3: Fitting TMVs everywhere adds needless tepid-water risk points and maintenance where no scald risk justifies them.
n.0: Lowering storage to 45°C to avoid TMVs creates a legionella risk and is never acceptable.
n.1: Removing hot water is impractical and is not how scald risk is managed.

TMVs & Scalding.q: On a healthcare TMV, at what point in the system should the blended (tepid) water temperature ideally be measured?
o: At the hot inlet to the valve before any blending occurs
At the cold water storage tank feeding the building
At the outlet or as close to it as practicable
At the calorifier flow connection in the plant room
TMVs & Scalding.w: The relevant delivered temperature is what reaches the user, so the blended water should be measured at or as near as practicable to the outlet.

n.0: The hot inlet reads storage/distribution temperature, not the safe delivered temperature.
n.3: The calorifier reading confirms storage control, not the outlet blend a user receives.
n.1: The cold tank temperature is a separate check and does not confirm the blended delivery.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Full-thickness scalds can occur very rapidly at high water temperatures. Which point best reflects this hazard?
o: Water below 60°C cannot cause a scald under any circumstances
Hotter water needs far less contact time to cause a serious scald than tepid water
Water at 41°C causes serious scalds within about one second
Scald severity depends only on volume of water, not its temperature
TMVs & Scalding.w: The higher the water temperature, the shorter the exposure needed to cause a serious burn, which is why hot deliveries to vulnerable users are blended down while storage stays hot.

n.2: Around 41°C is a safe bathing temperature and does not cause rapid scalding.
n.3: Temperature is the dominant factor in scald severity, not volume alone.
n.0: Water below 60°C can still scald, especially vulnerable people, given enough contact time.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why must hot water be stored at 60°C or above even though this temperature would scald if delivered directly?
o: To keep the stored water hot enough to control legionella, with TMVs preventing scalds at outlets
To reduce the electricity used by the immersion heater over a day
To allow the blended delivery to be set as high as 55°C safely
Because check valves only function correctly above 60°C
TMVs & Scalding.w: Storing at ≥60°C keeps legionella under control in the cylinder; the scald risk this creates at the tap is then managed locally by TMVs, not by cooling the store.

n.1: Higher storage temperature does not reduce energy use; it is required for microbial control.
n.3: Check valves are mechanical and are not dependent on a 60°C threshold.
n.2: Safe blended delivery is around 41°C, not 55°C, so this is not the reason for hot storage.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A TMV is being selected for a bath fill in a residential care setting. Which maximum blended delivery figure is the appropriate design target?
o: Around 44°C, within the recognised safe range for bathing
Around 60°C to match the storage temperature
Around 55°C to keep the bath water comfortably hot for longer
Whatever the incoming hot feed happens to deliver on the day
TMVs & Scalding.w: For baths and showers the blended delivery is kept within a safe range, with a maximum in the region of 43–44°C for a bath, to protect vulnerable bathers from scalding.

n.2: 55°C would present a serious scald risk and is well above the safe bathing range.
n.1: 60°C is the storage figure; delivering it to a bath would scald.
n.3: The whole point of the TMV is to control the delivered temperature rather than leaving it to the hot feed.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A ward TMV passes its fail-safe check but the outlet has very low flow and the valve interior is heavily scaled. What is the correct action?
o: Leave the valve and simply record the low flow for the next annual survey
Increase the blended set point to force water through the scale
No action – passing the fail-safe test is all that is required
Service and descale the valve and clean the strainers to restore correct function
TMVs & Scalding.w: Heavy scaling and reduced flow indicate the valve needs servicing, descaling and strainer cleaning; scale harbours bacteria and can eventually compromise blending and the fail-safe even if it currently passes.

n.2: A single passed test does not excuse leaving a heavily scaled, poorly performing valve in service.
n.1: Raising the set point compromises scald protection and does not remove the scale.
n.0: Deferring action on a scaled, low-flow valve allows the problem and the legionella risk to worsen.

TMVs & Scalding.q: How does fitting a TMV affect the temperature regime of the hot water system upstream of the valve?
o: The cold feed to the valve must be pre-warmed to help blending
The hot supply feeding the valve should be reduced to tepid to protect the valve
The whole hot system may be cooled once TMVs are on the main outlets
The hot feed and storage must remain at their normal hot temperatures up to the valve
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs only cool the water at the point of use; the storage and distribution up to the valve must stay hot (storage ≥60°C, distribution hot) to keep legionella under control.

n.1: The hot feed must stay hot; cooling it upstream would create a growth risk in the pipework.
n.2: Fitting TMVs does not license cooling the wider hot system.
n.0: Pre-warming the cold feed would undermine both blending accuracy and cold-water control.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which record is most useful for demonstrating ongoing control of both scald and legionella risk at a TMV?
o: The original purchase invoice for the valve and its packaging
The manufacturer's marketing brochure kept on file
A photograph of the valve taken when it was first installed
A log of servicing, disinfection, fail-safe tests and blended temperatures for that valve
TMVs & Scalding.w: A maintained log of servicing, cleaning/disinfection, fail-safe tests and recorded blended temperatures provides the evidence that the valve is being kept safe and effective over time.

n.0: A purchase invoice shows procurement, not ongoing safe operation.
n.2: An installation photo does not evidence continuing maintenance or performance.
n.1: A brochure describes the product but records nothing about this valve's upkeep.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A facilities team plans to feed several basins across a corridor from one centrally located TMV to save on valves. Why is this generally poor practice?
o: Central TMVs are prohibited in every type of building
It creates long runs of tepid blended water that favour legionella growth
It prevents the storage cylinder from reaching 60°C
It would make the blended water too hot for the furthest basin
TMVs & Scalding.w: Feeding distant outlets from one TMV produces long pipe runs holding tepid blended water in the growth range; TMVs should be sited close to the outlets they serve to minimise these tepid legs.

n.3: The problem is stagnant tepid pipework, not the water arriving too hot; long runs tend to cool, not overheat.
n.0: Central blending is not banned outright; the issue is the tepid dead-legs it creates.
n.2: TMV arrangement does not stop the cylinder heating to 60°C.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What should typically happen to the recorded blended temperatures of a TMV over successive routine checks if the valve is healthy?
o: They should climb steadily towards the storage temperature
They should alternate above and below the growth range at random
They should stay stable within the expected safe range each time
They should fall a little on every visit until the valve shuts off
TMVs & Scalding.w: A well-maintained TMV holds a consistent blended output within the safe range; stable readings are the sign of correct operation, whereas drift up or down signals a developing fault.

n.0: A rising trend towards storage temperature indicates the valve is failing towards a scald condition.
n.3: A steadily falling output indicates a developing fault, not healthy operation.
n.1: Random swings across the range indicate an unreliable, faulty valve, not a healthy one.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which of the following is a genuine benefit that a correctly maintained TMV provides?
o: It allows the cold water tank to be run at 30°C safely
It permanently disinfects the outlet so flushing is no longer required
It removes the need to keep any temperature records for that outlet
It lets vulnerable users receive safe-temperature water while storage stays hot
TMVs & Scalding.w: The core benefit of a TMV is that it delivers non-scalding water at the outlet for at-risk users while the system upstream stays hot enough to control legionella.

n.2: A TMV increases, rather than removes, the need for temperature and maintenance records.
n.0: Cold water should be kept below 20°C; a TMV does not license a warm cold tank.
n.1: A TMV provides no disinfection; outlets it serves may still need flushing if under-used.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A little-used TMV shower in a school changing room is only run during term time. What extra control is most relevant to managing its legionella risk?
o: Regular flushing of the outlet during periods of low or no use
Removing the strainers so the valve cannot become blocked
Disconnecting the cold feed while the school is closed
Raising the blended temperature to 50°C during the holidays
TMVs & Scalding.w: Infrequently used TMV outlets hold stagnant tepid water, so regular flushing to draw fresh water through is an important control alongside the valve's own servicing.

n.3: Raising the blended temperature to 50°C removes the scald protection the TMV exists to provide.
n.1: Strainers protect the valve and must be retained and cleaned, not removed.
n.2: Disconnecting the cold feed would trip the fail-safe and creates further stagnation, not a control.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Who is generally best placed to carry out the servicing, descaling and recalibration of TMVs?
o: A competent, suitably trained and equipped person following the maintenance regime
Any member of staff, using boiling water to sterilise the parts
Nobody – modern TMVs are sealed and never need internal work
Only the water supplier, who owns the incoming main
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMV maintenance requires a competent, trained person with the right equipment and knowledge of the valve, so that servicing, descaling, disinfection and recalibration are done correctly.

n.1: Untrained staff pouring boiling water over parts is unsafe and does not constitute proper servicing.
n.2: TMVs are not maintenance-free; their internals must be serviced regularly.
n.3: The water supplier is responsible for the main, not for maintaining the building's TMVs.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A TMV3-type valve is specified for a hospital bathroom rather than a basic domestic mixer. What is the main reason?
o: It removes the requirement to store hot water above 60°C
It meets a higher performance and fail-safe standard suited to high-risk healthcare users
It heats the water faster than a domestic mixing tap
It allows a single valve to serve the whole hospital wing
TMVs & Scalding.w: Healthcare settings serve high-risk users, so valves meeting the higher performance and fail-safe specification are specified to give reliable scald protection where the consequences of failure are most serious.

n.2: A TMV blends to a lower temperature; it does not heat water faster.
n.0: Storage must still be kept ≥60°C regardless of the valve grade.
n.3: Higher-spec valves are still sited close to outlets, not used to feed a whole wing.

TMVs & Scalding.q: An outlet has both a TMV and is only used a few times a year. From a water hygiene standpoint, what is the underlying tension the risk assessment must resolve?
o: Whether the cold and hot feeds should swap connections
Whether to store hot water above 70°C to offset the low use
Balancing the scald protection the TMV gives against the legionella risk it and low use create
Whether the valve should be painted to match the room decor
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV reduces scald risk but adds a tepid-water legionella risk that low use makes worse; the assessment must weigh whether the outlet is needed at all, and how to control both risks.

n.3: Decor is irrelevant to the water hygiene tension being assessed.
n.0: Swapping feeds is a wiring error, not the risk trade-off in question.
n.1: Storing at 70°C introduces its own scald and energy issues and does not resolve the tepid-water risk at the outlet.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What is the correct relationship between a TMV and the overall water safety approach for a building?
o: The TMV means cold water temperatures no longer need to be checked
The TMV is one local control that must sit within the wider water safety and temperature regime
The TMV replaces the need for a written scheme of control
The TMV overrides the monitoring of storage and distribution temperatures
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV is a point-of-use scald control that must be integrated with, not a substitute for, the building's wider legionella controls such as temperature monitoring and the written scheme.

n.2: A written scheme of control is still required; the TMV is one measure within it.
n.3: Storage and distribution temperatures must still be monitored; the TMV does not override them.
n.0: Cold water temperature checks remain necessary regardless of TMVs.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A contractor proposes removing the TMV from a staff kitchenette tap that has never presented a scald risk, to cut maintenance. How should this be judged?
o: Reject it because removing a TMV always raises the legionella risk
Reasonable if a risk assessment confirms there is no scald risk at that outlet
Accept it only if the storage temperature is lowered to compensate
Reject it because every tap must legally have a TMV
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs are justified by scald risk; where an assessment shows none, removing a redundant valve is sensible as it also removes a tepid-water maintenance point, provided the change is risk-assessed.

n.3: There is no requirement for every tap to have a TMV; they are fitted where scald risk justifies it.
n.0: Removing an unnecessary TMV reduces, not increases, tepid-water legionella risk points.
n.2: Storage must not be lowered; that is never an acceptable trade-off.

TMVs & Scalding.q: During disinfection of a hot water system to a high temperature, why do TMVs need particular attention?
o: They automatically raise the disinfection temperature at the outlet
They should be removed entirely and refitted only after the whole system cools
They must be run at their blended setting to protect them from the heat
They may need isolating or setting to pass hot water so their internals are disinfected without scalding an operator
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs will normally blend the hot disinfection water down, so they must be managed – isolated or set to pass hot water under controlled conditions – so their internals are disinfected while operators are protected from the hot flow.

n.2: Left at the blended setting, the valve internals and downstream leg may not reach disinfection temperature.
n.1: Wholesale removal is not the standard approach; controlled isolation or bypass is used.
n.0: A TMV lowers, not raises, the temperature reaching the outlet.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A basin TMV is delivering water at 47°C to a dementia care unit. How should this reading be treated?
o: Ignore it, because basin temperatures are not part of scald control
Acceptable, as anything under 50°C is regarded as safe for bathing
Acceptable, provided the hot feed to the valve is below 60°C
Too hot for the at-risk users – investigate and recommission the valve to the safe range
TMVs & Scalding.w: 47°C is above the safe blended range and presents a scald risk to vulnerable users, so the valve needs investigating and recommissioning back to the correct delivery temperature.

n.1: Under 50°C is not automatically safe; safe basin delivery is around 41°C, and 47°C can scald at-risk users.
n.2: The hot feed should be hot (near 60°C); a below-60°C feed would not make a 47°C delivery acceptable and would signal other problems.
n.0: Basin delivery temperature to vulnerable users is exactly what TMV scald control addresses.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which statement about commissioning a newly installed TMV is correct?
o: It can be left at the factory default with no on-site verification
It only needs commissioning once the outlet has been in use for a month
Its blended temperature should be set to match the storage temperature
It should be set and verified to deliver within the safe blended range and its fail-safe checked before use
TMVs & Scalding.w: A new TMV must be commissioned on site: the blended temperature set and verified within the safe range and the fail-safe function confirmed, before the outlet is put into service.

n.0: Factory defaults must be verified on site against the actual supplies; leaving them unchecked is unsafe.
n.1: Commissioning must happen before use, not after a month in service.
n.2: Setting the blend to storage temperature would deliver scalding water and defeats the valve's purpose.

TMVs & Scalding.q: An operative argues that because a TMV keeps the tap water tepid, that outlet no longer needs to be included in the legionella monitoring scheme. Why is this wrong?
o: Because the storage temperature alone guarantees safety at every outlet
Because the tap should instead be fed with unblended hot water
Because the tepid blended water and the valve internals are prime conditions for legionella and need monitoring
Because tepid water is always completely free of legionella
TMVs & Scalding.w: The very tepid water the TMV produces, together with the scale and biofilm inside the valve, sits in the ideal growth range, so TMV outlets need more, not less, monitoring and maintenance attention.

n.3: Tepid water is not legionella-free; it is in the range where the bacteria thrive.
n.0: Correct storage temperature does not by itself guarantee safety downstream of a blending valve.
n.1: Feeding the tap with unblended hot water would remove the scald protection the vulnerable users need.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why are showers and spray taps treated as a high legionella risk?
o: They break water into a fine spray of tiny droplets that can be breathed in
They are always fed from a cold water storage tank
They use more water than an ordinary tap
They run at a higher water pressure than baths
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Showers and spray taps create a fine breathable aerosol, the main route by which legionella bacteria reach the lungs and infect people.

n.2: Water volume is not what makes them a health risk; it is the aerosol they create.
n.1: Their feed source varies and is not the reason they are high risk.
n.3: Pressure alone does not cause infection; breathing in the spray does.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: How does a person usually catch Legionnaires' disease from a shower?
o: By getting shower water on their skin
By drinking water from the shower
By touching the shower head with bare hands
By breathing in fine water droplets from the spray
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Legionella infects people when they inhale the fine aerosol droplets a shower produces, so the bacteria reach deep into the lungs.

n.1: Swallowing water is not the usual route of infection for Legionnaires' disease.
n.2: Simple contact with a fitting does not cause the lung infection.
n.0: Water on the skin does not infect a healthy person; breathing in the spray does.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: How often should shower heads and hoses be cleaned, descaled and disinfected as a minimum?
o: Once a year
At least every three months
Once every two years
Only when they look dirty
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Guidance recommends cleaning, descaling and disinfecting shower heads and hoses at least quarterly, that is every three months.

n.0: Yearly is far too infrequent to control scale and biofilm in a shower head.
n.3: Waiting until it looks dirty is not acceptable; a routine quarterly schedule is required.
n.2: Two years would allow heavy scale and bacterial growth to build up.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A shower in a spare bedroom has not been used for several weeks. What is the correct action before it goes back into normal use?
o: Leave it alone as it will clear itself when someone uses it
Turn off its water supply permanently
Flush it through, running the water so any stagnant water is cleared
Only wipe the outside of the shower head
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A little-used outlet must be flushed so stagnant water sitting in the pipe and head is cleared before normal use.

n.0: Stagnant water does not clear itself; it needs deliberate flushing.
n.1: Turning it off permanently is only correct if it is truly redundant, not a spare that will be used again.
n.3: Wiping the outside does nothing about stagnant water or scale inside the head.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: How often should little-used (infrequently used) outlets be flushed as a minimum?
o: At least once a month
At least once a year
At least once a week
Only before an inspection
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Infrequently used outlets should be flushed at least weekly to stop water sitting stagnant and to keep the temperatures right.

n.0: Monthly is too infrequent and lets water stagnate between flushes.
n.1: Yearly leaves water standing for far too long.
n.3: Flushing only before an inspection ignores the real weekly requirement.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When flushing a little-used tap or shower, what tells you it has been flushed for long enough?
o: One minute has passed on the clock
The water stops running
The water looks clear
Hot water runs hot and cold water runs cold
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: You flush until the hot runs hot and the cold runs cold, which shows fresh water has drawn through and reached the right temperatures.

n.1: The water should not stop; you keep it running until temperatures are correct.
n.0: A fixed one minute may not be long enough to reach temperature on every outlet.
n.2: Clear-looking water can still be the wrong temperature and stagnant.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why should a little-used outlet be opened gently and slowly when you flush it?
o: Because the tap could break if opened quickly
To save water
To reduce the amount of spray and aerosol released into the air
To stop the pipes making a noise
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Opening gently limits the fine aerosol created, reducing the breathable spray that could carry legionella.

n.1: Saving water is not the reason; controlling aerosol is.
n.0: Preventing damage is not the health reason for opening gently.
n.3: Noise is not the concern; releasing less breathable spray is.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: An outlet has been disconnected and will never be used again. What should happen to the pipework serving it?
o: Leave it in place but flush it weekly
Fill the pipe with disinfectant and seal both ends
Remove the redundant pipework so it does not become a dead leg
Leave the pipe capped near the main so it can be reused later
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Permanently redundant pipework should be removed so it does not sit as a dead leg where stagnant water lets legionella grow.

n.3: A capped stub left on the main is exactly the dead leg that should be removed.
n.0: Flushing a pipe that will never be used is not the answer; remove it instead.
n.1: Sealing stagnant water in the pipe still leaves a dead leg harbouring bacteria.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: What is a 'dead leg' in a water system?
o: A length of pipe where water sits still because the outlet is little used or removed
The main incoming supply pipe to a building
A pipe fitted with a check valve
A pipe that carries only hot water
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A dead leg is a section of pipe where water can stagnate because it is rarely or never drawn off, letting bacteria multiply.

n.3: A hot pipe in regular use is not automatically a dead leg.
n.1: The busy incoming main is the opposite of a stagnant dead leg.
n.2: A check valve does not define a dead leg; stagnant, little-used pipe does.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why does scale building up inside a shower head make the legionella risk worse?
o: It makes the water come out colder
It blocks the water so no spray comes out at all
It changes the colour of the water
It gives biofilm and bacteria a rough surface to grow on and shelter in
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Scale gives biofilm and bacteria a rough sheltered surface to colonise, so removing scale by descaling reduces the risk.

n.1: Scale usually restricts and sprays the flow rather than stopping it completely.
n.0: Scale does not reliably cool the water; the concern is bacterial growth.
n.2: A colour change is not the health issue; harbouring bacteria is.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Before disinfecting a shower head, why is it important to descale and clean it first?
o: So the head shines and looks tidy for inspection
To make the head lighter to carry
So the disinfectant lasts longer in the bottle
Because scale and dirt can shield bacteria from the disinfectant
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Scale and dirt shelter bacteria and stop disinfectant reaching them, so cleaning and descaling first lets the disinfectant work.

n.0: Appearance is not the reason; effective disinfection is.
n.1: Weight of the head is irrelevant to the task.
n.2: How long the product lasts in the bottle is not the point.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: What is a flow straightener or strainer fitted in a spray tap or tap outlet?
o: A device that heats the water at the tap
A meter that records how much water is used
A valve that stops water flowing backwards
A small insert at the outlet that shapes the flow and can trap debris
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A flow straightener or strainer sits at the outlet to shape flow and can trap debris and scale, so it needs regular cleaning.

n.2: A backflow stop is a check valve, not a flow straightener.
n.0: It does not heat water; it shapes and screens the flow.
n.1: It does not measure water use.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: You find a spray tap in a washroom that is heavily scaled and barely spraying. What should you do?
o: Ignore it because the water is still coming out
Clean and descale the tap fitting and strainer, then report it if needed
Turn the water pressure up to force it through
Wrap tape around the outlet to hide the scale
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A scaled spray fitting should be cleaned and descaled so it works properly and does not harbour bacteria, and reported if a bigger fix is needed.

n.0: Ignoring scale lets bacteria and biofilm build up further.
n.2: Raising pressure does not remove scale and may worsen aerosol.
n.3: Hiding the scale does nothing to control the risk.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: After you flush a little-used outlet, what should you do next as part of the control scheme?
o: Turn off the outlet's supply
Nothing; flushing on its own is enough
Empty the storage tank
Record that you flushed it, noting the date
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Flushing must be recorded, including the date, so there is evidence the control scheme is being followed.

n.1: The task is not complete until it is recorded.
n.0: You do not shut off an outlet that is meant to stay in use.
n.2: Emptying a storage tank is not part of flushing an outlet.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When cleaning a shower head at a wash basin or in a tray, why lower the head down into the tray or basin before running it?
o: To keep the spray and aerosol down low and contained rather than sprayed into the air
To make the head easier to unscrew
To stop water splashing on the floor and being wasted
To warm the tray up first
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Lowering the head into the tray keeps any aerosol contained and low, reducing the breathable spray released while you work.

n.2: Preventing floor splashes and waste is not the health reason.
n.3: Warming the tray is irrelevant.
n.1: It does not help unscrew the head.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A cleaner reports a shower head that is clogged, dripping and covered in limescale. As the operative, what is the right response?
o: Spray air freshener near it to mask the smell
Take it out of use, clean, descale and disinfect it, and record the work
Tell them it is normal and to leave it
Just run the shower for a few minutes
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A scaled clogged head should be taken out of use, cleaned, descaled and disinfected, with the work recorded.

n.2: Heavy scale is not normal and must be dealt with.
n.3: Running it briefly does not remove scale or biofilm.
n.0: Masking a smell ignores the actual hygiene problem.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which type of outlet is generally considered a higher legionella risk because of the way it delivers water?
o: A slow-running mop-bucket tap
A garden bib tap outdoors
A bath filler that pours water in a stream
A spray tap that atomises water into a fine mist
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A spray tap atomises water into a fine mist, creating the breathable aerosol that makes it a higher risk.

n.2: A stream from a bath filler makes little aerosol compared with a spray.
n.1: An outdoor bib tap that pours a stream is a lower aerosol risk.
n.0: A slow stream into a bucket produces little breathable spray.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why are aerosol-forming outlets such as showers and spray taps a particular concern for vulnerable people?
o: They cannot be cleaned
They use hotter water than normal
The fine spray they create can be inhaled deep into the lungs
They are usually found only in hospitals
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The fine spray can be inhaled deep into the lungs, and people who are older, unwell or have weak immune systems are more likely to become ill.

n.1: They do not necessarily run hotter, and heat is not the inhalation risk.
n.3: Such outlets are found in many buildings, not only hospitals.
n.0: They can and must be cleaned regularly.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A little-used shower is only run for a few seconds each week 'to keep it ticking over'. Why is this not good enough?
o: It uses the wrong type of soap
It wastes too little water to matter
The hot may not reach hot and the cold may not reach cold, so stagnant water is not cleared
Showers should never be flushed at all
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A few seconds may not draw fresh water through or reach the correct hot and cold temperatures, so stagnant water is left in the system.

n.1: The problem is temperature and stagnation, not water waste.
n.0: Soap is not part of flushing an outlet.
n.3: Little-used showers should be flushed; that is exactly the control.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: What is biofilm, which can form inside shower hoses and heads?
o: A layer of limescale only
A protective plastic coating fitted at the factory
A cleaning product used on outlets
A thin slimy layer of bacteria and other matter clinging to the inside surface
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Biofilm is a thin slimy layer of bacteria and other matter that clings to internal surfaces and can shelter legionella.

n.1: It is not a factory coating; it is unwanted bacterial growth.
n.0: Scale is different from biofilm, though the two often occur together.
n.2: It is a problem to be removed, not a cleaning product.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: If you notice a shower hose that is split and covered in scale during your rounds, what should you do?
o: Cut the hose shorter yourself
Leave a note for the next shift only
Say nothing as it is not your job
Report it to the responsible person so it can be cleaned or replaced
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A fouled or damaged fitting should be reported to the responsible person so it can be cleaned, descaled or replaced.

n.2: Spotting and reporting hazards is part of the operative's duty.
n.0: Cutting the hose is not an appropriate fix and may not be your task.
n.1: A note for the next shift alone risks the fault being missed or delayed.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why should records of flushing and cleaning be kept accurate and up to date?
o: So the water bill can be checked
Because the water company demands them each week
To prove the control scheme is being carried out and to spot missed tasks
To show the outlet colour has not changed
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Accurate records prove the control scheme is being followed and help spot any outlets that have been missed.

n.3: Records are not about the colour of the outlet.
n.0: They are not for checking the water bill.
n.1: The reason is legionella control, not a weekly demand from the water company.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: An aerator is fitted to the end of a mixer tap. Why does it need regular cleaning?
o: It changes the taste of the water if left dirty
It measures the water temperature
It can collect scale and debris where bacteria can grow
It stops the tap from dripping
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: An aerator collects scale and debris at the outlet where bacteria can grow, so it must be cleaned regularly.

n.0: Taste is not the health concern; bacterial growth is.
n.3: An aerator is not a drip stopper.
n.1: It does not measure temperature.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A ward side-room is closed for a fortnight. To keep its shower and taps safe, staff should:
o: Leave the outlets shut and unused until the room reopens
Drain the whole building's cold water tank
Cap the outlets off permanently
Flush the outlets at least weekly until the room is back in use
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Outlets left little used should be flushed at least weekly so water does not stagnate while the room is closed.

n.0: Leaving them unused lets water stagnate and bacteria grow.
n.1: Draining the building's tank is a drastic, unnecessary step.
n.2: Capping permanently is wrong for outlets that will be used again soon.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which statement about the aerosol from a shower is correct?
o: Aerosol from a shower cannot carry bacteria
The finer the droplets, the more easily they can be breathed deep into the lungs
Only hot showers create any aerosol
The larger the droplets, the greater the risk of infection
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Finer droplets are more easily breathed deep into the lungs, which is why fine sprays are the main infection concern.

n.3: Larger droplets fall out of the air; fine droplets are the greater risk.
n.0: Aerosol can carry legionella; that is the whole concern.
n.2: Both hot and cold sprays can create aerosol.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When you clean a shower head that has been soaking in descaler, what should you do before it is used again?
o: Rinse it thoroughly so no cleaning chemical is left, then refit and disinfect as required
Paint it to seal the surface
Leave it to dry for a week first
Fit it straight back wet with descaler still on it
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The head must be rinsed thoroughly so no cleaning chemical remains before it is refitted and put back into use.

n.3: Leaving descaler on the head could contaminate the water and is unsafe.
n.2: A week's drying is unnecessary and takes the shower out of use needlessly.
n.1: Painting a shower head is not part of the cleaning process.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why must permanently redundant outlets be removed rather than just left turned off?
o: Turned-off outlets waste electricity
Turned-off taps rust the fastest
It makes the room look tidier
A capped-off but connected outlet leaves stagnant water in a dead leg
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: An outlet left connected but unused leaves stagnant water in a dead leg where legionella can multiply, so the pipework should be removed.

n.0: Water outlets do not use electricity, so that is not the reason.
n.1: Rust is not the legionella control reason.
n.2: Tidiness is not the health reason for removal.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A hotel has several rooms that are only booked occasionally. What is the best way to manage their showers between guests?
o: Turn off the hot water to those rooms
Flush them on a regular schedule, at least weekly, and record it
Leave them until the annual service
Only clean them when a guest complains
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Occasionally used showers should be flushed on a regular schedule, at least weekly, and the flushing recorded.

n.3: Waiting for a complaint is not proactive control.
n.2: An annual service leaves far too long between flushes.
n.0: Turning off the hot water can create its own risks and does not flush the outlet.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which of these is the main reason spray taps are commonly fitted in public washrooms even though they need careful management?
o: They save water compared with ordinary taps
They stop the sink from overflowing
They never need cleaning
They warm the water more quickly
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Spray taps are often fitted to save water, but because they atomise water they must be cleaned and descaled carefully to control legionella.

n.3: They do not heat water faster.
n.2: They in fact need regular cleaning, not none.
n.1: They do not prevent a sink overflowing.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: During flushing of a rarely used outlet, colleagues nearby are a concern. What is the sensible precaution?
o: Flush only with the window closed
Flush as fast and hard as possible to get it over with
Ask everyone to leave the building
Open the outlet gently to keep spray to a minimum and avoid unnecessary aerosol near people
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Opening gently keeps spray and aerosol to a minimum, reducing what people nearby might breathe in.

n.1: Fast, hard flushing throws up more aerosol.
n.2: Evacuating the building is a disproportionate response for routine flushing.
n.0: Closing the window does not reduce the aerosol created and may keep it in the room.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: What should be checked and cleaned on a spray tap besides the visible nozzle?
o: The strainer or flow straightener where debris and scale collect
The wall tiles behind the tap
Only the tap handle
The waste pipe under the sink
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The strainer or flow straightener collects debris and scale and must be cleaned as well as the visible nozzle.

n.2: Cleaning only the handle misses the parts in the water path.
n.3: The waste pipe is separate from the outlet fitting being cleaned.
n.1: Wall tiles are not part of the outlet's water hygiene.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why is warm, stagnant water in a little-used shower hose especially risky?
o: Warm water makes the hose stiffer
Warm still water is close to the temperature legionella grows best in
Warm water cannot be flushed away
Warm water changes colour
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Warm, still water sits in the range where legionella multiplies fastest, so it must be flushed out regularly.

n.2: Warm water can be flushed away; that is the control.
n.0: Hose stiffness is irrelevant to the risk.
n.3: Colour change is not the concern; bacterial growth is.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A gym shower block has a bank of showers, two of which are rarely used. What is the correct approach for those two?
o: Remove their heads and leave the pipes open
Assume the busy showers keep them safe
Include them in the weekly flushing regime and record it
Only clean them once a year
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The two rarely used showers should be flushed weekly and recorded, as busy neighbouring outlets do not keep their pipework safe.

n.0: Removing heads and leaving open pipes creates its own hazards.
n.1: Water in the little-used branches still stagnates regardless of the busy ones.
n.3: Once a year is far too infrequent for little-used outlets.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: What is the purpose of disinfecting a shower head after cleaning and descaling?
o: To make the metal shine
To seal the holes so it sprays harder
To kill remaining bacteria that cleaning and descaling did not remove
To make it smell pleasant
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Disinfection kills bacteria left behind after cleaning and descaling, completing the treatment of the head.

n.3: A pleasant smell is not the aim.
n.0: Shine is cosmetic, not the hygiene purpose.
n.1: Disinfecting does not and should not block the spray holes.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: An operative is told to flush little-used outlets 'when they get a chance'. Why is a fixed schedule better?
o: It makes sure every outlet is flushed at least weekly and none is forgotten
It reduces the number of outlets needing flushing
It looks more professional on paper only
It lets outlets be skipped when busy
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A fixed schedule ensures every little-used outlet is flushed at least weekly and none is overlooked.

n.2: The benefit is real control, not just paperwork appearance.
n.3: A good schedule prevents skipping, it does not permit it.
n.1: A schedule does not change how many outlets exist.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which outlet fitting is designed to mix air with water to give a softer, splash-free flow but can trap scale?
o: An aerator
A pressure gauge
A check valve
A stopcock
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: An aerator mixes air into the water for a softer flow and can trap scale and debris, so it needs regular cleaning.

n.2: A check valve stops backflow; it does not aerate the flow.
n.3: A stopcock is an isolating valve, not an outlet aerator.
n.1: A pressure gauge only measures pressure.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A shower head is so blocked with scale that only a fine high-pressure jet comes out. Why is this a particular concern?
o: The jet wastes hot water
A fine forceful spray can create more breathable aerosol
The water will taste different
The head will look untidy
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A fine forceful spray from a scaled head can create more breathable aerosol, increasing the chance of inhaling any bacteria present.

n.0: Water waste is not the health concern here.
n.3: Appearance is not the reason it is risky.
n.2: Taste is not the infection route; inhaled aerosol is.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When should you report a scaled or fouled outlet to the responsible person?
o: Only if it stops working completely
Never, unless someone asks you
At the end of the year
As soon as you notice it, rather than ignoring it
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A scaled or fouled outlet should be reported as soon as it is noticed so it can be dealt with promptly.

n.0: Waiting for total failure lets the problem grow and the risk increase.
n.2: Year-end reporting leaves a known fault unaddressed for far too long.
n.1: You should report faults you find, not stay silent until asked.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why is it important to flush the cold as well as the hot when flushing a little-used mixer outlet?
o: Stagnant water can sit in both the hot and the cold pipe, so both must be cleared
Cold water never carries bacteria
Only the hot pipe has a strainer
The cold side is fed from the same pipe as the hot
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Stagnant water can sit in both the hot and the cold supply to a mixer, so both sides must be run to clear them.

n.1: Cold water can carry bacteria, especially when lukewarm and stagnant.
n.2: Strainers are not only on the hot side; that is not the reason.
n.3: Hot and cold are fed by separate supplies to the mixer.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A caretaker keeps a written log of every shower head clean and descale. What is the main value of this log?
o: It records how much cleaning product is bought
It is only needed if there is an outbreak
It proves the caretaker works hard
It shows each head has been cleaned at least quarterly and flags any that are overdue
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The log shows every head has been cleaned at least quarterly and highlights any that are overdue for attention.

n.2: The log is about control evidence, not measuring effort.
n.0: It tracks the cleaning tasks, not product purchasing.
n.1: Records must be kept routinely, not only after an outbreak.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A washroom spray tap sprays unevenly and spits. What is the most likely hygiene-related cause an operative should check?
o: The sink is too small
The mirror above it is loose
Scale or debris in the strainer or spray outlet
The tap is the wrong colour
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Uneven spitting spray is commonly caused by scale or debris in the strainer or outlet, which should be cleaned.

n.3: Colour has nothing to do with how it sprays.
n.0: Sink size does not affect the spray pattern.
n.1: A loose mirror is unrelated to the tap's flow.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which action best reduces the aerosol you make when you have to open a stagnant outlet for flushing?
o: Open the valve slowly and, for a shower, keep the head low in the tray
Stand as close to the outlet as possible
Point the outlet upward into the room
Open the valve fully and quickly
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Opening slowly and keeping the shower head low in the tray keeps the aerosol contained and reduces what is released into the air.

n.3: Opening fully and quickly throws up more spray.
n.1: Standing close puts you in the aerosol you are trying to avoid.
n.2: Pointing the outlet up sprays aerosol into the room and towards people.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why should shower hoses, not just the heads, be included in cleaning and descaling?
o: Hoses carry the electrical earth
Hoses change the water pressure
Scale and biofilm also build up inside the hose where water sits
Hoses are more expensive than heads
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Scale and biofilm build up inside the hose as well as the head, so the hose must be cleaned or replaced too.

n.0: Hoses carry water, not an electrical earth.
n.3: Cost is not the reason they need cleaning.
n.1: The reason is bacterial growth inside, not pressure.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A little-used tap is flushed weekly but the flushing is never written down. What is wrong with this?
o: Flushing weekly is too often
Nothing, as long as the flushing happens
There is no record to prove the control is being done or to spot a missed week
The tap should be flushed monthly instead
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Without a record there is no evidence the flushing is being done and no easy way to spot a week that was missed.

n.1: Flushing without recording leaves the scheme unproven and hard to audit.
n.0: Weekly is the correct minimum, not too often.
n.3: Monthly would be too infrequent for a little-used outlet.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A room's shower will be permanently taken out of service in a refurbishment. What is the correct hygiene outcome?
o: Cap the shower off at the wall and leave the pipe behind it
Leave the shower fitted but never flush it
Fill the shower head with sealant
Remove the redundant pipework back to the live main so no dead leg is left
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Redundant pipework should be removed back to the live main so no dead leg of stagnant water is left behind.

n.0: Capping at the wall leaves a dead leg of stagnant water in the pipe.
n.1: Leaving it unflushed creates exactly the stagnant risk to avoid.
n.2: Sealing the head does nothing about the stagnant pipe behind it.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why is it good practice to run a shower for flushing with the head detached or held low rather than spraying freely?
o: It uses less soap
It reduces the fine spray released into the room air
It makes the water hotter
It cleans the inside of the head at the same time
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Directing the flow low or through a detached head reduces the fine spray released into the room, limiting breathable aerosol.

n.3: Flushing this way is about aerosol control, not cleaning the head.
n.2: It does not change the water temperature.
n.0: Soap is not involved in flushing.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: An operative finds an outlet that no one can explain and that appears never to be used. What is the correct first step?
o: Paint over it
Report it to the responsible person so it can be assessed and, if redundant, removed
Cut it off immediately without telling anyone
Start using it daily so it is no longer little used
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: An unexplained, apparently unused outlet should be reported so it can be assessed and, if redundant, removed to avoid a dead leg.

n.2: Cutting it off yourself without authority or assessment is not appropriate.
n.3: Forcing daily use of an unnecessary outlet is not the right solution.
n.0: Painting it does nothing about the stagnation risk.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which best describes why regular quarterly cleaning of heads and hoses works together with weekly flushing of little-used outlets?
o: They are alternatives, so you only ever need one of them
Both are only for hot outlets
Cleaning removes scale and biofilm while flushing keeps water fresh, and both are needed
Flushing replaces the need to clean the head
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Cleaning and descaling remove scale and biofilm, while flushing keeps water fresh; together they control the risk at the outlet.

n.0: They are complementary controls, not alternatives.
n.1: Both apply to cold as well as hot outlets.
n.3: Flushing does not remove built-up scale and biofilm, so cleaning is still needed.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A shower used every day by many people still needs its head cleaned and descaled on a routine. Why?
o: Only little-used showers grow scale
Frequent use means it never needs cleaning
Scale and biofilm can still build up in the head regardless of how often it is used
Busy showers clean themselves
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Scale and biofilm can still form in the head of a busy shower, so routine quarterly cleaning and descaling is still needed.

n.1: Frequent use does not remove the need for cleaning.
n.0: Busy showers scale up too, not only little-used ones.
n.3: Water flow alone does not clean out scale and biofilm.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which single statement best sums up why showers and spray taps get so much attention in water hygiene?
o: They are the outlets that turn water into a breathable spray, so they must be flushed, cleaned and kept scale-free
They are the cheapest outlets to fit in a building
They are the only outlets fed with hot water
They are the outlets used least often in most buildings
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Showers and spray taps turn water into a breathable spray, which is the main way legionella reaches people, so they must be flushed when little used and cleaned and descaled regularly.

n.1: Cost is not the reason they are a priority for hygiene.
n.2: They are not the only outlets fed with hot water.
n.3: They are not necessarily the least-used outlets; the concern is the aerosol they create.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why are showers and spray taps considered a particular legionella risk?
o: They use more water than ordinary taps
They cannot be cleaned once installed
They create a fine spray or aerosol that can be breathed in
They are always fed from the coldest part of the system
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Showers and spray taps break the water into a fine aerosol, which is the main way legionella bacteria reach the lungs.

n.0: Water usage is not what makes them risky; it is the aerosol they produce.
n.3: Their feed temperature varies; the risk comes from the spray, not from being cold-fed.
n.1: Shower heads and spray fittings are designed to be removed, cleaned and disinfected.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: How often should shower heads and hoses normally be cleaned, descaled and disinfected?
o: Once a year is always enough
Only when they become blocked
At least every three months (quarterly)
Once every five years
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Shower heads and hoses are cleaned, descaled and disinfected at least quarterly to stop scale and biofilm harbouring legionella.

n.3: Five years is far too long and would let biofilm and legionella build up in the fitting.
n.1: Waiting for a blockage means the fitting is already fouled and possibly contaminated.
n.0: Annual cleaning is not frequent enough for aerosol-producing shower fittings.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: How often must a little-used outlet be flushed to help control legionella?
o: It never needs flushing if it looks clean
At least weekly, running it until hot runs hot and cold runs cold
Only when someone reports a smell
Once every six months
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Infrequently used outlets are flushed at least weekly so that fresh water replaces the stagnant water where legionella can grow.

n.3: Six months lets water stagnate for far too long and allows legionella to multiply.
n.2: Flushing is a planned weekly control, not something done only after a complaint.
n.0: Stagnant water can be contaminated even when the outlet looks perfectly clean.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When flushing a little-used outlet, how should you run it to reduce aerosol release?
o: Run it for two seconds only
Blast it at full pressure with the door open
Only run the cold side and never the hot
Open it gently and run it fully until hot is hot and cold is cold
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The outlet is run steadily until the temperatures reach their normal hot and cold, drawing through fresh water while limiting spray.

n.1: A high-pressure blast maximises aerosol, the very thing that spreads legionella.
n.0: Two seconds does not draw fresh water through or reach the correct temperatures.
n.2: Both hot and cold sides must be flushed so neither leg stagnates.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: You find a shower in a spare room that has not been used for several weeks. What should you do?
o: Flush it through, then clean and disinfect the head, and add it to the weekly flush list
Leave it, since nobody is using that room
Turn the shower on for one second and move on
Remove the cold feed so only hot water is available
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: An unused shower holds stagnant water in a fitting that makes aerosol, so it is flushed, the head cleaned and disinfected, and put on the flush routine.

n.1: Leaving stagnant water in an aerosol-producing shower is a clear legionella risk.
n.3: Removing the cold feed causes scalding and does not deal with the stagnation.
n.2: A one-second burst releases aerosol without properly flushing through fresh water.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: An outlet has been out of use for months and is never going to be used again. What is the best legionella control?
o: Leave it capped at the tap and forget about it
Just close the isolation valve behind it
Flush it once and then leave it permanently
Remove the redundant outlet and pipework back to the main supply
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A permanently disused outlet is best removed back to the live pipe so there is no dead leg of stagnant water to grow legionella.

n.0: A capped tap still leaves a dead leg of stagnant water feeding it.
n.2: A single flush does nothing once the outlet stagnates again for months.
n.1: An isolated but connected pipe still holds standing water that can be drawn back into the system.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why should spray-tap fittings and flow straighteners be cleaned and descaled regularly?
o: They change the colour of the water if left dirty
Cleaning them increases the water pressure
They make the tap harder to turn
Scale and debris trap biofilm and legionella and make more aerosol
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Scale and deposits in spray fittings harbour biofilm where legionella grows and worsen the aerosol, so they are cleaned and descaled on schedule.

n.0: Water discolouration is not the legionella reason these fittings are maintained.
n.2: Stiffness of the tap handle is unrelated to the legionella control task.
n.1: The aim is legionella control, not boosting pressure.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: While cleaning a shower head you notice it is furred with scale and slime. What should you do?
o: Descale and disinfect it fully, wearing PPE, and record what you found
Rinse it under the tap and refit it
Refit it as it is because it still sprays
Throw it in the bin and leave the shower with no head
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Scale and slime hold legionella, so the head is properly descaled and disinfected with PPE worn, and the finding is recorded.

n.1: A quick rinse leaves the scale and biofilm that harbour legionella in place.
n.2: Refitting a fouled head keeps a contaminated aerosol source in service.
n.3: Leaving no head is not a controlled repair and the finding still needs recording.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why are showers and spray taps regarded as higher-risk outlets for Legionella infection than an ordinary swan-neck tap?
o: They use more water per minute, so any contamination is diluted
They break the water into a fine breathable aerosol that can be inhaled deep into the lungs
They are fitted lower down, so the pipework is always cooler
They always deliver water above 60 degrees C, which scalds users
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Showers and spray taps atomise water into a fine aerosol of respirable droplets; inhaling this aerosol is the main route by which Legionella causes infection, so these outlets need particular control.

n.3: Showers are typically blended to a safe usable temperature and do not reliably deliver water at 60 degrees C or above; the risk is aerosol, not scalding.
n.0: Higher flow does not dilute the hazard; it simply produces more contaminated aerosol to inhale.
n.2: Mounting height is not the reason; the aerosol produced at the outlet is what creates the inhalation risk.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Under HSG274 Part 2, how often should shower heads and hoses normally be cleaned, descaled and disinfected as a minimum?
o: Only when a user complains about the spray
Once every two years
Annually, at the same time as the tank inspection
At least quarterly (every three months)
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: HSG274 Part 2 recommends dismantling, cleaning, descaling and disinfecting shower heads and hoses at least every three months, because scale and biofilm accumulate quickly in these fittings.

n.1: A two-year interval would allow extensive scale and biofilm to build up in the head and hose between cleans.
n.0: Cleaning must be a planned, scheduled control, not something left until a user notices a problem.
n.2: Annual cleaning is far too infrequent for aerosol-generating fittings that foul rapidly.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A little-used shower in a site changing block is on the flushing regime. How often should it be flushed as a minimum?
o: At least weekly, running it until the hot runs hot and the cold runs cold
Once a month is sufficient for a shower
Only before the annual site audit
Whenever someone happens to want a shower
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Infrequently used outlets, including showers, should be flushed at least weekly, running each until the hot reaches hot and the cold reaches cold, to prevent stagnation in the branch and fitting.

n.1: Monthly is too long an interval; water stagnating for a month in a warm branch encourages Legionella growth.
n.2: Flushing is an ongoing weekly control, not a task done only around an audit.
n.3: Relying on chance use gives no reliable control; a documented weekly flush is required.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When flushing a little-used spray tap or shower to limit the release of aerosol, what is the recommended technique?
